rows.heading: Administration
rows.groupTitle: Minister's administrative role and delegation power
rows.groupReason: Identifies the responsible authority and the specific delegation power in one short administrative rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the Minister is in charge of the administration and enforcement of the Bituminous Shale Act and may designate a person to act on his behalf.

evidenceText: The Minister is in charge of the administration and enforcement of this Act and may designate a person to act on his behalf.

rows.sourceMapReason: One-sentence provision assigning the Minister responsibility for administration and enforcement of the Act and granting a delegation power; a single recall task.

rows.heading: Ownership of bituminous shale
rows.groupTitle: Crown ownership of bituminous shale and status of 1973 licences
rows.groupReason: Both subsections address one recall task: the legal basis of Crown ownership of bituminous shale and how prior 1973 licence agreements relate to that ownership.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that bituminous shale, its products, and by-products are Crown property separate from the soil, that other mineral dispositions do not include bituminous shale rights except 1973 licences, and that those 1973 licence agreements are subject to this Act and its regulations.

evidenceText: vested in the Crown in right of the Province
no other lease, licence, grant or other disposition of mines, minerals or oil and natural gas shall be construed as to include rights to bituminous shale
all those licence agreements are subject to this Act and the regulations

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3 is a short, self-contained ownership declaration: Crown vesting of bituminous shale separate from soil, the interpretive exclusion from other mineral dispositions, and the subordination of 1973 licences. The two subsections are tightly interdependent and form one coherent ownership concept.

rows.heading: Exploration rights
rows.groupTitle: Exploration rights: required authorizations by activity stage
rows.groupReason: The three prohibitions share one actor and modality and form a single escalating authorization matrix that a learner recalls as a set.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the specific authorization required for each of the three activity stages: exploration, drilling a bituminous shale evaluation well, and mining or developing a bituminous shale deposit.
rows.sourceMapReason: Three escalating prohibitions with progressively narrowing authorization lists form one coherent recall framework: what authorization is required at each activity stage (exploration, evaluation drilling, mining/development).

rows.heading: Bituminous shale evaluation wells
rows.groupTitle: Application of Oil and Natural Gas Act to bituminous shale evaluation wells
rows.groupReason: 5(1) extends ONGA drilling rules by reference; 5(2) permits the Minister to vary those requirements where conditions warrant.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the Oil and Natural Gas Act and its regulations with respect to drilling apply mutatis mutandis to a bituminous shale evaluation well, and that the Minister may vary those requirements in his opinion where conditions warrant.
rows.sourceMapReason: Tightly interdependent rule/exception pair: ONGA drilling rules apply mutatis mutandis to bituminous shale evaluation wells, subject to a Ministerial power to vary requirements.

rows.heading: Access
rows.groupTitle: Enforcement Access and Inspection Powers
rows.groupReason: All four sub-paragraphs answer the same recall question: what may a Minister-authorized enforcement person do, and under what conditions?
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the preconditions (reasonable time, Minister-issued identification card) and the four specific access, inspection, sampling, and testing powers granted to persons authorized by the Minister under section 6.

evidenceText: Persons authorized by the Minister to enforce the provisions of this Act and the regulations, at any reasonable time and upon the presentation of an identification card issued by the Minister
may take samples or carry out any tests or examination desired.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 grants a single coherent enforcement access power to Minister-authorized persons, with four enumerated facets (a)–(d) sharing the same actor, preconditions (reasonable time, identification card), and permissive modality, forming one recall task.

rows.heading: Conflicts of interest
rows.groupTitle: Conflicts of interest for enforcement employees
rows.groupReason: The prohibition on monetary interest and its category F offence plus forfeiture consequence are one recallable rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what monetary interests are prohibited for provincial employees administering the Act and the offence and forfeiture consequences of violation.
rows.sourceMapReason: Subsection (1) states the prohibition and (2) its directly dependent offence-and-forfeiture consequence; together they form one tightly interdependent conflict-of-interest rule.

rows.heading: Summons to witness, disclosure of information
rows.groupTitle: Summons and document production protection for the Minister and employees
rows.groupReason: 8(1) combines two related process restrictions—no official-capacity summons and no document production without a court or judge order—into one recall task about when judicial process may reach the Minister or provincial employees under the Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that no summons may require the attendance of the Minister or a provincial employee in his official capacity under the Act, and that documents in official custody may not be produced without an order of the court or a judge.

evidenceText: A summons to witness shall not issue out of any court requiring the attendance of the Minister or any employee of the Province in his official capacity under this Act, nor shall any document in his official custody or possession be produced without an order of the court or a judge thereof.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 8 contains two independently operative rules with different actors, triggers, and modalities: 8(1) restricts court process against the Minister and employees in official capacity, while 8(2) imposes a non-disclosure duty on enforcement employees triggered by Ministerial certification. Each is a separate recall task.

rows.heading: Summons to witness, disclosure of information
rows.groupTitle: Prohibition on employee disclosure of certified non-public information
rows.groupReason: 8(2) creates a distinct non-disclosure duty for enforcement employees, triggered by the Minister's certification that information is not in the public interest to divulge—a different actor, trigger, and legal modality from 8(1).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain that an employee responsible for administration and enforcement of the Act shall not disclose information obtained in official capacity that the Minister certifies is not in the public interest to divulge.

evidenceText: Any employee responsible for the administration and enforcement of this Act shall not disclose any information obtained by him in his official capacity that the Minister certifies is not in the public interest to be divulged.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 8 contains two independently operative rules with different actors, triggers, and modalities: 8(1) restricts court process against the Minister and employees in official capacity, while 8(2) imposes a non-disclosure duty on enforcement employees triggered by Ministerial certification. Each is a separate recall task.

rows.heading: Crown land
rows.groupTitle: Crown land exploration consent and Ministerial conditions
rows.groupReason: One short operative rule: permission to enter Crown lands for bituminous shale exploration conditioned on the Minister's consent and terms and conditions he prescribes, subject to the Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which Crown lands may be entered and explored for bituminous shale, including the role of the Minister's consent and prescribed terms and conditions.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 9 is a single, tightly interdependent rule granting conditional permission to enter Crown lands for bituminous shale exploration, subject to Ministerial consent and prescribed terms. It forms one recallable concept and is distinct from Section 10's broader right-of-entry and compensation regime.

rows.heading: Right of entry
rows.groupTitle: Compensation for entry on Crown lands
rows.groupReason: Crown-land compensation has its own payee (Crown in the right of the Province), applicant for court determination (the Minister), and payment direction (Minister of Finance and Treasury Board), making it a distinct recall task from the non-Crown regime.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the compensation liability, the payee (Crown in the right of the Province), the court-determination trigger and applicant (Minister), and the final payee (Minister of Finance and Treasury Board) when a person enters Crown land for bituminous shale exploration or production.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 10 contains three independently recallable concepts: the entry-authorization prohibition and resulting surface right (10(1)–(2)), and two distinct compensation regimes that differ by land type, payee, and application mechanism (10(3) Crown lands vs. 10(4) non-Crown lands).

rows.heading: Right of entry
rows.groupTitle: Entry authorization and scope of surface right
rows.groupReason: The prohibition on unauthorized entry and the positive scope of the surface right are tightly interdependent and answer one recall question: what must exist before entry, and what does entry entitle the holder to do.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the two lawful pathways for entering non-Crown lands for bituminous shale exploration (agreement or Minister's special order) and the scope of the resulting right to use and possess the necessary surface of the licence, permit, or lease area.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 10 contains three independently recallable concepts: the entry-authorization prohibition and resulting surface right (10(1)–(2)), and two distinct compensation regimes that differ by land type, payee, and application mechanism (10(3) Crown lands vs. 10(4) non-Crown lands).

rows.heading: Right of entry
rows.groupTitle: Compensation for entry on non-Crown lands
rows.groupReason: Non-Crown-land compensation differs from the Crown-land regime in payee (interested person), the applicant for court determination (either party), and the scope of compensable damage (land or chattels), forming a separate recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the compensation liability to a person having an interest, the scope of compensable loss (land or chattels), and the court-determination mechanism (either party may apply) when a person enters non-Crown land for bituminous shale exploration or production.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 10 contains three independently recallable concepts: the entry-authorization prohibition and resulting surface right (10(1)–(2)), and two distinct compensation regimes that differ by land type, payee, and application mechanism (10(3) Crown lands vs. 10(4) non-Crown lands).

rows.heading: Special order to enter and use land
rows.groupTitle: Application for special order, five-day notice, and substituted service
rows.groupReason: The right to apply when agreement fails, the mandatory five-clear-day written notice precondition, and the substituted-service exception form one coherent application-stage recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the applicant's right to seek a special order, the five-clear-day written notice requirement, and the Minister's substituted-service power where service difficulties exist.

evidenceText: may apply in writing to the Minister for a special order to enter and use such land
the applicant has served upon the owner, tenant or occupier of the land, five clear days prior to the making of the application, written notice of the intention to make the said application
the Minister may order substituted service in such manner as he determines

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 11 contains three materially distinct procedural stages—application and notice, Minister's hearing and decision, and compensation/security for entry—each creating independently recallable rules with different actors and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Special order to enter and use land
rows.groupTitle: Compensation determination, order effectiveness, and security before entry

evidenceText: the determination of the compensation shall be referred to The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick or any judge thereof acting under Part II of the Expropriation Act by either party

the special order is effective upon the date of issue, and the Minister may require the licensee, geophysical licensee, permittee or lessee to give security in the form as prescribed in section 34 to ensure payment of the compensation

rows.heading: Special order to enter and use land
rows.groupTitle: Minister's hearing and decision on special order application
rows.groupReason: The Minister's mandatory hearing deadline, discretionary notice direction, and sole-discretion grant-or-deny power without reasons constitute a distinct decision-stage recall task separate from the application and compensation stages.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the Minister's duty to fix a hearing within ten clear days, the power to direct hearing notice, and the sole-discretion authority to grant or deny the special order without giving reasons.

evidenceText: shall fix a date for the hearing of the application which shall not be later than ten clear days after the notice of the application has been served and delivered
may in his sole discretion and without giving reasons therefor, grant or deny such special order upon such terms and conditions as he considers proper

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 11 contains three materially distinct procedural stages—application and notice, Minister's hearing and decision, and compensation/security for entry—each creating independently recallable rules with different actors and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Geophysical exploration
rows.groupTitle: Geophysical exploration: applicable regime and non-interference duty
rows.groupReason: Both subsections are short and jointly state the governing regime (ONG Act applies) and the specific prohibition (non-interference with listed rights-holders); recalling them separately would fragment one small framework.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that ONG Act geophysical-exploration provisions and licence-granting rules apply mutatis mutandis to bituminous shale, and identify the categories of rights-holders whose operations a geophysical explorer must not interfere with.

evidenceText: All provisions and regulations of the Oil and Natural Gas Act with respect to geophysical exploration and the granting of geophysical licenses apply mutatis mutandis to any geophysical exploration for bituminous shale under this Act

A person who performs geophysical exploration for the purposes of bituminous shale shall not interfere with the operations of any holder of a mining or mineral claim or mining lease under the Mining Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 12 is a short, thematically unified provision: subsection (1) incorporates ONG Act geophysical-exploration rules by reference and subsection (2) adds a specific non-interference prohibition. Together they form one recall task on the geophysical-exploration framework for bituminous shale.

rows.heading: Licence to search
rows.groupTitle: Licence to search: granting power, exclusivity limits, and tender prerequisite
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(3) form one interdependent mechanism: the Minister's granting power is expressly subject to the one-licence-per-area and no-overlap-with-permit-or-lease rules in (2) and the mandatory tender step in (3).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Minister's discretionary power to grant a licence to search for bituminous shale, the prohibition on granting more than one licence for the same area or for land with a permit or lease in force, and the requirement to call for tenders before granting.
rows.sourceMapReason: Short, tightly interdependent provision: the granting power in (1) is expressly subject to the exclusivity limits in (2) and the tender prerequisite in (3), forming one licence-to-search mechanism.

rows.heading: Size of licence area
rows.groupTitle: Size limits for a licence area
rows.groupReason: One provision, one concept: the quantitative bounds (max 81, min 25, boundary exception, absolute floor ½ section) that govern every licence area under the Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the maximum, minimum, and absolute minimum size of a licence area and identify the single exception that relaxes the minimum.

evidenceText: A licence area shall not exceed eighty-one sections and shall not be less than twenty-five sections except where the licence area is adjacent to a boundary of the Province, but in no case shall a licence area be less than one-half of a section.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 14 is a single, self-contained rule setting maximum, minimum, and absolute-floor size limits for a licence area, with one boundary-adjacency exception. All elements are tightly interdependent and answer one recall question.

rows.heading: Validity of licence to search
rows.groupTitle: Licence to search – validity term and renewal procedure
rows.groupReason: Subsections 15(1) and 15(2) together define the initial three-year term, renewal limits, and the written application requirements for renewal.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the initial term, maximum consecutive annual renewal periods, and the written application requirements (timing, form, accompanying fee and deposit) for renewing a licence to search.
rows.sourceMapReason: Short two-subsection provision stating licence-to-search validity terms and renewal application procedure; forms one integrated recall concept.

rows.heading: Work deposits
rows.groupTitle: Work deposits: exploratory work duty and deposit requirements
rows.groupReason: The three subsections form one interdependent rule: the annual work obligation, the pre-granting deposit securing the initial term, and the renewal deposit maintenance condition.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the licensee's annual exploratory work obligation, the initial deposit the Minister must require before granting a licence to search, and the deposit maintenance condition that applies to each renewal period.

evidenceText: The licensee shall each year during the term and continuation of the licence to search do or cause to be done on the area for which the licence to search was granted, exploratory work to the satisfaction of the Minister in an amount prescribed by regulation.

the Minister shall require the licensee to deposit with the Minister of Finance and Treasury Board in accordance with section 34 an amount at least equivalent to the work requirement prescribed by regulation for the initial term
Every renewal of a licence to search is subject to the licensee maintaining his deposit with the Minister in an amount at least equivalent to the work requirement for the term of the renewal period.

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent work-deposit mechanism: the licensee's annual exploratory work duty plus the initial and renewal deposit requirements that secure it.

rows.heading: Development permits
rows.groupTitle: Development permit application, area selection, and grant
rows.groupReason: Subsections 17(1)–(4) together describe who may apply, the permitted area options, the Minister's granting authority, and the operative effect on the search licence.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the application requirements, area options, and the effect on the licence to search when a development permit is granted under s. 17.

evidenceText: he may apply to the Minister in the manner prescribed by regulation for a development permit, the area of which is to include any pilot operation site
The licensee may select to be included in his development permit all of his licence area, or a portion of his licence area which shall consist of a single block
Notwithstanding subsection 15(1), upon the granting of a development permit, the permittee's licence to search expires with respect to the permit area

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 17 covers two distinct recall tasks: acquiring a development permit (application, area selection, grant, and the resulting expiry of the search licence) versus maintaining it (duration and renewal procedure).

rows.heading: Development permits
rows.groupTitle: Development permit duration and renewal
rows.groupReason: Subsections 17(5)–(6) set the initial term, maximum renewal periods, and the written renewal application with fee and deposit, forming one temporal and procedural recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the initial term, maximum renewal periods, and the renewal application requirements for a development permit under s. 17.

evidenceText: A development permit is valid for an initial term of one year and may be renewed by the Minister in accordance with the regulations at the permittee's option for a maximum of four consecutive annual periods

An application for renewal of a development permit shall be made in writing to the Minister at least thirty days prior to the expiry date of the development permit or any renewal thereof and shall be accompanied by the fee and deposit prescribed by regulation

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 17 covers two distinct recall tasks: acquiring a development permit (application, area selection, grant, and the resulting expiry of the search licence) versus maintaining it (duration and renewal procedure).

rows.heading: Work deposits
rows.groupTitle: Work deposits securing development-permit work obligations
rows.groupReason: One coherent deposit-and-work-obligation mechanism spanning initial grant and renewal.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the permittee's annual development work obligation, the pre-grant deposit the Minister must require (including the section 34 form), and the deposit-maintenance condition on every renewal.

evidenceText: The permittee shall each year during the term and continuation of the development permit carry out or cause to be carried out on the permit area development to the satisfaction of the Minister in an amount prescribed by regulation.

Before a development permit is granted, the Minister shall require the licensee to deposit with the Minister of Finance and Treasury Board in accordance with section 34 an amount at least equivalent to the work requirement prescribed by regulation for the initial term of the development permit.

Every renewal of a development permit is subject to the permittee maintaining his deposit with the Minister in an amount at least equivalent to the work requirement for the term of the renewal period.

rows.sourceMapReason: Three tightly interdependent subsections form one work-deposit mechanism: the annual work obligation, the pre-grant deposit securing it, and the renewal deposit condition. Recalling them separately would fragment a single concept.

rows.heading: Conversion to lease
rows.groupTitle: Conversion to lease: application, area determination criteria, grant, and permit expiry
rows.groupReason: Subsections 1–4 form the coherent permittee-to-lease conversion process: the application right, the Minister's area-determination factors, the regulatory grant, and the automatic expiry of the development permit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how a permittee applies for a lease, the factors the Minister must consider in determining the lease area, the Minister's granting power under the regulations, and the effect of a granted lease on the underlying development permit.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 18 contains the operative conversion-to-lease mechanism (subsections 1–4) and a separate 1981-date transitional deeming rule (subsection 5) that are independently recallable.

rows.heading: Conversion to lease

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 18 contains the operative conversion-to-lease mechanism (subsections 1–4) and a separate 1981-date transitional deeming rule (subsection 5) that are independently recallable.

rows.heading: Lease from Crown lands

rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who may apply for a Crown lands lease, the form of application, and the lands to which the lease may extend.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19 addresses two distinct lease-lifecycle stages with different actors, triggers, and modalities: initial grant to a permittee (19(1)) versus transfer of an existing lease to another lessee with a mandatory new-lease grant and minimum area (19(2)).

rows.heading: Lease from Crown lands

evidenceText: the Minister may, upon written application by the lessee, approve the transfer of the whole or part of the lease area to another lessee, and shall upon such transfer grant a new lease to such transferee upon such terms and conditions as are prescribed by the Minister, but each transfer shall not be for less than one section in area

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19 addresses two distinct lease-lifecycle stages with different actors, triggers, and modalities: initial grant to a permittee (19(1)) versus transfer of an existing lease to another lessee with a mandatory new-lease grant and minimum area (19(2)).

rows.heading: Abandon, release or surrender of development permit or lease

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 20 grants a single right (release in whole sections) with a directly dependent minimum-area condition; the two subsections form one tightly coupled recall unit.

rows.heading: Production rights of permittee or lessee
rows.groupTitle: Exclusive production right and oil/gas priority condition

the oil and natural gas shall be produced first, in a manner approved by the Minister.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 21 grants the permittee or lessee an exclusive production right and immediately conditions it with an oil-and-gas priority rule; the two subsections form one coherent right-plus-limitation unit that a learner would recall together.

rows.heading: Term of lease
rows.groupTitle: Bituminous Shale Lease Term and Renewal Conditions

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the initial term of a bituminous shale lease, the structure of renewal periods, and the two conditions that must be satisfied for a renewal to be granted.
rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained provision establishing the initial lease term and both renewal conditions as one coherent rule set.

rows.heading: Rental reductions
rows.groupTitle: Rental reduction for exploration work (s. 23)

the rental shall not be reduced pursuant to subsection (1) for any year following a year in which commercial production has commenced.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 23 is a self-contained rental-reduction mechanism: one Minister's power, its application conditions, a carry-forward rule, and a post-production cutoff, all interdependent parts of a single recall task.

rows.heading: Forfeiture

the licence to search, development permit or lease, as the case may be, shall be cancelled by the Minister.

rows.heading: Forfeiture

rows.heading: Payment of royalty for resources other than timber
rows.groupTitle: Royalty payment duty for non-timber resources
rows.groupReason: Single rule linking the trigger (extracting, harvesting, or taking a prescribed resource under a licence of occupation) to the obligation (paying prescribed royalties to the Crown).

evidenceText: Any person who extracts, harvests or takes a resource prescribed by regulation under the authority of a licence of occupation shall pay to the Crown the royalties prescribed by regulation.

rows.heading: Classes of timber on Crown Lands

evidenceText: Timber on Crown Lands shall be classed by species or groups of species as veneer logs, saw logs, pulpwood, poles, fuel wood, Christmas trees and such other classes as may be prescribed by regulation.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 57 states one mandatory timber-classification rule with enumerated categories and a regulatory extension mechanism; it forms a single coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Payment of royalty and charges for timber

evidenceText: Every person who harvests or takes possession of timber on Crown Lands under a license, sub-license or permit, shall pay to the Crown a royalty for the timber harvested and such other charges as may be prescribed by regulation.
A sub-licensee shall remit his royalty to the Crown through the licensee by whom his sub-license was issued.

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent payment obligation: the general duty to pay royalty and charges on Crown Lands timber plus the sub-licensee remittance channel, recalled as a single concept.

the royalty that would have been payable if the timber had been harvested as authorized under this or any other Act, and

rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the two components of the Crown timber royalty, the annual review requirement for the FMV amount, and the conditions and 75% limit on the Minister's royalty reduction power.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 59 is a short, cohesive provision defining the Crown timber royalty formula, its annual review, and the Minister's reduction power as one recallable financial rule.

rows.heading: Interest

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative rule creating a mandatory interest duty on unpaid Crown royalties, charges, penalties, sale prices, and rentals; rate delegated to regulation. Self-contained with no need to split or combine.

rows.heading: Lien in favour of Minister
rows.groupTitle: Creation, scope, and operation of the Minister's lien

evidenceText: A lien in favour of the Minister attaches to all timber harvested on Crown Lands, when harvested, and continues until all royalties, sale price, charges and interest thereon in respect of the timber have been paid.
A lien arising pursuant to subsection (1) does not require registration or filing and attaches to any processed wood into which timber that is subject to the lien may be converted.

evidenceText: A lien under this section has priority over every charge, pledge, claim, lien, privilege or other encumbrance in respect of such timber or processed wood in favour of any other person, whether arising before or after a lien arises under this section.

Notwithstanding subsection (3), where a third party, for value, in good faith and without advice of a lien, has acquired any interest in timber or processed wood harvested on Crown Lands, the lien arising in favour of the Minister under subsection (1) is subject to such interest.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 61 contains two distinct recall tasks: the lien's creation, scope, and operational characteristics versus its priority ranking and the BFP exception to that priority.

rows.groupTitle: Purchaser's protection from estate debts and claims
rows.groupReason: Defines the conditions (good faith, for value, from PR or from beneficiary to whom PR conveyed) under which a purchaser's title is discharged, plus the specific-charge exception and the additional release from beneficial-claim holders when buying from the PR.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the conditions for a purchaser to hold real property freed from the deceased's debts, the specific-charge exception, and the additional discharge from beneficial-claim holders when the purchase is from the personal representative.

evidenceText: holds the same freed and discharged from all debts or liabilities of the deceased owner, except such as are specifically charged thereon otherwise than by his will

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 14 contains two distinct recall tasks: the purchaser's title protection (14(1)) and the continuing estate-debt liability plus the beneficiary's personal liability on sale (14(2)). Different actors, different legal effects, and different modalities (discharge vs. obligation) justify separate StudyUnits.

rows.heading: Rights respecting purchase, liability respecting conveyance
rows.groupTitle: Continuing estate-debt liability and beneficiary's personal liability on sale
rows.groupReason: States the continuing liability of property vested in a beneficiary for estate debts while it remains in their hands, and the personal liability the beneficiary assumes upon a good-faith sale or mortgage, capped at the property's prior liability value.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that property vested in a beneficially entitled person remains liable for estate debts so long as it is not held by a good-faith purchaser, and that the beneficiary becomes personally liable up to the property's prior liability value upon sale or mortgage in good faith.

evidenceText: shall continue to be liable to answer the debts of the deceased owner so long as it remains vested in that person or in any person claiming under him not being a purchaser in good faith and for value
he shall be personally liable for the debts to the extent to which such real property was liable when vested in the personal representative, but not beyond the value thereof

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 14 contains two distinct recall tasks: the purchaser's title protection (14(1)) and the continuing estate-debt liability plus the beneficiary's personal liability on sale (14(2)). Different actors, different legal effects, and different modalities (discharge vs. obligation) justify separate StudyUnits.

rows.heading: Two or more personal representatives
rows.groupTitle: Concurrence requirement and proving-executor exception for dispositions of devolved real property
rows.groupReason: The concurrence rule and the proving-executor exception are interdependent halves of one disposition-authority test.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when a conveyance, mortgage, lease, or other disposition of devolved real property requires concurrence of all personal representatives or a Court order, and when a proving executor may act alone with the same effect as full concurrence.

evidenceText: a conveyance, mortgage, lease or other disposition of real property devolving under this Act shall not be made without the concurrence therein of all such representatives, or an order of the Court

any conveyance, mortgage, lease or other disposition of the real property may be made by the proving executor or executors for the time being, and shall be as effectual without an order of the Court, as if all the persons named as executors had concurred therein

rows.sourceMapReason: Single rule plus its directly dependent exception form one recall task: when may a disposition of devolved real property be made with multiple personal representatives?

rows.heading: Sale of property free from dower or curtesy
rows.groupTitle: Sale of estate property free from dower or curtesy
rows.groupReason: Procedure, legal effect, and payment options are one coherent mechanism for clearing dower/curtesy interests on estate property.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the procedure a personal representative follows to obtain a court order for sale of estate property free from curtesy or dower, the effect of that order on the tenant's interest and the purchaser's title, and the court's options for providing a reasonable satisfaction to the tenant out of the purchase money.
rows.sourceMapReason: The three subsections form one tight, interdependent mechanism: the application procedure, the legal effect on the tenant's interest, and the court's payment options for selling estate property free from dower or curtesy.

rows.heading: Application of Act
rows.groupTitle: Cumulative application of Act to personal representatives
rows.groupReason: One operative rule: the Act supplements rather than displaces other sources of a personal representative's authority.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that rights and immunities under the Devolution of Estates Act for personal representatives are in addition to, and not in derogation of, powers conferred by any other Act or by the will.

evidenceText: The rights and immunities conferred by this Act upon personal representatives are in addition to and not in derogation of the powers conferred by any other Act or by the will.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single-sentence savings clause stating the Act's rights and immunities for personal representatives are cumulative with, not exclusive of, powers under other Acts or by will; forms one coherent legal principle.

rows.heading: Effect on real property of registration of will
rows.groupTitle: Vesting of Devised Real Estate by Will Registration
rows.groupReason: The trigger (Registry Office recording per Registry Act s. 25), the vesting effect, and the Probate Court Act limitation are one recallable rule about how real property passes on registered wills.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the condition that triggers automatic vesting of devised real estate in the devisee upon will registration, the extent of the interest vested, and the saving for the Probate Court Act.

evidenceText: if a will is recorded in a Registry Office as provided by section 25 of the Registry Act the recording of the will has the effect of vesting any real estate devised by the will in the person to whom it is devised, to the extent of the interest so devised therein, but such real estate is subject to the provisions of the Probate Court Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 18 states a single self-contained vesting rule: recording a will at a Registry Office vests devised real estate in the devisee, subject to the Probate Court Act. The trigger, effect, and limitation form one tightly interdependent concept.

rows.heading: Vesting of property not disposed of by representative
rows.groupTitle: Automatic vesting of undistributed estate property after two years
rows.groupReason: One rule: after two years the property vests automatically in the beneficially entitled persons or their assigns without a deed from the representative, regardless of whether probate was granted.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State which estate property automatically vests in the beneficially entitled persons or their assigns if not distributed within two years of death, the applicable property types and value threshold, and that no conveyance by the personal representative is required.

evidenceText: Money and securities for money to a value of twenty-five hundred dollars, personal chattels or real property not disposed of by the personal representatives, or conveyed to, divided or distributed among the persons beneficially entitled thereto within two years after the death of the deceased shall, whether probate or letters of administration have or have not been taken out, be thenceforward vested in the persons beneficially entitled thereto under the will or upon the intestacy, or their assigns, without any conveyance by the personal representatives.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19 is a single coherent vesting rule: undistributed estate property automatically vests in beneficially entitled persons after two years, without conveyance. The property scope, time trigger, and vesting effect are interdependent parts of one recallable rule.

rows.heading: Instate leaving widow and one child, widow and children or widow and issue of child
rows.groupTitle: Widow's share in intestacy: one child, multiple children, and predeceased child's issue
rows.groupReason: All subsections define the widow's entitlement in the intestacy scenario, with the marital property component and residue fraction varying by number of surviving children plus a representational rule for predeceased children's issue.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what the widow receives (marital property interest plus the applicable fraction of the residue) when the intestate leaves one child versus multiple children, and explain the representational effect when a predeceased child's issue is alive at the date of death.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 22 is a short, self-contained rule set defining the widow's share in an intestacy across three closely interdependent scenarios (one child, multiple children, predeceased child's issue), forming one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Per stirpes distribution among issue
rows.groupTitle: Per stirpes distribution among issue
rows.groupReason: Establishes the core intestate rule that issue take per stirpes, subject to the widow's rights.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the per stirpes distribution rule that applies when an intestate dies leaving issue, including the widow's rights qualifier.
rows.sourceMapReason: A single operative rule: per stirpes distribution among issue, subject to the widow's rights. One recall task, no internal split warranted.

rows.heading: Intestate leaving widow and no issue
rows.groupTitle: Intestate leaving widow but no issue
rows.groupReason: One recall task: identify the trigger condition and the resulting devolution of the entire estate to the widow.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the rule that where an intestate dies leaving a widow but no issue, his estate goes to his widow.
rows.sourceMapReason: Single-sentence intestate succession rule with one trigger (widow, no issue) and one outcome (estate to widow); no internal complexity warranting a split.

rows.heading: Intestate leaving no widow and no issue
rows.groupTitle: Intestate estate to parents: no widow, no issue
rows.groupReason: One trigger (no widow, no issue), one primary outcome (equal shares to both living parents), and one dependent condition (survivor takes the whole estate) form a single rule set.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State to whom the estate devolves, and in what shares, when an intestate dies leaving no widow or issue but one or both parents are living.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 25 states one self-contained intestate succession rule: where the deceased leaves no widow and no issue, the estate passes to the father and mother in equal shares, or to the surviving parent. The equal-shares rule and its dependent survivorship modification form a single recallable concept.

rows.heading: Intestate leaving no widow or issue, father or mother
rows.groupTitle: Intestate estate to brothers and sisters; representation for predeceased sibling
rows.groupReason: One recall task: identify the sibling level as the takers and the representation rule for a deceased sibling's children.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who takes the estate when the intestate leaves no widow, issue, father, or mother, and how the share of a predeceased sibling passes to that sibling's children.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 26 states a single coherent intestacy rule: brothers and sisters take in equal shares, with children of a predeceased sibling taking that parent's share by representation.

rows.heading: Intestate leaving only niece or nephew
rows.groupTitle: Intestate estate passing to nephews and nieces (no representation)
rows.groupReason: One trigger, one beneficiary class, equal-shares rule, and the no-representation qualifier form a single recall task in the intestate hierarchy.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which an intestate estate passes to nephews and nieces, the sharing rule, and why representation is not admitted at this level.

evidenceText: If an intestate dies leaving no widow, issue, father, mother, brother or sister, his estate shall go to his nephews and nieces in equal shares and in no case shall representation be admitted.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 27 is a single, self-contained intestate succession rule: one trigger, one beneficiary class, one sharing rule, and one key qualifier (no representation). It forms one coherent recall task distinct from s.26 (siblings, with representation) and s.28 (next of kin of equal degree).

rows.heading: Intestate leaving no immediate family
rows.groupTitle: Intestate estate: next-of-kin fallback distribution
rows.groupReason: One rule: when all closer relatives are absent, the estate passes equally to the nearest surviving kin of equal degree, without representation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the trigger condition (no widow, issue, parents, siblings, or nephews/nieces survive), the equal-degree distribution among next of kin, and the prohibition on representation under s. 28.

evidenceText: If an intestate dies leaving no widow, issue, father, mother, brother, sister, nephew or niece, his estate shall be distributed equally among the next of kin of equal degree of consanguinity to the intestate and in no case shall representation be admitted.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 28 is a short, self-contained fallback distribution rule: a trigger (absence of all closer kin), an equal-share distribution among next of kin of equal degree, and a no-representation limitation. These elements form one recallable intestate-succession concept.

rows.heading: Computation of degrees of kindred
rows.groupTitle: Computation of degrees of kindred and half-blood equality
rows.groupReason: The upward-downward counting method and the half-blood equality rule are tightly interdependent; the equality rule depends on the computed degree, so they form one coherent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the method for computing degrees of kindred (upward to nearest common ancestor, then downward) and the rule that half-blood kindred inherit equally with whole-blood kindred in the same degree.

evidenceText: degrees of kindred shall be computed by counting upward from the intestate to the nearest common ancestor and then downward to the relative
the kindred of the half-blood shall inherit equally with those of the whole-blood in the same degree

rows.sourceMapReason: Short self-contained provision establishing both the degree-of-kindred computation method and the half-blood/whole-blood equality rule; the two rules are interdependent and form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Rights of posthumous child respecting intestacy
rows.groupTitle: Posthumous Child Inheritance in Intestacy
rows.groupReason: One indivisible rule: posthumous descendants and relatives of the intestate take their inheritance as if born before death and surviving the intestate.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the rule under section 30 governing how descendants and relatives of the intestate who are begotten before but born after the intestate's death inherit in intestacy.

evidenceText: Descendants and relatives of the intestate, begotten before his death but born thereafter, shall inherit as if they had been born in the lifetime of the intestate and had survived him.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single operative rule establishing that descendants and relatives begotten before but born after the intestate's death inherit in intestacy as if born during the intestate's lifetime and surviving him.

rows.heading: Advancement to child by intestate
rows.groupTitle: Advancement to child by wholly intestate person
rows.groupReason: All three subsections form one coherent advancement rule: the distribution effect, the deemed-valuation rule, and the onus of proof are each needed to apply the rule correctly.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how a portion advanced to a child of a wholly intestate person is reckoned in distribution, how the value of the advancement is determined, and who bears the onus of proving that an advancement was made.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 31 is a self-contained advancement (hotchpot) rule for wholly intestate estates; its substantive distribution rule, valuation mechanism, and evidentiary burden are tightly interdependent parts of one recall task.

rows.heading: Disposition of property not left by will
rows.groupTitle: Disposition of Estate Property Not Covered by Will
rows.groupReason: One-sentence rule stating that undisposed estate is distributed as if the testator died intestate and had left no other estate; the 'no other estate' qualifier is the operative detail a learner must recall.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the rule for distributing estate property not disposed of by will, including the requirement that distribution proceeds as if the testator had died intestate and had left no other estate.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 32 is a single operative rule for partial intestacy: undisposed estate is distributed as if the testator died intestate and left no other estate. It is short but substantively self-contained with one clear recall task.

rows.heading: Intestate woman
rows.groupTitle: Equal intestate distribution for women (s. 36)
rows.groupReason: The section imposes one rule (gender-equal intestate distribution) and one scope list (the cross-referenced sections); recalling them together answers the single question of how a woman's intestate estate is distributed.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the principle governing distribution of a woman's intestate estate and identify which sections (22–28, 30, 35) supply the operative distribution rules by cross-reference.

evidenceText: The estate of a woman dying intestate shall be distributed in the same proportions and in the same manner as the estate of a man so dying

the word "widower" being substituted for "widow", the word "her" for "his", the word "she" for "he," and the word "her" for "him," where such words respectively occur in sections 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 30 and 35

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 36 states a single operative rule: a woman's intestate estate is distributed in the same proportions and manner as a man's, with grammatical gender substitutions applied across sections 22–28, 30, and 35. This is one tightly interdependent concept best recalled as a unit.

rows.heading: Devolution of real property under mortgage
rows.groupTitle: Devolution of Mortgaged Estate on Mortgagee's Death
rows.groupReason: One rule with tightly interdependent condition, devolution result, qualification, and deemed-heir fiction for mortgage trusts and powers.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State to whom a mortgaged estate devolves on the mortgagee's death absent testamentary disposition, the rights it remains subject to, and the personal representative's deemed status for mortgage-created trusts and powers.

evidenceText: the same shall on his death, in the absence of any testamentary disposition, devolve to and become vested in his personal representative, but subject to all the like rights, equities and obligations
his personal representative for the time being shall be deemed in law his heir for the purposes of all trusts and powers created by the said mortgage

rows.sourceMapReason: Single coherent rule: devolution of a mortgaged estate on the mortgagee's death, with its condition, qualification, and deemed-heir fiction all serving one recall task.

rows.heading: Claim to profit or benefit
rows.groupTitle: Prescriptive protection for claims to profits or benefits (30-year and 60-year thresholds)
rows.groupReason: The 30-year limitation and the 60-year absolute-right rule are two tiers of one protection mechanism for the same profit or benefit, with the 60-year exception depending on the same factual predicate.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the 30-year and 60-year prescriptive thresholds for a claim to a profit or benefit, the limitation on defeating a 30-year claim by showing it did not exist from time immemorial, and the deed-or-writing consent exception to the 60-year absolute right.
rows.sourceMapReason: Subsections 1(1) and 1(2) form one escalating protection regime for profits or benefits: a 30-year limitation on defeating a claim and a 60-year elevation to an absolute right with a deed-or-writing exception. They share the same subject, actors, and legal concept.

rows.heading: Claim to general easement
rows.groupTitle: Prescriptive easement periods and their legal effects
rows.groupReason: The 20-year tier (limited defense) and 40-year tier (absolute and indefeasible unless express written consent) form one progressive prescriptive-easement framework that a learner must recall together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the 20-year and 40-year prescriptive enjoyment periods for general easements, the subject matter covered, and the distinct legal effect of each tier including the express-written-consent exception at 40 years.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 2 states the two-tier prescriptive easement rule (20-year and 40-year enjoyment) for ways, easements, watercourses, and water use; the tiers are tightly interdependent stages of one concept.

rows.heading: Action respecting easement
rows.groupTitle: Measuring and interrupting easement periods
rows.groupReason: The temporal-measurement rule and the interruption standard are tightly interdependent qualifiers on the same 20/40-year periods and form one recallable procedural concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State how the statutory periods in sections 1 and 2 are measured from a suit or action and what act or matter constitutes an interruption of enjoyment.

evidenceText: Each of the periods of years mentioned in sections 1 and 2 shall be taken to be the period next before a suit or action in which the claim or matter to which such period relates was or is brought into question

no act or other matter shall be deemed an interruption within the meaning of those two sections, unless it has been submitted to, or acquiesced in, for one year after the party interrupted has had notice of it and of the person making or authorizing it to be made

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3 is a short, self-contained procedural rule governing how the 20/40-year periods in sections 1 and 2 are measured from a suit and what constitutes a valid interruption; both sentences form one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Pleadings
rows.groupTitle: Pleading requirements for easement actions (s. 4)
rows.groupReason: All three subsections together state the complete pleading framework: what the claimant must allege and what the opposing party must specially set out in answer.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the sufficiency rules for alleging an easement right in pleadings (s. 4(1)–(2)) and the obligation on the opposing party to specially allege any proviso, exception, incapacity, disability, contract, or other matter in answer (s. 4(3)).
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 4 is a coherent set of pleading rules for easement actions: sufficiency of the claimant's allegation (4(1)–(2)) and the opposing party's obligation to specially allege exceptions (4(3)). The subsections are tightly interdependent procedural mechanics and form one recall task.

rows.heading: Presumption in favour of claim
rows.groupTitle: No presumption for periods shorter than the Act specifies
rows.groupReason: One operative prohibition: the minimum enjoyment period fixed by the Act cannot be shortened by judicial presumption in favour of a claimant.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that no presumption in favour of a claim to a profit, benefit, way, watercourse, or other easement may rest on proof of enjoyment for less than the period the Act specifies for that type of claim.

evidenceText: no presumption shall be allowed or made in favour or support of any claim on proof of the exercise or enjoyment of the right or matter claimed for any less period of time or number of years than for such period or number mentioned in this Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 5 states a single, self-contained prohibition: no presumption may support an easement claim based on enjoyment shorter than the Act's applicable period. One recallable rule, one actor (the court/adjudicator), one modality (prohibition).

rows.heading: Limitation of actions
rows.groupTitle: Exclusions from limitation period computation (s. 6)
rows.groupReason: The provision pairs a single carve-out with two exclusion grounds that together answer one recall question: when do periods stop running for easement claims?
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two grounds on which time is excluded from computation of limitation periods for easement claims under s. 6, and identify the carve-out where the right or claim is declared absolute and indefeasible.

evidenceText: Except only in cases where the right or claim is declared by this Act to be absolute and indefeasible
the time during which any person otherwise capable of resisting a claim to any of the matters mentioned in the previous sections is mentally incompetent, a minor, or a tenant for life
the time during which any action or suit has been pending, and has been diligently prosecuted until abated by the death of a party to it

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 states a self-contained operative rule: two specific exclusions from limitation period computation, subject to a single carve-out for absolute and indefeasible rights. The rule, carve-out, and both grounds form one recall task.

rows.heading: Effect of term of years on claim for easement or water
rows.groupTitle: Exclusion of term-of-years enjoyment from the 40-year prescriptive period
rows.groupReason: The provision states one rule with a trigger (term of life or term exceeding three years), an effect (exclusion from the 40-year period), and two limiting conditions (three-year claim window; reversion-holder resistance), all of which must be recalled together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when enjoyment under a term of life or a term of years exceeding three years is excluded from the 40-year prescriptive computation and identify the two conditions that must be met for the exclusion to apply.

evidenceText: the time of the enjoyment of the way or other matter during the continuance of the term shall be excluded in the computation of the period of 40 years, in case the claim is within three years next after the end or sooner determination of the term resisted by any person entitled to any reversion expectant on the determination of it

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 7 states one self-contained rule: when land or water is held under a term of life or a term of years exceeding three years, the enjoyment during that term is excluded from the 40-year prescriptive computation, subject to two conditions (claim within three years of the term's end, and resistance by a reversion holder). All components are tightly interdependent and form a single recallable rule.

rows.heading: Easement respecting light or air
rows.groupTitle: Easement respecting light or air: no acquisition by mere use
rows.groupReason: Prohibition on acquiring a blocking light-and-air right by prescription, plus the pre-April 10, 1875 preservation carve-out, form one recallable rule with its exception.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that no easement of light or air can be acquired by mere use to prevent building on adjoining land, and that this does not affect rights already acquired before April 10, 1875.

evidenceText: shall acquire or be held to have acquired, by the mere use of light and air through the windows, any right so as to prevent the erection of any building or other structures on the adjoining land
nothing in this Act shall deprive any person of any rights or easement that the person may have acquired before April 10, 1875

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent prohibition on acquiring light-and-air easements by use, with a directly dependent pre-1875 preservation exception; splitting would fragment a single rule.

rows.heading: Easement respecting cable or wire
rows.groupTitle: No Prescription Easement for Wires or Cables
rows.groupReason: States the prohibition: wire or cable easements attached to or passing over land or buildings cannot be acquired by prescription, present or future.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that no easement in respect of a wire or cable attached to or passing over land or a building can be deemed or will be acquired by prescription.

evidenceText: No easement in respect of a wire or cable attached to land or a building or passing over land or a building shall be deemed to have been acquired or shall hereafter be acquired by prescription.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative rule prohibiting acquisition of wire or cable easements by prescription; independently recallable as a distinct easement limitation separate from light/air (s. 8) and local-government water (s. 10).

rows.heading: Easement respecting property of a local government
rows.groupTitle: Prohibition on prescriptive acquisition over local government water supply property
rows.groupReason: One legal rule: a notwithstanding prohibition on prescriptive acquisition of easements, watercourses, water use, and title over land connected with a local government water supply, carved back only if the prescription period was already complete before the local government's acquisition.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the scope of the prohibition on acquiring by prescription any easement, watercourse, water use, or title over land forming part of or connected with a local government's water supply, and the single exception where the prescription term was complete before the local government's acquisition.

evidenceText: no person shall be capable of acquiring or be deemed to have acquired by prescription a claim to any way or other easement or to any watercourse or to the use of any water

when the land in respect of which the title or a way or other easement is claimed, or the watercourse or use of water sought to be prescribed is a portion of, or connected with the water supply of a local government, unless the adverse possession or the term of prescription was complete before the acquisition by the local government of the land or water or right in or to the land or water

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 10 is a single, self-contained prohibition on prescriptive acquisition of easements and water rights over local government water supply property, with a defined scope and one exception, forming one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Electronic Transactions Act – Section 1 Definitions
rows.groupReason: All four defined terms form the interpretive vocabulary for the Act and are best recalled as a single definitional set.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the statutory meaning of each defined term: 'electronic' (includes digital and optical), 'electronic signature' (electronic information created or adopted to sign a document and in, attached to, or associated with the document), 'information' (includes a document), and 'legal requirement' (a requirement of an Act, regulation or other subordinate legislation under an Act, or of the common law of New Brunswick).
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 1 establishes the four defined terms that govern interpretation throughout the Electronic Transactions Act; together they form one short definitional framework a learner must recall before applying any operative section.

rows.heading: Interpretation
rows.groupTitle: Scope of Legal-Requirement Provisions
rows.groupReason: States the operative scope rule: the Act's legal-requirement provisions reach both obligation-creating and consequence-providing laws.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State whether the Act's legal-requirement provisions apply to laws that create obligations, that provide consequences for doing or not doing something, or both.

evidenceText: The provisions of this Act relating to legal requirements apply whether the law (a) creates an obligation, or (b) provides consequences for doing something or for not doing something.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single-sentence interpretation clause that draws the scope boundary for the Act's legal-requirement provisions (obligations vs. consequences); narrow but independently recallable.

rows.heading: Act does not require use or acceptance of electronic information
rows.groupTitle: No compulsion to use or accept electronic information
rows.groupReason: One operative sentence establishing that the Act is permissive and does not mandate electronic information on any person.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that nothing in the Electronic Transactions Act requires a person to use or accept electronic information.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 4 states a single, self-contained legal rule — the Act imposes no obligation on any person to use or accept electronic information — with no internal structure warranting split or combine.

rows.heading: Application
rows.groupTitle: Application: Conflict Ordering and Regulatory Exclusion
rows.groupReason: Both subsections answer the same recall question: how does this Act apply in relation to other legislation and regulatory exclusions?
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the other Act prevails in a conflict with this Act and identify that the Act does not apply to matters excluded by regulation.

evidenceText: If there is a conflict between this Act and any other Act that expressly authorizes, prohibits or regulates the use of electronic information, the other Act prevails.
This Act does not apply to any Act, legal requirement, information, transaction or other matter that is excluded by regulation.

rows.sourceMapReason: Two one-sentence subsections defining the Act's application scope (statutory conflict ordering and regulatory exclusion) form one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: This Act binds the Crown
rows.groupTitle: Binding of the Crown
rows.groupReason: One sentence establishing that the Electronic Transactions Act applies to and binds the Crown.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the Electronic Transactions Act binds the Crown under section 6.

evidenceText: This Act binds the Crown.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 states a single substantive legal rule: the Act binds the Crown. It is a recallable scope fact with no grouping complexity.

rows.heading: Legal effect
rows.groupTitle: No denial of legal effect solely for electronic form
rows.groupReason: Single operative rule with its section 4 limitation forming one recallable principle.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that information shall not be denied legal effect or enforceability solely on the ground that it is electronic, subject to section 4.

evidenceText: information shall not be denied legal effect or enforceability solely on the ground that the information is electronic

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 7 states one clear operative rule — electronic information shall not be denied legal effect or enforceability solely because it is electronic — subject to the section 4 limitation. No split or combine needed.

rows.heading: Information in writing
rows.groupTitle: Satisfying a Legal Writing Requirement with Electronic Information
rows.groupReason: One recall task: the accessibility standard that electronic information must meet to satisfy a legal writing requirement, read with the Act's definition of 'legal requirement.'
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the condition (accessible so as to be usable for subsequent reference) under which electronic information satisfies a legal requirement that information be in writing, and identify what counts as a 'legal requirement' under the Act.

evidenceText: A legal requirement that information be in writing is satisfied by electronic information that is accessible so as to be usable for subsequent reference.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 8 is a short, self-contained operative rule stating when electronic information satisfies a legal writing requirement. It has no internal structure warranting a split and is distinct from the adjacent sections 7 (legal effect) and 9 (forms).

rows.heading: Forms
rows.groupTitle: Electronic Information Satisfying a Form Requirement
rows.groupReason: One operative rule defining the test (same or substantially the same form) under which electronic information satisfies a legal form requirement.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the test under which electronic information satisfies a legal requirement that information be in or on a particular form.

evidenceText: A legal requirement that information be in or on a particular form is satisfied by electronic information that is in or on the same or substantially the same form.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 9 states a single, self-contained satisfaction rule: electronic information meets a form requirement if it is in or on the same or substantially the same form. It is a distinct recall task separate from the writing (s.8) and original (s.10) satisfaction rules in the same Act.

rows.heading: Originals
rows.groupTitle: Electronic Information Satisfying an Original Requirement
rows.groupReason: The general rule, integrity/reliability criteria, and format-conversion extension form one interdependent recall unit on when electronic information counts as an original.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which electronic information satisfies a legal requirement for an original, including the integrity criterion (complete and unaltered apart from normal transmission changes), the reliability standard (purpose and all circumstances), and the effect of format conversion.

evidenceText: A legal requirement that information be an original is satisfied by electronic information if there exists a reliable assurance as to the integrity of that information from the time it was created.

Information remains an original for the purposes of this section even though it has been converted from non-electronic to electronic format, or from electronic to non-electronic format, if it continues to meet the requirements of subsections (1) and (2).

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 10 is a self-contained rule on electronic originals: 10(1) states the general requirement, 10(2) defines the integrity criterion and reliability standard, and 10(3) extends the rule across format conversions. All three are tightly interdependent and answer one recall task.

rows.heading: Signatures
rows.groupTitle: Electronic signatures satisfying legal signature requirements
rows.groupReason: The general rule in 11(1) and the two permissible forms in 11(2) are interdependent and form one recallable concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that an electronic signature satisfies a legal requirement for a person's signature and identify the two permissible forms: an electronic representation of a manual signature, or electronic information in which the person provides their name and clearly indicates it is being provided as their signature.

evidenceText: A legal requirement for the signature of a person is satisfied by an electronic signature.
an electronic representation of the manual signature of the person signing the document
electronic information by which the person signing the document (i) provides his or her name, and (ii) indicates clearly that the name is being provided as his or her signature to the document.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 11 states one coherent rule — electronic signatures satisfy legal signature requirements and the forms they may take — that functions as a single recall task.

rows.heading: Retention of information
rows.groupTitle: Conditions for electronic retention to satisfy a legal retention requirement
rows.groupReason: The three conditions (format, accessibility, supplementary identifying information) and the non-electronic format option in 12(2) are interdependent parts of one rule on when electronic retention is legally sufficient.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the three conditions that must all be met for electronic retention to satisfy a legal retention requirement, and state the permissive rule allowing non-electronic format for initially electronic information.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 12 states one coherent rule — when electronic retention satisfies a legal retention requirement — with three interdependent conditions in 12(1) and a closely tied permissive format variant in 12(2). All pieces answer the same recall question and form a single legal concept.

rows.heading: Provision of written information
rows.groupTitle: Electronic satisfaction of written-information requirements (s. 13)
rows.groupReason: The three subsections form one rule-with-condition structure: the main electronic-satisfaction test, the multi-copy corollary, and the inhibition carve-out that modifies the retention requirement in subsection (1).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the conditions under which electronic information satisfies a legal requirement for written information to be provided, the effect on a multiple-copy requirement, and when information is deemed not capable of being retained due to provider-imposed printing or storage inhibition.

evidenceText: A legal requirement that written information be provided to a person is satisfied by the provision of electronic information that is accessible by that person and is capable of being retained by that person so as to be usable for subsequent reference.
A legal requirement that more than one copy of written information be provided to a person at the same time is satisfied by the provision of a single electronic version of that information.
electronic information shall be deemed not to be capable of being retained if the person providing the information inhibits the printing or storage of the information

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 is a short, tightly interdependent three-subsection rule on when electronic information satisfies a legal requirement for written information to be provided, including the multi-copy shortcut and the printing/storage inhibition limitation; the subsections form one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Mail
rows.groupTitle: Electronic satisfaction of a mail delivery requirement
rows.groupReason: One rule: electronic delivery discharges a legal requirement for mail delivery.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the condition under which delivering information electronically satisfies a legal requirement that the information be delivered by mail.

evidenceText: A legal requirement that information be delivered by mail is satisfied by delivering the information electronically.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative rule stating that electronic delivery satisfies a mail-delivery requirement; one recall task with no structural basis to split or combine.

rows.heading: Registered mail
rows.groupTitle: Electronic satisfaction of a registered-mail delivery requirement
rows.groupReason: Both subsections state one recallable rule: electronic delivery with a request for acknowledgment plus recipient acknowledgment satisfies a registered-mail requirement, and the electronic acknowledgment must carry the recipient's electronic signature.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two conditions under which electronic delivery satisfies a legal registered-mail requirement and identify the signature requirement that applies when the recipient acknowledges receipt electronically.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 15 is a short, self-contained operative rule stating the two conditions for electronic delivery to satisfy a registered-mail requirement and the signature requirement on the acknowledgment. The two subsections form one tightly interdependent rule/condition pair.

rows.heading: Effective electronic means
rows.groupTitle: Effective electronic means – determination power, legal effect, and non-exclusivity
rows.groupReason: Definition of actor, scope of matters, determination power, legal effect, and non-exclusivity limitation are mutually dependent pieces of one operative rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who the responsible authority is, what it may determine about the form, nature, and conditions of acceptable electronic information, the legal effect of that determination, and the non-exclusivity limitation under section 16.
rows.sourceMapReason: All five subsections form one tightly interdependent mechanism: the definition of responsible authority, the scope of covered matters, the determination power, its legal effect, and the non-exclusivity limitation. Recalling them separately would fragment a single operative rule.

rows.heading: Time of sending and receipt
rows.groupTitle: Presumed time of receipt and place exclusion
rows.groupReason: 17(2) establishes a two-branch presumption for receipt (designated system vs. other system) and 17(3) carves out place determinations, together forming the receipt-side recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the two-branch presumption for when electronic information is received and note that section 17 does not determine the place of sending or receipt.

evidenceText: Electronic information is presumed to be received
when it enters an information system designated or used by the addressee for the purpose of receiving information of the type sent and it is capable of being retrieved and processed by the addressee
Nothing in this section shall be interpreted as determining the place from which electronic information is sent nor the place at which it is received

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 17 contains two distinct recall tasks—when electronic information is sent (a definitional rule) and when it is presumed received (a presumption)—each with its own scenarios and legal modality, justifying separate study units.

rows.heading: Time of sending and receipt
rows.groupTitle: Time of sending electronic information
rows.groupReason: 17(1) defines two distinct sending triggers (cross-system vs. same-system) and a party-agreement override, forming one coherent recall task on when sending occurs.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two scenarios for when electronic information is considered sent and the effect of sender-addressee agreement under s. 17(1).

evidenceText: Unless the sender and the addressee agree otherwise, electronic information is sent
when it enters an information system outside the control of the sender
if the sender and the addressee are in the same information system, when the sender takes the appropriate steps to make the information accessible to the addressee

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 17 contains two distinct recall tasks—when electronic information is sent (a definitional rule) and when it is presumed received (a presumption)—each with its own scenarios and legal modality, justifying separate study units.

rows.heading: Electronic agents
rows.groupTitle: Electronic agents: definition and permission for electronic transactions
rows.groupReason: The local definition of 'electronic agent' (no individual review at the time of response) and the permissive rule allowing contracts or transactions by agent interaction are inseparable for recall.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Define 'electronic agent' as used in ss. 18–19 and state the two forms of interaction by which a contract or other transaction may be entered into under s. 18(2).
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 18 is a short, self-contained provision: subsection (1) defines 'electronic agent' for ss. 18–19 and subsection (2) grants a permission to enter contracts or transactions via electronic agents. The definition and the permission are tightly interdependent and form one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Human error
rows.groupTitle: Cancellation for human error in electronic transactions (s. 19)
rows.groupReason: All five subsections together define when cancellation is available, what the cancelling individual must do, the other person's reciprocal duty, preservation of other remedies, and the agent extension.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two conditions for cancelling a transaction entered through an electronic agent, the three duties of the cancelling individual, the other person's return-or-destroy obligation, and the extension where the individual acted on behalf of another person.
