rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19 is a self-contained cancellation mechanism for human error in electronic transactions, with interdependent trigger, conditions of exercise, reciprocal duty, savings clause, and agent extension forming one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Regulations
rows.groupTitle: Regulation-making power under the Electronic Transactions Act
rows.groupReason: The enumerated regulatory subjects, the general-or-specific scoping rule, and the consumer-contract elaboration are all facets of one regulation-making power and recall best as a single unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the subject matters for which the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make regulations under this Act, including the specific authority over electronically entered consumer contracts and the requirement that regulations may be general or specific.

evidenceText: The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make regulations
Regulations under this section may be general or specific, both as to the persons to whom and the subject-matter to which they relate.

Regulations under paragraph (1)(g) may include provisions relating to the substantive, formal and procedural requirements of a consumer contract or other consumer transaction, to its enforceability and to the remedies that may arise in relation to it.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single regulation-making power with eight enumerated subject matters in 20(1), a general scoping rule in 20(2), and a consumer-contract elaboration in 20(3) that specifies one enumerated item; together they form one coherent regulatory-authority concept.

rows.heading: Possession of lands
rows.groupTitle: Attorney General's power to take possession of or recover escheated or forfeited lands
rows.groupReason: Covers the triggers (intestate death without lawful heirs or forfeiture), the Attorney General's two recovery options, the no-inquisition rule, and the standard-procedure note as one integrated recovery mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the circumstances under which lands become liable to escheat or forfeiture, the two actions available to the Attorney General (taking possession in the Crown's name or bringing a recovery action), the dispensation of any prior inquisition, and the applicable procedural form of the action.

evidenceText: the Attorney General may cause possession of them to be taken in the name of the Crown, or in case possession is withheld the Attorney General may cause an action to be brought for the recovery of them, without any inquisition being first necessary
The proceedings in such an action may be in all respects similar to those in other actions for the recovery of land

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 1 is a short, self-contained operative provision creating the Attorney General's power to take possession of or recover escheated or forfeited lands and dispensing with any prior inquisition; 1(2) is a direct procedural supplement to the recovery action in 1(1), so both form one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Grant of lands
rows.groupTitle: Grant of escheated or forfeited lands by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council
rows.groupReason: The grant power, its procedural conditions (no entry or inquisition required, no Crown possession required), and the grantee's recovery right form one short, interdependent mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Lieutenant-Governor in Council's power to grant escheated or forfeited lands, the procedural conditions under which the grant may be made, and the grantee's right to institute recovery proceedings if possession is withheld.

evidenceText: The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make any grant of lands, tenements or hereditaments that have so escheated or become forfeited
Any such grant may be made without actual entry or inquisition being first necessary, and although the lands, tenements or hereditaments are not in the actual possession of the Crown
the person to whom the grant is made is entitled to institute proceedings for the recovery of them

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 2 is a short, self-contained provision (three subsections) stating the Lieutenant-Governor in Council's grant power over escheated or forfeited lands, the procedural conditions under which the grant operates, and the grantee's recovery right; together they form one coherent 'Grant of lands' concept.

rows.heading: Relief from forfeiture
rows.groupTitle: Relief from forfeiture: waiver or release by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council
rows.groupReason: The power to waive or release a forfeiture, its vesting effect, and the permissible terms (consideration and conditions) are one coherent recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Lieutenant-Governor in Council's power to waive or release a forfeiture of land, the effect of the relief on vesting, and the conditions governing its exercise.

evidenceText: the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may waive or release any right that the Crown has become entitled to, so as by the waiver or release to vest the property either absolutely or otherwise in the persons who would have been entitled to it but for the forfeiture
A waiver or release may be either for valuable consideration or otherwise, and may be on such terms and conditions as to the Lieutenant-Governor in Council seem fit

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3 is a short, self-contained power provision: 3(1) grants the Lieutenant-Governor in Council the authority to waive or release a forfeiture of land and states the vesting effect, and 3(2) supplies the directly dependent terms of exercise (consideration and conditions). The two subsections form one tightly coupled rule/condition structure best recalled together.

rows.heading: Assignment of personal property
rows.groupTitle: Assignment of escheated or forfeited personal property by the Lieutenant-Governor in Council
rows.groupReason: One power, one actor, one modality; triggers and purposes are all subordinate to the same discretionary grant and are best recalled together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the triggers (intestacy without heirs or forfeiture), the enumerated purposes for assignment, and the discretionary standard under which the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may assign Crown personal property under s. 4 of the Escheats and Forfeitures Act.

evidenceText: The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make any assignment of personal property to which the Crown is entitled by reason of the person last entitled to it having died intestate or without leaving any kin or other persons entitled to succeed to it

or may make an assignment of any portion of such personal property for the purpose of transferring or restoring it to any person having a moral claim to it, or on the person to whom it had belonged, or for carrying into effect any disposition of it that the person may have contemplated, or of rewarding any person making discovery of the escheat or forfeiture, as to the Lieutenant-Governor in Council seems proper.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 4 is a single discretionary power granted to the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, with defined triggers (intestacy without heirs, forfeiture) and enumerated purposes, all under one 'may make' modality and one 'seems proper' standard. It forms one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Sale of personal property
rows.groupTitle: Sale of forfeited personal property and disposition of proceeds
rows.groupReason: Subsections 5(1) and 5(2) together state the sale power (actor, trigger, method) and the mandatory disposition of proceeds; recalling them separately would fragment one small mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who may sell Crown-forfeited personal property, the two permissible sale methods, and the mandatory destination of the sale proceeds.

evidenceText: the Minister of Finance and Treasury Board may sell the property, either by public auction or private sale
The proceeds of any such sale shall become part of the Consolidated Fund.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 5 is a short, self-contained provision granting the Minister of Finance and Treasury Board power to sell forfeited personal property and directing proceeds to the Consolidated Fund. Both subsections form one recallable mechanism.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Evidence Act key definitions: court, witness, business, and other terms
rows.groupReason: All eight definitions operate together to set the Act's interpretive scope and are one recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Evidence Act's defined terms—especially the broadened meanings of 'court,' 'witness,' and 'business'—and how each extends the Act's application beyond its ordinary sense.

evidenceText: "court" includes a judge, arbitrator, umpire, commission, tribunal and any other body or person having by law or consent of parties authority to receive evidence
"witness" includes party to an action, suit or judicial proceeding when entitled or compellable to be examined
"business" includes every kind of business, profession, trade, occupation and the operation of institutions whether carried on for profit or not

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 1 defines eight key terms that collectively establish the interpretive scope of the Evidence Act and form one coherent definitional framework best recalled as a single unit.

rows.heading: No incompetency by reason of interest or crime
rows.groupTitle: Incompetency by reason of interest or crime
rows.groupReason: States the general rule that neither interest in the matter nor commission of a crime renders a person incompetent to give evidence.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two grounds—interest and crime—that do not render a person incompetent to give evidence under section 2.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 2 states a single general competency rule removing interest and crime as grounds for incompetency to give evidence; one standalone StudyUnit.

rows.heading: Competency and compellability of parties and spouses
rows.groupTitle: Competency and compellability of parties and spouses
rows.groupReason: One coherent rule naming the persons competent and compellable as witnesses and the modes of giving evidence in court proceedings.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the persons who are competent and compellable to give evidence under s. 3(1) (parties, persons on whose behalf proceedings are brought, and their spouses), the proceedings to which it applies, and the permitted modes of testifying.

evidenceText: the parties thereto and the persons in whose behalf the action, matter or proceeding is brought or instituted, or opposed or defended, and the spouses of such parties and persons, are, except as hereinafter excepted, competent and compellable to give evidence either viva voce or by deposition according to the practice of the court

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3(1) is a single operative rule identifying which persons are competent and compellable witnesses; repealed 3(2) contributes no study content.

rows.heading: Evidence of spouse re sexual intercourse
rows.groupTitle: Spousal competency: evidence of sexual intercourse
rows.groupReason: One permission rule (spouse may give evidence) with one subject, one temporal scope, and one 'without limiting' qualifier to s.3(1); all pieces recall together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the scope of a spouse's competency to give evidence about sexual intercourse under s.3.1, including the temporal coverage (before or during the marriage) and the relationship to the general rule in s.3(1).

evidenceText: a spouse may, in an action, matter or other proceeding in any court, give evidence that he or she did or did not have sexual intercourse with the other party to the marriage at any time, or within any period of time, before or during the marriage

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3.1 states a single, self-contained spousal competency permission for sexual-intercourse evidence with a clear temporal scope, operating as a specific confirmation within s.3(1) without limiting it.

rows.heading: Evidence for or against spouse
rows.groupTitle: Spousal competency to give evidence for or against spouse
rows.groupReason: One rule answering a single recall question: the scope of spousal competency to testify in any court proceeding.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a spouse is competent to give evidence for or against his or her spouse on the trial of an issue, matter, or question, or on an inquiry arising in any action, matter, or other proceeding in any court.

evidenceText: a spouse is competent to give evidence for or against his or her spouse

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 4 states a single, self-contained competency rule: a spouse is competent to give evidence for or against his or her spouse in any court proceeding. No internal subdivisions warrant splitting.

rows.heading: Non-compellability of person charged or spouse of person charged
rows.groupTitle: Competence and non-compellability of charged person and spouse
rows.groupReason: The competence grant and the non-compellability bar operate as a single rule governing the same actors in the same proceeding type.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the evidentiary status (competent but not compellable) of a person charged and that person's spouse on a prosecution for a provincial statute violation or penalty, including where the charge is joint.

evidenceText: the person charged and his or her spouse are competent witnesses, whether the person so charged is charged solely or jointly with another person; but neither such person nor his or her spouse is compellable to testify.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 5 is a short, self-contained rule pairing witness competence with non-compellability for a charged person and spouse in provincial prosecutions; the two clauses are tightly interdependent and form one recall task.

rows.heading: Compellability of witness respecting disclosure of indebtedness
rows.groupTitle: Compellability of witness: debt and civil suit exposure
rows.groupReason: Single operative rule removing a specific compellability objection (debt or civil suit exposure) that forms one recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the rule and its scope: a witness cannot refuse to answer a question relevant to the matter in issue solely because the answer may establish or tend to establish indebtedness or civil suit exposure, whether the suit is brought by the Crown or any other person.

evidenceText: A witness cannot by law refuse to answer a question relative to the matter in issue by reason only that the answering of the question may establish or tend to establish that he owes a debt or is otherwise subject to a civil suit, either at the instance of the Crown, or of any other person.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 is a single, self-contained compellability rule: a witness cannot refuse to answer a relevant question solely because the answer may expose the witness to a debt or civil suit, by the Crown or any person. One coherent recall task with no internal subdivisions warranting a split.

rows.heading: Compellability of witness respecting disclosure of criminal act
rows.groupTitle: Compellability of witness and use restriction for compelled testimony
rows.groupReason: The section pairs a compellability duty with a directly dependent evidentiary use restriction and perjury exception as one recallable rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the proceedings in which a witness may not refuse to answer on the ground that the answer may show criminal liability, and state the restriction on using compelled evidence against the witness with its perjury exception.

evidenceText: no person shall be excused from answering any question upon the ground that the answer to such question may tend to render him liable to a prosecution, penalty or forfeiture
no evidence so given shall be used or receivable in evidence against such person in any proceeding instituted against him other than a prosecution for perjury in giving such evidence

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 7 states a single coherent evidentiary rule: a witness must answer self-incriminating questions in specified proceedings, but compelled testimony is restricted from use against the witness except for perjury. The compellability duty and its use restriction are tightly interdependent rule/qualification clauses joined in one sentence.

rows.heading: Non-compellability of accused or spouse of accused
rows.groupTitle: Non-compellability of accused and spouse (s. 9)
rows.groupReason: One recall task: identify who is protected, the scope of the protection (for or against), and the provincial-offence limitation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who section 9 renders non-compellable, the direction of evidence covered (for or against), and the offence-type limitation.

evidenceText: Nothing herein renders a person charged with an offence against a law of this Province compellable to give evidence for or against himself or herself, or his or her spouse compellable to give evidence for or against such person.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 9 is a short, self-contained non-compellability rule covering two protected persons (accused and spouse) within a single recallable concept; no split is warranted.

rows.heading: Compellability of spouses
rows.groupTitle: Compellability of spouses (s. 10)
rows.groupReason: Creates the spousal communication privilege: no spouse may be compelled to disclose communications made during the marriage.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the rule in s. 10 that a spouse cannot be compelled to disclose any communication made to them by their spouse during the marriage, and identify the temporal limit (during the marriage).

evidenceText: Nothing in this Act renders a spouse compellable to disclose any communication made to him or her by his or her spouse during their marriage.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single-sentence provision establishing a self-contained non-compellability rule for spousal communications during marriage, distinct from the s. 9 accused-testimony rule.

rows.heading: Application of Act
rows.groupTitle: Evidence Act scope: exclusion of federal criminal prosecutions for provincial breaches
rows.groupReason: One sentence establishing the Act's inapplicability to federal criminal prosecutions for provincial breaches; a single recall task on the boundary of the Act's scope.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the circumstance in which the Evidence Act does not apply to a prosecution under federal criminal law for a breach of a provincial statute.

evidenceText: Nothing herein extends or applies to any prosecution instituted under and by virtue of the criminal laws of Canada for any breach of a provincial statute.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 11 states a single, clear scope limitation: the Evidence Act does not extend to prosecutions under federal criminal law for breaches of provincial statutes. This is an operative boundary rule a learner must recall to know when the Act's evidence rules apply.

rows.heading: Power of court to administer oath
rows.groupTitle: Power of court to administer oath
rows.groupReason: One short enabling provision: identifies the actor (every court) and the scope (witnesses legally called before it) of oath-administration power.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the power granted to every court to administer an oath and identify the class of witnesses to whom it applies.

evidenceText: Every court is hereby empowered to administer an oath to all such witnesses as are legally called before it.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative sentence granting every court the power to administer an oath to witnesses legally called before it; one foundational recall task.

rows.heading: Manner of taking oath
rows.groupTitle: Manner of administering an oath
rows.groupReason: Covers the default oath-administration form (holding scripture without kissing) and the alternative form when a person objects on conscience grounds, both answering the same recall question.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the default manner of administering an oath and the alternative form applicable when a person objects to the standard manner or declares it not binding on his conscience.

evidenceText: it may be administered to a person while such person holds in his hand a copy of the Old or New Testament without requiring him to kiss the same

when he objects to being sworn in this manner or declares that the oath so administered is not binding upon his conscience, then in such manner and form and with such ceremonies as he declares to be binding

rows.sourceMapReason: A single short procedural rule governing the manner of administering an oath, including the default form and the conscience-based alternative, forming one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Solemn affirmation or declaration
rows.groupTitle: Right to solemn affirmation in lieu of oath
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) together establish the triggering conditions, the duty on the court, the required words, and the legal effect of solemn affirmation as one integrated evidentiary mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the conditions under which a witness may affirm instead of being sworn, the mandatory words of affirmation, and the legal force given to a solemn affirmation under section 14 of the Evidence Act.
rows.sourceMapReason: Short self-contained provision establishing the right to solemn affirmation in lieu of oath and its legal equivalence to a sworn oath.

rows.heading: Disbelief in oath
rows.groupTitle: Oath validity not defeated by disbelief
rows.groupReason: One rule covering both the oath-taker and the oath-administering person, scoped by the universal phrase 'for any purpose.'
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that an oath's validity is unaffected, for any purpose, by the fact that either the person taking it or the person administering it did not believe in its binding effect at the time.

evidenceText: the fact that the person to whom it was administered and by whom it was taken did not at the time of taking the oath believe in the binding effect of the oath does not, for any purpose, affect the validity of the oath

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 15 states a single operative rule: disbelief in the binding effect of an oath does not affect its validity for any purpose. One recall task, no split or combine needed.

rows.heading: Solemn declaration respecting written document
rows.groupTitle: Solemn declaration: authorized officers, form, purpose, and legal effect
rows.groupReason: The section prescribes one mechanism—authorized officers, voluntary condition, form, purpose, and oath-equivalence—that a learner recalls as a unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the officers who may receive a solemn declaration under section 16, the condition that the declaration be voluntary, its purpose, and its legal equivalence to an oath.

evidenceText: Any Notary Public, Commissioner for taking affidavits to be read in The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick or other functionary authorized by law to administer an oath may receive the solemn declaration of any person voluntarily making the same before him
in attestation of the truth of any fact or of any account rendered in writing
knowing that it is of the same force and effect as if made under oath, and by virtue of the Evidence Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 16 establishes a single coherent procedural mechanism: who may receive a solemn declaration, the voluntary condition, the prescribed form, the purpose, and its equivalence to an oath. These elements are tightly interdependent and answer one recall task.

rows.heading: Proof of adversity of witness
rows.groupTitle: Impeaching one's own adverse witness
rows.groupReason: Covers the full rule/exception/condition structure of s. 17 as one coherent impeachment framework.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the prohibition on general bad character evidence, the conditions under which a producing party may contradict an adverse witness, and the notice requirement before proving a prior inconsistent statement.

evidenceText: The party producing a witness shall not be allowed to impeach his credit by general evidence of bad character

if the witness in the opinion of the judge proves adverse, contradict him by other evidence, or by leave of the judge prove that he has made at other times a statement inconsistent with his present testimony
the circumstances of the supposed statement, sufficient to designate the particular occasion, must be mentioned to the witness and he must be asked whether or not he has made such statement

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 17 is a single rule/exception/condition structure governing impeachment of one's own witness: a prohibition, a conditional permission to contradict, and a procedural precondition. The pieces are tightly interdependent and form one recall task.

rows.heading: Contradiction of witness on cross-examination
rows.groupTitle: Contradiction of Witness on Cross-Examination
rows.groupReason: The cross-examination trigger, the permission to give proof of a prior inconsistent statement, and the mandatory preliminary step of designating the occasion form one interdependent procedural rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the condition under which proof of a prior inconsistent statement may be given on cross-examination and the mandatory step of mentioning the circumstances sufficient to designate the particular occasion before such proof.

evidenceText: before such proof can be given, the circumstances of the supposed statement, sufficient to designate the particular occasion, must be mentioned to the witness and he must be asked whether or not he has made such statement

rows.sourceMapReason: Single procedural rule governing contradiction of a witness on cross-examination; the trigger, permission to give proof, and mandatory preliminary step form one interdependent concept.

rows.heading: Examination of witness respecting previous statements in writing
rows.groupTitle: Examining a witness on previous written statements
rows.groupReason: Three interdependent elements—permission to examine without showing the writing, the attention-call prerequisite for contradiction, and the judge's power to require production—form one recallable procedural unit about using a witness's prior written statements.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when a witness may be examined on previous written statements, what must be done before the writing is used to contradict the witness, and the judge's power to require and use the writing during trial.

evidenceText: A witness may be examined as to previous statements made by him in writing, or reduced into writing, relative to the subject matter of the cause, without such writing being shown to him
if it is intended to contradict such witness by the writing, before such contradictory proof can be given, his attention must be called to those parts of the writing
it is competent for the judge at any time during the trial to require the production of the writing for his own inspection

rows.sourceMapReason: Short single-paragraph provision stating one coherent procedure for examining a witness on previous written statements, the contradiction prerequisite, and the judge's inspection power, all operating on the same document in the same examination context.

rows.heading: Examination of witness respecting prior conviction, certificate of conviction
rows.groupTitle: Examining and Proving a Witness's Prior Criminal Conviction
rows.groupReason: One recall task: the trigger for proving a prior conviction and the certificate requirements that make it sufficient evidence.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a witness may be questioned about a prior criminal conviction, the effect of denial or refusal to answer, and the requirements for a court certificate to constitute sufficient evidence of the conviction without further proof of signature or official character.

evidenceText: A witness in any cause may be questioned as to whether he has been convicted of any crime; and upon being so questioned, if he either denies the fact or refuses to answer, the opposite party may prove such conviction.
is, upon proof of the identity of the person, sufficient evidence of the said conviction without proof of the signature or official character of the person appearing to have signed the same.

rows.sourceMapReason: Both subsections form one coherent evidentiary procedure: the right to question a witness about a prior conviction and the certificate mechanism for proving it. They are short, tightly interdependent, and answer a single recall prompt.

rows.heading: Necessity of proof of instrument by attesting witness
rows.groupTitle: Proof of instrument without attesting witness
rows.groupReason: One evidentiary permission rule with a single condition (attestation not requisite to validity) and a single consequence (instrument may be proved by admission or otherwise as if unattested).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when proof by an attesting witness is not required and identify the alternative means by which such an instrument may be proved.

evidenceText: It is not necessary to prove by the attesting witness an instrument to the validity of which attestation is not requisite, and such an instrument may be proved by admission or otherwise, as if there had been no attesting witness thereto.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 21 states one self-contained evidentiary rule: when attestation is not requisite to an instrument's validity, proof by attesting witness is unnecessary and the instrument may be proved by admission or otherwise. It is a single recallable permission rule with no internal sub-parts warranting a split.

rows.heading: Resolution of dispute respecting genuineness of handwriting
rows.groupTitle: Handwriting Comparison Evidence
rows.groupReason: All elements—precondition (genuine writing proved to court satisfaction), actor (witnesses), and admissibility effect (writings and witness evidence before court or jury)—form one interdependent rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the precondition, performing actor, and evidentiary effect when comparing a disputed writing with a genuine writing to establish or negate genuineness before a court or jury.

evidenceText: Comparison of a disputed writing with any writing proved to the satisfaction of the court to be genuine shall be permitted to be made by witnesses, and such writings and the evidence of witnesses respecting the same may be submitted to the court or jury as evidence of the genuineness or otherwise of the writing in dispute.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 22 states one complete evidentiary rule: the conditions, performing actor, and admissibility effect of handwriting comparison to resolve a genuineness dispute.

rows.heading: Expert opinion witnesses
rows.groupTitle: Limit on expert opinion witnesses without court leave
rows.groupReason: One numeric cap rule with a single actor (either side), single trigger (intent to call expert witnesses), and one consequence threshold (leave required beyond three).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the statutory limit on expert opinion witnesses either side may call in an action without court leave and the scope of that limit per issue.

evidenceText: not more than three of such witnesses may be called by either side to give opinion evidence on any issue in the action without the leave of the court.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 23 is a single, self-contained procedural rule capping expert opinion witnesses at three per side per issue without court leave.

rows.heading: Child of tender years
rows.groupTitle: Receiving a Child of Tender Years' Evidence Without an Oath
rows.groupReason: The provision sets out the court's opinion-based conditions (child does not understand the nature of an oath, possesses sufficient intelligence, understands the duty of speaking the truth) that together permit receiving a child's evidence without an oath.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a child of tender years' evidence may be received in an action without being given upon oath, including the role of the court's opinion on the child's understanding and intelligence.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 24(1) states a single cohesive evidentiary permission: the conditions under which a child of tender years' evidence may be received without an oath. All conditions are interdependent parts of one rule, forming one recallable unit. Subsection (2) is repealed and carries no operative content.

rows.heading: Recording of evidence and proceedings, admissibility
rows.groupTitle: Permitted recording methods and transcript admissibility under s. 25
rows.groupReason: The two subsections form one interdependent rule: who may record and by what methods, and when the resulting certified transcript is admissible.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the three permitted recording methods in 25(1) and state the certification and admissibility requirements for a transcript under 25(2), including that approval or signature by the witness or parties is not required.

evidenceText: an Official Shorthand Reporter, Special Court Shorthand Reporter or other person, who is authorized to record evidence and proceedings in an action or a legal proceeding may record the evidence and proceedings

a transcript of the whole or part of any evidence or proceedings that has been recorded in accordance with subsection (1) and that has been certified as a true report of the evidence or proceedings by the person who recorded the evidence or proceedings, or by the judge or other person who presided over the action or proceedings and that is otherwise admissible by law, is admissible in evidence

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsection 25(1) (permitted recording methods) and 25(2) (admissibility and certification of the resulting transcript) are tightly interlocked: 25(2) expressly applies only to evidence 'recorded in accordance with subsection (1),' making them one coherent recording-and-admissibility mechanism best studied as a single unit.

rows.heading: Destruction and preservation of records
rows.groupTitle: Destruction of recorded evidence and proceedings
rows.groupReason: Subsections (0.1), (1), and (2) form one complete rule: the circumstances and timeframes within which a recorder may or must preserve a record, split by whether a certified transcript exists.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the destruction timeframes applicable to a recorder depending on whether a certified transcript was made, including the thirty-day window and the regulation-prescribed period, and the scope limitation to proceedings before boards, commissions, tribunals, bodies, or commissioners.

evidenceText: where a transcript of evidence or proceedings recorded in accordance with subsection 25(1) has been made and certified in accordance with subsection 25(2), the Official Shorthand Reporter, Special Court Shorthand Reporter, or other person who recorded the evidence and proceedings may, after the expiration of thirty days from the day on which the transcript was made and certified, destroy the record or erase any recording thereof.

shall not destroy the record or erase any recording thereof for such period after it has been made as the Minister of Justice may by regulation prescribe, but after that period has expired, he may destroy the record or erase the recording thereof.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 26 contains two distinct procedural mechanisms: destruction timeframes governing recorders, and the preservation-order process governing interested persons. Each answers a different recall question and involves a different primary actor.

rows.heading: Destruction and preservation of records
rows.groupTitle: Preservation orders for records of evidence and proceedings
rows.groupReason: Subsections (3) through (6) form the complete preservation-order procedure: the right to apply without notice, the normal and fallback application routes, the discretion standard, and the binding effect of a served order.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the preservation-order process: who may apply and without what notice, to whom the application is normally made and the fallback to the Minister of Justice when the original body has ceased to have authority, the discretion standard under which the order is made, and the preservation duty imposed on the record holder upon service.

evidenceText: An interested person, without notice to any other person, may apply for an order providing for the preservation for a specified period of any record made under subsection 25(1).

In the case of any record of evidence or proceedings before any board, commission, tribunal, body or commissioner that or who has ceased to have authority to act in the matter in respect of which the evidence was given or the proceedings were held, an application for an order under subsection (3) is to be made to the Minister of Justice.

Where an order made under subsection (5) is served on the person making or having possession of the record referred to in the order, that person shall preserve it for the period specified in the order.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 26 contains two distinct procedural mechanisms: destruction timeframes governing recorders, and the preservation-order process governing interested persons. Each answers a different recall question and involves a different primary actor.

rows.heading: Civil liability of witness respecting disobedience of summons to witness
rows.groupTitle: Civil liability for witness's disobedience of summons to witness
rows.groupReason: One rule tying the conditions for a witness's default to the damages action available to the serving party.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the conditions under which a witness's default on a summons triggers civil liability and the scope of the damages action available to the person who served the summons.

evidenceText: A witness served in due time with a summons to witness issued out of a court in this province and paid his proper attendance money, who makes default in obeying such summons to witness without any lawful and reasonable impediment, is, in addition to any penalty he may incur as for a contempt of court or by law, liable to an action on the part of the person by whom, or on whose behalf, he is served with the summons to witness, for any damage that such person may sustain or be put to by reason of such default.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 28 states one self-contained civil liability rule with its triggering conditions and remedy in a single sentence; no independent recall tasks justify a split.

rows.heading: Bringing up prisoner as witness
rows.groupTitle: Bringing up a prisoner as a witness (s. 29)
rows.groupReason: The three subsections form one procedural sequence: issuing the order, the custodian's tender condition, the return and continuous-custody fiction, and officer immunity.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the application requirements, eligible persons, tender condition on the custodian, the return and continuous-custody fiction, and the officer immunity provided by s. 29 of the Evidence Act.

evidenceText: A judge of The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick, upon application on affidavit of either party to a suit pending in his court, may issue an order under his hand and the seal of the court for bringing up before the court any prisoner confined in a jail, or person under any sentence or under commitment for trial, or under process in a civil suit, to be examined as a witness

he shall be returned forthwith by the officer who has him in charge to the jail or prison, and such person shall, for the purpose of serving or completing the term of his imprisonment, be deemed to have remained continuously in such jail or prison
No sheriff, jailer or other officer is liable to any action or prosecution for acting in obedience to any such order

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 29 is a self-contained procedural mechanism (order to bring up, return and continuous-custody fiction, officer immunity) that functions as one recallable unit; all three subsections describe one procedural flow from application through return.

rows.heading: Order of commissioner respecting witness
rows.groupTitle: Commissioner's power to order witness attendance under a foreign commission
rows.groupReason: The entire section states one power and its scope; the trigger (foreign commission), actor (named commissioner), and scope (attendance plus named documents at appointed time and place) form a single recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the conditions under which a commissioner named in a foreign commission may order a New Brunswick witness to attend with specified documents, and the requirements the order must state.

evidenceText: When a commission is issued from any court of any other province, state or kingdom for the examination of a witness in this Province by a commissioner named in the commission, such commissioner may make an order for the attendance of the witness, with such books, papers, documents or writings of any kind as may be in the custody, power or possession of such witness, to be mentioned in such order, at such time and place as the commissioner appoints.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 is a single, self-contained power provision: when a commission from another jurisdiction is issued, the named commissioner may order the witness's attendance with specified documents at an appointed time and place. One actor, one trigger, one recall task.

rows.heading: Order of commissioner respecting attachment of witness
rows.groupTitle: Attachment application procedure for defaulting commission witness
rows.groupReason: Prerequisites, two default triggers, authorized applicants, and the judge's mandatory show-cause order are interdependent parts of one attachment application procedure.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the service and expense-tendering prerequisites, the two witness-default triggers, who may apply to a judge of The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick, and the judge's mandatory show-cause order upon receipt of the supporting affidavit.

evidenceText: after any such order is served on the witness and reasonable expenses are tendered in the manner prescribed by law or the practice of The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick
the commissioner or the attorney or agent of any of the parties to the action, proceeding or suit in which the commission is issued may apply to a judge of The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick

who shall forthwith, upon an affidavit of such service, refusal or default, order such witness to appear before him at such time and place as he appoints, to show cause why an attachment should not be issued

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 31 is a single-paragraph procedural provision establishing the attachment application procedure for a commission witness who defaults; its prerequisites, triggers, authorized applicants, and the judge's mandatory show-cause order form one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Order of judge respecting attachment of witness
rows.groupTitle: Judge's orders at a witness-attachment hearing
rows.groupReason: The mandatory attachment order, its good-and-sufficient-cause exception, and the judge's discretionary costs and enforcement powers are all one judicial decision at the same hearing and are best recalled together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the judge's mandatory duty to issue attachment, the exception for good and sufficient cause, and the judge's discretionary powers to order further relief, costs of neglect or default, and enforcement by attachment.

evidenceText: The judge is hereby required to issue such attachment, unless good and sufficient cause is shown to the contrary, and to make such further order in the matter with reference to such witness and such examination, and the costs and expenses thereof, and of such neglect, refusal or default as he may deem proper, and may order the witness to pay all costs and expenses incurred by such neglect, refusal or default, and may enforce such payment by attachment.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 32 is a short, self-contained provision setting out the judge's mandatory and discretionary orders at a witness-attachment hearing, forming one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Admissibility of evidence given at former trial
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility of Former Trial Testimony
rows.groupReason: One interdependent admissibility rule: same-party requirement, permissible evidence sources (judge's notes or certified stenographic record), and three witness-unavailability grounds must be recalled together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which testimony given on a former trial may be admitted, including the party-identity requirement, the two acceptable evidence sources, and the grounds for witness unavailability (death, absence from the Province, or sickness or inability to attend).
rows.sourceMapReason: Single self-contained admissibility rule whose party requirement, evidence-source options, and witness-unavailability conditions are interdependent and form one recall task.

rows.heading: Notice respecting production of judge’s notes
rows.groupTitle: Notice and production of judge's notes at a subsequent trial
rows.groupReason: The notice duty and the judge's two production options form one compact procedural rule that a learner can recall as a single unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the notice requirement that applies when judge's notes are required on a trial and describe the two options available to the judge who took the notes.

evidenceText: notice shall be given to the judge who took the same, and he may either produce and read the same in court, or may transmit them to the presiding judge to be read by him on such subsequent trial

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 34 is a short, self-contained procedural rule: a notice duty on the party requiring judge's notes and two options for the judge to produce or transmit them. The two elements are tightly interdependent and form one recallable procedure.

rows.heading: Admissibility of evidence given at prior proceedings
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility conditions for prior proceeding testimony
rows.groupReason: Subsection (1) sets out three cumulative conditions that must all be satisfied for prior proceeding testimony or an unsworn statement to be admissible; they form one interdependent test.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the three cumulative conditions (qualifying prior forum, witness unavailability, and prior representation with opportunity to examine) required for testimony or an unsworn statement from a prior proceeding to be admissible.

evidenceText: where testimony has been given or an unsworn statement has been made by a person before a court of record in Canada, a royal commission, a board of inquiry or any other board, commission, tribunal or body
where such person is dead or unfit by reason of his bodily or mental condition to attend as a witness or if he is outside the Province and it is not reasonably practicable to secure his attendance

the party against whom such evidence or unsworn statement is tendered or his predecessor in interest or other privy was represented before such previous court, commission, board, tribunal or body and either called such person or had an opportunity to examine or question such person

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 35 contains a substantive admissibility rule with three cumulative conditions (s. 35(1)) and two distinct prima facie proof mechanisms for tendering that evidence (ss. 35(2)–(3)); these raise different recall tasks for a learner.

rows.heading: Admissibility of evidence given at prior proceedings
rows.groupTitle: Prima facie proof of prior proceeding testimony
rows.groupReason: Subsections (2) and (3) each establish a separate prima facie proof mechanism—printed copies from official printers and certified transcripts from proper custody—for tendering the prior testimony in evidence.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the requirements for a printed copy of, or a certified transcript of, prior proceeding testimony to constitute prima facie proof of that testimony.

evidenceText: What purports to be a copy of the testimony or statement of such person and purports to have been printed by or on behalf of such court, commission, board, tribunal or body or by or on behalf of the King's Printer or other official printer

What purports to be a transcript of the evidence or statement of such person produced from proper custody and purports to be certified by a shorthand reporter who recorded or transcribed such evidence or statement or purports to be certified by the presiding officer, is prima facie proof thereof

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 35 contains a substantive admissibility rule with three cumulative conditions (s. 35(1)) and two distinct prima facie proof mechanisms for tendering that evidence (ss. 35(2)–(3)); these raise different recall tasks for a learner.

rows.heading: Admissibility of copy of public record
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility of copies of public records (s. 36, Evidence Act)
rows.groupReason: The section states one coherent rule: the covered documents, the two alternative proof methods, and the resulting evidentiary effect, all of which a learner must recall together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State which documents and public offices are covered, the two methods by which a copy may be proved or certified, and the evidentiary effect of such proof in all courts.

evidenceText: shall without proof of the official character or handwriting of such officer be deemed and taken in all courts to be as good and sufficient evidence of such record, grant, letters patent, surrender, escheat, inquisition, lease, licence, conveyance, map, plan, record of survey, document or writing as the original or any exemplification thereof under the Great Seal.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 36 is a single undivided evidentiary rule covering the documents, proving methods, and legal effect for copies of public records; all elements are interdependent and form one recall task.

rows.heading: Admissibility of copy of parts of public record
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility of Partial Exemplifications of Crown Records
rows.groupReason: One rule: when only parts of specific Crown-related records are necessary, exemplifications of those parts suffice in any court in the Province.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the categories of public records covered by section 37 and the condition under which a partial exemplification is admissible in evidence without requiring the whole document to be exemplified.

evidenceText: exemplifications of such parts that may be so necessary may be received in evidence in any court in this Province without requiring the whole of the record, roll, inquisition, surrender, escheat, lease, licence, judgment or conveyance to be exemplified.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 37 is a single, self-contained evidentiary rule permitting partial exemplifications of Crown-related public records to be admitted without proving the whole document. One coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Effect of omissions from copy of public record
rows.groupTitle: Omissions permissible in copies of public records
rows.groupReason: Single rule defining which clauses may be omitted from a copy and the condition protecting the copy from evidentiary rejection.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify which clauses may be omitted from a certified or examined copy of a public record admissible under section 36 and the condition under which such an omission does not result in rejection of the copy.

evidenceText: it is not necessary to copy the conditions contained in such grant, letters patent, surrender, escheat, inquisition, lease, licence or conveyance, on the part of the grantees, lessees or licensees, their heirs or assigns, to be observed or performed

no such exemplification, examined or certified copy shall be rejected in evidence on account of the omission of such clauses, if such omission does not prejudice the opposite party or affect the merits in question

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent evidentiary rule: copies of public records may omit non-pertinent clauses without rejection, subject to a prejudice-and-merits limitation.

rows.heading: Annexation of certified plan to public record
rows.groupTitle: Evidentiary requirement for public records referencing an annexed plat or plan
rows.groupReason: One rule with one exception: the plan must accompany the copy, unless the responsible official certifies none exists. Splitting the exception from the rule would fragment a single admissibility condition.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the evidentiary condition that applies to a certified copy of a public record that references an annexed plat or plan, and identify the certificate exception and who may issue it.

evidenceText: no exemplification or copy of such record, grant, letters patent, surrender, escheat, inquisition, lease, licence or conveyance shall be received in evidence unless there is annexed thereto a true transcript or copy of such plat or plan

unless it is proved by the certificate of the Minister of Natural Resources or other public officer of the Province having charge of the original, or otherwise to the satisfaction of the court at which the evidence may be tendered, that there is no such plat or plan entered in or attached to the said grant

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 39 states one coherent evidentiary rule: a copy of a public record referencing an annexed plat or plan is inadmissible without that plan, subject to a certificate exception from the Minister of Natural Resources or other public officer having charge of the original. The rule and its exception are tightly interdependent and form a single recallable concept directly relevant to surveying practice.

rows.heading: Certificate of Minister of Natural Resources
rows.groupTitle: Evidentiary effect of Minister of Natural Resources certified survey copies
rows.groupReason: Admissibility condition, prima facie evidence effect, and no-proof-of-official-character-or-handwriting clause are interdependent halves of one recall task: the evidentiary status of a certified survey copy.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the admissibility condition, the prima facie evidence effect, and the self-authentication rule (no proof of official character or handwriting) for a Minister of Natural Resources or deputy-certified copy of a plan or record of survey on file in the Minister's office.

evidenceText: is admissible in evidence in all cases where the original plan or record of survey would be admissible in evidence
shall, without proof of official character or handwriting, be deemed and taken to be prima facie evidence of such original plan or record of survey

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent evidentiary rule covering admissibility, prima facie effect, and self-authentication of Minister of Natural Resources certified survey copies; no independent split warranted.

rows.heading: Proof of copies of letters patent and grants issued under the Nova Scotia Grants Act
rows.groupTitle: Proof of Pre-1784 Nova Scotia Land Grants by Certified or Examined Copies
rows.groupReason: Extends the Act's existing copy-proof method to one defined class of historic Nova Scotia grants; a single recallable evidentiary rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the class of pre-1784 Nova Scotia grants registered under the 26th-year George III Act and the permissible methods of proving them by certified or examined copies in the same manner as current provincial grants.

evidenceText: may be proved by certified or examined copies thereof, or of the material parts thereof, in like manner as hereinbefore provided in respect to grants passed under the Great Seal of the Province

rows.sourceMapReason: One narrow operative evidentiary permission extending the Act's standard certified-or-examined-copy proof method to a specific class of pre-1784 Nova Scotia land grants registered under the George III registration Act.

rows.heading: Costs respecting making of copies of public records
rows.groupTitle: Taxation of costs for copies of public records given in evidence
rows.groupReason: One coherent cost-recovery rule covering the scope of documents, the taxing officer's role, and the review path.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that expenses of exemplifying or copying records, grants, plats, plans, and other documents given in evidence under the Act may be charged and allowed in taxation of costs, in whole or in part, by the taxing officer of the pending court, with review as in ordinary cases.

evidenceText: may be charged and allowed in the taxation of costs, in whole or in part, by the taxing officer of the court wherein the suit may be pending, whose decision thereupon may be reviewed as in ordinary cases.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 42 is a single, self-contained costs-taxation rule: it permits charging copying/exemplification expenses for public records given in evidence under the Act, assigns the taxing officer as decision-maker, and provides for review as in ordinary cases. All elements form one recall task.

rows.heading: Admissibility of public records
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility of Government Reports and Publications as Evidence
rows.groupReason: One operative admissibility rule specifying document types, subject matters, preparer authority, and the relevance condition for public records.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the categories of government reports, publications, and statements that are admissible as evidence of the matters stated therein and the relevance condition that limits that admissibility.

evidenceText: Any report, publication or statement on any matter of science, technology, geography, population, natural resources, engineering or other matter of fact or fact and opinion purporting to have been prepared by or under the authority of any department or branch of the Government of Canada or of the Province or of any other province is, in so far as relevant, admissible as evidence of the matters stated therein.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 43 states a single, self-contained admissibility rule for government reports, publications, and statements; all its elements (document types, subject matters, preparer authority, relevance condition) define one evidentiary test.

rows.heading: Investigative report
rows.groupTitle: Privilege of investigative reports in civil proceedings
rows.groupReason: The provision states the two alternative grounds for privilege (dominant-purpose litigation submission, or any opinion expressed regardless of purpose) and the resulting protection from disclosure and production in civil proceedings as one interdependent rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two grounds on which an investigative report is privileged from disclosure and production in civil proceedings under s. 43.1.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 43.1 is a single, self-contained privilege rule with two alternative grounds and one legal effect, forming one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Solicitor and client communication
rows.groupTitle: Solicitor-client privilege preserved against auditor disclosure
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) together state the complete non-waiver rule for auditor-related disclosure, covering both actual disclosure and preparatory intention; recalling one without the other would fragment the concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the circumstances in which solicitor-client privilege is not lost or waived by disclosure to the client's auditor, reference in financial statements and notes, or the preparatory intention of such disclosure.

evidenceText: Any privilege that exists in relation to any communication between a solicitor and client is not lost or waived because all or part of the communication is

The fact that any communication between a solicitor and client is prepared or made with the intention that it will be furnished or disclosed to the client's auditor for the purpose of assisting the auditor in the performance of an audit does not prevent the creation of, or give rise to the waiver of, a privilege

rows.sourceMapReason: Two subsections form one interdependent rule: privilege survives actual auditor disclosure or financial-statement reference (s.1) and is neither prevented from arising nor waived by the intention of such disclosure (s.2).

rows.heading: Hospital committee
rows.groupTitle: Hospital Committee Privilege for Witnesses
rows.groupReason: The definitions, three-limbed excuse, carve-outs for statutory records and patient medical records, the medical-advisory-committee exclusion, and the no-excuse-for-participants rule are mutually dependent parts of one privilege rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the scope of the witness excuse under s. 43.3(2), the exceptions in s. 43.3(3), the medical advisory committee exclusion in s. 43.3(4), and the rule in s. 43.3(5) that committee participation does not itself excuse a witness.

evidenceText: A witness, whether a party to a legal proceeding or not, is excused from
Subsection (2) does not apply to
a committee referred to in subsection (2) does not include a medical advisory committee exercising its functions respecting surgical and other privileges of the medical staff

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 43.3 establishes one coherent evidentiary privilege: a witness's excuse from testifying about or producing material connected to regional health authority committees, with tightly interdependent definitions, scope, exceptions, committee exclusion, and participant rule that together form a single recallable privilege concept.

rows.heading: Telegraph message or despatch
rows.groupTitle: Telegraph message or despatch: notice requirement and prima facie evidentiary effect
rows.groupReason: The notice precondition and the resulting prima facie evidence and presumption are inseparable: the notice is the sole trigger for the evidentiary effect, so they form one recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the ten-day notice requirement for offering a telegraph message or despatch not in the opposite party's possession, and identify the prima facie evidence and presumption that attach once the Court is satisfied the notice was properly given.

evidenceText: he may, at least ten days before offering the same in evidence, give to the opposite party, his solicitor or attorney, notice of his intention to offer such telegraph message or despatch in evidence, together with a copy of such message or despatch

such telegraph message or despatch shall, if otherwise admissible, be received and admitted as prima facie evidence of its having been dated, directed, written and signed by the person whose name appears therein as the sender thereof

it shall in such case be presumed, until proved to the contrary, that the same was sent and signed by the person by whom it purports to have been sent and signed, and at the date, and from the place, and to the person mentioned therein respectively

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 44 is a single cohesive evidentiary rule: a notice precondition tightly coupled to the resulting prima facie evidence and presumption, forming one recall task.

rows.heading: Secondary evidence, prima facie evidence, agreed upon meaning
rows.groupTitle: Agreed-upon meaning of figures and words in telegraph messages
rows.groupReason: A construction rule governing how coded or abbreviated language is interpreted in telegraph messages for evidentiary purposes.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how figures, words, or phrases carrying an agreed-upon meaning between sender and receiver are treated in a telegraph message under sections 43–45.

evidenceText: such signature, address or writing shall, for the purposes of this and the last preceding two sections, be taken to be the word, number, name, phrase or sentence so agreed upon and recognized between the sender and receiver

rows.sourceMapReason: The three subsections address independently recallable evidentiary rules with distinct triggers and legal effects: admissibility mechanics (45(1)), an evidentiary presumption (45(2)), and an interpretive construction rule (45(3)).

rows.heading: Secondary evidence, prima facie evidence, agreed upon meaning
rows.groupTitle: Prima facie evidence of telegraph transmission and receipt
rows.groupReason: Establishes a specific evidentiary presumption triggered by proof of delivery at a telegraph office.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the prima facie evidentiary effect of proving that a telegraph message was delivered at a telegraph office and received thereat for transmission.

evidenceText: shall be prima facie evidence that the same was transmitted in due course, and received by the person to whom it was addressed

rows.sourceMapReason: The three subsections address independently recallable evidentiary rules with distinct triggers and legal effects: admissibility mechanics (45(1)), an evidentiary presumption (45(2)), and an interpretive construction rule (45(3)).

rows.heading: Secondary evidence, prima facie evidence, agreed upon meaning
rows.groupTitle: Secondary evidence of telegraph message sent to opposite party
rows.groupReason: Covers the notice-to-produce condition, the secondary-evidence fallback when the message is not produced, and the original-document status when it is.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the conditions under which a party may give secondary evidence of a telegraph message sent to the opposite party and the evidentiary status if the message is produced under notice.

evidenceText: such party may give secondary evidence thereof
it shall, if otherwise admissible, be received in evidence the same as an original document

rows.sourceMapReason: The three subsections address independently recallable evidentiary rules with distinct triggers and legal effects: admissibility mechanics (45(1)), an evidentiary presumption (45(2)), and an interpretive construction rule (45(3)).

rows.heading: Book or record in bank
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility and conditions for bank book or record entries
rows.groupReason: The prima facie evidentiary rule and its four admission conditions form one tightly coupled recall unit: the rule is inoperative without the conditions, and the conditions specify the proof mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the prima facie evidentiary effect of a copy of a bank book or record entry and the four conditions that must be proved for its admission, including who may give proof and the permissible forms of proof.

evidenceText: a copy of an entry in any book or record kept in a bank shall in all actions be received as prima facie evidence of such entry and of the matters, transactions and accounts therein recorded

the book or record was at the time of the making of the entry one of the ordinary books or records of the bank and that the entry was made in the usual and ordinary course of business, and that the book or record is in the custody or control of the bank and that such copy is a true copy thereof, which proof may be given by the manager or accountant of the bank and may be given orally or by affidavit

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 46 contains four distinct recall tasks with different actors, modalities, and procedural stages: the core admissibility rule with its conditions, a separate protection for bank officers, an inspection-order mechanism with its notice requirement, and a standalone costs rule.

rows.heading: Book or record in bank
rows.groupTitle: Costs of applications under section 46
rows.groupReason: A standalone costs rule with a specific bank-default carve-out and a distinct enforcement mechanism (enforceable as if the bank were a party), separately recallable from the substantive evidentiary and procedural rules.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the court's discretion over costs of section 46 applications, the specific condition under which a bank may be ordered to pay those costs, and the enforcement mechanism available against a bank.

evidenceText: The costs of an application to a court or judge under or for the purposes of this section, and the costs of anything done or to be done under an order of a court or judge made under or for the purposes of this section, shall be in the discretion of the court or judge, who may order the same or any part thereof to be paid to any party by the bank, where the same has been occasioned by any default or delay on the part of the bank, and any such order against a bank may be enforced as if the bank were a party to the proceeding

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 46 contains four distinct recall tasks with different actors, modalities, and procedural stages: the core admissibility rule with its conditions, a separate protection for bank officers, an inspection-order mechanism with its notice requirement, and a standalone costs rule.

rows.heading: Book or record in bank
rows.groupTitle: Court-ordered inspection of bank records and notice requirement
rows.groupReason: The court's inspection power and its attendant notice requirement form one procedural mechanism: the notice rule operates only in connection with the inspection application and is needed to recall the full procedure.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the court or judge's power to order inspection and copying of bank entries on a party's application, and the two-tier notice requirement (two clear days to the account holder, or to the bank where service on the account holder is not possible).

evidenceText: On the application of any party to an action a court or judge may order that such party be at liberty to inspect and take copies of any entries in the books or records of a bank for any of the purposes of such proceedings

Notice of an application under subsection (4) shall be served upon the person whose account is to be inspected at least two clear days before the hearing of the application; if it is shown to the satisfaction of the court or judge that such service cannot be effected, then such notice shall be served upon the bank

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 46 contains four distinct recall tasks with different actors, modalities, and procedural stages: the core admissibility rule with its conditions, a separate protection for bank officers, an inspection-order mechanism with its notice requirement, and a standalone costs rule.

rows.heading: Book or record in bank
rows.groupTitle: Protection of bank officers from compulsion
rows.groupReason: A distinct protection rule with a different actor (bank officer), a different legal modality (immunity from compulsion), and a specific exception (court order for special cause), separately recallable from the admissibility rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when a bank officer is protected from being compellable to produce bank books or records or to appear as a witness, and identify the sole exception to that protection.

evidenceText: An officer of a bank shall not in any legal proceeding to which the bank is not a party be compellable to produce any book or record the contents of which can be proved under this section, or to appear as a witness to prove the matters, transactions and accounts therein recorded unless by order of a court or judge made for special cause

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 46 contains four distinct recall tasks with different actors, modalities, and procedural stages: the core admissibility rule with its conditions, a separate protection for bank officers, an inspection-order mechanism with its notice requirement, and a standalone costs rule.

rows.heading: Microfilms
rows.groupTitle: Premature Destruction Limitation and Government Exception
rows.groupReason: The six-year destruction limitation, its two triggering dates, the court's discretionary refusal power, and the government/Bank of Canada carve-out form a tightly interdependent rule-and-exception unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the six-year premature-destruction rule, identify the two triggering dates (whichever is later), the court's power to refuse admission, and the exception for prints tendered or made by a government or the Bank of Canada.

evidenceText: the court may refuse to admit in evidence under this section a print from a photograph film of the object
Where the photographic print is tendered or made by a government or the Bank of Canada, subsection (3) does not apply

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 47 contains three independently recallable concepts: the core admissibility conditions for photographic prints, the premature-destruction limitation with its government exception, and the separate proof-of-compliance mechanism. Each creates a distinct recall task.

rows.heading: Microfilms
rows.groupTitle: Microfilm Admissibility: Qualifying Documents and Conditions
rows.groupReason: Definitions of person and photographic film are integral to the core rule stating which documents qualify and the established-practice condition for admissibility.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the types of documents that may be photographed, the established-practice and permanent-record conditions, and the evidentiary effect of a photographic print under s. 47(2).
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 47 contains three independently recallable concepts: the core admissibility conditions for photographic prints, the premature-destruction limitation with its government exception, and the separate proof-of-compliance mechanism. Each creates a distinct recall task.

rows.heading: Microfilms
rows.groupTitle: Proof of Compliance with Microfilm Conditions
rows.groupReason: The mechanism for proving compliance (any person with knowledge, orally or by affidavit, notarial copy substitution) is a distinct procedural recall task from the substantive admissibility conditions.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who may give proof of compliance with s. 47 conditions, the permissible forms of proof (oral or notarial affidavit), and the admissibility of a notarial copy in lieu of the original affidavit.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 47 contains three independently recallable concepts: the core admissibility conditions for photographic prints, the premature-destruction limitation with its government exception, and the separate proof-of-compliance mechanism. Each creates a distinct recall task.

rows.heading: Document copied and stored electronically
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility of printouts from electronically copied documents
rows.groupReason: Subsections 1–3 form one interdependent rule: the local definitions, the admissibility trigger, and the three mandatory conditions that must all be met before a printout is admissible.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three conditions (electronic imaging in established practice, destruction of the original after copying, and true-copy status) that must all be satisfied for a printout of an electronically copied document to be admissible in evidence.

evidenceText: a printout of the document generated by or produced from a computer record or other electronic medium is admissible in evidence in all cases and for all purposes for which the original document would have been admissible.
A printout described in subsection (2) is not admissible in evidence unless
the original document was destroyed after being copied and recorded or stored in accordance with paragraph (a), and
the printout is a true copy of the original document.

rows.sourceMapReason: The section contains a substantive admissibility rule with three conditions (subs 1–3) and a separate proof-of-compliance mechanism (sub 4) that create distinct recall tasks: the conditions for admissibility versus the method and form of proving compliance.

rows.heading: Document copied and stored electronically
rows.groupTitle: Proof of compliance with electronic copying requirements
rows.groupReason: Subsection 4 is a distinct procedural mechanism specifying who may give proof, in what form, and the admissibility of a notarial copy, creating a separate recall task from the underlying admissibility rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who may give proof of compliance with the electronic copying requirements, the acceptable forms of that proof (oral or affidavit sworn before a notary public), and the rule on admissibility of a notarial copy of the affidavit.

evidenceText: Proof of compliance with the requirements of this section may be given by any person who has knowledge, or who has informed himself or herself, of the facts, either orally or by affidavit sworn before a notary public, and unless the court otherwise orders, a notarial copy of any such affidavit is admissible in evidence in lieu of the original affidavit.

rows.sourceMapReason: The section contains a substantive admissibility rule with three conditions (subs 1–3) and a separate proof-of-compliance mechanism (sub 4) that create distinct recall tasks: the conditions for admissibility versus the method and form of proving compliance.

rows.heading: Document created in electronic form and stored electronically
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility of printouts from electronically created documents (s. 47.2)
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(3) jointly state when a printout is admissible, the two mandatory conditions, and the proof method; they answer one integrated recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a printout of an electronically created and stored document is admissible in evidence and identify who may give proof of compliance and in what form.

evidenceText: a printout of the document generated by or produced from a computer record or other electronic medium is admissible in evidence in all cases and for all purposes for which the document would have been admissible had it been created in a tangible form
the contents of the document being tendered are as originally recorded and stored and have not been altered
Proof of compliance with the requirements of this section may be given by the author of the document or any other person who has knowledge

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 47.2 is a self-contained evidentiary rule: subsection (1) states the admissibility principle for printouts of electronically created documents, (2) sets the two mandatory conditions, and (3) provides the proof mechanism. Together they form one coherent recall unit answering 'when and how is a printout of an electronically created document admissible?'

rows.heading: Entries in books of accounts
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility and prima facie effect of deceased person's book entries
rows.groupReason: One coherent admissibility rule: trigger, handwriting proof, prima facie effect, and ordinary-course condition are mutually dependent.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the triggering context, handwriting-proof requirements, prima facie evidentiary effect, and ordinary-course-of-business condition for admitting a deceased person's book entries under s. 48.

evidenceText: where the rights or liabilities of the estate of a deceased person are in question, entries in the books of accounts of such deceased person are, on proof of their being in the handwriting of the deceased, or of a clerk who is shown to the satisfaction of the court to be dead or incapable of testifying by reason of insanity or imbecility, admissible in evidence, and shall be taken as prima facie proof of the correctness of the statements contained in such entries, if the court is satisfied on view of the same or otherwise, that they were made in the ordinary course of business.
