rows.sourceMapReason: Single self-contained evidentiary rule with interdependent trigger, authentication, evidentiary effect, and ordinary-course condition that form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Record or entry of act, condition or event
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility of Business Records (s. 49)
rows.groupReason: One admissibility rule whose conditions (regular course of business, identity, near-time) are interdependent and answer a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions the court must be satisfied of before admitting a record or entry made in the regular course of a business under section 49.

evidenceText: a record or entry of an act, condition or event made in the regular course of a business is, in so far as relevant, admissible as evidence of the matters stated therein if the court is satisfied as to its identity and that it was made at or near the time of the act, condition or event.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single self-contained evidentiary admissibility rule with three interdependent satisfaction conditions forming one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Written report or finding of facts of expert
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility criteria for a written expert report
rows.groupReason: Subsection (1) sets the expert's qualification conditions, the report's content requirement, and the court's justice gate as one admissibility rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the qualifications the preparing expert must satisfy, the report's content requirement, and the court's substantial-injustice condition for admitting a written expert report under s. 50(1).

evidenceText: a written report or finding of facts prepared by an expert not being a party to the cause, nor an employee of a party, except for the purposes of making such report or finding, nor financially interested in the result of the controversy
if, in the opinion of the court, no substantial injustice will be done the opposite party

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 50 contains two independently recallable recall tasks: the substantive admissibility criteria in subsection (1) and the procedural pre-offer requirements plus adverse-party rights in subsections (2) and (3).

rows.heading: Written report or finding of facts of expert
rows.groupTitle: Pre-offer notice requirements and adverse-party protections
rows.groupReason: Subsections (2) and (3) together state the offering party's procedural duties (notice, copy, inspection, names) and the adverse party's cross-examination and unavailability rights, forming one procedural-protections unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the notice, copy, inspection, and naming obligations the offering party must satisfy before tendering the report, and the adverse party's right to cross-examine informants and the effect of an informant's unavailability.

evidenceText: the party offering it has given notice to the adverse party of his intention to offer it in evidence together with a copy of the report or finding
Any person who has furnished any information on which such report or finding is based may be called as a witness and cross-examined by the adverse party

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 50 contains two independently recallable recall tasks: the substantive admissibility criteria in subsection (1) and the procedural pre-offer requirements plus adverse-party rights in subsections (2) and (3).

rows.heading: Register of or declaration respecting ships
rows.groupTitle: Proof and presumptive effect of ship registers and certificates
rows.groupReason: Covers the three permitted methods of proof and the resulting presumptive-proof effect for ship registers and certificates of registry as one coherent evidentiary rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the three methods by which a British or Canadian ship register or declaration may be proved in court and identify the presumptive-proof effect attached to a produced register or certificate of registry.

evidenceText: may be proved in any court either by the production of the original, or by an examined copy thereof, or by a copy thereof purporting to be certified under the hand of the person having charge of the original
shall be received in evidence in any court as presumptive proof of all the matters contained or recited in such register

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 51 is a single, self-contained evidentiary rule specifying both the methods of proving ship registers and their presumptive-proof effect; the two parts are tightly interdependent and form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Proof of births, deaths and marriages
rows.groupTitle: Certified marriage, birth, and death records as prima facie evidence
rows.groupReason: Both subsections state the same rule that certified copies of civil vital-statistics records, certified by the appropriate registrar or custodial official, are prima facie evidence of the facts stated.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify which certified copies of marriage (52(1)) and birth or death (52(2)) records qualify as prima facie evidence in court and name the certifying authorities for each registration system.

evidenceText: shall be prima facie evidence in any court of the facts therein stated without proof of appointment or signature
shall be prima facie evidence in any court of law in this Province of the facts therein stated

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 52 groups two distinct evidentiary shortcuts: certified civil vital-statistics records (52(1)–(2)) and military death/service certificates (52(3)–(4)), which differ in certifying authority, legal-effect language, and subject matter.

rows.heading: Proof of births, deaths and marriages
rows.groupTitle: Military death and active-service certificates as prima facie proof
rows.groupReason: These subsections create a distinct evidentiary rule for military certificates, adding proof of the signatory's office, authority, and signature beyond what the civil-record provisions provide.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a National Defence Act death certificate (52(3)) or an armed-forces active-service certificate (52(4)) is prima facie proof of the stated fact and of the signatory's office, authority, and signature without further proof.

evidenceText: is prima facie proof for any purpose to which the authority of the Legislature of New Brunswick extends, that the person so named died on that date, and also the office, authority and signature of the person signing the certificate

is prima facie proof for any purpose to which the authority of the Legislature of New Brunswick extends that the person so named was on active service during that period, and also of the office, authority and signature of the person signing the certificate

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 52 groups two distinct evidentiary shortcuts: certified civil vital-statistics records (52(1)–(2)) and military death/service certificates (52(3)–(4)), which differ in certifying authority, legal-effect language, and subject matter.

rows.heading: Copies of foreign letters patent or certificate of incorporation
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility of certified foreign letters patent or certificates of incorporation
rows.groupReason: One coherent notarial-certification admissibility rule with a jurisdictional scope, a comparison requirement, a prima facie effect, and a King's Bench ten-day service condition that are mutually dependent.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the notarial certification requirements, the jurisdictions and document types covered, the prima facie evidentiary effect, and the ten-day pre-service condition in The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick for certified foreign letters patent or certificates of incorporation.

evidenceText: a certificate purporting to be that of a notary public, under his notarial seal of office, to the effect that the document to which it is attached is a true copy or transcript of any letters patent
such certificate is prima facie evidence that the letters patent, certificate of incorporation or other document so certified, is a true copy

a copy of such certified copy of letters patent, certificate of incorporation or other document, and of the certificate of such notary public, is served upon the attorney of the opposite party, at least ten days before the same is offered in evidence

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 53 is a single interlocking mechanism: notarial certification of foreign incorporation documents, their prima facie evidentiary effect, and a Court of King's Bench service condition. The elements are tightly interdependent and form one recallable admissibility rule.

rows.heading: Prima facie evidence of incorporation
rows.groupTitle: Prima facie evidence effect of certified incorporation documents
rows.groupReason: One evidentiary rule with two tightly linked objects of proof (due incorporation; right to sue/be sued by corporate name) flowing from the same certified document.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the evidentiary effect of a certified copy of letters patent, certificate of incorporation, or other incorporation document under section 54 and the two matters it constitutes prima facie evidence of.

evidenceText: is prima facie evidence of the due incorporation of the company, society, or association mentioned therein, and of its right to sue and be sued by its corporate name therein mentioned

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 54 states a single focused evidentiary rule: a certified copy of incorporation documents is prima facie evidence of due incorporation and the right to sue or be sued by corporate name. One coherent recall task, no internal split warranted.

rows.heading: Obtaining incorporation in place where document issued
rows.groupTitle: Prima facie evidence of mode of incorporation by document type
rows.groupReason: The no-need-to-prove shortcut and the prima facie evidence rule for mode of incorporation are interdependent halves of one evidentiary mechanism addressed in a single paragraph.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the evidentiary effect when a copy of letters patent or a certificate of incorporation is offered under sections 53–54: no separate proof of the local incorporation method is required, and the document is prima facie evidence of incorporation by the corresponding mode (letters patent or certificate of incorporation).

evidenceText: it is not necessary to prove whether in the place where such letters patent or certificate of incorporation was issued, incorporation is obtained by letters patent or by certificate of incorporation

the copy of letters patent, certificate of incorporation or other document as provided for and mentioned in the said section are prima facie evidence that incorporation is obtained, in the place where the same is issued, by letters patent if letters patent are offered in evidence, or by certificate of incorporation if a certificate of incorporation is offered in evidence

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 55 is a short, self-contained evidentiary rule stating that a copy of letters patent or certificate of incorporation offered under sections 53–54 is prima facie evidence of the mode of incorporation without requiring proof of local incorporation practice. It forms one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Contract by foreign corporation
rows.groupTitle: Proving contracts of a foreign corporation (s. 57)
rows.groupReason: One evidentiary rule with a single trigger, proof standard, mandatory admission effect, and override clause; recalling them separately would fragment a single mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the proof requirement for admitting a foreign corporation's contract into evidence in a New Brunswick court and the effect of that proof on the court's admission duty.

evidenceText: it is only necessary for the party seeking to prove the contract or engagement, or to put the same in evidence before the court, to prove that such contract or engagement has been duly signed or issued by the accredited agent or officer of such foreign corporation in this Province
the court before which the trial is had shall admit the same in evidence, and the same shall be considered as duly proved without any other evidence of the execution thereof
any law, usage or custom to the contrary notwithstanding

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 57 states one self-contained evidentiary rule: the simplified proof requirement and mandatory admission for contracts of a foreign corporation doing business in the Province, with an override clause. All elements (trigger, proof standard, effect, notwithstanding clause) are tightly interdependent and form a single recallable rule.

rows.heading: Bankruptcy proceedings in England
rows.groupTitle: Sufficiency of office copies of English bankruptcy proceedings
rows.groupReason: One operative evidentiary rule linking the trigger, document requirements, and legal effect into a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which office copies of English bankruptcy proceedings are deemed sufficient evidence in a provincial court without further proof.

evidenceText: the production of office copies of all or any such proceedings, purporting to be under the hands of the commissioner and registrar, and also professing to be under the seal of the Court of Bankruptcy for the district in which such bankrupt has been declared and adjudged bankrupt, shall in all cases be held and deemed to be sufficient evidence of the facts recited in such documents without any further proof of them

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 58 is a single, self-contained evidentiary rule: it states the trigger (need to prove English bankruptcy proceedings in a provincial court), the qualifying documents (office copies under the hands of the commissioner and registrar with the Court of Bankruptcy seal), and the legal effect (deemed sufficient evidence without further proof). These elements are tightly interdependent and form one recallable unit.

rows.heading: The London Gazette, as evidence of
rows.groupTitle: London Gazette as sufficient proof of bankruptcy proceedings
rows.groupReason: One evidentiary shortcut rule: the Gazette entry itself is sufficient proof, no further evidence required, conditioned on the Gazette purporting to be published by Royal authority.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when and how the London Gazette is received as sufficient proof of bankruptcy proceedings and the condition attached to its admissibility.

evidenceText: The London Gazette, purporting to be published by Royal authority, shall in all cases be received in evidence as sufficient proof of the proceedings in bankruptcy contained in such Gazette.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 59 is a single, self-contained evidentiary rule: the London Gazette, purporting to be published by Royal authority, is sufficient proof of bankruptcy proceedings contained in it, requiring no further evidence. One recall task, no internal splits.

rows.heading: Instruments registered in Scotland
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility of certified copies of Scottish Sheriff Court instruments
rows.groupReason: One coherent admissibility rule: qualifying Scottish instruments, the required form of the copy (officer's hand plus sheriff's seal), and the three affidavit authentication requirements form a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a copy of a deed, last will or testament, or other instrument registered in a Scottish Sheriff Court is admissible in a New Brunswick court, including who must issue the copy, what seal it must bear, and what the authenticating affidavit must establish.

evidenceText: a copy of such deed, last will or testament, or other instrument under the hand of the deputy sheriff, clerk of the county or other officer having the custody of the court books, and the seal of the sheriff, shall in all cases be admitted in evidence

if such copy is authenticated by affidavit that the same has been collated or compared with the original document, and is a true and correct copy thereof, and also that the seal affixed to such copy is the seal of the Sheriff Court, having the custody of the said original document

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 60 is a single, self-contained evidentiary rule specifying the admissibility conditions for copies of instruments registered in Scottish Sheriff Court books; the qualifying documents, required form of the copy, and affidavit requirements are interdependent parts of one admissibility test.

rows.heading: Quebec notarial documents
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility and notice requirement for Quebec notarial certified copies
rows.groupReason: Covers the qualifying document, its prima facie evidentiary effect (general and for marriage certificates), and the ten-day written notice precondition as one admissibility rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the evidentiary effect of a certified copy of a Quebec notarial act or instrument and the ten-day written notice to the adverse party required before it is admitted in evidence.

evidenceText: shall be received in evidence in all courts as prima facie evidence of the original, and of the due execution thereof as appears by such copy, and if such document is a certificate of a marriage in Quebec, such certified copy is prima facie evidence of such marriage

at least ten days notice in writing of the intention to offer the same in evidence, accompanied by a copy of such certified copy, shall be given to the adverse party, and the due service of which notice and copy being proved by affidavit or otherwise to the satisfaction of the court

rows.sourceMapReason: Single cohesive evidentiary rule: the prima facie evidentiary effect of certified Quebec notarial copies and their built-in ten-day notice precondition form one interdependent admissibility rule.

rows.heading: Statutes and public documents
rows.groupTitle: Prima facie evidence of Statutes and Ordinances
rows.groupReason: The scope, evidentiary effect, venues, and two alternative documentary modes form one recallable evidentiary rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two modes by which prima facie evidence of a Statute or Ordinance may be given in New Brunswick courts and the range of jurisdictions and time periods the provision covers.

evidenceText: whether such Statute or Ordinance was passed before or after the passing of the Constitution Act, 1867
by the production of what purports to be a copy of the official Gazette for Canada, or the province or territory, purporting to contain a copy of such Statute or Ordinance
purporting to be published or printed by or by the authority of the official or King's Printer for Canada or the province or territory

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 62 is a single, self-contained evidentiary rule: it states the scope (Statutes and Ordinances of Canada, the Province, other provinces, territories, before or after 1867), the effect (prima facie evidence), the venues (all courts of the Province), and two alternative documentary modes. The modes are alternatives within one rule and should be recalled together.

rows.heading: Proclamations, orders, regulations and appointments by a provincial government
rows.groupTitle: Prima facie evidence modes for provincial proclamations, orders, regulations, and appointments
rows.groupReason: 63(1) establishes a permissive evidentiary rule listing three distinct production modes for proving any of four types of provincial government instruments; a learner must recall who may issue the instrument and the three acceptable modes.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the issuing authorities and the three modes by which prima facie evidence of a provincial proclamation, order, regulation, or appointment may be given in court.

evidenceText: Prima facie evidence of any proclamation, order, regulation or appointment made or issued by a Lieutenant-Governor or a Lieutenant-Governor in Council of this or any other Province of Canada, or of any Territory of Canada, or other Chief Executive Officer or Administrator for the time being of the Government of the Province or Territory, or by or under the authority of any member of the Executive Council, being the head of any department of the Government of the Province or Territory, may be given in any court or tribunal
(a) by the production of a copy of the Official Gazette for the Province or Territory, purporting to contain a notice of such proclamation, order, regulation or appointment

(c) by the production of a copy or extract of such proclamation, order, regulation or appointment, certified to be a true copy by the clerk or assistant or acting clerk of the Executive Council, or by the head of any department of the Provincial Government or Territorial Government, or by his deputy or acting deputy, as the case may be.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 63 contains two distinct legal mechanisms: a permissive prima facie evidence rule with three specified modes (63(1)) and a mandatory judicial notice rule for proclamations bringing enactments into force (63(2)). They differ in modality, scope of instruments covered, and the actor bearing the obligation, making them independently recallable.

rows.heading: Proclamations, orders, regulations and appointments by a provincial government
rows.groupTitle: Judicial notice of Lieutenant-Governor proclamations bringing enactments into force
rows.groupReason: 63(2) imposes a mandatory judicial notice obligation on all courts and judges, a distinct legal mechanism from the permissive evidentiary rule in 63(1), limited to proclamations bringing an enactment or provision into force.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the mandatory judicial notice obligation that applies to all courts and judges in the Province when a Lieutenant-Governor proclaims an enactment or provision into force.

evidenceText: All proclamations made by the Lieutenant-Governor proclaiming an enactment or any provision thereof into force shall be judicially noticed by all courts and judges in the Province.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 63 contains two distinct legal mechanisms: a permissive prima facie evidence rule with three specified modes (63(1)) and a mandatory judicial notice rule for proclamations bringing enactments into force (63(2)). They differ in modality, scope of instruments covered, and the actor bearing the obligation, making them independently recallable.

rows.heading: Prima facie evidence
rows.groupTitle: Prima facie evidence of federal proclamations, orders, regulations and appointments
rows.groupReason: All four modes are alternative methods of proving the same category of federal instrument and must be recalled as a set to know what is available in practice.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the four modes by which prima facie evidence of a federal proclamation, order, regulation, or appointment may be given in New Brunswick courts and proceedings, and match the appropriate certification authority to the type of instrument.

evidenceText: Prima facie evidence of any proclamation, order, regulation or appointment, made or issued before or after the passing of this Act by the Governor-General, or by the Governor-General in Council, or other Chief Executive Officer, or Administrator for the time being of the Government of Canada, or by or under the authority of any Minister or head of any department of the Government of Canada, may be given in all courts in this Province
by production of a copy of the Canada Gazette, purporting to contain a notice of any such proclamation, order, regulation or appointment
of a copy or extract purporting to be certified to be a true copy thereof by the clerk, or assistant or acting clerk of the King's Privy Council for Canada

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 64 is a self-contained provision listing four alternative modes of giving prima facie evidence of federal instruments; the modes are interdependent alternatives answering one recall question.

rows.heading: Handwriting or official position, forma
rows.groupTitle: No Proof of Handwriting or Position for Certifiers Under the Act
rows.groupReason: Removes the proof burden on a party tendering a certified copy and sets the permissible form of that copy; both clauses answer the same recall question about what a court requires (or does not) for a certified copy under the Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what proof of the certifier's handwriting or official position is (or is not) required for a certified copy or extract of a proclamation, order, regulation, or appointment, and what forms the copy may take.

evidenceText: No proof is required of the handwriting or official position of any person certifying, in pursuance of this Act, to the truth of any copy of, or extract from any proclamation, order, regulation or appointment
any such copy or extract may be in print or in writing, or partly in print and partly in writing

rows.sourceMapReason: A single short operative rule: no separate proof of the certifier's handwriting or official position is required for copies certified under the Act, and the copy may be in print, writing, or both. One coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Official notices in the Canada Gazette, or Royal Gazette
rows.groupTitle: Prima facie evidence of official Gazette and legislative appendix publications
rows.groupReason: One coherent evidentiary rule covering two publication categories that share the same prima facie evidentiary effect, naturally recalled together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the categories of official publications covered by section 67 and state that they are prima facie evidence of the originals and of their contents.

evidenceText: All copies of official and other notices, advertisements and documents published or printed in the Canada Gazette or in The Royal Gazette, and all matters contained in the appendix to a volume of the Acts of the Legislature purporting to be published or printed by or by the authority of the King's Printer, are prima facie evidence of the originals, and of the contents thereof.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 67 is a single, self-contained evidentiary rule granting prima facie evidentiary status to official publications in the Canada Gazette, The Royal Gazette, and legislative appendices printed by the King's Printer.

rows.heading: Documents in possession of officers of Executive Council
rows.groupTitle: Privilege objection for documents in possession of Executive Council officers
rows.groupReason: The trigger (officer holding official documents while called as witness), the entitlement to object on privilege, and the equivalence to a personal objection are interdependent parts of one evidentiary rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a deputy head or other departmental officer may raise a privilege objection on behalf of a Member of the Executive Council or department head, and the legal effect of that objection.

evidenceText: he is entitled, acting herein by the direction and on behalf of the Member of the Executive Council or head of the department, to object to produce the documents on the ground that they are privileged

such objection may be taken by him in the same manner, and shall have the same effect, as if the Member of the Executive Council or head of the department were personally present and made the objection

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 68 is a single, self-contained evidentiary rule: a deputy head or departmental officer holding official documents may raise a privilege objection on behalf of the Member of the Executive Council or department head, with the same manner and effect as a personal objection. All elements are interdependent and form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Canadian or provincial government account books
rows.groupTitle: Prima facie evidence of government account book entries
rows.groupReason: The prima facie evidence rule and its three proving conditions are tightly interdependent; recalling them separately fragments one concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the evidentiary effect of a copy of a government account book entry and the three matters the department officer's oath or affidavit must prove.

evidenceText: a copy of any entry in any book of account kept in any department of the Government of Canada or of this Province shall be received as prima facie evidence of such entry, and of the matters, transactions and accounts therein recorded

proved by the oath or affidavit of an officer of such department that such book was, at the time of the making of the entry, one of the ordinary books kept in such department, that the entry was apparently, and as the deponent believes, made in the usual and ordinary course of business of such department, and that such copy is a true copy thereof

rows.sourceMapReason: One self-contained evidentiary rule: the prima facie evidence effect and its three proving conditions form a single recall unit.

rows.heading: Judicial notice
rows.groupTitle: Mandatory judicial notice of legislation
rows.groupReason: One recallable rule: the five categories subject to mandatory judicial notice and the in-section definition of Imperial Parliament that makes category (a) operable.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the five categories of legislation for which judicial notice is mandatory under s. 70(1) and state the s. 70(2) definition of 'Imperial Parliament'.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 70 states one mandatory evidentiary rule (courts shall take judicial notice of five categories of legislation) with a directly interdependent in-section definition; all five enumerated categories answer the same recall question.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Definitions for the State Documents Evidence Provisions (ss. 72–74)
rows.groupReason: All definitions in s. 71 are scoped to ss. 72–74 and jointly determine the scope of the state-documents evidence regime; they form one recall unit on what counts as a state document and how political entities are classified for evidentiary purposes.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the four categories of 'state document' under s. 71 and the political-entity taxonomy (dominion, British possession, foreign state, Imperial, federal, provincial) that determines which type of state document applies in ss. 72–74.

evidenceText: "state document" includes(document d'État)
"dominion" includes kingdom, empire, republic, commonwealth, state, province, territory, colony, possession, and protectorate

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 71 is a single scoped definitions section for sections 72–74, whose terms form one interdependent taxonomy of political entities and state-document categories; splitting them would fragment one definitional framework.

rows.heading: Imperial state document
rows.groupTitle: Modes of proving an Imperial state document
rows.groupReason: The five alternative proof modes (a)–(e) are parallel permissive options for the same evidentiary purpose and are best recalled as a single list.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the five alternative modes by which the existence and contents of an Imperial state document may be proved under section 72.

evidenceText: The existence and the whole or any part of the contents of an Imperial state document may be proved in any of the following modes:

by the production of a copy thereof purporting to be certified as a true copy by the minister or head, or by the deputy minister or deputy head, of any department of the Imperial Government or purporting to be an exemplification thereof under the Imperial Great Seal

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 72 is a self-contained evidentiary rule listing five parallel permissive modes for proving an Imperial state document; all five answer the same recall question and involve the same trigger and modality, so they form one StudyUnit.

rows.heading: Federal or provincial state document
rows.groupTitle: Modes of Proving a Federal or Provincial State Document
rows.groupReason: The three modes—gazette/Acts production, King's Printer production, and certified copy or Great Seal exemplification—are parallel alternatives for the same evidentiary purpose and should be recalled together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the three statutory modes by which the existence or contents of a federal or provincial state document may be proved, including the authorized certifying officers and the Great Seal exemplification path.

evidenceText: The existence and the whole or any part of the contents of any federal or provincial state document may be proved in any of the following modes

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 73 sets out three parallel alternative modes of proving a federal or provincial state document; all three answer the same recall question and form one coherent evidentiary rule.

rows.heading: State document of British possession or foreign state
rows.groupTitle: Modes of proof for state documents of a British possession or foreign state
rows.groupReason: Covers both the official-printing mode (a) and the certification or exemplification mode (b) as alternative proofs under one section.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the two modes by which the existence or contents of a state document of a British possession or foreign state may be proved under section 74, including the qualifying printers under mode (a) and the qualifying certifiers or seal authorities under mode (b).

evidenceText: The existence and the whole or any part of the contents of any state document of a British possession or foreign state may be proved in any of the following modes

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 74 sets out two alternative modes of proving state documents of a British possession or foreign state; the section is short and self-contained as one evidentiary rule.

rows.heading: Proof of signature, position or seal
rows.groupTitle: Evidentiary dispensation for certified copies under ss. 72–74
rows.groupReason: A single operative rule listing the specific facts dispensed from proof when tendering copies or extracts under ss. 72–74.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the specific items that do not need to be proved—certifying signature, official position, Great Seal or state seal, existence of the original, and custody—when a copy or extract is admissible under ss. 72, 73, or 74.

evidenceText: It is not necessary to prove the signature or official position of the person printing or certifying any copy or extract admissible in evidence under section 72, 73 or 74 or to prove the Great Seal or other state seal affixed thereto or to prove that the original document or the public records from which the copy or extract purports to be made in fact existed, or were deposited or kept in the custody of the person so certifying.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 75 is a self-contained evidentiary dispensation stating what need not be proved for copies or extracts admissible under ss. 72–74; one coherent rule with no natural split point.

rows.heading: Construction by judge of British, Colonial or foreign statutes
rows.groupTitle: Judge's Construction of British, Colonial, or Foreign Statutes
rows.groupReason: All three subsections form one two-tier procedural rule (mandatory vs. permissive judicial construction authority) plus a brief evidence-savings clause that is inseparable from the rule it preserves.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the legislatures for which a judge must decide a statutory construction question (s. 76(1)), those for which the judge may do so or express an opinion without misdirection (s. 76(2)), and the evidence-savings protection in s. 76(3).

evidenceText: the judge before whom such trial is pending shall decide such question in like manner as if the question had arisen under an Act of the Legislature of this Province
it shall not be deemed misdirection in the judge to express his opinion to the jury
No evidence in relation to the construction or meaning of any foreign, Canadian or colonial law, that would be heretofore admissible, shall be excluded by reason hereof.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short, coherent three-subsection procedural rule on how a judge handles statutory construction questions for non-New Brunswick legislation; the two-tier jurisdictional rule and the evidence-savings clause form one interdependent unit.

rows.heading: Judicial documents
rows.groupTitle: Proving judicial documents from other courts by authenticated copy
rows.groupReason: Subsection (1) defines the covered documents, the originating courts, and the two authentication alternatives; subsection (2) states the evidentiary effect that completes the rule. Together they answer how a judicial document from another court is proved by copy.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify which judicial documents from specified courts may be proved by authenticated copy, the two authentication methods (court seal or judge's signature with a no-seal statement), and the evidentiary effect that dispenses with proof of the seal, signature, or judicial character.

evidenceText:
the authenticated copy being admissible in evidence must either

(a)
be sealed with the seal of said British, foreign, Canadian, provincial or colonial court making, issuing or otherwise giving existence to any such judgment, decree, order or other judicial proceeding

the same shall respectively be admitted in evidence in every case in which the original document could have been received in evidence without proof of the seal, where a seal is attached, or of the truth of the statement attached thereto or thereon where no seal is attached, and without proof of the signature or the judicial character of the person purporting to have signed the statement where no seal is attached.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 77 establishes one coherent evidentiary procedure: which judicial documents from specified courts may be proved by copy, the two alternative authentication methods, and the resulting evidentiary effect. Subsections (1) and (2) are tightly interdependent and form a single recall task.

rows.heading: Oaths, affidavits, affirmations and statutory declarations
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility of out-of-province oath documents without further proof
rows.groupReason: Subsection (3) sets distinct formal-document requirements (signature, office shown, appropriate seal) under which an out-of-province oath document is admissible without further proof.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the formal document requirements (signature, office below signature, and applicable seal or stamp) and the resulting evidentiary consequence that dispels the need for further proof of signature, office, character, seal, or jurisdiction.

evidenceText: is admissible in evidence without proof of his signature or of his office or official character or of the seal or stamp and without proof that he was exercising his functions or had jurisdiction or authority in the place in which the oath, affidavit, affirmation or statutory declaration was administered, sworn, affirmed or made.

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsections (1) and (2) together state when an out-of-NB oath, affidavit, affirmation, or statutory declaration is valid, while subsection (3) states a separate evidentiary rule on admissibility without further proof.

rows.heading: Oaths, affidavits, affirmations and statutory declarations
rows.groupTitle: Validity of oaths and affidavits made outside New Brunswick
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) together define the full set of persons before whom an out-of-NB oath, affidavit, affirmation, or statutory declaration is valid and effectual.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the categories of persons before whom an oath, affidavit, affirmation, or statutory declaration made outside New Brunswick is valid and effectual as if made before a commissioner for taking affidavits within New Brunswick.
rows.sourceMapReason: Subsections (1) and (2) together state when an out-of-NB oath, affidavit, affirmation, or statutory declaration is valid, while subsection (3) states a separate evidentiary rule on admissibility without further proof.

rows.heading: Registered decrees of British, Canadian and New Brunswick Courts of Record
rows.groupTitle: Evidence of Registered Decrees of Courts of Record
rows.groupReason: One evidentiary rule covering the certification requirements and evidentiary effect for proving registered decrees by copy.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the certification requirements for putting a registered decree, decretal, or other order of a Court of Record in evidence by copy and the resulting evidentiary effect in any court action.

evidenceText: may be put in evidence by a party in any action in any court, and shall be received as evidence of such decree, decretal or other order and of the contents thereof

rows.sourceMapReason: Single-rule evidence provision stating how registered decrees of Courts of Record may be proved by certified copy; one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Copy of instrument as evidence
rows.groupTitle: Certified copy of registered instrument as evidence
rows.groupReason: One recall task: the scope, evidentiary effect, and all prerequisites (affidavit, ten-day notice, proof of service) for admitting a certified copy of a registered instrument in the absence of the original.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a certified copy of a registered instrument (other than a will) is admissible as evidence of its contents, including the required affidavit, ten-day written notice, and proof of service.

evidenceText: he may produce in evidence a copy of the registry of such instrument certified by the registrar of deeds for the county where the same is registered, which copy shall, in the absence of the original instrument, be received and allowed as evidence of the contents thereof

it shall appear to the court by affidavit that such original is not under the control of the party, and that he does not know where the same may be found, and at least ten days notice in writing shall be given to the adverse party, his attorney or agent

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 80 states one coherent evidentiary rule: a certified copy of a registered instrument (other than a will) is admissible in the absence of the original, subject to affidavit and ten-day notice prerequisites that operate as a single procedural gate.

rows.heading: Party out of the Province
rows.groupTitle: Substitute affidavit by agent or attorney when party is out of the Province
rows.groupReason: The provision states one mechanism: the agent or attorney's affidavit requirements, the service step, and the evidentiary effect form a single recall unit for the out-of-Province scenario.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions that allow an agent or attorney to make a substitute affidavit for a party out of the Province, the required affidavit contents, the service requirement, and the evidentiary effect under section 81.

evidenceText: his agent in the Province or attorney in the suit, may make an affidavit of the non-residence of such person, and that he, the agent or attorney, as the case may be, has not the possession of the original instrument and does not know where the same is or may be found

on service upon the adverse party, or his attorney or agent, of the copies of affidavit and notice, and upon the affidavit of such service, as required by section 80, such certified copy shall be received in evidence as fully and effectually as if the party had himself made the affidavit and given the notice required by section 80

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 81 is a self-contained procedural mechanism: when a party is out of the Province, the agent or attorney may substitute an affidavit meeting specified content requirements, and the certified copy is then admitted as if the party had acted. One coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Registered will or copy as evidence, costs
rows.groupTitle: Costs of certified copies under sections 80, 81, and 82
rows.groupReason: A distinct cost-allocation rule covering certified copies under sections 80, 81, and 82, separate from the evidentiary mechanism in s. 82(1).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that costs of certified copies under sections 80, 81, and 82, together with connected proceeding costs, are taxed and allowed to the party procuring them when costs are awarded against the other party.

evidenceText: The costs of the certified copies provided for by this section and sections 80 and 81 together with the costs of the proceedings therewith connected, shall be taxed and allowed to the party procuring such copies, in case costs are awarded to him against the other party in such suit or proceeding

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 82 contains a distinct evidentiary admissibility and notice rule (s. 82(1)) and a separate cost-allocation rule for certified copies (s. 82(2)); these answer different recall questions and involve different legal modalities.

rows.heading: Registered will or copy as evidence, costs
rows.groupTitle: Evidentiary admission and notice for registered wills and copies
rows.groupReason: The qualification, certified form, evidentiary effect, and ten-day notice precondition form one interdependent evidentiary procedure best recalled as a single unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall what qualifies for admission as a certified registry copy of a registered will, the evidentiary effect of that copy, and the ten-day written notice precondition with attached copy and proof of service.

evidenceText: he may produce in evidence a copy of such registry, certified by the registrar of deeds for the county where the same is registered, which copy shall be received and allowed as evidence of the contents of such will and prima facie of its validity and due execution

at least ten days notice in writing shall be given to the adverse party, or the attorney or agent of such adverse party, of the intention to offer the same in evidence, such notice to be accompanied by a copy of such certified copy, the due service thereof being proved by affidavit or otherwise to the satisfaction of the court

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 82 contains a distinct evidentiary admissibility and notice rule (s. 82(1)) and a separate cost-allocation rule for certified copies (s. 82(2)); these answer different recall questions and involve different legal modalities.

rows.heading: Application of sections 80, 81 and 82 to the Crown
rows.groupTitle: Application of registered-instrument evidence provisions to Crown proceedings
rows.groupReason: One operative rule: sections 80–82 extend to Crown proceedings, and the affidavit of loss may be made by the Crown's attorney or other officer.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State how sections 80, 81, and 82 apply to Crown actions or proceedings and identify who may make the required affidavit of loss on behalf of the Crown.

evidenceText: The provisions of sections 80, 81, and 82 apply to actions or proceedings by or on behalf of the Crown, and the affidavit of the loss of the conveyance or instrument required, may be made by the attorney or other officer acting on behalf of the Crown.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 83 is a short, self-contained extension rule stating that sections 80–82 apply to Crown proceedings and that the affidavit of loss may be made by the Crown's attorney or other officer. It forms one recallable concept distinct from the underlying provisions.

rows.heading: Certified copies
rows.groupTitle: Admissibility of Certified Copies of Registered Instruments
rows.groupReason: One rule with two alternative exceptions; recalling the restriction and exceptions together captures the full admissibility test for certified copies of registered instruments.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the general restriction on receiving a certified copy of the registry of an instrument or conveyance in evidence and the two alternative conditions under which it may be admitted under section 84.

evidenceText: No certified copy of the registry of any instrument or conveyance shall be received in evidence, otherwise than is provided by this Act or by the Registry Act, unless by the consent of parties, or unless it appears to the court at which the trial is had that the original instrument or, if there are duplicate instruments, one of such duplicate originals is in the possession of the adverse party, and not in the possession of the party offering such evidence, and that due notice has been given to produce the same.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 84 states a single self-contained evidence rule: a certified copy of the registry of an instrument or conveyance is inadmissible except as provided by this Act or the Registry Act, with two alternative exceptions (consent of parties; court finding the original in the adverse party's possession with due notice given). The restriction and both exceptions form one recall task.

rows.heading: Notices of sale
rows.groupTitle: Evidentiary proof of mortgage notices of sale
rows.groupReason: All four subsections form one interdependent evidentiary mechanism for proving a mortgage notice of sale, including its conditions and the POA extension.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the prima facie evidentiary effect of a duly registered mortgage notice of sale, the section 80 notice-and-affidavit precondition for offering a certified copy, the additional power-of-attorney proof requirement, and the exemption from proving the registrar's signature.

evidenceText: shall on production without further proof either of the signature to the notice or to the certificate of the proof or of the signature of the registrar, be received in all courts as prima facie evidence of the signing of the said notice
Where such notice of sale has been executed under a power of attorney, it is necessary to prove the execution and the due registry or filing of such power of attorney
The signature of the registrar to any certificate mentioned in this section need not be proved.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 85 is one coherent evidentiary rule: it sets the prima facie effect of a duly registered mortgage notice of sale, the section 80 notice precondition for certified copies, the additional power-of-attorney proof requirement, and the registrar signature exemption, all serving the single recall task of how to prove a mortgage sale notice in court.

rows.heading: Pre-Personal Property Security Act chattel security documents
rows.groupTitle: Evidentiary effect of certified copies of pre-PPSA chattel security documents
rows.groupReason: One coherent rule: the scope of covered documents, the certification requirement, and the resulting admissibility and proof effect form a single recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the evidentiary status and probative effect of a certified copy of a writing registered under the Assignment of Book Debts Act, the Bills of Sale Act, the Conditional Sales Act, the Corporation Securities Registration Act, or the Forest Products Loans Act before repeal of those Acts.

evidenceText: A copy of any writing registered under the Assignment of Book Debts Act, the Bills of Sale Act, the Conditional Sales Act, the Corporation Securities Registration Act or the Forest Products Loans Act before the repeal of those Acts, certified by the person in whose office the same is filed as a true copy, is receivable as evidence and is, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, proof of the execution and registration of the original and of all matters of which the original would be evidence.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 86 is a single, self-contained evidentiary rule governing the admissibility and probative effect of certified copies of chattel security documents registered under five specific Acts before their repeal. One recall task: what makes the copy admissible and what it proves.

rows.heading: Documents filed in Registry Office
rows.groupTitle: Evidentiary effect of registrar of deeds certified copy
rows.groupReason: One coherent evidentiary mechanism: the certified-copy requirement, its court-wide evidentiary effect on filing, and the date/time certification extension are interdependent and recalled together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a registrar of deeds certified copy is admissible as evidence of filing in all courts, and what a time or day statement in the certificate proves.

evidenceText: a writing purporting to be a true copy of such document, and to be certified by such registrar under his hand as having been filed in his office, and to be a true copy of the document so filed is, in all courts, evidence of the filing of such document
if such certificate certifies that such document was filed at any time, or on any day, it is evidence that the same was filed on the day or at the time so specified

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 87 is a self-contained evidentiary rule establishing the effect of a registrar of deeds certified copy and its time-certification extension; no split or combine is warranted.

rows.heading: Copy of by-law, rule or regulation
rows.groupTitle: Evidentiary effect of certified by-law or regulation copies
rows.groupReason: Single rule specifying who certifies, what the certificate must state, and the prima facie proof of passage, existence, and (conditionally) date for certified copies of local government by-laws, rules, and regulations.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the required certifying officer, the mandatory certificate content, the prima facie evidentiary effect on passage and existence, and the additional conditional effect when the certificate states the passage date.

evidenceText: certified by the Minister of Local Government or clerk of the local government, as the case may be, to have been compared with the original and to be a true copy, is without proof of the official character of the Minister or clerk, or of his or her handwriting, prima facie evidence in all courts of the passage and existence of the by-law, rule or regulation

if the certificate states the date on which the by-law, rule or regulation was passed, as shown by the original record, prima facie evidence that the by-law, rule or regulation was passed on the date certified

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 88 is one coherent evidentiary rule: it sets the certification requirement, identifies the certifying officer, states the prima facie effect (passage, existence, and conditionally date), and dispenses with proof of official character or handwriting. All elements serve a single recall task.

rows.heading: Copy of record book
rows.groupTitle: Prima facie evidence of county record book
rows.groupReason: One evidentiary shortcut rule with a clear trigger (Minister's certification), a clear effect (prima facie evidence of contents and due signing), and a clear source document (county record book under the Counties Act).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what document, certification, and evidentiary effect section 89 attaches to a certified copy of the county record book.

evidenceText: certified by the Minister of Local Government to be a true copy of such record book, or extract therefrom, is prima facie evidence in all courts of the contents of such record book
the book containing such entry was duly signed by the warden or chairman and secretary as provided by such Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 89 is a single, self-contained evidentiary rule: a Minister-of-Local-Government-certified copy of a county record book is prima facie evidence of its contents and of due signing. One recall task, no subsections, no distinct sub-rules to separate.

rows.heading: Proof of appointment of parish or county officer
rows.groupTitle: Certificate as sufficient proof of parish or county officer appointment
rows.groupReason: A learner should recall that a certificate under the hand of the Minister of Local Government stating the appointment, time, and manner is sufficient proof, and that it is admissible without proof of the Minister's signature or official character.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the certificate that constitutes sufficient proof of a parish or county officer's appointment and the admissibility rule that dispenses with proof of the Minister of Local Government's signature or official character.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 90 is a self-contained evidentiary rule: 90(1) specifies the certificate that constitutes sufficient proof of a parish or county officer's appointment, and 90(2) provides the admissibility shortcut for that same certificate. The two subsections are tightly interdependent and form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Seal of Mayor
rows.groupTitle: Authentication of Mayor's Acts by the Mayor's Seal
rows.groupReason: One recall task: what authentication suffices for a mayor's act under the local government's corporate seal, and what exception applies.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the seal of the mayor is sufficient authentication of the mayor's act done under the corporate seal of the local government for use as evidence in court, and that this does not extend to a corporate act.

evidenceText: the seal of the mayor is sufficient authentication of the act, unless the act is a corporate act

rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained evidentiary rule: the mayor's seal suffices to authenticate the mayor's non-corporate acts done under the local government's corporate seal, with a tightly coupled corporate-act exception.

rows.heading: Liability of joint contractor
rows.groupTitle: Liability of Representatives of a Deceased Joint Contractor
rows.groupReason: Single rule governing when a joint obligation may be pursued against a deceased co-contractor's estate as if joint and several, including the incorporated-entity limitation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when an interested party may bring action against the representatives of a deceased joint contractor, the joint-and-several character of that proceeding despite a surviving co-obligor, and the limitation for chartered-bank stockholders or incorporated-company members.

evidenceText: may proceed by action against the representatives of the deceased contractor or obligor, in the same manner as if the contract, obligation or promise had been joint and several

the property and effects of stockholders in chartered banks or the members of other incorporated companies, shall not be liable to a greater extent than they would have been if this section had not been passed

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent rule on suing representatives of a deceased joint contractor, with a scope clarification and a chartered-bank/incorporated-company limitation forming a single recallable concept.

rows.heading: Sale of realty by executor
rows.groupTitle: Executor's power to execute testamentary real-estate directions
rows.groupReason: The trigger (unappointed direction in a will), the operative grant (executor shall and may act), and the scope qualifier (same effect as if specifically appointed) are interdependent and form one recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which an executor named in a will may carry out a testamentary direction to sell, dispose of, appoint, mortgage, encumber, or lease real estate, and the scope of that power relative to a specific appointment.

evidenceText: Where there is in a will of a deceased person a direction, whether express or implied, to sell, dispose of, appoint, mortgage, encumber or lease any real estate, and no person is by the said will, or some codicil thereto, or otherwise by the testator appointed to execute and carry the same into effect, the executor, if any, named in the will, shall and may execute and carry into effect every such direction
in as full, large and ample a manner, and with the same legal effect as if the executor was appointed by the testator to execute and carry the same into effect

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 2 states one coherent rule: when a will contains a direction to deal with real estate and no other person is appointed, the named executor shall and may carry out that direction with full effect as if specifically appointed.

rows.heading: Sale of realty by administrator
rows.groupTitle: Administrator's exercise of executor's real-estate powers under a will
rows.groupReason: One rule with two preconditions (will-embedded power; granting of letters of administration with the will annexed) and one operative effect (grantee exercises the power with identical scope and legal effect).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two preconditions under which a grantee of letters of administration with the will annexed may exercise the executor's real-estate powers and state the scope and legal effect of that exercise.

evidenceText: letters of administration with the will annexed have been by The Probate Court of New Brunswick granted to any person, that person shall and may exercise every such power, and sell, dispose of, appoint, mortgage, encumber or lease the real estate, and any estate or interest therein, in as full, large and ample a manner, and with the same legal effect as the said executor might have done.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3 states one coherent rule: a grantee of letters of administration with the will annexed steps into the executor's real-estate powers under the will, with identical scope and legal effect. Single actor, single trigger, single modality.

rows.heading: Death of executor before testator
rows.groupTitle: Administrator's power to execute testamentary real-estate dispositions where executor dies before testator
rows.groupReason: One rule with trigger conditions (no appointee or pre-death executor; letters of administration granted) and a single legal effect (administrator executes with same force as a testator's appointee).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which an administrator with the will annexed may sell, dispose of, appoint, mortgage, encumber, or lease real estate under a testamentary power where no person is appointed or the executor dies before the testator, and the legal effect of that exercise.

evidenceText: no person is by the said will or otherwise by the testator appointed to execute the power, or in case the executor or other person appointed to execute the power dies before the testator, and letters of administration with the will annexed have been by The Probate Court of New Brunswick granted to any person, that person shall and may execute every such power

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 4 is a single coherent rule granting an administrator with the will annexed power to execute testamentary real-estate dispositions when no appointee exists or the executor dies before the testator. One recallable concept; no split warranted.

rows.heading: Liability of executors and administrators
rows.groupTitle: Liability standard for executors exercising sections 2–4 powers
rows.groupReason: One recall task: identify the actor, the triggering powers (ss. 2–4), the assets covered, and the two-prong standard (testator-appointed or law/Court-appointed) that sets the executor's or administrator's liability and duty level.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the liability and duty standard that applies to an executor or administrator with the will annexed when exercising the additional powers in sections 2, 3, and 4, including how the standard is measured when the testator did or did not appoint a specific person to execute those powers.

evidenceText: be subject to all the liabilities, and compellable to discharge all the duties of whatsoever kind, that, as respects the acts to be done by him under such powers, would have been imposed upon an executor or other person appointed by the testator to execute the same

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 5 is a single, tightly interdependent liability rule: it sets one standard of duties and liabilities for an executor or administrator exercising the statutory powers in sections 2, 3, and 4, measured against what would have been owed had the testator personally appointed the actor. No internal split is warranted.

rows.heading: Sale of realty to satisfy legacy
rows.groupTitle: Conditions, methods, and mortgage terms for raising money from charged realty
rows.groupReason: Prerequisites, permitted sale/mortgage methods, and mortgage-term discretion form one recallable operative power under section 6.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a devisee in trust may sell or mortgage charged real estate to satisfy a debt or legacy, the permitted methods, and the discretion over mortgage interest rate and repayment periods.

evidenceText: it shall be lawful for the said devisee in trust, notwithstanding any trusts actually declared by the testator, to raise such debts, legacy or money as aforesaid by a sale and absolute disposition by public auction or private contract of the said real estate, or any part thereof, or by a mortgage of the same, or partly in one mode and partly in the other

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 creates one coherent power—prerequisites, sale/mortgage methods, and mortgage-term discretion—for raising money from charged realty, naturally recalled as a single operative rule.

rows.heading: Powers of successors of executors and administrators
rows.groupTitle: Extension of section 6 powers to successors of the devisee in trust

evidenceText: The powers conferred by section 6 extend to every person in whom the estate devised is for the time being vested by survivorship, descent or devise, or to any person who may be appointed under any power in the will, or by The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick, or The Probate Court of New Brunswick, to succeed to the trusteeship vested in such devisee in trust as aforesaid.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 7 is a single, coherent rule extending the section 6 sale-and-mortgage powers to successors of the devisee in trust (by survivorship, descent, devise, or court appointment). It creates a distinct recall task: identifying the class of persons who hold the power after the original trusteeship changes hands.

rows.heading: Powers of executors to mortgage realty
rows.groupTitle: Executor power to sell or mortgage charged realty without a trust devise
rows.groupReason: Single operative rule: executors step into the devisee-in-trust raising power when no whole-estate trust devise exists, with a built-in limitation on the scope of the sale or mortgage.

evidenceText: the executors for the time being named in the will, if any, shall have the same or the like power of raising the said money as is hereinbefore vested in the devisee in trust of the said real estate
any sale or mortgage under this Act shall operate only on the estate and interest of the testator, and shall not render it unnecessary to get in any outstanding subsisting legal estate

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 8 grants executors a specific power (sell or mortgage charged real estate) under a defined condition (no trust devise of the whole estate) and attaches a scope limitation on the resulting sale or mortgage. These elements form one coherent rule with a single recall task: when and how executors exercise the raising power, and its limit to the testator's estate and interest.

rows.heading: Duty of inquiry by purchasers of realty from estate

evidenceText: Purchasers or mortgagees shall not be bound to inquire whether the powers conferred by sections 6, 7 and 8 or any of them have been duly and correctly exercised by the persons acting in virtue thereof.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative rule removing purchasers' and mortgagees' duty to inquire into the proper exercise of sections 6–8 powers; one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Application of sections 6 to 9

evidenceText: The provisions contained in sections 6 to 9 shall not extend to a devise to any person in fee or for the testator's whole estate and interest charged with debts or legacies, nor shall they affect the power of any such devisee or devisees to sell or mortgage as he or they may by law now do.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short exclusion provision stating when sections 6–9 do not apply (devises in fee or for the whole estate charged with debts or legacies) and preserving the devisee's existing sell/mortgage power; one coherent boundary concept.

rows.heading: Effect of contingent liabilities of estate

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions an executor must satisfy (satisfied accrued claims, set aside a sufficient fund for ascertained future sums, assigned the lease to a purchaser) to distribute the estate without personal liability for subsequent lease claims, and identify the lessor's preserved right to follow the assets to distributees.

evidenceText: he shall be at liberty to distribute the estate of the deceased to and amongst the parties entitled thereto respectively without appropriating any part, or further part, as the case may be, of the personal estate of the deceased to meet any future liability under the said lease

the executor so distributing the residuary estate shall not, after having assigned the said lease or agreement for a lease, and having where necessary set apart a sufficient fund as aforesaid, be personally liable in respect of any subsequent claim

Nothing herein contained shall prejudice the right of the lessor, or those claiming under him, to follow the assets of the deceased into the hands of the persons to or amongst whom the said assets may have been distributed

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 11 states one conditional rule (executor's protection from personal liability for future lease claims once accrued liabilities are satisfied, a sufficient fund is set aside, and the lease is assigned) directly coupled with a savings clause preserving the lessor's right to trace assets to distributees. The two subsections form a tightly interdependent rule-and-limitation pair best recalled together.

rows.heading: Liability of executor for contingent liabilities

evidenceText: he shall be at liberty to distribute the residuary estate of the deceased to and amongst the parties entitled thereto respectively, without appropriating any part, or further part, as the case may be, of the personal estate of the deceased to meet any future liability

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 12 states one coherent protection rule: conditions and relief for an executor dealing with chief rent or rent charge conveyances, plus the grantor's reserved right to follow assets as a directly dependent qualification.

rows.heading: Testator erroneously presumed dead

evidenceText: all acts done under the authority of the appointment or probate, shall, notwithstanding it may thereafter appear that the presumption of death was erroneous, be as valid and effectual as such acts would have been had the person been dead

the person erroneously presumed to be dead shall, subject to the provisions of sections 15 and 16, have the right to recover from the person acting as executor, any part of the estate remaining in his or her hands undistributed, and no more

be entitled to recover from any one who received any portion of his or her estate as one of his or her next of kin, or as a devisee, legatee or heir, or as the spouse of such person presumed dead, the portion so received, or the value thereof

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 states one coherent legal response to an erroneous presumption of death: validity of acts under the grant plus the limited recovery rights of the person erroneously presumed dead. rows.heading: Recovery of estates where later will discovered

evidenceText: all acts done under the authority of such will or grant of administration shall, notwithstanding it may afterwards appear that the deceased had left a will, or left a will that superseded that of which probate was granted or that was annexed to the said letters, or notwithstanding that it appears that the will admitted to probate or administration was not duly executed, or was for any reason invalid, be as valid and effectual

upon the revocation of the grant of probate or administration, the new personal representative of the deceased shall, subject to the provisions of sections 15 and 16 have the right to recover from the person acting as executor as aforesaid, any part of the estate remaining in his or her hands undistributed, and no more

shall, subject to the provisions of the Statutes of Limitations, be entitled to recover from any one who erroneously received any portion of the estate of the deceased as one of his or her next of kin, or as a devisee, legatee, or heir, or as the spouse of the deceased, the portion so received or the value thereof

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 14 states one coherent legal consequence when a later or valid will is discovered after a prior grant: prior acts remain valid, and the new personal representative has defined recovery rights subject to ss. 15–16 and the Statutes of Limitations.

rows.heading: Costs and expenses where later will discovered

evidenceText: An executor as referred to in sections 13 and 14 shall have the right to retain out of any amount remaining in his hands undistributed his proper costs and expenses in the administration of the estate.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 15 creates a single, specific right: an executor acting under a later-invalidated will or grant (per s. 13 or 14) may retain proper administration costs from undistributed estate funds. rows.heading: Fraud of executors

unless the thing so done was in pursuance of a contract for valuable consideration made before he was aware to the effect aforesaid

rows.sourceMapReason: A single fraud-and-awareness exception to executor protection under sections 13–15, with one prior-contract carve-out; all elements are interdependent and form one recallable rule.
