rows.groupReason: One coherent mechanism: the lessee's power to surrender by registration, the encumbrance-holder consent condition, and the vesting effect form a single recallable concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the consent requirements, the registration form, and the vesting effect of a registered surrender of lease under s. 28.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 28 is a short, tightly interdependent provision stating the surrender procedure, the additional encumbrance-consent condition, and the vesting effect; all three subsections answer one coherent recall task on surrendering a registered lease.

rows.heading: Registration of assignment
rows.groupTitle: Registration of assignments of registered instruments
rows.groupReason: The section states the assignment mechanism, the deemed-transferee rule for a mortgagee's charge, the vesting effects on the assignee, and the trusts exception as one procedure.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how a registered mortgage, lease, or debenture is assigned by registration, the rights and obligations that pass to the assignee, the deemed-transferee rule for a mortgagee's charge, and the trusts carve-out.
rows.sourceMapReason: All five subsections form one coherent assignment mechanism for registered instruments: the registration requirement, a deemed-transferee rule for a mortgagee's charge, the vesting effects, and the trusts carve-out.

rows.heading: Registration of caveat
rows.groupTitle: Registrar General examination and caveat withdrawal order
rows.groupReason: The Registrar General's examination, the two specific grounds for a withdrawal order, the appeal window, and the service requirement for that order form a distinct recall task centred on a different actor and trigger.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two grounds on which the Registrar General may order a caveat withdrawn, the appeal window, and the persons who must receive a copy of the withdrawal order.

evidenceText: Where in the opinion of the Registrar General a caveat forwarded to him pursuant to subsection (2) has been improperly registered in that the interest claimed thereunder is not an interest in land or should be registered in the form of an instrument that creates an interest or passes an estate in the land, he shall make an order directing the registrar, after the expiration of such time as the Registrar General shall specify in the order, unless an appeal is taken within that time, to withdraw the caveat from registration.

A copy of the order referred to in subsection (3) shall, when it is sent to the registrar, be given to the registered owner of the land and to any person having a registered estate or interest affected by the caveat and to the caveator or his solicitor who filed the caveat.

rows.sourceMapReason: The section pairs a registration permission with the registrar's immediate duties, then shifts to a different actor (Registrar General) with distinct examination grounds and a separate withdrawal-order procedure. These create independently recallable legal tasks.

rows.heading: Registration of caveat
rows.groupTitle: Caveat registration right and registrar's immediate duties
rows.groupReason: The registration right, form requirement, and the registrar's two immediate duties (notice and forwarding) all occur at the registration event and form one procedural recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who may register a caveat, the form requirement, and the registrar's two immediate duties upon registration.

evidenceText: Any person claiming to be interested in any registered land may register a caveat in prescribed form against the land.

the registrar shall forthwith (a) give a notice of the caveat to the registered owner of the land and to any person having a registered estate or interest therein affected by the caveat; and (b) subject to the regulations, forward the caveat to the Registrar General who shall thereupon examine the caveat and inquire into the interest claimed thereunder.

rows.sourceMapReason: The section pairs a registration permission with the registrar's immediate duties, then shifts to a different actor (Registrar General) with distinct examination grounds and a separate withdrawal-order procedure. These create independently recallable legal tasks.

rows.heading: Effect of registration
rows.groupTitle: Effect of caveat registration on land and registrar
rows.groupReason: 31(1) states both the limitation (no estate created or passed) and the registrar's duty to subject other registrations to the caveator's claim.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what a registered caveat does and does not create in the land, and the registrar's obligation regarding other instruments while the caveat remains in force and registered.

evidenceText: it shall not have the effect of creating any interest in or passing any estate in that land but, while it is registered and remains in force, the registrar shall not register any other instrument affecting the land described in the caveat except subject to the caveator's claim as stated in the caveat

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 31 contains two distinct legal concepts: the operative effect of caveat registration on the land and the registrar's duty (31(1)), and the separate mechanism for assigning a caveat (31(2)-(3)).

rows.heading: Effect of registration
rows.groupTitle: Assignment of a caveat
rows.groupReason: 31(2) grants the power to assign a caveat and 31(3) defines the effect of registered assignment on rights, powers, and obligations.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how a caveator may assign a caveat and what rights, powers, limitations, and obligations pass to the assignee upon registration of the assignment.

evidenceText: A caveator may assign his claim and rights under a caveat, and such assignment may be evidenced by the registration of an assignment in prescribed form.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 31 contains two distinct legal concepts: the operative effect of caveat registration on the land and the registrar's duty (31(1)), and the separate mechanism for assigning a caveat (31(2)-(3)).

rows.heading: Application by owner
rows.groupTitle: Court application for caveat removal
rows.groupReason: Covers the three applicant categories, the court's show-cause and ordering powers, and the proof-of-service requirement as one recallable procedure.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the persons who may apply to the court regarding a registered caveat, the court's show-cause and ordering powers upon such application, and the proof-of-service requirement on the caveator.

evidenceText: Upon application by the owner, by a person claiming an interest in the land against which a caveat is registered or by the registrar, the court may require the caveator to show cause why the caveat should not be removed from registration
the court may, upon proof that the caveator has been served and upon such evidence as it requires, make such order in respect of the caveat as it thinks fit

rows.sourceMapReason: Single short procedural rule: the applicants, the court's show-cause and ordering powers, and the proof-of-service requirement form one cohesive caveat-removal mechanism.

rows.heading: Notice of request to withdraw caveat
rows.groupTitle: Registrar's notice duty and 30-day caveat lapse
rows.groupReason: The written-request trigger, the registrar's prescribed-form notice duty, and the 30-day lapse-with-extension-exception form one tightly linked rule a learner must recall together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the registrar's duty to give prescribed-form notice to the caveator on a written withdrawal request and explain when the caveat ceases to be registered and what filing prevents lapse.

evidenceText: the registrar shall, on receipt of a request to have the caveat withdrawn from registration, in writing made by the owner or person claiming an interest in land affected by a caveat, give a notice in prescribed form to the caveator

A caveat ceases to be registered upon the expiration of thirty days from the giving of the notice pursuant to subsection (1), unless within that time the caveator files with the registrar a court order extending the period of registration of the caveat

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 33 contains two distinct procedural stages with different primary actors: the registrar's notice-and-lapse mechanism (33(1)–(2)) and the court extension procedure with its own expiration rule (33(3)–(4)). Each forms an independently recallable recall task for land-titles study.

rows.heading: Notice of request to withdraw caveat
rows.groupTitle: Court extension order and expiration of extended caveat period
rows.groupReason: The caveator's right to apply to court, the court's discretion on notice, and the separate lapse rule for the end of an extended period are a distinct procedural stage involving different actors from the registrar's notice duty.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the caveator's right to apply to court for an extending order, the notice the court may require, and the condition under which a caveat ceases at the end of an extended period.

evidenceText: The caveator may apply to the court for an order referred to in subsection (2), and the court may, on such notice as it considers proper to the owner and any other person the court considers should be given notice, make such order.
the caveat ceases to be registered at the expiration of the extended period set out in the order unless, before the expiration of the extended period, a further extending order is filed.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 33 contains two distinct procedural stages with different primary actors: the registrar's notice-and-lapse mechanism (33(1)–(2)) and the court extension procedure with its own expiration rule (33(3)–(4)). Each forms an independently recallable recall task for land-titles study.

rows.heading: Instrument to withdraw caveat
rows.groupTitle: Instrument to withdraw a registered caveat
rows.groupReason: One recall task: the form, registration location, and partial-withdrawal scope of the caveat withdrawal instrument.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the requirements for the instrument that withdraws a registered caveat, including that it must be in prescribed form, registered in the land titles office for the district, and may operate in whole or in part or as to all or any of the affected land.

evidenceText: A registered caveat may be withdrawn from registration in whole or in part or as to all or any of the land affected thereby by an instrument in prescribed form registered in the land titles office for the district in which the land is situated.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 34 is a single, self-contained procedural rule stating the instrument mechanism for withdrawing a registered caveat; it creates a distinct recall task separate from the notice process in s.33 or the remedies in s.35.

rows.heading: Action for damages, restraining order
rows.groupTitle: Damages action for wrongfully registered caveat
rows.groupReason: Creates a private right of action with enumerated grounds (wrongful, vexatious, unreasonable period, without reasonable cause) and a defined liable party.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the enumerated grounds for a damages action arising from a caveat registration and the party against whom the action lies.

evidenceText: Any person who has sustained damage or incurred costs or expenses by reason of a caveat having been registered, or having been allowed to remain registered, wrongfully or vexatiously or for an unreasonable period of time or without reasonable cause, has a cause of action therefor against the caveator or his personal representative.

rows.sourceMapReason: The two subsections create distinct recall tasks: a private cause of action for wrongfully registered caveats (35(1)) and a separate court power to restrain re-registration (35(2)). Different actors, modalities, and legal effects warrant separate StudyUnits.

rows.heading: Action for damages, restraining order
rows.groupTitle: Restraining order against re-registration of caveat
rows.groupReason: Grants the court a discretionary power to restrain re-registration in the same matter, triggered by specific court decisions on caveat proceedings.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the triggering court decisions (withdrawal/removal or refusal to extend a caveat) and the scope and parties bound by the restraining order.

evidenceText: Where the court orders the withdrawal or removal of a caveat or declines to extend the registration of a caveat, it may also grant an order restraining the caveator or any party to the application from registering another caveat in the same matter.

rows.sourceMapReason: The two subsections create distinct recall tasks: a private cause of action for wrongfully registered caveats (35(1)) and a separate court power to restrain re-registration (35(2)). Different actors, modalities, and legal effects warrant separate StudyUnits.

rows.heading: Registration of stop order to prohibit registration
rows.groupTitle: Stop order: grounds, effect, notice, and duration
rows.groupReason: The Registrar General's grounds for issuing a stop order, the prohibition on registration, the notice duty, and the duration rule are interdependent pieces of one operative rule a learner must recall together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the grounds on which the Registrar General may issue a stop order, the effect of a registered stop order on instrument registration (including the receipt carve-out), the registrar's notice duty, and the stop order's duration.

evidenceText: he may issue and register a stop order to prohibit the registration of any instrument affecting the land
the registrar shall forthwith give a notice of the stop order to the registered owner

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 36 establishes the stop order mechanism (grounds, power, effect, notice, duration) as one coherent rule in 36(1)–(3), while 36(4) creates a separate judicial review procedure with a different trigger, different actors, and a distinct court power.

rows.heading: Registration of stop order to prohibit registration
rows.groupTitle: Judicial review of refusal to withdraw a stop order
rows.groupReason: Section 36(4) creates a distinct judicial review procedure with a different trigger (refusal to withdraw), different applicants (owner or person claiming an interest), and a different court power (show cause, order as it thinks fit).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain who may apply to court, the trigger for review, and the court's powers when the Registrar General refuses upon request to withdraw a registered stop order.

evidenceText: the court may require the Registrar General to show cause why the stop order should not be withdrawn from registration and the court may upon such evidence as it requires make such order as it thinks fit

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 36 establishes the stop order mechanism (grounds, power, effect, notice, duration) as one coherent rule in 36(1)–(3), while 36(4) creates a separate judicial review procedure with a different trigger, different actors, and a distinct court power.

rows.heading: Registration of affidavit to prevent registration
rows.groupTitle: Affidavit to prevent registration: filing, effect, and release
rows.groupReason: 37(1) sets out one coherent mechanism: the registered owner's affidavit alleging special or unusual circumstances, the Registrar General's authorization, the prohibition on registering the instrument, and the two release conditions.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the requirements for filing an affidavit to prevent registration, its operative effect on the registrar, and the two conditions under which the prohibition is lifted.

evidenceText: the Registrar General may authorize the registration of the affidavit and while it is registered and remains in force the registrar shall not register the instrument referred to therein unless the deponent withdraws the affidavit or a court order has been filed with the registrar establishing the title of the claimant under the instrument

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 37 contains two independently recallable concepts: the filing mechanism, operative effect, and release conditions for an affidavit to prevent registration (37(1)), and a separate cause of action for wrongful or vexatious registration of the affidavit (37(2)). The actors, legal modalities, and recall tasks differ between the mechanism and the remedy.

rows.heading: Registration of affidavit to prevent registration
rows.groupTitle: Cause of action for wrongful affidavit registration
rows.groupReason: 37(2) creates a distinct remedial cause of action with its own grounds (wrongful, vexatious, without reasonable cause) and defendant (deponent or personal representative), separate from the registration mechanism in 37(1).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the grounds, the class of claimant, and the defendant for a cause of action arising from wrongful or vexatious registration of an affidavit to prevent registration.

evidenceText: Any person who has sustained damage or incurred costs or expenses by reason of an affidavit referred to in subsection (1) having been registered or having been allowed to remain registered, wrongfully or vexatiously or without reasonable cause, has a cause of action therefor against the deponent or his personal representative.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 37 contains two independently recallable concepts: the filing mechanism, operative effect, and release conditions for an affidavit to prevent registration (37(1)), and a separate cause of action for wrongful or vexatious registration of the affidavit (37(2)). The actors, legal modalities, and recall tasks differ between the mechanism and the remedy.

rows.heading: Registration of certificate of pending litigation
rows.groupTitle: Registration and removal of certificate of pending litigation
rows.groupReason: One recallable mechanism: what may be registered, by what instrument it may be removed, and the two specific grounds that trigger removal.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the requirements for registering a certificate of pending litigation against land and the two grounds on which it may be removed from registration.

evidenceText: A certificate of pending litigation in prescribed form may be registered against land described therein and may be removed from registration by the registration of a court order or a certificate of the clerk of the court for the judicial district in which the action was commenced
(a) has been discontinued; or (b) has been disposed of by a judgment in favour of the defendant and no appeal has been taken within the time limited for so doing.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 38 is a short, self-contained registration mechanism (register and remove a certificate of pending litigation) with tightly interdependent registration, removal, and ground provisions that form one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Registration of instrument severing or consolidating registered land
rows.groupTitle: Registrar's obligation to register severance or consolidation instruments
rows.groupReason: Single rule with two interdependent preconditions governing the registrar's registration duty for severance or consolidation instruments.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two conditions that must be satisfied before the registrar is obliged to register an instrument severing or consolidating registered land under the Land Titles Act.

evidenceText: The registrar is not obliged to register an instrument severing or consolidating registered land unless he is satisfied that the provisions of the Community Planning Act have been complied with, if it is applicable, and he is provided with such documentation as is necessary to enable him to register the instrument in accordance with this Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 39 states one clear registration precondition for severing or consolidating instruments, forming a single recallable rule.

rows.heading: Application to register memorial of judgment
rows.groupTitle: Grounds that do not invalidate a judgment registration application
rows.groupReason: Section 40(3) lists four enumerated variations in name, co-ownership, leasehold/life interest, and estate/personal-representative designation that do not render the application incomplete or in improper form.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Enumerate the specific name-spelling, co-registration, leasehold/life-interest, and estate/personal-representative circumstances under which an application to register a judgment is not defective.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 40 contains three independently recallable concepts: the filing procedure and registrar's duty, enumerated completeness safeguards, and a substantive non-severance rule for joint tenancies.

rows.heading: Application to register memorial of judgment
rows.groupTitle: Filing requirements for judgment registration and registrar's duty
rows.groupReason: Subsections 40(1), (4), (5), and (6) together define who files, the prescribed form, the annexed judgment copy, the multiple-parcel option, and the registrar's mandatory registration duty.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who must file an application to register a judgment against registered land, the required form and annex, the option to cover multiple parcels, and the registrar's duty to register when satisfied the application is in order.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 40 contains three independently recallable concepts: the filing procedure and registrar's duty, enumerated completeness safeguards, and a substantive non-severance rule for joint tenancies.

rows.heading: Application to register memorial of judgment
rows.groupTitle: Non-severance of joint tenancy by judgment registration
rows.groupReason: Section 40(2) states a substantive rule that registration of a judgment does not sever a joint tenancy, a distinct legal effect separate from the filing procedure.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that registration of a judgment against registered land does not have the effect of severing a joint tenancy.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 40 contains three independently recallable concepts: the filing procedure and registrar's duty, enumerated completeness safeguards, and a substantive non-severance rule for joint tenancies.

rows.heading: Effect of registration of memorial of judgment
rows.groupTitle: Effect of Registered Judgment on Debtor's Interest
rows.groupReason: States when and how a registered judgment binds the debtor's interest and cross-references the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the legal effect of a registered judgment on the judgment debtor's interest in registered land and identify the statute governing the specifics of that effect.

evidenceText: While a judgment is registered and remains in force it binds the interest of the judgment debtor who is an owner of the land or an estate or interest therein against which it is registered as provided in the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single short provision stating one operative rule: the binding effect of a registered judgment on the judgment debtor's interest in registered land.

rows.groupTitle: Registered judgment and joint tenancy on death before severance
rows.groupReason: The two subsections are mirror death scenarios in a joint tenancy that together define the complete rule on whether a registered judgment survives a co-tenant's death.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain whether a registered judgment binds the surviving joint tenant's interest when the judgment debtor dies before severance, and whether it binds the judgment debtor's interest when the other joint tenant dies before severance.

evidenceText: the judgment does not bind the interest that the surviving joint tenant holds in the land after the death of the judgment debtor
the judgment binds the interest that the judgment debtor holds in the land after the death of the other joint tenant

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 41.1 sets out a self-contained rule on the effect of a registered judgment in a joint tenancy upon death before severance, with two mirror scenarios producing opposite outcomes; both subsections form one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Notice of registration to owner
rows.groupTitle: Registrar's duty to notify owner upon judgment registration
rows.groupReason: Single operative duty: the registrar must promptly notify the affected landowner when a judgment is registered against their registered land.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when the registrar must give notice of a judgment registration and to whom the notice is directed.

evidenceText: Upon the registration of a judgment against registered land, the registrar shall forthwith give notice of such registration to the owner of the interest in the land against which it is registered.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 42 imposes a single, clear procedural duty on the registrar: give notice to the owner upon registration of a judgment against registered land. One actor, one trigger, one obligation — one recallable unit.

rows.heading: Notice to judgment creditor, cessation of registration, extension of registration period, registration of assignment
rows.groupTitle: Registration and effect of assignment of registered judgment
rows.groupReason: Subsections (7)-(8) together state both the registration requirement for an assignment and its legal effect (passing of the assignor's section 41 interest with corresponding limitations), forming one coherent concept distinct from the cessation/extension mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain that a registered judgment may be assigned in prescribed form, and that upon registration the assignor's section 41 interest passes to the assignee subject to the same limitations as if named in the original judgment.

evidenceText: The assignment of a judgment that has been registered may be registered if made in prescribed form

the interest of the assignor as set forth in section 41 with all rights, powers and privileges thereto appertaining passes to the assignee and the assignee thereupon is subject to the same limitations as if named in the original judgment to the extent of the interest assigned

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 43 covers three materially distinct recall tasks: the owner's notice-and-cessation procedure, the court extension mechanism, and the registration and effect of judgment assignment. Each involves different actors, triggers, and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Notice to judgment creditor, cessation of registration, extension of registration period, registration of assignment
rows.groupTitle: Extension of judgment registration period
rows.groupReason: Subsections (5)-(6) establish the creditor's application right, the court's power to grant extension on notice to the owner, and the further-extension mechanism, forming one distinct recall task from the initial cessation procedure.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State how a judgment creditor applies to the court to extend registration, what notice the court must give, and how a further extension may be obtained before the original extended period expires.

evidenceText: A judgment creditor may apply to the court for an order referred to in subsection (4), and the court may, on notice to the owner of the interest in the land against which the judgment is registered, make such order

The registration period of a judgment that has been extended pursuant to subsections (4) and (5) may be further extended by an order of the court filed before the expiration of the original extended registration period

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 43 covers three materially distinct recall tasks: the owner's notice-and-cessation procedure, the court extension mechanism, and the registration and effect of judgment assignment. Each involves different actors, triggers, and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Notice to judgment creditor, cessation of registration, extension of registration period, registration of assignment
rows.groupTitle: Notice to judgment creditor and cessation of registration
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)-(4) form one interdependent procedural sequence: who may request, required affidavit grounds, registrar's duty to serve, and the 90-day cessation rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who may request notice to a judgment creditor, the affidavit grounds required (wrong debtor/trustee, or unenforceable/satisfied debt), the registrar's duty to serve, and the 90-day cessation trigger.

evidenceText: the registered owner or any person claiming an interest in the land against which a judgment is registered may, in writing, request the registrar to give to the judgment creditor a notice in prescribed form
the judgment debtor (i) is not the same person as the owner, or (ii) holds the land as trustee; or (b) the judgment debt (i) is not enforceable, or (ii) is satisfied
A judgment ceases to be registered upon the expiration of ninety days from the giving of the notice

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 43 covers three materially distinct recall tasks: the owner's notice-and-cessation procedure, the court extension mechanism, and the registration and effect of judgment assignment. Each involves different actors, triggers, and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Instrument withdrawing memorial of judgment
rows.groupTitle: Withdrawal of a Registered Judgment
rows.groupReason: The provision defines the mechanism, scope, and filing location for withdrawing a registered judgment; all elements answer one recall question.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the required instrument form, the permitted scope of withdrawal (whole or part, all or any affected land), and the correct land titles office at which the withdrawal instrument must be registered.

evidenceText: A registered judgment may be withdrawn or removed from registration in whole or in part or as to all or any land affected thereby by an instrument in prescribed form registered in the land titles office for the district in which the land is situated.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 44 states one self-contained procedural rule for withdrawing a registered judgment: the instrument requirement, scope of withdrawal, and filing location form a single recallable concept.

rows.heading: Action for damages against judgment creditor
rows.groupTitle: Action for damages against judgment creditor
rows.groupReason: The cause of action and its deeming criterion for wrongful registration are tightly interdependent and answer one recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the persons who may bring a cause of action for damages arising from a judgment registered wrongfully, vexatiously, or without reasonable cause, the parties against whom the action lies, and the specific deeming criterion in 45(2) concerning failure to take reasonable steps to ensure the judgment debtor is the registered owner.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 45 creates a single coherent cause of action for damages from wrongful judgment registration, with subsection (2) supplying the deeming criterion that directly qualifies subsection (1); the two subsections form one recallable legal rule.

rows.heading: Paramountcy of Act
rows.groupTitle: Paramountcy of the Land Titles Act over the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act
rows.groupReason: Establishes that the Land Titles Act governs judgment registration against registered land where it conflicts with the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify which statute applies when its judgment-registration provisions (sections 40–45) conflict with the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act.

evidenceText: Where there is a conflict between the provisions of the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act and section 40, 41, 42, 43, 44 or 45 of this Act, the provisions of this Act apply.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained paramountcy rule: the Land Titles Act prevails over the Enforcement of Money Judgments Act for sections 40–45. One clear recall task.

rows.heading: Registration or filing of power of attorney
rows.groupTitle: Proving execution of an instrument under a power of attorney
rows.groupReason: General rule/exception/carve-back structure governing statutory-declaration proof of execution under a POA, including the electronic-format exception and the paper-instrument carve-back in s.47(6).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when a statutory declaration is required to prove execution under a power of attorney, the electronic-format exception in s.47(5), and the paper-instrument carve-back preserving s.47(4) in s.47(6).

evidenceText: Where an instrument required to be registered is executed under a power of attorney, execution shall be proved by a statutory declaration in prescribed form.
A statutory declaration is not required to accompany an instrument in electronic format that is submitted for registration.

Notwithstanding that an electronic instrument is not required to be accompanied by a statutory declaration, subsection (4) applies to those instruments in paper format that a subscriber is required to have in his or her possession under paragraph 17.2(3)(a).

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 47 contains two distinct recall tasks: registering or filing a power of attorney and the registrar's recognition duty (s.47(1)–(3)), and proving execution of instruments under a POA with electronic-format exceptions (s.47(4)–(6)).

rows.heading: Registration or filing of power of attorney
rows.groupTitle: Registration or filing of a power of attorney and registrar recognition
rows.groupReason: Interdependent permission-and-effect structure: when a POA may be registered versus filed, and the registrar's duty to recognize it while in force.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a power of attorney may be registered or filed with the registrar and the registrar's duty to recognize it for its stated purpose while it remains in force.

evidenceText: A power of attorney that describes registered land by its approved parcel identifier may be registered as to that land.
A power of attorney that has been filed or registered shall be recognized by the registrar for the purpose for which it was executed while it remains in force.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 47 contains two distinct recall tasks: registering or filing a power of attorney and the registrar's recognition duty (s.47(1)–(3)), and proving execution of instruments under a POA with electronic-format exceptions (s.47(4)–(6)).

rows.heading: Registration of instrument containing conditions or covenants
rows.groupTitle: Private discharge of conditions and covenants
rows.groupReason: Private discharge by registration of a party-executed instrument is a separate mechanism from court discharge, involving different actors and a different trigger.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify that a condition or covenant may be discharged in whole or in part, as to the whole or any part of the affected land, by registration of an instrument executed by the parties entitled to enforce it.

evidenceText: A condition or covenant may be discharged in whole or in part as to the whole or any part of the land affected thereby by the registration of an instrument executed by the parties entitled to enforce the condition or covenant.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 48 contains three distinct recall tasks: registration permission with binding effect on successive owners (including court modification/discharge as a direct qualification), limits of what registration does not accomplish, and private discharge by the parties.

rows.heading: Registration of instrument containing conditions or covenants
rows.groupTitle: Registration of conditions and covenants: binding effect and court modification or discharge
rows.groupReason: The registration permission, the binding notice effect on successive owners, and the three court modification/discharge grounds are linked by a rule-and-exception structure in one subsection and form a single interdependent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that an instrument containing a condition or covenant may be registered on land being or already registered, that every successive owner is affected with notice and bound if it runs with the land, and that a court may modify or discharge it on three grounds: benefit to principally interested persons, conflict with a zoning by-law, official plan, or development scheme in the public interest, or offence against public policy or prohibition by law.

evidenceText: There may be registered, in respect of any land that is being or has been registered, an instrument containing a condition or covenant.

Every successive owner of the land is affected with notice of the condition or covenant and is bound thereby if it is of such nature as to run with the land, but any such condition or covenant may be modified or discharged by order of the court

the condition or covenant conflicts with the provisions of a zoning by-law, official plan or development scheme issued, made or established under the authority of an enactment and the modification or discharge is in the public interest
the condition or covenant offends public policy or is prohibited by law

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 48 contains three distinct recall tasks: registration permission with binding effect on successive owners (including court modification/discharge as a direct qualification), limits of what registration does not accomplish, and private discharge by the parties.

rows.heading: Registration of instrument containing conditions or covenants
rows.groupTitle: Limits of registration of conditions and covenants
rows.groupReason: Registration's two negative limits—no creation of running and no registrar determination—form a distinct recall task separate from what registration does accomplish.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that registration of a condition or covenant does not make it run with the land if its nature or expression would not otherwise annex it, and does not constitute a determination by the registrar of its essential nature or enforceability.

evidenceText: The registration of an instrument containing a condition or covenant intended to run with the land or annexed thereto does not
make the condition or covenant run with the land if, on account of its nature or of the manner in which it is expressed, it would not otherwise be annexed to or run with the land
constitute a determination by the registrar of its essential nature or enforceability

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 48 contains three distinct recall tasks: registration permission with binding effect on successive owners (including court modification/discharge as a direct qualification), limits of what registration does not accomplish, and private discharge by the parties.

rows.heading: Conditions and covenants in a transfer
rows.groupTitle: Numbering and reference of conditions and covenants in transfers
rows.groupReason: The three subsections form one procedural mechanism: number assignment by the Registrar General, designation of that number in a transfer, and the rule that a registered condition or covenant need not be repeated in subsequent transfers.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how the Registrar General assigns a number to a condition or covenant upon application, how an owner designates that number in a transfer, and the effect that a registered condition or covenant need not be repeated in any subsequent transfer.
rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained numbering mechanism for referencing conditions and covenants in transfers; all three subsections form one interdependent procedural rule.

rows.heading: Instrument evidencing expropriation of registered land
rows.groupTitle: Registrar's duty to receive expropriation instruments and power to request documentation
rows.groupReason: One actor (the registrar) performs one duty and exercises one power in the same expropriation-registration step; recalling them separately would fragment a single short procedural rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the registrar's duty to receive instruments evidencing expropriation of registered land under a federal or provincial enactment and the registrar's power to request further documentation to carry out the Act's intent and purpose.

evidenceText: The registrar shall receive instruments evidencing an expropriation of registered land pursuant to an enactment of Canada or the Province and he may request such further documentation as he determines necessary to carry out the intent and purpose of this Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 49 is a short, self-contained rule giving the registrar a duty to receive expropriation instruments and a discretionary power to request further documentation. The two elements share one actor, one triggering event, and one transactional moment, so they form a single coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Bankruptcy proceedings
rows.groupTitle: Owner's challenge to a bankruptcy registration and restoration of title
rows.groupReason: Provides the owner's written challenge mechanism, the supporting affidavit requirement, the 30-day cure period for the trustee, and the automatic restoration of the prior registered owner.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the steps an owner must take to challenge a bankruptcy registration, the affidavit content required, the 30-day period and its effect, and the consequence when the receiving order ceases to affect the land.

evidenceText: The owner may, in writing, request the registrar to give to the trustee a notice in prescribed form

a request under subsection (3) shall be accompanied by an affidavit of the owner or some person having knowledge of the facts to the effect that the bankrupt named in the receiving order or assignment is not the same person as the owner

the receiving order or assignment shall cease to affect the land upon the expiration of thirty days from the giving of the notice unless within that time the trustee files with the registrar a court order confirming that the bankrupt is the owner
the registrar shall register as owner the person who would have been the registered owner if the receiving order or assignment had not been registered

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 50 contains two independently recallable mechanisms: the registrar's registration-and-notice duties upon a bankruptcy filing (50(1)–(2)) and the owner's challenge procedure with its affidavit, 30-day window, and restoration rules (50(3)–(6)).

rows.heading: Bankruptcy proceedings
rows.groupTitle: Registration of a bankruptcy receiving order or assignment
rows.groupReason: Sets out the registrar's mandatory registration, notice, and interest-only scope duties when a trustee files a bankruptcy receiving order under s. 74 of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the registrar's registration and notice duties upon a bankruptcy receiving order and the rule that an interest-only registration is confined to that interest.

evidenceText: the registrar shall register the title to the land in the name of the trustee as such and forthwith give a notice of the registration to the owner of the land and to each owner of a registered interest or estate in the land affected by the registration
A receiving order or assignment that relates only to an interest in registered land shall be registered as to that interest

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 50 contains two independently recallable mechanisms: the registrar's registration-and-notice duties upon a bankruptcy filing (50(1)–(2)) and the owner's challenge procedure with its affidavit, 30-day window, and restoration rules (50(3)–(6)).

rows.heading: Tax sale proceedings
rows.groupTitle: Registrar's non-inquiry duty and title transfer in tax sale
rows.groupReason: Subsection (3) imposes a distinct limitation on the registrar (no duty to inquire into irregularities) and an affirmative duty to register title in the purchaser's name upon presentation of the tax sale deed or transfer.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the registrar's non-inquiry duty regarding tax sale irregularities and the obligation to register title in the purchaser's name upon presentation of the tax sale deed or transfer.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 51 covers two distinct procedural stages of tax sale registration: the certificate phase (registration and cancellation on redemption) and the final title-transfer phase with the registrar's non-inquiry protection. Different actors, triggers, and legal modalities justify separate recall units.

rows.heading: Tax sale proceedings
rows.groupTitle: Registration and redemption of tax sale certificate
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) form the certificate lifecycle: the purchaser's permission to register the certificate and the mandatory filing and cancellation on redemption.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the purchaser's right to register a certificate of tax sale and the redemption notice filing and cancellation duties when land is redeemed within the redemption period.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 51 covers two distinct procedural stages of tax sale registration: the certificate phase (registration and cancellation on redemption) and the final title-transfer phase with the registrar's non-inquiry protection. Different actors, triggers, and legal modalities justify separate recall units.

rows.heading: Registration of claimant as owner
rows.groupTitle: Registration of claimant as owner – filing and Registrar General order
rows.groupReason: Subsections 52(1) and (2) form one short filing-to-registration procedure with different actors (claimant, registrar, Registrar General) operating in a single sequence.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the triggering events, the claimant's filing duty, the registrar's forwarding duty, and the Registrar General's satisfaction criteria (appeal period expired and proper identification for judgments; legal entitlement for other documents) that together lead to a registration order.
rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent procedural mechanism: enumerated claim triggers, claimant filing duty, registrar forwarding, and Registrar General satisfaction criteria leading to a registration order.

rows.heading: Transmission on death
rows.groupTitle: Purchaser protection from a personal representative and Devolution of Estates Act exclusion
rows.groupReason: Subsections (6) and (8) together define the legal effects of transmission: the purchaser's right to clean title subject to registered encumbrances and the exclusion of the Devolution of Estates Act's devolution rules for registered land.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the rights of a good-faith purchaser for value from a personal representative (freed from the deceased's debts and claims, subject to registered encumbrances, no duty to apply purchase money) and the non-application of Devolution of Estates Act sections 18 and 19 to registered land.

evidenceText: A person purchasing real property in good faith and for value from the personal representative of a deceased registered owner in a manner authorized by this Act is entitled to hold it freed and discharged from any debts or liabilities of the deceased owner and from all claims of the persons beneficially entitled thereto
Sections 18 and 19 of the Devolution of Estates Act do not apply with respect to registered land.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 53 contains three distinct recall tasks: the transmission registration procedure, the registrar's duty to verify a personal representative's authority over any executed instrument, and the purchaser-protection regime with the Devolution of Estates Act exclusion.

rows.heading: Transmission on death
rows.groupTitle: Registrar's duty regarding instruments executed by a personal representative
rows.groupReason: Subsection (5) imposes a distinct refusal duty on the registrar for any instrument by a personal representative, broader in scope than the specific transmission application procedure.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the registrar's obligation to refuse registration of an instrument executed by a personal representative unless documents establishing the representative's right to act are provided, noting the caveat exception.

evidenceText: The registrar shall not register any instrument executed by the personal representative of a deceased registered owner, except a caveat, unless the instrument to be registered is accompanied by such other documents as are necessary to establish his right to execute such instrument.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 53 contains three distinct recall tasks: the transmission registration procedure, the registrar's duty to verify a personal representative's authority over any executed instrument, and the purchaser-protection regime with the Devolution of Estates Act exclusion.

rows.heading: Transmission on death
rows.groupTitle: Transmission registration on death: mechanism and procedure
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1), (2), (4), and (7) together state the rule, the application procedure, the partial-interest limitation, and the Registrar General approval gate as one registration mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State how title to registered land passes on death, the personal representative's application requirements, the partial-interest rule, and the Registrar General approval requirement.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 53 contains three distinct recall tasks: the transmission registration procedure, the registrar's duty to verify a personal representative's authority over any executed instrument, and the purchaser-protection regime with the Devolution of Estates Act exclusion.

rows.heading: Implied covenants in instruments
rows.groupTitle: Force, succession, joint and several liability, and pleading of implied covenants
rows.groupReason: Subsections (4)–(6) are general operational rules applying to all implied covenants under the section: their legal force and succession, joint and several binding of multiple executors, and the manner of pleading breach in an action.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the general legal effect of covenants declared to be implied in an instrument: their force as if set out at length (s. 54(4)), their joint and several operation when multiple persons execute as one party (s. 54(5)), and the manner of alleging them in a breach action (s. 54(6)).

evidenceText: shall, unless it is expressly negatived or modified in the instrument, have the same force and effect and be enforced in the same manner as if it had been set out at length in the instrument
shall be construed to bind the persons jointly and severally unless expressly stated to the contrary

the covenant alleged to be broken may be set forth and it is lawful to allege, in the same manner as if the covenant had been expressed in words in the instrument, that the party to the instrument did so covenant

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 54 contains distinct implied covenants with different actors, triggers, and legal effects (transferor's further-assurance covenant vs. transferee's mortgage-payment covenant), plus separate general rules on force, succession, joint and several liability, and pleading that form a coherent operational set.

rows.heading: Implied covenants in instruments
rows.groupTitle: Transferee's implied covenant to pay mortgage money and indemnify transferor
rows.groupReason: Different actor (transferee, not transferor), different trigger (transfer of land subject to a mortgage), and different content (payment and indemnification duty) make this an independently recallable covenant.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the implied covenant that attaches to a transferee of registered land subject to a mortgage under s. 54(3): the duty to pay the secured money at the rate and time specified and to indemnify and keep harmless the transferor from liability on the mortgage covenants.

evidenceText: there shall be implied a covenant by the transferee with the transferor that the transferee will pay the principal money, interest, annuity or rent charge secured by the mortgage at the rate and at the time specified in the mortgage and will indemnify and keep harmless the transferor

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 54 contains distinct implied covenants with different actors, triggers, and legal effects (transferor's further-assurance covenant vs. transferee's mortgage-payment covenant), plus separate general rules on force, succession, joint and several liability, and pleading that form a coherent operational set.

rows.heading: Implied covenants in instruments
rows.groupTitle: Transferor's and mortgagor's implied covenant of further assurance
rows.groupReason: Both subsections state the transferor's or mortgagor's implied covenant to execute further instruments, differing only in scope (all registered instruments vs. prescribed-form transfers and mortgages) and in express succession language.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the content and scope of the implied covenant of further assurance that attaches to a transferor or mortgagor in a registered instrument under s. 54(1) and s. 54(2). The source does not use the term 'further assurance' itself; it states the covenant to do acts and execute further instruments necessary to give effect to the instrument's covenants, conditions and purposes, extended in s. 54(2) to heirs, executors, administrators and assigns for transfers and mortgages in prescribed form.

evidenceText: there shall be implied a covenant by the transferor or mortgagor that he will do such acts and execute such instruments as, in accordance with this Act, are necessary to give effect to all covenants, conditions and purposes

the transferor or the mortgagor, his heirs, executors, administrators and assigns will do such other acts and execute such further instruments for further, better and more perfectly and absolutely transferring or mortgaging the said lands

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 54 contains distinct implied covenants with different actors, triggers, and legal effects (transferor's further-assurance covenant vs. transferee's mortgage-payment covenant), plus separate general rules on force, succession, joint and several liability, and pleading that form a coherent operational set.

rows.heading: Proof of execution
rows.groupTitle: Execution exceptions, Registrar General override, and electronic instrument paper rule
rows.groupReason: Subsections (5)–(7) create a distinct recall task: which instruments are categorically exempt, the Registrar General's case-by-case override power, and the special rule applying execution requirements to the paper format of electronic instruments.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: List the classes of instruments exempt from the execution requirements, identify the Registrar General's authority to direct registration notwithstanding those requirements, and state how subsections (1) and (2) apply to the paper format of electronic instruments.

evidenceText: The requirements of subsections (1) and (2) do not apply to a caveat, claim for lien under the Construction Remedies Act, judgment, order of the Registrar General, document issued by the Crown under an enactment of the Province, document issued pursuant to the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada), affidavit under section 37 or such class of instruments as may be prescribed
the Registrar General, upon being satisfied of the due execution of the instrument, may direct the registrar to register it
subsections (1) and (2) apply to those instruments in paper format that a subscriber is required to have in his or her possession under paragraph 17.2(3)(a)

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 55 contains two distinct recall tasks: the core execution/proof requirements (signing, witnessing, affidavit, oath administration) and the exceptions, Registrar General override, and electronic-instrument paper rule. These support separate recall prompts.

rows.heading: Proof of execution
rows.groupTitle: Instrument execution and proof of execution requirements
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(4) together answer how an instrument must be signed, witnessed, and proven, including who may administer the oath and the certificate form.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the signing and witnessing requirements for an individual and corporate instrument, the required accompanying affidavit or certificate of execution, and who may administer the oath for an affidavit of execution within or outside the Province.

evidenceText: signed by the parties required to sign it in the presence of one or more witnesses each of whom is at least sixteen years of age
shall be accompanied by an affidavit of execution, a certificate of execution or, in the case of a corporation, an affidavit of corporate execution
A certificate of execution shall be in prescribed form and shall be signed by a notary public and sealed with his notarial seal

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 55 contains two distinct recall tasks: the core execution/proof requirements (signing, witnessing, affidavit, oath administration) and the exceptions, Registrar General override, and electronic-instrument paper rule. These support separate recall prompts.

rows.heading: Address for service
rows.groupTitle: Address for service in the land titles system
rows.groupReason: All three subsections together define the complete address-for-service mechanism from initial filing through update to legal effect on service.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the address requirement for instruments presented to the registrar, the method a person may use to update a name or address, and the legal effect of the last address on file for service of notices under the Act.

evidenceText: shall contain an address of the applicant, transferee, mortgagee, lessee, assignee or claimant
A person may notify the registrar in writing of a change of his name or address
The last address of a person on file with the registrar is the address for service of all notices and documents given pursuant to this Act

rows.sourceMapReason: The three subsections form one unified address-for-service mechanism: filing requirement, update permission, and legal effect of the address on file.

rows.heading: Method of service
rows.groupTitle: Method of service for notices under the Land Titles Act
rows.groupReason: Both subsections together define the permissible service methods and the fallback, forming one procedural rule a practitioner must recall.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the permissible methods for serving a notice under the Land Titles Act and the fallback method when personal service cannot be effected.

evidenceText: shall be given by any method recognized as personal service for the purposes of the Rules of Court or, if such personal service cannot be effected, in the manner directed by the Registrar General

Unless otherwise provided by subsection (1), any notice or document required by this Act to be given to or by any person shall be given by any method recognized as personal service for the purposes of the Rules of Court or in the manner directed by the Registrar General

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 57 states a single coherent procedural rule: notices under the Act are served by personal service per the Rules of Court or as directed by the Registrar General, with a fallback when personal service fails. Both subsections are tightly interdependent (57(2) expressly defers to 57(1)) and form one recallable service method.

rows.heading: Registered land in trust
rows.groupTitle: Registration and disposition restrictions for registered land in trust
rows.groupReason: Subsections 58(1) and 58(2) together establish the required registration form for disclosed trusts and the disposition restriction that follows.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the registrar's registration requirement when an instrument discloses a trust and the condition that must be met before a disposition of land registered in trust may be registered.
rows.sourceMapReason: Two short, interdependent subsections forming one concept: how registered land in trust is recorded and the resulting restriction on dispositions.

rows.heading: Trust must be in accordance with Act
rows.groupTitle: Trusts not recorded on the title register
rows.groupReason: The prohibition on registering trust notices and the registrar's resulting duty to register the trustee as absolute owner form a single recallable rule about trust treatment in land registration.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the rule that no notice of trust may be entered on the title register and explain how the registrar must treat an instrument containing such a notice, including the trustee's registration status.

evidenceText: no memorandum, entry or record shall be made upon the title register of any notice of trust, whether express, implied or constructive
the registrar shall treat any instrument containing any such notice as if there were no trust and the trustee named therein shall be registered as the absolute and beneficial owner of the land

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 59 is a short, self-contained rule: trusts are not noted on the title register, and the registrar must treat the trustee as absolute and beneficial owner. The two subsections state a prohibition and its operational consequence as one interdependent rule.

rows.heading: Seals and consideration
rows.groupTitle: Seals and consideration for land titles instruments
rows.groupReason: The three subsections form one cohesive execution rule: the general permission (no seal or stated consideration needed), its legal effect (same as sealed), and the corporate exception, all answering one recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when a paper land titles instrument may be executed without seal or stated consideration, the legal effect such an instrument carries, and the separate requirement that a corporation affix its corporate seal when it has one.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 60 is a short, self-contained provision stating the general rule on seals and consideration, the legal effect of unsealed instruments, and the corporate-seal exception as one interdependent rule/exception structure.

rows.heading: Unregistered instrument or interest
rows.groupTitle: Registered land shut-out rule and fraud exception
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) together state the core rule that a dealing party need not inquire into registration circumstances and is not affected by notice of unregistered interests, with the fraud carve-out and the rule that mere knowledge is not imputed as fraud.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the registered-land shut-out rule: a person dealing with the owner is not bound to inquire into registration circumstances and is not affected by direct, implied, or constructive notice of unregistered instruments or interests, except in the case of fraud by that person, and mere knowledge of an unregistered interest is not of itself imputed as fraud.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 61 contains the general registered-land shut-out rule with its fraud limitation (61(1)–(2)) and a distinct PPSA-registration rule with its own fraud analysis (61(3)–(4)); these are independently recallable legal rules a learner would be tested on separately.

rows.heading: Unregistered instrument or interest
rows.groupTitle: PPSA registration effect on registered-land dealings
rows.groupReason: Subsections (3) and (4) create a distinct rule: PPSA registrations do not affect a dealing party in registered land (subject to s. 49 PPSA), and knowledge or constructive knowledge of a PPSA registration is not evidence of fraud under the general shut-out rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain that, subject to section 49 of the Personal Property Security Act, a registration in the Personal Property Registry does not affect a person dealing with registered land, and that knowledge or constructive knowledge of such a registration is not evidence of fraud for purposes of the general shut-out rule.

evidenceText: Subject to section 49 of the Personal Property Security Act, no person contracting or dealing with or taking or proposing to take a transfer of or an interest in registered land from the owner is affected by a registration in the Personal Property Registry whether or not that person has notice or knowledge of the registration.

The fact that a person referred to in subsection (3) has knowledge of a registration in the Personal Property Registry, or that that person could have obtained knowledge by searching the Personal Property Registry, is not evidence of fraud for the purposes of subsection (1).

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 61 contains the general registered-land shut-out rule with its fraud limitation (61(1)–(2)) and a distinct PPSA-registration rule with its own fraud analysis (61(3)–(4)); these are independently recallable legal rules a learner would be tested on separately.

rows.heading: Certificate of registered ownership
rows.groupTitle: Certificate of registered ownership: request, contents, and evidentiary effect
rows.groupReason: All three subsections describe the same instrument's availability, mandatory contents, and legal effect; recalling them separately would fragment one concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who may request a certificate of registered ownership, what it must contain, what it is subject to, and its evidentiary effect in courts and proceedings.

evidenceText: Any person may upon payment of the prescribed fee require the registrar to issue a certificate of registered ownership, in the prescribed form, in respect of any parcel of registered land.

Every certificate of registered ownership under this Act shall contain a statement of the registered owner's interest in the land referred to therein and is subject to the exceptions and reservations stated therein, overriding incidents and the provisions of this Act and the regulations.

Every certificate of registered ownership under this Act shall be evidence in all courts and in every proceeding of the particulars contained therein as of the date and at the time the certificate was issued.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 63 describes one instrument (certificate of registered ownership) across three tightly interdependent subsections: the request mechanism, required contents, and evidentiary effect. Together they form a single coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Instrument to state tenancy
rows.groupTitle: Requirement to state tenancy in co-ownership instruments
rows.groupReason: The mandatory statement requirement and the Property Act default are two sides of one co-ownership instrument rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that an instrument granting, transferring, conveying, or assigning land to two or more persons must state whether the grantees are intended to take as joint tenants or as tenants in common, and that if the instrument is silent the grantees take in accordance with the Property Act.

evidenceText: the instrument shall state whether the persons in whose favour it is executed are intended to take as joint tenants or as tenants in common
if the instrument does not so state the persons to whom the land, estate or interest is granted, transferred, conveyed or assigned take in accordance with the Property Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 64 states one tightly interdependent rule: instruments granting land to two or more persons must state the intended tenancy (joint or common), with a default to the Property Act if silent. The duty and its default consequence form a single recall task.

rows.heading: Survivorship in joint tenancy
rows.groupTitle: Survivorship registration for joint tenants under the Land Titles Act
rows.groupReason: Covers the trigger, the application and document requirements, and the registrar's registration duty as one coherent survivorship procedure.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a joint tenant's death triggers survivorship registration, the application and document requirements, and the registrar's obligation to register in the survivor's name.

evidenceText: Where two or more persons are registered owners as joint tenants of any land or interest therein and one of the owners dies, the registrar shall, upon the filing with him of an application in prescribed form accompanied by such other documents as are, in the opinion of the Registrar General, necessary, register the land or interest therein in the name of the survivor as owner.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 65 is a single, self-contained survivorship rule for registered joint tenancies: trigger (death of a joint tenant), procedure (application in prescribed form plus documents the Registrar General deems necessary), and the registrar's duty to register in the survivor's name. One recall task, no split warranted.

rows.heading: Entry of “No Survivorship”
rows.groupTitle: No Survivorship entry: creation and legal effect
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) together define what the entry is, the consent requirement, the threshold trigger, and the operative restriction on registered dispositions.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when a 'No Survivorship' entry may be made, the consent and threshold requirements, and the restriction it imposes on registered dispositions upon an owner's death or reduction below the specified number.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 66 contains two distinct recall tasks: the creation and meaning of the 'No Survivorship' entry (subs. 1–2, owner consent and effect) and the judge's separate procedural duties and powers when making the court order (sub. 3).

rows.heading: Entry of “No Survivorship”
rows.groupTitle: Judge's duties and powers in making No Survivorship orders
rows.groupReason: Subsection (3) assigns the judge a distinct procedural duty (notice and show-cause) and a separate power to order transfer or other protective measures when making the court order.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the judge's obligation to advertise notice and allow a show-cause period, and the powers to order transfer to new owners or make other just orders for protection of beneficially interested persons.

evidenceText: the judge shall, if considered requisite, cause notice of the application to be properly advertised, and in such a case appoint a period of time within which any person interested may show cause why the order should not be made

the judge may order the transfer of the land to any new owner or owners, solely or jointly, with or in the place of any existing owner or owners, or make such order in the premises as seems just for the protection of the persons beneficially interested

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 66 contains two distinct recall tasks: the creation and meaning of the 'No Survivorship' entry (subs. 1–2, owner consent and effect) and the judge's separate procedural duties and powers when making the court order (sub. 3).

rows.heading: Action of ejectment or recovery
rows.groupTitle: Recovery of registered land: prohibition and exceptions
rows.groupReason: The general no-action rule and its three exceptions (mortgagee, lessor, fraud victim) are inseparable for correct recall of when registered title may be challenged by recovery.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the general prohibition on actions of ejectment or recovery against a registered owner and identify each of the three statutory exceptions.

evidenceText: No action of ejectment or other action for the recovery of registered land shall lie against the owner under this Act, except in the case of
a mortgagee, as against a mortgagor in default;
a lessor, as against a lessee in default;

a person deprived of land by fraud, as against the person who through the fraud has been registered as owner, or as against a person deriving title otherwise than as a transferee bona fide for value from or through such owner through fraud.

rows.sourceMapReason: General prohibition on recovery actions against registered owners with three short, directly dependent exceptions forming a single coherent recall task on title security.

rows.heading: Cases where registrar may rectify
rows.groupTitle: Registrar's rectification power, enumerated grounds, and notice requirement
rows.groupReason: The two rectification pathways and the four specific grounds with their attached notice duty form a single independently recallable concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two pathways by which the registrar may rectify the title register, identify the four enumerated grounds, and describe the notice obligation that applies before rectifying under those grounds.

evidenceText: the registrar may rectify the title register in any case and at any time with the consent of all persons interested, as well as in the following cases

but in any case referred to in paragraph (a), (b), (c) or (d) the registrar shall first give notice of his intention to rectify the title register to all persons appearing to be interested or affected by such rectification.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 68 sets out the registrar's rectification power with two pathways (consent-based and four enumerated grounds) plus a mandatory notice step; these pieces form one coherent recall task on when and how the title register may be rectified.

rows.heading: Powers of registrar
rows.groupTitle: Registrar's powers to cancel entries and recall documents
rows.groupReason: Covers both corrective powers of the registrar: cancelling stale register entries and recalling, correcting, or cancelling erroneously issued documents.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the two situations in which the registrar may cancel a title-register entry or recall, correct, or cancel a document, including the specific error conditions and the regulatory condition on entry cancellation.

evidenceText: cancel any entry in the title register when he is satisfied that the entry has ceased to affect the title to the land to which the entry relates

recall a document issued by him if it has been issued in error, if it contains a clerical error or if an omission has been made therefrom, and may cause the necessary corrections to be made therein or cancel the document

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 69 grants the registrar two short, closely related corrective powers (cancel a title-register entry; recall/correct/cancel a document). Both are permissive powers of the same actor in the same register-maintenance context, forming one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Court order respecting rectification
rows.groupTitle: Court power to order rectification of the title register
rows.groupReason: The three cases in 70(1) enumerate the court's rectification power, and 70(2) adds the procedural cross-reference to section 79; together they form one recall task on when and how rectification may be ordered.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three cases in which the court may order rectification of the title register under section 70(1) and identify that the application must be made in the manner prescribed in section 79.

evidenceText: the court may make an order directing the registrar to rectify the title register in the following cases
has been obtained, made or omitted by fraud, wrongful act or mistake
An application to the court for an order directing the registrar to rectify the title register shall be made in the manner prescribed in section 79

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 70 states the court's power to order rectification in three enumerated cases and the procedural requirement to follow section 79, forming one coherent recall unit on rectification grounds and application procedure.

rows.heading: Rectification and registered owner in possession
rows.groupTitle: Protection of registered owner in possession against rectification
rows.groupReason: The general prohibition and its three enumerated exceptions (fault/knowledge, void disposition, and general injustice) are interdependent and answer one recall question: when may rectification affect a registered owner in possession.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the rule that the title register shall not be rectified to detrimentally affect a registered owner in possession and identify the three exceptions that permit rectification against such an owner.

evidenceText: The title register shall not be rectified so as to affect detrimentally the title of the registered owner who is in possession unless
such owner had knowledge of the omission, fraud or mistake in consequence of which the rectification is sought, or caused such omission, fraud or mistake or substantially contributed to it
the immediate disposition to him was void, or the disposition to the person through whom he claims otherwise than for valuable consideration was void
for any other reason, in any particular case it is considered that it would be unjust not to rectify the register against him

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 71 states a single protective rule (no rectification against a registered owner in possession) with three directly dependent exceptions, forming one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Notation of rectification
rows.groupTitle: Notation of rectification and its retroactive effect
