rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what the registrar must record in the title register upon rectification, what the registrar must not do to the erroneous entry, and from what time the register is deemed rectified.

evidenceText: he shall make a notation of the rectification and the date thereof in the title register in the prescribed manner but he shall not erase or remove any erroneous entry or memorandum from the title register
the title register shall be deemed to be and to have been rectified from the time

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 72 is a short, self-contained procedural rule: the registrar's notation duty and prohibition (72(1)) together with the retroactive deeming effect of the rectification (72(2)). The subsections are tightly interdependent and form one recallable concept—how a rectification is recorded and when it is deemed effective.

rows.heading: Indemnification on rectification
rows.groupTitle: Indemnification on rectification – entitlement, exceptions, and forged dispositions
rows.groupReason: The entitlement, six exceptions, and the forged-disposition deeming rule form one recallable indemnification framework; the exceptions directly modify the entitlement and the deeming rule operates only for the purposes of subsection (1).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the four categories of damage that trigger the right to indemnification, the six statutory exceptions to indemnification, and the deeming rule applying to a good faith purchaser under a forged disposition when the title register is rectified.

evidenceText: Any person who suffers damage by reason of the rectification of the title register, an error or omission in the title register which is not rectified, an error or omission in a certificate of registered ownership or the loss or destruction of any document lodged at a land titles office for inspection or safe custody is entitled to be indemnified

an owner of any registered land or encumbrance claiming in good faith and for valuable consideration under a forged disposition shall, where the title register is rectified, be deemed to have suffered damage by reason of such rectification

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 73 is a single coherent indemnification framework: one entitlement rule, six tightly interdependent exceptions, and a narrow deeming provision for forged dispositions, all operating under one heading.

rows.heading: Award of indemnity
rows.groupTitle: Award of indemnity: Registrar General determination, conditions, and court fallback
rows.groupReason: Both subsections form one coherent two-stage indemnity-award pathway (administrative determination then judicial fallback) that a learner should recall together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Registrar General's power to determine and award indemnity subject to Service New Brunswick approval and claimant consent, the separate expense award available whether or not a right of indemnity is found, and the claimant's right to apply to court where no award is made under subsection (1).

evidenceText: the Registrar General may determine whether or not a right of indemnity has arisen under this Act, and where he determines that such a right has arisen he may, with the approval of Service New Brunswick and with the consent of the claimant, award the claimant an amount as indemnity
the claimant may, whether or not he has made an application under subsection (1), apply to the court for an award of indemnity

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 74 is a short, self-contained procedural provision setting out the administrative and judicial pathways for obtaining an indemnity award under the Land Titles Act.

rows.heading: Payment
rows.groupTitle: Condition and timing of indemnity payment
rows.groupReason: One coherent rule: payment is triggered by an indemnity award and conditioned on the claimant executing an assignment of related enforcement rights to the Registrar General.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the condition the person being indemnified must satisfy (executing an assignment of related rights to the Registrar General) and the timing obligation (payment forthwith) before an indemnity award is paid.

evidenceText: it shall be paid forthwith to the person being indemnified upon such person executing in favour of the Registrar General an assignment of any rights which such person would have been entitled to enforce

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 75 is a short, self-contained procedural rule: an indemnity payment is owed forthwith once the claimant executes an assignment of related rights to the Registrar General. The trigger, obligation, and condition are tightly interdependent and form one recall task.

rows.heading: Recovery of payment from third parties
rows.groupTitle: Registrar General's recovery power after indemnity payment
rows.groupReason: One statutory power grant with a single trigger (indemnity paid) and actor (Registrar General); the recovery-from-at-fault-party and enforcement-of-rights components are joined alternatives within the same sentence and answer one recall question.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Registrar General's two recovery mechanisms available after an indemnity is paid under the Act: proceedings against a person who caused or substantially contributed to the damage by fraud or negligence, and enforcement of any express or implied agreement or other right the indemnified person would have held.

evidenceText: the Registrar General may take proceedings to recover the amount so paid from any person who has caused or substantially contributed to the damage by his fraud or negligence
to enforce any express or implied agreement or other right which the person who is indemnified would have been entitled to enforce

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 76 grants the Registrar General a single, coherent recovery power triggered by indemnity payment, with two closely joined components (recovery from at-fault third parties and enforcement of the indemnified person's rights) that form one recallable mechanism.

rows.heading: Agreements with respect to liability

rows.sourceMapReason: Single permissive power granting Service New Brunswick authority to enter liability-sharing agreements with the Law Society of New Brunswick or other persons regarding Registrar General indemnities under section 76.

rows.heading: Time of valuation

at the time when the error or omission that caused the damage was made, where the title register is not rectified
immediately before the time of rectification, where the title register is rectified

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 77 states a single coherent valuation rule for indemnity: a fair-market-value cap with two time points, plus a tightly linked good-faith improvements addition in the same calculation. One recall unit suffices.

rows.heading: Two year limitation period

evidenceText: Any application for indemnity under any provision of this Act shall be commenced within and not later than two years from the date that the applicant knew of the event that occasioned the damage.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 78 is a single, self-contained limitation period for indemnity applications under the Act; one recall task with no need to combine or split.

rows.heading: Application to court

rows.heading: Application to court

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 79 contains four distinct procedural stages with different recall tasks: the written-reasons right, the application and pre-application notice, limitations on the application, and the court's hearing powers.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 79 contains four distinct procedural stages with different recall tasks: the written-reasons right, the application and pre-application notice, limitations on the application, and the court's hearing powers.

rows.sourceMapReason: Two short subsections form one coherent conflict-resolution rule about this Act's statutory hierarchy relative to other public and private Acts; they are best recalled together as a single concept.

rows.heading: General limitation periods

rows.heading: Continuous act or omission

rows.heading: Application of Part 2

rows.heading: Judgments

rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain when an unauthorized disposition of a marital home may be set aside and how reliance on a verifying affidavit establishes good faith and lack of notice.

evidenceText: the disposition may be set aside on an application under section 22 unless the person holding the interest at the time of the application acquired it for value, in good faith and without notice that the property was at the time of the disposition a marital home

shall, unless the person to whom the disposition is made had actual notice to the contrary, be deemed to have acquired the property in good faith and without notice that it was at the time of the disposition a marital home

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19 contains two independently recallable concepts: the disposition prohibition with its five enumerated exceptions (s.19(1)) and the set-aside remedy with BFP protection and affidavit mechanism (ss.19(2)–(3)).

rows.heading: Spouses’ rights on disposition
rows.groupTitle: Division of marital home disposition proceeds and unequal-division factors
rows.groupReason: The default equal-division rule and the Court's unequal-division power with its six enumerated factors form one coherent rule/exception structure requiring joint recall.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the default one-half entitlement to net proceeds from disposition of a marital home and identify the six factors the Court weighs when ordering an unequal division under subsection (2).
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 20 contains a division rule with enumerated court factors, a separate trust obligation on a different actor, and short termination/deeming boundary provisions that form distinct recall tasks.

rows.heading: Spouses’ rights on disposition
rows.groupTitle: Termination of spouses' rights and deeming of expropriation
rows.groupReason: Both are short boundary provisions: 20(4) terminates the subsection (1)–(2) rights on ceasing to be a spouse, and 20(5) deems expropriation a disposition for this section.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when a spouse's subsection (1)–(2) rights terminate and that an expropriation of a marital home interest is deemed a disposition for the purposes of section 20.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 20 contains a division rule with enumerated court factors, a separate trust obligation on a different actor, and short termination/deeming boundary provisions that form distinct recall tasks.

rows.heading: Spouses’ rights on disposition
rows.groupTitle: Trust obligation on net proceeds held by a spouse or third party
rows.groupReason: The trust obligation binds a different actor (the holder, possibly a third party) and imposes a distinct legal mechanism (holding in trust) separate from the spouses' entitlement rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain that a spouse or other person holding net proceeds from disposition of a marital home holds them in trust to be divided per subsection (1), a subsection (2) order, or a domestic contract.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 20 contains a division rule with enumerated court factors, a separate trust obligation on a different actor, and short termination/deeming boundary provisions that form distinct recall tasks.

rows.heading: Spouses’ right to redemption or relief against forfeiture
rows.groupTitle: Spouse's right to redemption, relief against forfeiture, notice, and payment application (s. 21)
rows.groupReason: Both subsections create one spousal protection in enforcement or forfeiture proceedings: the substantive right and the operational rule for applying payments toward that right.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the rights a spouse with s. 18 possession holds in a proceeding to realize on a lien, encumbrance, execution, or forfeiture against a marital home, and how a redemption or relief payment made by that spouse must be applied.

evidenceText: the spouse who has a right of possession by virtue of section 18 has the same right to redemption or relief against forfeiture as the other spouse has and is entitled to any notice respecting the claim and its enforcement or realization to which the other spouse is entitled
the payment shall be applied in satisfaction of the claim giving rise to the lien, encumbrance, execution or forfeiture

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 21 grants a spouse with s. 18 possession a redemption/relief right and notice entitlement in enforcement proceedings, and s. 21(2) specifies how redemption payments are applied; the two subsections form one coherent spousal-protection mechanism that is independently recallable.

rows.heading: Application by spouse or interested party respecting marital home
rows.groupTitle: Court determination of marital home status and extent
rows.groupReason: Standalone declaratory power: the Court's authority to determine marital-home status and extent on application.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what the Court may determine under s. 22(a) on application by a spouse or interested party.

evidenceText: determine whether or not the property is or includes a marital home and, if so, the extent of the marital home

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 22 is a menu of five distinct Court powers on application, each with a different trigger, conditions, and legal effect; each is independently recallable as a separate study concept.

rows.heading: Application by spouse or interested party respecting marital home
rows.groupTitle: Court authorization of disposition without spouse consent
rows.groupReason: Distinct authorization power with three enumerated grounds for proceeding without the other spouse's consent, subject to terms and conditions.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three grounds on which the Court may authorize a disposition of a marital-home interest without the other spouse's consent, and note that terms and conditions may include comparable accommodation or payment.

evidenceText: authorize a disposition of any interest in the marital home if the Court finds that the spouse whose consent is required
cannot be found or is not available
is not capable of giving or withholding consent
is unreasonably withholding consent

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 22 is a menu of five distinct Court powers on application, each with a different trigger, conditions, and legal effect; each is independently recallable as a separate study concept.

rows.heading: Application by spouse or interested party respecting marital home
rows.groupTitle: Court dispensation from section 21 notice
rows.groupReason: Narrow procedural power allowing the Court to waive the notice requirement imposed by section 21.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the Court may, on application, dispense with any notice required under section 21.

evidenceText: dispense with any notice required to be given under section 21

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 22 is a menu of five distinct Court powers on application, each with a different trigger, conditions, and legal effect; each is independently recallable as a separate study concept.

rows.heading: Application by spouse or interested party respecting marital home
rows.groupTitle: Setting aside unauthorized disposition and revesting
rows.groupReason: Remedial power to set aside a disposition made contrary to s. 19(1) and re-vest the interest on terms the Court considers appropriate.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Court's power under s. 22(d) to set aside a disposition made in contravention of s. 19(1) and re-vest the interest on appropriate terms and conditions.

evidenceText: direct the setting aside of any disposition of an interest in the marital home contrary to subsection 19(1) and the revesting of the interest or any part of the interest on such terms and subject to such conditions as the Court considers appropriate

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 22 is a menu of five distinct Court powers on application, each with a different trigger, conditions, and legal effect; each is independently recallable as a separate study concept.

rows.heading: Application by spouse or interested party respecting marital home
rows.groupTitle: Remedy for false affidavit under section 19(3)
rows.groupReason: Fraud-specific remedy: the Court may order substitution of property or setting aside money/security where a false s. 19(3) affidavit was sworn or knowingly relied upon.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall who is subject to the s. 22(e) order, the trigger (false affidavit under s. 19(3)), and the available remedies (substitute property or set aside money/security).

evidenceText: if a false affidavit is given under subsection 19(3), direct the person who swore the false affidavit, or any person who knew at the time it was sworn that the affidavit was false and who subsequently conveyed the property, to substitute other property for the marital home or direct the person to set aside money or security in its place

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 22 is a menu of five distinct Court powers on application, each with a different trigger, conditions, and legal effect; each is independently recallable as a separate study concept.

rows.heading: Order for exclusive possession
rows.groupTitle: Court's exclusive possession powers under s.23(1)
rows.groupReason: Covers the five types of orders available and the temporary-relief qualifier, answering 'what can the Court order in an exclusive possession application?'
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the five categories of orders the Court may make under s.23(1)(a)–(e) and the provision that such orders may be temporary relief pending another application.

evidenceText: the Court on application may, by order, (a) direct that one spouse be given exclusive possession of a marital home or part of it
An order may be made under subsection (1) for temporary relief pending the bringing or disposition of another application under this Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 23 contains two independently recallable concepts: the range of orders the Court may make (23(1)(a)–(e), 23(2)) and the substantive test for granting plus the automatic cessation rule (23(3), 23(4)).

rows.heading: Order for exclusive possession
rows.groupTitle: Test for and cessation of exclusive possession orders (s.23(3)–(4))
rows.groupReason: The 'only if' granting test and the automatic cessation-on-death rule are a separate recall task from the list of available powers.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two alternative grounds under s.23(3) that must be satisfied before an exclusive possession order may be made, and identify the automatic cessation trigger in s.23(4).

evidenceText: an order under subsection (1) for exclusive possession may be made only if, in the opinion of the Court, other provision for shelter is not adequate in the circumstances or it is in the best interests of a child
An order made under paragraph (1)(a), (c), (d) or (e) ceases to apply on the death of either spouse.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 23 contains two independently recallable concepts: the range of orders the Court may make (23(1)(a)–(e), 23(2)) and the substantive test for granting plus the automatic cessation rule (23(3), 23(4)).

rows.heading: Discharge, variation, suspension of order
rows.groupTitle: Discharge, variation, and suspension of s. 22(b) and s. 23 orders
rows.groupReason: Both subsections state the same Court power (discharge, vary, suspend) applied to different order types with different standards, forming one recall task: identifying who may apply, which orders are reviewable, and the applicable satisfaction standard for each.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the applicant, the order type subject to review, and the applicable standard (material change in circumstances for s. 23(1)(a),(c),(d),(e) orders; no longer appropriate for s. 22(b) terms and conditions) under s. 24.

evidenceText: the Court may discharge, vary or suspend the order if it is satisfied that there has been a material change in circumstances
the Court may discharge, vary or suspend the terms and conditions if the Court is satisfied that the terms and conditions are no longer appropriate

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 24 contains a single coherent review mechanism — the Court's power to discharge, vary, or suspend its own orders in this Part — applied to two order types with distinct standards. The two subsections contrast the applicable standard (material change in circumstances vs. no longer appropriate) within one recall task.

rows.heading: Interim orders
rows.groupTitle: Interim orders for delivering up, safekeeping, and preservation of marital home or household goods
rows.groupReason: One court power with a single trigger (application under this Part), standard (as it considers necessary), and object set (marital home or household goods) forms one recallable unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Court's interim-order power on an application under this Part, the 'as it considers necessary' standard, and the three permitted order types (delivering up, safekeeping, preservation) applied to the marital home or household goods.

evidenceText: the Court may make such interim orders as it considers necessary for the delivering up, safekeeping and preservation of the marital home or household goods.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single-sentence provision granting the Court one discrete interim-order power over the marital home or household goods; no internal structure warrants splitting.

rows.heading: Spouses’ right to possession of household goods
rows.groupTitle: Spousal right of possession of household goods and its termination
rows.groupReason: Subsection (1) states the equal possession right and its three statutory limitations; subsection (2) provides the sole termination condition. Together they answer one recall question about the scope and duration of the right.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the spousal right to equal possession of household goods, the three limitations subject to which it applies, and the event that terminates the right.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 26 creates a substantive spousal right to equal possession of household goods with three stated limitations and a clear termination trigger; both subsections form one tightly interdependent rule-and-boundary pair suitable for a single recall task.

rows.heading: Order in respect of household goods
rows.groupTitle: Application for household goods order and pendency restraint
rows.groupReason: The application right, its scope limitation excluding goods already covered by a marital home order, and the other spouse's pendency non-disposal duty form one procedural step with a distinct recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who may apply for a household goods order, the exclusion for goods already covered by a marital home exclusive possession order, and the other spouse's duty not to dispose of specified goods during pendency absent written consent or Court leave.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 27 contains two procedurally distinct stages with different actors and modalities: (1) the spouse's right to apply and the other spouse's pendency duty, and (2) the Court's order-making power and mandatory decision criteria.

rows.heading: Order in respect of household goods
rows.groupTitle: Court's order-making power and decision criteria for household goods
rows.groupReason: The Court's discretionary powers (exclusive possession, non-disposition, incidental provisions) and the mandatory factors it must consider are a distinct recall task from the application and pendency rules.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what the Court may order in respect of household goods and the factors it must consider in exercising that power, including the applicant's need for daily life and family responsibilities.

evidenceText: the Court may order the following, and may impose such incidental, supplemental and consequential provisions as the Court considers necessary
In determining whether to exercise its powers under subsection (3) in respect of household goods, the Court shall consider

the extent to which the household goods are needed by the applicant to satisfy the ordinary requirements of his or her daily life, including any requirements arising from the family responsibilities of the applicant

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 27 contains two procedurally distinct stages with different actors and modalities: (1) the spouse's right to apply and the other spouse's pendency duty, and (2) the Court's order-making power and mandatory decision criteria.

rows.heading: Termination or variation of order
rows.groupTitle: Termination and variation of household goods orders (s. 28)
rows.groupReason: Both subsections address the same question—how a s. 27(3) order ends or changes—through automatic termination and discretionary court modification, respectively.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three automatic termination triggers (divorce, declaration of nullity, death of a spouse) for a s. 27(3) order and the Court's power on either spouse's application to vary, discharge, or suspend the order upon a material change in circumstances.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 28 is a short, cohesive provision governing the complete fate of s. 27(3) orders: automatic termination events in (1) and discretionary judicial modification in (2). Together they form one lifecycle rule that a learner would recall as a unit.

rows.heading: Order to pay for wrongful disposition of household goods
rows.groupTitle: Pre-order wrongful disposition of household goods by the defendant
rows.groupReason: The three timing windows define when the defendant's disposition is wrongful in the pre-order context and are tightly interdependent conditions for the Court's payment power.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three timing windows for wrongful pre-order disposition under s.29(1)(a)–(c) and the Court's power to order the defendant to pay a fair and reasonable amount for the applicant's loss of use and enjoyment of the household goods.

evidenceText: within the period of three months immediately before the date of the application
on or after the date of the application but before the service of notice of the application on the defendant
the Court may order the defendant to pay to the applicant in respect of the loss of use and enjoyment of those household goods such amount as the Court considers fair and reasonable

rows.sourceMapReason: The three subsections create distinct recall tasks: s.29(1) targets the defendant spouse's pre-order disposition with three timing windows, while s.29(2) and s.29(3) address post-order contravention dispositions targeting a third party with notice and the other spouse respectively.

rows.heading: Order to pay for wrongful disposition of household goods
rows.groupTitle: Liability for disposition in contravention of household-goods orders
rows.groupReason: Both subsections impose liability for post-order contravention dispositions but target different responsible parties — a third party with notice (s.29(2)) and the other spouse (s.29(3)) — forming a coherent contrast for recall.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Distinguish the third-party liability under s.29(2) from the other-spouse liability under s.29(3) for disposing household goods in contravention of a s.27(2) prohibition, a s.27(3) order, or a s.23(1)(d) order, and the Court's power to order a fair and reasonable payment for loss of use and enjoyment.

evidenceText: to a person having notice that household goods are being disposed of in contravention of any of them, the Court, on application by the spouse who applied for an order in respect of the household goods, may order that person to pay to the applicant
the Court, on application of the spouse in whose favour the order in respect of the household goods was made, may order the other spouse to pay to the applicant

rows.sourceMapReason: The three subsections create distinct recall tasks: s.29(1) targets the defendant spouse's pre-order disposition with three timing windows, while s.29(2) and s.29(3) address post-order contravention dispositions targeting a third party with notice and the other spouse respectively.

rows.heading: Registration of notice of order in respect of household goods
rows.groupTitle: Registration of household-goods order notice and its deemed-notice effect
rows.groupReason: One mechanism: registration of a s. 27(3) or 23(1)(d) order in the Personal Property Registry, its deemed-notice effect for s. 29(2) purposes, and the two exceptions (serial-numbered goods not described by serial number; consumer goods at or under $1,000).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who may register a household-goods order notice, the registry and governing regulations, the deemed-notice effect of registration under s. 29(2), and the two exceptions in s. 30(4) (serial-numbered goods and low-value consumer goods).

evidenceText: the registration under subsection (1) of a notice of an order affecting household goods shall be deemed to be notice of the order and its terms to that person

Subsection (3) does not apply to (a) a disposition of household goods that are serial numbered goods within the meaning of the regulations under the Personal Property Security Act unless the goods were described by serial number in the registration

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 is a self-contained registration mechanism: it grants a spouse permission to register a household-goods order notice, states that registration is deemed notice to third persons under s. 29(2), and carves out two exceptions. The subsections are tightly interdependent and form one recallable legal concept.

rows.heading: Consideration of circumstances by Court
rows.groupTitle: Court's duty to consider circumstances and expenditure under s. 29
rows.groupReason: Single judicial-consideration directive with two decision points (whether to exercise s. 29 powers; amount of payment) and two enumerated expenditure factors forming one recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two decision contexts in which the Court must have regard to all circumstances under s. 31 and name the two specific expenditure factors the provision calls out.

evidenceText: the Court shall have regard to all the circumstances, including any expenditure incurred or to be incurred by the applicant by reason of the loss of the use and enjoyment of any household goods and any expenditure incurred in providing a substitute or replacement for those household goods.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 31 is a single, self-contained court-guidance provision directing the Court to consider all circumstances, including two specific expenditure factors, when exercising s. 29 powers. One recall task; no split needed.

rows.heading: Effect of sale or the giving of a security interest in household goods without consent of spouse
rows.groupTitle: Effect of selling or encumbering household goods without spousal consent
rows.groupReason: The rule, its delivery/possession trigger, and the spousal consent and joinder requirement are tightly interdependent and form one recallable protection concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when a sale or security interest in household goods conveys no right, title, or interest, and identify the spousal consent and joinder conditions required for the transaction to be effective.

evidenceText: the sale or the security agreement shall not convey any right, title or interest in the household goods unless the spouse of that person consents to the sale or the security agreement and joins in the instrument evidencing the sale or in the security agreement

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 32 is a single coherent protection rule: a sale or security interest in household goods not accompanied by immediate delivery and possession change conveys no interest unless the spouse consents and joins the instrument.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Part 3 Definitions: Domestic Contract, Marriage Contract, Separation Agreement
rows.groupReason: The umbrella 'domestic contract' definition and its two component terms determine which agreements are governed by Part 3.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the three types of agreements that fall under the Part 3 definition of 'domestic contract' and the specific section under which each is entered into.

evidenceText: "domestic contract" means a marriage contract, separation agreement or an agreement entered into under section 35.
"marriage contract" means an agreement entered into under section 34.
"separation agreement" means an agreement entered into under section 36.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 33 defines the three agreement types that constitute a 'domestic contract' under Part 3, establishing the scope of the entire domestic-contract regime.

rows.heading: Marriage contract
rows.groupTitle: Marriage contract: timing, scope, and child-related prohibition
rows.groupReason: Subsection (1) grants the permission and scope; subsection (2) directly limits that permission by prohibiting agreements on child parenting time and decision-making responsibility.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when spouses may enter a marriage contract, the matters it may cover, and identify the specific child-related matters that may not be agreed to under section 34(2).
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 34 is a short, self-contained provision granting permission to enter a marriage contract and directly restricting its scope with a prohibition on child parenting and decision-making agreements; the two subsections form one interdependent rule/limitation unit.

rows.heading: Domestic contract
rows.groupTitle: Domestic contract: scope, limits, and effect of subsequent marriage
rows.groupReason: Permission, scope, parenting-time prohibition, and deeming-upon-marriage rules for cohabiting unmarried persons form one coherent domestic contract concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who may enter a domestic contract, the matters it may and may not cover, and its legal character if the parties subsequently marry.
rows.sourceMapReason: Short, coherent provision defining the domestic contract for cohabiting unmarried persons: permission and scope (35(1)), the parenting-time prohibition (35(2)), and the deeming rule upon subsequent marriage (35(3)) form one recallable unit.

rows.heading: Separation agreement
rows.groupTitle: Separation agreement – eligibility and scope
rows.groupReason: The eligibility criteria and the four enumerated matters (property, support, parenting time/decision-making, and other settlement matters) form one coherent recall task: what a s. 36 separation agreement is and who may make it.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who may enter a separation agreement under s. 36 and list the matters the agreement may address, including the right to parenting time or decision-making responsibility.

evidenceText: Two persons who cohabited and are living separate and apart or who are cohabiting and agree to live separate and apart may enter into a separation agreement
the right to parenting time or decision-making responsibility with respect to their children

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 36 creates a specific permission with distinct eligibility criteria and enumerated scope, setting it apart from the s. 35 domestic contract for cohabitants still together.

rows.heading: Execution of domestic contract
rows.groupTitle: Execution formalities for domestic contracts
rows.groupReason: The three formal requirements are co-dependent conditions for a single legal rule and are best recalled as one set.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the three execution formalities a domestic contract or any agreement to amend or rescind a domestic contract must satisfy under section 37.

evidenceText: A domestic contract and any agreement to amend or rescind a domestic contract shall be in writing, shall be signed by the parties to be bound and shall be witnessed.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 37 states one tightly interdependent set of execution formalities (writing, signature, witness) for domestic contracts and amendments; all three requirements answer a single recall task and form one coherent unit.

rows.heading: Capacity to contract
rows.groupTitle: Minor's capacity to enter a marriage contract or separation agreement
rows.groupReason: Standalone rule: a minor's capacity to contract is derived from marriage capacity and is conditional on Court approval, which may be given before or after execution.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the capacity requirement for a minor to enter a marriage contract or separation agreement and the timing flexibility for Court approval.

evidenceText: A minor who has capacity to contract marriage has capacity to enter into a marriage contract or a separation agreement that is approved by the Court, whether the approval is given before or after the contract is entered into.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 38 contains two materially distinct capacity rules: a minor's own capacity tied to marriage capacity, and a separate agency rule naming specific statutory representatives for a person without capacity. Different actors, triggers, and legal instruments support separate recall tasks.

rows.heading: Capacity to contract
rows.groupTitle: Authorized persons to contract on behalf of a person without capacity
rows.groupReason: Separate agency rule identifying two authorized actors (representative and Public Trustee) with specific statutory sources and fallback conditions, all subject to Court approval.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who may enter a domestic contract or give a waiver or consent on behalf of a person without capacity, the conditions triggering each authorized person, and the requirement of Court approval.

evidenceText: Subject to the approval of the Court, the following persons may enter into a domestic contract or give any waiver or consent under this Act on behalf of a person who does not have the capacity to do so
the person's representative appointed under the Supported Decision-Making and Representation Act
the Public Trustee appointed under the Public Trustee Act, if the representative is the spouse of the person or if the person does not have a representative

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 38 contains two materially distinct capacity rules: a minor's own capacity tied to marriage capacity, and a separate agency rule naming specific statutory representatives for a person without capacity. Different actors, triggers, and legal instruments support separate recall tasks.

rows.heading: Best interests of child paramount
rows.groupTitle: Court power to disregard domestic contract provisions on child matters
rows.groupReason: One recall task: the scope, actor, standard, and trigger for the Court's power to disregard a domestic contract provision regarding child support, parenting time, or decision-making responsibility.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the matters covered, the actor, the discretionary power, and the best-interests standard under which the Court may disregard a domestic contract provision pertaining to a child.

evidenceText: the Court may disregard any provision of a domestic contract pertaining to it if, in the opinion of the Court, to do so is in the best interests of the child

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative rule granting the Court a discretionary power to override a domestic contract provision on child matters under a best-interests standard.

rows.heading: Effect of chastity provision
rows.groupTitle: Voidness of chastity provisions in domestic contracts
rows.groupReason: 40(1) sets the general voidness rule and its remarriage/cohabitation saving; 40(2) recharacterizes pre-1981 chastity conditions rather than voiding them. Together they form one complete rule on the legal effect of a chastity-based condition.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when a chastity-based provision in a separation agreement or marriage contract is void, identify the remarriage/cohabitation contingency that remains effective, and explain the different treatment for separation agreements made before January 1, 1981.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 40 states a single coherent rule: chastity-based conditions in domestic contracts are void, with a direct exception preserving remarriage/cohabitation contingencies, plus a pre-1981 recharacterization rule. Both subsections answer the same recall question and are tightly interdependent.

rows.heading: Paramountcy of domestic contract provision
rows.groupTitle: Paramountcy of domestic contract over the Act
rows.groupReason: The provision and its subject-to limits form one tightly interdependent rule a learner must recall as a unit: the contract prevails, but sections 39 and 43 qualify that paramountcy.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the rule that a domestic contract prevails over a conflicting provision of the Act, and identify the two sections that limit that paramountcy.

evidenceText: Subject to sections 39 and 43, if there is a conflict between a provision of this Act and a domestic contract, the domestic contract prevails.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 42 states a single core rule: domestic contracts prevail over the Act in case of conflict, subject to sections 39 and 43. This is one independently recallable legal principle with no internal structure warranting a split.

rows.heading: Court may disregard provision of domestic contract
rows.groupTitle: Court power to disregard domestic contract provision
rows.groupReason: The power, the inequity standard, and the two alternative conditions form a single recallable rule about when the Court may set aside a domestic contract provision.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two alternative conditions (pre-1981 contract without contemplation of this Part, or absence of independent legal advice) under which the Court may disregard a domestic contract provision as inequitable in all the circumstances.

evidenceText: The Court may disregard any provision of a domestic contract if the Court is of the opinion that to apply the provision would be inequitable in all the circumstances of the case if
the domestic contract was made before January 1, 1981, and was not made in contemplation of the commencement of this Part
the spouse who challenges the provision entered into the domestic contract without receiving legal advice from a person independent of any legal adviser of the other spouse

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 43 states one coherent judicial power (Court may disregard a domestic contract provision) with a single inequity standard and two alternative triggering conditions that are tightly interdependent and answer one recall question.

rows.heading: Application by interested third party respecting property rights
rows.groupTitle: Third-party application, Court's remedial powers, and Part 1 bar

Together they define the scope and limit of the third-party application.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who may apply under s. 44(1), the four specific orders the Court may make, and the circumstance in which s. 44(8) prohibits the application.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 44 contains four independently recallable legal concepts: the application grant with its Part 1 bar, the contribution-assessment standard with its presumption, the disclosure-and-confidentiality procedure, and the Court's protective and enforcement powers.

rows.heading: Application by interested third party respecting property rights
rows.groupTitle: Contribution assessment standard and equal-contribution presumption
rows.groupReason: Subsection (2) sets the standard for recognizing and valuing contributions (work, money, money's worth) without regard to marital relationship, and subsection (3) adds the presumption of equal contribution and the onus on the spouse claiming the larger share.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the types of contribution that give rise to a property interest, the exclusion of the 'reasonable spouse' standard, the presumption of equal contribution, and which party bears the onus to rebut it.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 44 contains four independently recallable legal concepts: the application grant with its Part 1 bar, the contribution-assessment standard with its presumption, the disclosure-and-confidentiality procedure, and the Court's protective and enforcement powers.

rows.heading: Application by interested third party respecting property rights
rows.groupTitle: Mandatory contribution disclosure and confidentiality protection
rows.groupReason: Subsection (4) requires each party to file and serve a verified statement of contribution in the form prescribed by the Rules of Court; subsection (5) allows the Court to order confidentiality where public disclosure would cause hardship.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the filing and service requirements for the contribution statement under s. 44(4) and the Court's power under s. 44(5) to treat the statement and cross-examination as confidential.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 44 contains four independently recallable legal concepts: the application grant with its Part 1 bar, the contribution-assessment standard with its presumption, the disclosure-and-confidentiality procedure, and the Court's protective and enforcement powers.

rows.heading: Application by interested third party respecting property rights
rows.groupTitle: Court's interim protective orders and enforcement of security
rows.groupReason: Subsection (7) authorizes interim orders restraining disposition or impoverishment and for safekeeping during the application; subsection (6) provides for sale of property to realize a security or charge the Court has already ordered.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the grounds and scope of interim protective orders under s. 44(7) and the sale mechanism available under s. 44(6) to realize a court-ordered security or charge.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 44 contains four independently recallable legal concepts: the application grant with its Part 1 bar, the contribution-assessment standard with its presumption, the disclosure-and-confidentiality procedure, and the Court's protective and enforcement powers.

rows.heading: Habitual residence

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent applicability framework: 46(1) sets the habitual-residence trigger for Parts 1–3, and 46(2)–(3) provide the interdependent fallback for spouses outside that trigger.

rows.heading: Application of Act to property

evidenceText: this Act applies in respect of property whether situated within or outside the Province
the Court shall, as is necessary, take into account property of the parties wherever situated

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 47 states one coherent application rule: the Act reaches property inside and outside the Province (subject to the Court's general limitations on foreign land), and the Court must consider property wherever situated when dividing property.

rows.heading: Orders registrable under Registry Act

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that an order made under the Marital Property Act affecting land is registrable under the Registry Act.

evidenceText: An order made under this Act affecting land is registrable under the Registry Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 48 states a single operative rule: orders under the Act affecting land are registrable under the Registry Act. It is short but creates a distinct, recallable registrability status for MPA orders.

rows.heading: Effect of statutory right to division or possession of property
rows.groupTitle: Legal Effect of Division and Possession Rights on Property Disposition
rows.groupReason: A single operative rule defining what the statutory rights do and do not create, with one stated exception.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that a spouse's statutory right to division (ss. 2, 3, 4) or possession (ss. 18, 23, 26) does not constitute an interest in the other spouse's property and does not prevent the owning spouse from disposing of that property, unless otherwise provided in the Act or by a court order under the Act.

evidenceText: does not constitute an interest in property owned by the other spouse and, except if otherwise provided in this Act or an order made under this Act, shall not be construed so as to prevent the spouse who owns marital property from disposing of that property as if this Act had not been passed

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 49 states one coherent legal rule: the statutory rights to division or possession do not constitute a property interest and do not restrict the owning spouse's power of disposition unless the Act or a court order provides otherwise.

rows.heading: Dower

rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) form one rule plus its directly dependent temporal exception; recalling them separately would fragment a single short legal fact.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 50 states a single rule-and-exception structure: the common law right of dower is abolished, subject to a defined historic temporal boundary. Both subsections are tightly interdependent and form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Application of section, measurement in Canadian system of units

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Lieutenant-Governor in Council's Order-in-Council designation power and the rule that a Canadian system of units measurement in a designated instrument is deemed an equivalent International System of Units measurement under the Canadian Metric Practice Guide (CAN3-Z234.1-79).
rows.sourceMapReason: Short two-subsection provision creating a designation power and a deemed-equivalence rule for metric measurements in designated instruments; the subsections form one coherent mechanism.

rows.heading: Interpretation
rows.groupTitle: Sand, gravel, clay and soil as minerals: definition and interpretive limits

rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the conditions under which sand, gravel, clay and soil are minerals in Crown-reserved grants and Crown Lands, state their property separateness from the soil, and recall that the provision is not a change of prior law nor an expropriation under the Expropriation Act.

evidenceText: all sand, gravel, clay and soil used or to be used for their chemical or special physical properties, or both, or taken for contained minerals, are minerals and are property separate from the soil and constitute a property that is independent from that of the soil, and ownership of such minerals is vested in the Crown
Subsection (1) shall not be deemed to be nor to involve an expropriation within the meaning of the Expropriation Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsections (1)–(5) form one interpretive/definitional package establishing when sand, gravel, clay and soil are minerals; subsection (6) is a distinct payment exemption with its own actor, temporal trigger, and legal effect.

rows.heading: Interpretation

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the royalty and rent exemption available to a person who worked a sand, gravel, clay or soil deposit before May 18, 1986 and the purposes for which the exemption applies.

evidenceText: a person who, before May 18, 1986, worked any deposit of sand, gravel, clay or soil for the purpose of using it for its chemical or special physical properties, or both, or for its contained minerals, shall not hereafter be required to pay any royalty or rent

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsections (1)–(5) form one interpretive/definitional package establishing when sand, gravel, clay and soil are minerals; subsection (6) is a distinct payment exemption with its own actor, temporal trigger, and legal effect.

rows.heading: Provision to add certainty to definition of mineral
rows.groupTitle: Express Mineral Inclusions for Greater Certainty (s. 1.2)

rows.heading: Application
rows.groupTitle: Application and Non-Derogation of the Mining Act
rows.groupReason: Both subsections together set the Act's scope: 2(1) defines positive application to Crown minerals and all mines; 2(2) preserves fire-legislation obligations. They form one coherent boundary-setting rule.

evidenceText: This Act and the regulations apply to minerals the ownership of which is vested in the Crown and to all mines, including those where any or all of the mining is in relation to minerals the ownership of which is not vested in the Crown.
Nothing in this Act or the regulations exempts a person acting under this Act or the regulations from the application of the Forest Fires Act or the Fire Prevention Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 2 is a short, self-contained application provision defining the Act's positive scope (Crown minerals and all mines) and its non-derogation from fire legislation; both subsections jointly establish the Act's jurisdictional boundary as one recall task.

rows.heading: Administration
rows.groupTitle: Minister's administrative authority and Crown mine control
rows.groupReason: Both subsections define the Minister's single administrative role; recalling them separately would fragment one concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Minister's responsibility for administration and enforcement of the Act and regulations, the power to designate persons to act on the Minister's behalf, and the Minister's administration and control of all Crown mines and minerals.

evidenceText: The Minister is responsible for the administration and enforcement of this Act and the regulations and may designate persons to act on his behalf.
Subject to this Act, the Minister has the administration and control of all mines and minerals the ownership of which is vested in the Crown.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short institutional section establishing the Minister's administration, enforcement, and Crown mine control roles as one coherent administrative authority concept.

rows.heading: Appointment of Recorder and other officers
rows.groupTitle: Appointment of Recorder and other mining officers
rows.groupReason: Both subsections together establish the standard Civil Service appointment rule and the specified-term exception, forming one coherent staffing rule for the mining office.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State how the Minister appoints a Recorder and other officers under the Civil Service Act and the three categories of specified-term employment permitted notwithstanding the Civil Service Act.

evidenceText: The Minister shall appoint from among persons employed under the Civil Service Act a Recorder and such other officers as he may determine.
Notwithstanding the Civil Service Act, the Minister may employ for a specified term any person

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 4 creates a Civil Service appointment duty for the Recorder and officers in 4(1) and a notwithstanding-permission for specified-term outside employment in 4(2); both answer the same recall question and the Recorder role is referenced in the Act's definitions.

rows.heading: Powers of Minister
rows.groupTitle: Minister's inspection, sampling, and entry powers
rows.groupReason: All five sub-items are the Minister's oversight powers exercisable at any reasonable time to carry out Act responsibilities; they share one actor, one trigger, and one purpose.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recount the five powers the Minister may exercise at any reasonable time—entry and inspection of mines and claim/lease land, sampling and testing, access to books and records, and entry upon private land without trespass liability (in the absence of actual damage or subject to tolls)—to carry out responsibilities under the Mining Act and regulations.

evidenceText: The Minister may, at any reasonable time,
enter upon the land covered by a mineral claim or mining lease and into a mine for the purpose of making inspections and inquiries
enter upon private land and travel along private roads without being liable for trespass, in the absence of actual damage, or subject to tolls

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 5 is a single enumerated list of Ministerial inspection, sampling, record-access, and private-land entry powers, all shared by the same actor under the same trigger and purpose; it forms one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Minister may enter into agreements

evidenceText: The Minister, with the approval of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, may enter into and amend from time to time agreements with Canada, a provincial government or a person with respect to exploration for minerals, development or production of minerals or any other matter in relation to this Act or the regulations.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 is a single, self-contained ministerial power: the Minister may enter into and amend mining-related agreements with specified counterparties, subject to Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval. rows.heading: Disposal of registered mineral claim

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 7 states one coherent ministerial disposal power for expired, cancelled, or surrendered mineral claims and mining leases, tightly linked to a notice-triggered suspension of specified prospecting and registration provisions.

rows.heading: Extension of time by Minister

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the three prerequisites for an application, the ministerial standard (necessary for better management of Crown minerals), the scope of extendable time, and the ancillary power to prescribe payment to a person aggrieved under section 8 of the Mining Act.

evidenceText: Upon application accompanied by payment of the fee prescribed by regulation and upon good cause being shown, the Minister may, being of the opinion that it is necessary to do so for the better management of minerals the ownership of which is vested in the Crown, extend the time fixed or allowed for doing anything or taking any proceeding under this Act or the regulations and he may prescribe payment by the applicant to a person aggrieved by such extension of time.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 8 states one coherent ministerial power with tightly coupled prerequisites, a discretionary standard, a scope, and an ancillary payment power; all pieces answer the single recall task of when and how the Minister may extend time under the Act.

rows.heading: Application for extension of time

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 9 sets a short, interdependent rule: general post-deadline extension permission in 9(1) qualified by a specific 21-day advance filing requirement for required-work extensions in 9(2). The two subsections are tightly linked (9(1) is expressly subject to 9(2)) and form one recallable procedural concept.

rows.heading: Extension respecting required work

evidenceText: An extension of time under section 8 for the performance of required work does not relieve the applicant from performing, in addition to the work for which the extension of time was granted, the minimum annual required work.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative rule clarifying that a section 8 extension does not relieve the applicant of the minimum annual required work; one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Waiver or reduction of required work
rows.groupTitle: Minister's power to waive or reduce required work

evidenceText: the Minister may, upon submission of proof satisfactory to him that no further work is warranted at that time, waive or reduce required work in respect of a mineral claim or mining lease for such period of time as he may determine

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 11 is a single self-contained discretionary power: the Minister may waive or reduce required work on a mineral claim or mining lease when proof shows no further work is warranted, for a period the Minister determines. One recallable concept; no split warranted.

rows.heading: Function and authority of Board

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 contains at least six independently recallable legal concepts: the Board's jurisdictional scope, inspection and reporting powers, cancellation/reinstatement orders with registry effects, property-damage compensation, conditional work relief, and procedural costs/enforcement rules.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 contains at least six independently recallable legal concepts: the Board's jurisdictional scope, inspection and reporting powers, cancellation/reinstatement orders with registry effects, property-damage compensation, conditional work relief, and procedural costs/enforcement rules.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 contains at least six independently recallable legal concepts: the Board's jurisdictional scope, inspection and reporting powers, cancellation/reinstatement orders with registry effects, property-damage compensation, conditional work relief, and procedural costs/enforcement rules.

rows.heading: Function and authority of Board

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 contains at least six independently recallable legal concepts: the Board's jurisdictional scope, inspection and reporting powers, cancellation/reinstatement orders with registry effects, property-damage compensation, conditional work relief, and procedural costs/enforcement rules.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 contains at least six independently recallable legal concepts: the Board's jurisdictional scope, inspection and reporting powers, cancellation/reinstatement orders with registry effects, property-damage compensation, conditional work relief, and procedural costs/enforcement rules.

rows.heading: Powers and duties of Recorder

any claim map referred to in subsection (3) and any document filed in the Recorder's office or submitted to the Recorder shall be open to public inspection during normal office hours and, on payment of the fee prescribed by regulation, the Recorder shall provide copies

rows.heading: Mineral claims registry

rows.heading: Registration information

rows.heading: Registration information

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 14.2 contains two distinct recall tasks: the electronic-means duty covering both information and payment, and the authorization restriction with its certification effect. Each group involves a different legal modality and actor focus.

the integrity of the registry will be maintained
the Recorder shall enter the information with respect to the registration into the registry

rows.heading: Correcting an entry in registry

rows.groupReason: Three interdependent payment and proof-of-payment conditions that together constitute the complete pre-registration checklist for a vesting order.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the three obligations the applicant must satisfy—paying debts, liabilities, and taxes; paying Board-ordered compensation to the owner and tenant; and furnishing proof of payment to the applicable registrar—before submitting a vesting order for registration.

evidenceText: pay all debts, liabilities and taxes owing on the private land

provide the registrar of deeds for the county in which the private land is located or the registrar of land titles for the land registration district in which the private land is located, as the case may be, with proof of payment of the debts, liabilities, taxes and compensation in the form and manner required by the Board.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short self-contained section listing three pre-registration prerequisites for a vesting order; all share the same actor (applicant), trigger (prior to submitting for registration), and duty modality, forming one coherent recall checklist.

rows.heading: Effect of registration
rows.groupTitle: Effect of registering a vesting order
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(2) state when registration takes effect and the resulting fee-simple vesting with its easement/right-of-way exception; subsections (3)–(4) characterize the vesting order as an instrument and exclude s. 44/55, all answering one recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when a vesting order takes effect, the nature of the resulting fee-simple vesting, the easements and rights-of-way that survive registration, and the legal characterization of the vesting order under the Registry Act and Land Titles Act.

evidenceText: A vesting order comes into effect on its registration in the registry office established under the Registry Act for the county in which the private land is located or in the land titles office established in the Land Titles Act for the district in which the private land is located, as the case may be.

the private land is vested in the applicant in fee simple, free and clear from all encumbrances, other than a right-of-way or easement for the conveyance, transmission or transportation of water, oil, gas, electricity or telecommunication or for the disposal of sewage or any other easement or right-of-way, however created, on, over or in respect of the private land.

rows.sourceMapReason: All four subsections coherently state the timing, substantive property effect, and legal characterization of vesting-order registration as one integrated rule.

rows.heading: Notify Recorder of registration
rows.groupTitle: Applicant's Duty to Notify Recorder of Vesting Order Registration
rows.groupReason: One obligation with a defined actor (applicant), trigger (registration of the vesting order), recipient (Recorder), and 30-day deadline; independently recallable procedural requirement.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the applicant's obligation to notify the Recorder of a vesting order registration and the 30-day deadline by which it must be done.

evidenceText: Within 30 days after the registration of the vesting order, the applicant shall notify the Recorder of the registration.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single, self-contained procedural duty: the applicant must notify the Recorder within 30 days after vesting order registration. One clear recall task with distinct actor, trigger, timeframe, and action.

rows.heading: Costs and expenses
rows.groupTitle: Applicant's liability for costs and expenses
rows.groupReason: One duty (applicant pays owner's and Minister's costs) plus its six enumerated categories answer a single recall question about the scope of the applicant's cost liability.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the applicant is liable for costs and expenses incurred by the owner and the Minister, and identify the six categories of recoverable costs listed in subsection (2).

evidenceText: The applicant is liable to pay the costs and expenses incurred by the owner and the Minister in relation to an application and a hearing under this Part.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 112.2 states one cost-liability duty on the applicant and the categories that define its scope; subsections (1) and (2) are tightly interdependent and form a single recallable rule.

rows.heading: Security for costs and expenses
rows.groupTitle: Security deposit for costs and expenses in vesting order applications
rows.groupReason: Deposit duty, excess-return rule, and insufficiency reimbursement form one conditional mechanism tied to the same security instrument.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when and how the applicant must deposit security with the Board, the Board's obligation to return excess, and the Minister's duty to reimburse the owner and right to recover from the applicant under section 112.22 when security is insufficient.
rows.sourceMapReason: The three subsections form one interdependent security-deposit mechanism — applicant's deposit duty, Board's return of excess, and Minister's reimbursement/recovery on insufficiency — that a learner recalls as a single procedural rule.

rows.heading: Certificate for costs and expenses
rows.groupTitle: Certificate for costs: demand, court judgment, and interest
rows.groupReason: One interdependent recovery procedure from demand through court judgment, including certificate contents, filing costs, and the applicable interest rate.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Minister's step-by-step procedure to recover costs when applicant security is insufficient, including the 30-day demand, certificate contents, court judgment effect, filing-cost recovery, and the prescribed interest rate.

evidenceText: the Minister may send a registered letter to the applicant demanding payment within 30 days
the certificate may be filed in the Court and shall be entered and recorded in the Court and, when so entered and recorded, becomes a judgment of the Court
the amount bears interest at the rate prescribed in subsection 9(1) of New Brunswick Regulation 84-247 under the Revenue Administration Act

rows.sourceMapReason: A single sequential enforcement procedure (demand letter, certificate, court judgment, filing costs, interest) for recovering costs when applicant security is insufficient; the steps are interdependent and form one recall task.

rows.heading: Hearings
rows.groupTitle: Application for Board adjudication under Part XIII
rows.groupReason: Defines who may apply, the scope of matters (s. 13(1)), the exclusion for Part XII.1, and the precondition of filing a notice of dispute.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the person entitled to apply to the Board, the scope of matters covered, the Part XII.1 exclusion, and the filing precondition in s. 113(1).

evidenceText: a person seeking redress with respect to any question, disagreement, matter or claim referred to in subsection 13(1), other than a matter concerning the acquisition of private lands under Part XII.1, may apply to the Board for an adjudication under this Part

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 113 contains six independently recallable hearing-procedure concepts: access to adjudication, Board conduct of hearings, summary hearing, registry effects of pending proceedings, compliance and court enforcement, and time management. Each creates a distinct recall task for a learner.

rows.heading: Hearings
rows.groupTitle: Board hearing procedures: notification and default
rows.groupReason: Covers the Board's duty to notify parties, affected persons, and the Recorder, and its power to proceed without a party who has received notice.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify whom the Board must notify upon an application and the condition under which the Board may proceed and determine in the absence of a notified party.

evidenceText: The Board shall notify all persons who are parties and all persons who the Board considers are affected and should be notified and the Recorder of an application under subsection (1)
When the Board is satisfied that a party has received notice of the hearing, the Board may proceed to conduct the hearing and make a determination in the absence of that party

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 113 contains six independently recallable hearing-procedure concepts: access to adjudication, Board conduct of hearings, summary hearing, registry effects of pending proceedings, compliance and court enforcement, and time management. Each creates a distinct recall task for a learner.

rows.heading: Hearings
rows.groupTitle: Summary hearing with finality
rows.groupReason: Creates a distinct procedural path: summary hearing conditioned on written party approval, with the consequence that the decision is final.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions for a summary hearing under s. 113(6) and the effect of that procedure on the finality of the Board's decision.

evidenceText: the Board may, with the approval in writing of the parties, proceed to summarily hear the parties and may, with or without reasons, base its decision solely on that hearing in which case the Board's decision shall be final

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 113 contains six independently recallable hearing-procedure concepts: access to adjudication, Board conduct of hearings, summary hearing, registry effects of pending proceedings, compliance and court enforcement, and time management. Each creates a distinct recall task for a learner.

rows.heading: Hearings
rows.groupTitle: Effect of pending Board proceedings on recording and leasing
rows.groupReason: Imposes a prohibition on the Recorder and a suspension on mining lease applications where the land is the subject of a pending Board application or an appealable decision.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two grounds on which the Recorder shall not record a mineral claim and a mining lease application shall not be considered under s. 113(10).

evidenceText: The Recorder shall not record a mineral claim and an application for a mining lease shall not be considered where the land covered by the mineral claim or in respect of which the application for a mining lease is made is at the time of the filing of the application to record or of the making of the application for the mining lease, (a) the subject of an application before the Board; or (b) the subject of a decision or order of the Board and the time within which an appeal from the decision or order may be made has not expired

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 113 contains six independently recallable hearing-procedure concepts: access to adjudication, Board conduct of hearings, summary hearing, registry effects of pending proceedings, compliance and court enforcement, and time management.
