rows.heading: Hearings
rows.groupTitle: Compliance with and court enforcement of Board decisions
rows.groupReason: Sets the 30-day compliance obligation, the mechanism for a Board order to become a court judgment, and the recovery of enforcement costs.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the compliance deadline for Board decisions, how an order is enforced through The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick, and how filing and recording costs are recovered.

evidenceText: Within thirty days after the date the decision was mailed or within such other time as may be specified by order of the Board in its decision, each of the parties shall comply with the decision of the Board and any orders made by the Board

A copy of any order made by the Board may be filed in The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick and shall be entered and recorded in the Court and, when so entered and recorded, becomes a judgment of the Court and may be enforced as such

All reasonable costs and charges attendant upon the filing, entering and recording of an order under subsection (14) shall be recovered in like manner as if the amount thereof had been included in the order

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 113 contains six independently recallable hearing-procedure concepts: access to adjudication, Board conduct of hearings, summary hearing, registry effects of pending proceedings, compliance and court enforcement, and time management. Each creates a distinct recall task for a learner.

rows.heading: Hearings
rows.groupTitle: Board's power to extend or abridge time
rows.groupReason: Grants the Board a general power to extend or abridge any fixed time in relation to an application, whether or not expired.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Board's power under s. 113(13) to extend or abridge time fixed for anything in relation to an application.

evidenceText: The Board may extend the time fixed for doing anything in relation to an application before him under this Act, whether or not the time fixed has expired, and he may abridge the time fixed for doing anything in relation to an application before him under this Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 113 contains six independently recallable hearing-procedure concepts: access to adjudication, Board conduct of hearings, summary hearing, registry effects of pending proceedings, compliance and court enforcement, and time management. Each creates a distinct recall task for a learner.

rows.heading: Appeals
rows.groupTitle: Right to Appeal and Filing Procedure
rows.groupReason: These subsections form the initiating procedure: who may appeal, the 30-day limit, the grounds, the forum, service requirements, the Board's document delivery duty, and the role of the Rules of Court.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the parties entitled to appeal a Board decision under s. 114, the 30-day time limit, the grounds of error of law or jurisdiction, the forum, the service and document-delivery requirements, and the application of the Rules of Court.

evidenceText: A party to any question, disagreement, matter or claim may, within 30 days after being notified of a decision or order of the Board under section 112.13 or subsection 113(8), as the case may be, apply by Notice of Application to a judge of The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick to review and set aside the order or decision on the grounds of any error of law or of jurisdiction.

The Notice of Application referred to in subsection (1) shall be served by the applicant on the other parties to the proceedings, and on the Board and the Recorder, in accordance with the Rules of Court.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 114 contains a complete appeals procedure with two naturally distinct recall tasks: initiating the appeal (right, grounds, time limit, service, governing rules) and the post-filing process (hearing, remedies, stay, and collateral effects on recordings and leases).

rows.heading: Appeals
rows.groupTitle: Hearing, Remedies, and Operative Effects of an Appeal
rows.groupReason: These subsections cover the post-filing process: the judge's evidentiary power, the automatic stay, the judge's remedial options, the effectiveness-date order for dismissed s. 113(8) appeals, and the Recorder's recording and lease-application restriction during a pending appeal.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the judge's evidentiary power, the automatic stay of the Board's decision, the judge's remedial options (set aside, dismiss, or substitute), the effectiveness-date order for a dismissed s. 113(8) appeal, and the Recorder's prohibition on recording a mineral claim or considering a lease application during a pending s. 114 appeal.

evidenceText: An application under subsection (1) stays the operation of the decision or order in respect of which the application is made.

The Recorder shall not record a mineral claim and an application for a mining lease shall not be considered if the land covered by the mineral claim or in respect of which the application for a mining lease is made is at the time of the filing of the application to record or of the making of the application for the mining lease the subject of an application under this section.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 114 contains a complete appeals procedure with two naturally distinct recall tasks: initiating the appeal (right, grounds, time limit, service, governing rules) and the post-filing process (hearing, remedies, stay, and collateral effects on recordings and leases).

rows.heading: Regulations
rows.groupTitle: Scope of Mining Act Regulatory Power
rows.groupReason: All subsections constitute one regulatory enabling framework, from the enumerated subject matters to the inapplicability declaration power in subsection (2).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the subject matters the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may regulate under the Mining Act, including mineral definition, security, environmental reclamation, fees, royalties, and the New Brunswick Mineral and Petroleum Grid, and recognize the power to declare a regulation inapplicable to a specific mineral claim, mining lease, or mine.
rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent regulatory enabling provision; all subsections define the scope of Lieutenant-Governor in Council regulatory power under the Mining Act and answer a single recall question.

rows.heading: Offences
rows.groupTitle: Offences under section 116
rows.groupReason: The four remaining prohibitions (a)–(c) and (e) share one legal modality and form a single short offences list.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify each of the four acts prohibited by section 116(1) of the Mining Act, including the specific survey-mark protections in subsection (a) and the Board-order compliance duty in subsection (e).

evidenceText: No person shall do any of the following:
without lawful authority under this Act, deface, alter, remove or disturb any picket, boundary line, figure, writing or other mark lawfully placed, standing or made under this Act;
obstruct the Minister or an officer appointed under this Act in the execution of their powers and duties;
fail to comply with a decision or order made by the Board under this Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 116 lists four operative prohibitions in a single 'no person shall' structure; the short list forms one coherent recall task of identifying the Mining Act offences.

rows.heading: No interference with mining
rows.groupTitle: Prohibition on interference with mining
rows.groupReason: The prohibition's actors, scope, and lawful-authority condition in subsection (1) plus the cumulative prosecution-and-civil-liability rule in subsection (2) are one tightly interdependent legal rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who is bound by the prohibition on interfering with mining, what 'lawful authority' qualifies, and that liability to prosecution is in addition to civil liability for a violation.

evidenceText: No prospector, holder of a mineral claim or mining lease or operator of a mine, or an agent thereof, shall without lawful authority interfere with mining on land covered by the mineral claim, mining lease or mine of any other holder of a mineral claim or mining lease or operator of a mine.
A person's liability to prosecution for a violation of subsection (1) is in addition to any civil liability.

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsection (1) is a specific prohibition with defined actors and conditions; subsection (2) directly adds cumulative liability for its violation. Together they form one coherent mining-interference rule.

rows.heading: Offences generally
rows.groupTitle: Offence categorization under the Mining Act
rows.groupReason: All four subsections together define how Mining Act offences are created and assigned to categories under the Provincial Offences Procedure Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the default and prescribed offence categories for regulatory violations and the Schedule A offence-to-category mapping under section 117.1.

evidenceText: A person who violates or fails to comply with a provision of the regulations commits an offence that is, subject to subsection (2), punishable under Part II of the Provincial Offences Procedure Act as a category B offence.
A person who violates or fails to comply with a provision of this Act that is listed in Column I of Schedule A commits an offence.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 117.1 establishes the unified offence-categorization framework for the Mining Act: default regulatory category, prescribed-category override, and Schedule A mapping. The four short subsections form one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Continuing offences
rows.groupTitle: Fine calculation for continuing offences
rows.groupReason: The trigger (offence continuing more than one day) and the parallel minimum/maximum fine multipliers form one interdependent penalty-calculation rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State how the minimum and maximum fines are calculated when an offence under the Mining Act or its regulations continues for more than one day.

evidenceText: the minimum fine that may be imposed is the minimum fine set by the Provincial Offences Procedure Act multiplied by the number of days during which the offence continues
the maximum fine that may be imposed is the maximum fine set by the Provincial Offences Procedure Act multiplied by the number of days during which the offence continues

rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained penalty-calculation rule for continuing offences with independent recall value as a distinct enforcement consequence.

rows.heading: Parties
rows.groupTitle: Individual liability for corporate offences (s. 119)
rows.groupReason: One sentence covering covered persons, triggering conduct, and the consequence of personal criminal liability independent of corporate prosecution.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify which corporate actors (officer, director, employee, agent) are personally liable for a Mining Act offence, the conduct that triggers that liability (directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in, or participated), and the effect that liability exists whether or not the corporation was prosecuted or convicted.

evidenceText: any officer, director, employee or agent of that corporation who directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in or participated in the commission of the offence is a party to and commits the offence

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 119 states one coherent rule: which corporate actors are personally liable for a corporate offence and under what conduct. All elements (covered persons, triggering conduct, punishment, independence from corporate prosecution) serve a single recall task.

rows.heading: Liability of corporation
rows.groupTitle: Corporate Liability Preserved Alongside Individual Liability
rows.groupReason: States the corporation remains liable for its offence even where an individual is also liable under section 119.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a corporation that committed an offence under the Mining Act is not relieved of its own liability merely because an officer, director, employee, or agent is separately held liable under section 119.

evidenceText: Nothing in section 119 relieves the corporation that committed an offence under this Act from liability therefor.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative rule: section 119's individual liability does not relieve the corporation of its own liability. One clear recall task; no split needed.

rows.heading: Neglect or failure of corporation
rows.groupTitle: Attribution of Corporate Agent Conduct to the Corporation (s. 121)
rows.groupReason: Single attribution rule identifying the covered actors, the scope condition, and the legal effect of attributing agent conduct to the corporation under the Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that under s. 121, the act, omission, neglect, or failure of a corporation's officer, director, employee, or agent acting within the scope of employment or instructions is the act, omission, neglect, or failure of the corporation in construing and enforcing the Act.

evidenceText: the act, omission, neglect or failure of an officer, director, employee or agent of a corporation, acting within the scope of his employment or instructions, is the act, omission, neglect or failure of the corporation

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 121 states a single, self-contained attribution rule: an officer, director, employee, or agent's act, omission, neglect, or failure within the scope of employment or instructions is the corporation's own act, omission, neglect, or failure for construing and enforcing the Act. One recallable concept; no split or combine warranted.

rows.heading: Certificate of Recorder as evidence

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the evidentiary status of the Recorder's certificate, the notice-and-copy precondition for its reception, and the opposing party's right to require the Recorder's attendance for cross-examination with leave.
rows.sourceMapReason: A short, self-contained evidentiary mechanism: the Recorder's certificate rule, its notice precondition, and the cross-examination safeguard form one interdependent procedure.

rows.heading: Dissolution of a town or village

rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the triggering recommendation, the required Minister's recommendation, the Lieutenant-Governor in Council's dissolution-by-regulation power, and who may be appointed to carry out dissolution actions.

rows.heading: Dissolution of a town or village
rows.groupTitle: Matters the dissolution regulation may provide for

rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the enumerated matters the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may provide for in a dissolution regulation, including disposition of assets and liabilities, adjustment of ratepayers' rights, tax discharge, continuance or discontinuance of by-laws and services, claims, vesting of property in the Crown in right of the Province, and incidental matters.

rows.heading: Incorporation of city

rows.groupReason: One rule, one actor, one prerequisite, one result; no independent sub-concepts warrant splitting.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who may incorporate a town as a city, the minimum population required, and the municipality type that is the starting point.

evidenceText: The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may incorporate a town having a population of ten thousand or more as a city.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single self-contained rule stating the Lieutenant-Governor in Council's power to incorporate a town as a city at a ten-thousand population threshold; one actor, one condition, one outcome.

rows.heading: Office of mayor and council on incorporation
rows.groupTitle: Continuity of mayor and council on village-to-town or town-to-city incorporation
rows.groupReason: Single rule with one trigger (village→town or town→city incorporation), one effect (sitting mayor and council continue), and one endpoint (until new council elected and takes office).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what happens to the sitting mayor and council when a village is incorporated as a town or a town is incorporated as a city, and when their term ends.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 17 is a short, self-contained rule stating that the sitting mayor and council of a village or town continue in office after incorporation as a higher-tier municipality until a new council is elected and takes office. One coherent continuity-of-office concept.

rows.heading: Order in Council is conclusive evidence
rows.groupTitle: Conclusive evidence effect of Order in Council
rows.groupReason: Single legal rule on what the Order in Council conclusively establishes for municipal structural changes.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two matters an Order in Council effecting incorporation, amalgamation, annexation, or decrement is conclusive evidence of.

evidenceText: An Order in Council effecting an incorporation, amalgamation, annexation, or decrement is conclusive evidence that all conditions precedent for the making of the order have been complied with and that the municipality or rural community thereby created and enlarged or decreased is duly incorporated.

rows.sourceMapReason: One short, self-contained rule: an Order in Council effecting structural change is conclusive evidence of conditions-precedent compliance and due incorporation.

rows.heading: Procedure and rules for first elections
rows.groupTitle: Applicability of the Municipal Elections Act and OIC supremacy in first elections
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (8) together establish the hierarchy: the Municipal Elections Act applies to first elections subject to this section, and an Order in Council under paragraph 19(1)(e) prevails over this section in a conflict.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that the Municipal Elections Act governs first elections under paragraph 19(1)(e) except as provided in section 19.01 or an Order in Council, and that the Order in Council prevails over section 19.01 where a conflict arises.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19.01 contains four distinct recall tasks: the governing-instrument hierarchy, candidate residency qualifications, ward ballot/voting mechanics, and electoral administration logistics (polling divisions, notices, voters lists). Each answers a different exam question and is independently testable.

rows.heading: Procedure and rules for first elections
rows.groupTitle: Candidate residency requirements in first elections
rows.groupReason: Subsections (3) and (4.01) set two distinct residency-based candidate qualification rules: a six-month municipal residency for mayor or councillor, and a ward-residency-at-nomination rule for ward councillor candidates in ward-divided municipalities.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a candidate for mayor or councillor in a first election must have resided within the municipality boundaries for at least six months before the election, and that a ward councillor candidate must be resident in the ward at the time of nomination.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19.01 contains four distinct recall tasks: the governing-instrument hierarchy, candidate residency qualifications, ward ballot/voting mechanics, and electoral administration logistics (polling divisions, notices, voters lists). Each answers a different exam question and is independently testable.

rows.heading: Procedure and rules for first elections
rows.groupTitle: Ward-specific voting restrictions and ballot paper structure in first elections
rows.groupReason: Subsection (4.1) imposes the ward-voting restriction and mandates a separate ballot paper per ward listing mayor, ward councillor, and at-large councillor candidates; subsection (4.2) carves out mayor and councillor-at-large candidates from the ward-voting restriction.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that in a ward-divided municipality, ward voters vote only for candidates nominated for that ward (unless the Order in Council provides otherwise), a separate ballot paper is prepared for each ward listing candidates for mayor, ward councillor, and councillor at large, and the ward-voting restriction does not apply to mayor or councillor-at-large candidates.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19.01 contains four distinct recall tasks: the governing-instrument hierarchy, candidate residency qualifications, ward ballot/voting mechanics, and electoral administration logistics (polling divisions, notices, voters lists). rows.heading: Procedure and rules for first elections
rows.groupTitle: Polling divisions, Notice of Election, and voters lists for first elections
rows.groupReason: Subsections (2), (5), (6), and (7) govern the administrative logistics of a first election: polling division changes when concurrent with a quadrennial election, Notice of Election for the post-change municipality, the default preliminary voters list, and the Municipal Electoral Officer's discretion to prepare a new voters list.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that when a first election coincides with a quadrennial election the Municipal Electoral Officer may revise polling divisions after December 31 of the prior year and must give Notice of Election only for the municipality as described in the Order in Council, that the preliminary voters list is the most recent previous list except in concurrent elections, and that the Municipal Electoral Officer may prepare a new voters list if advisable.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19.01 contains four distinct recall tasks: the governing-instrument hierarchy, candidate residency qualifications, ward ballot/voting mechanics, and electoral administration logistics (polling divisions, notices, voters lists). rows.heading: Continuance of borrowing authority in an amalgamation proceeding
rows.groupTitle: Continuance of borrowing authority in an amalgamation
rows.groupReason: The trigger (amalgamation OIC under s. 19), the Minister's written-authorization condition, and the notwithstanding override are all parts of one operational rule that should be recalled together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the trigger, the required Ministerial authorization, and the notwithstanding override that permit a former municipality's outstanding Municipal Capital Borrowing Act authority to continue in the name of a new municipality after an amalgamation Order in Council.

evidenceText: where an Order in Council is made under section 19 effecting an amalgamation, any outstanding authority of a former municipality to borrow money granted and approved under the Municipal Capital Borrowing Act may, with the written authorization of the Minister, continue in the name of the new municipality

rows.sourceMapReason: Single short provision creating one permissive rule with a clear trigger, condition, and override; no structural basis to split or combine.

rows.heading: Basic planning statement, municipal plan, rural plan, zoning by-law or other by-law of new municipality
rows.groupTitle: Council review and reporting duty for deemed planning instruments
rows.groupReason: Subsection (3) imposes a separate affirmative duty on the council with a distinct five-year timeframe and a written-report-to-Minister requirement, forming an independently recallable concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the council's duty to review a deemed planning instrument within five years after incorporation and to report the results in writing to the Minister.

evidenceText: The council of a newly incorporated municipality shall conduct a review of any basic planning statement, municipal plan, rural plan, zoning by-law or other by-law deemed to be such under subsection (1) or (2) within five years after the effective date of the incorporation and shall report the results of the review to the Minister in writing.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19.1 contains a coherent deeming-and-persistence mechanism in subsections (1), (2), and (4), and a separately structured council review-and-reporting duty in subsection (3) with its own actor, trigger, timeframe, and recipient.

rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how an Order in Council designating a Community Planning Act instrument deems it validly enacted for a newly incorporated municipality and that the instrument remains in force until repealed by the council.

evidenceText: shall be deemed to be the basic planning statement, municipal plan, rural plan, zoning by-law or other by-law, as designated in the Order in Council, of the municipality as of the effective date of the incorporation and shall be deemed to be validly enacted as such

rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) set out the two distinct annexation triggers and identify which planning instrument is deemed to apply in each scenario.

evidenceText: when an unincorporated contiguous area is annexed to a municipality, any rural plan under subsection 77(2.1) or 77.2(1) of the Community Planning Act or any portion of a rural plan or any other regulation under the Community Planning Act that is designated in the Order in Council effecting the annexation shall be deemed to be the basic planning statement, municipal plan, rural plan, zoning by-law or other by-law, as designated in the Order in Council, of the annexed area

when an area that is part of one municipality is annexed to another municipality, the zoning by-law or the zoning provisions in the rural plan of the municipality from which the area is annexed shall be deemed to be the zoning by-law or the zoning provisions of the annexed area

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19.2 contains two distinct recall themes: the deemed-enactment triggers for the two annexation scenarios, and the post-annexation operation rules (conflict resolution, council review duty, continuing force).

rows.heading: By-laws of former municipalities

rows.sourceMapReason: All four subsections state one coherent rule—by-laws survive and extend through different types of municipal structural change—forming a single recallable concept of by-law continuity.

rows.heading: Assets and liabilities of former municipalities

evidenceText: all the assets and liabilities of the former municipality or municipalities and its or their local commissions are assets and liabilities of the new municipality and the new municipality for all purposes stands in the place and stead of the former municipality or municipalities.

rows.heading: Assets and liabilities of former municipalities

evidenceText: When the territorial limits of a municipality are decreased, the assets and liabilities of the former municipality and its local commissions shall be adjusted in accordance with an agreement between the municipality and the Minister.

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsections 21(1) and 21(2) address materially different triggers (structural creation events vs. territorial decrease) with different legal mechanisms (automatic transfer vs. Minister agreement), forming two independently recallable rules.

rows.heading: Establishment of local service district

evidenceText: Where on November 9, 1966 any service contained in the First Schedule is provided in any area outside the territorial limits of a municipality the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may establish the area as a local service district for the provision of that service.

rows.heading: Definition of service for purposes of sections 23.1 to 27.01

rows.sourceMapReason: Single definitional provision setting the scope of 'service' for sections 23.1 to 27.01, with one clear inclusion and one clear exclusion forming one coherent recall task.

rows.groupReason: Single permissive grant identifying the actor (council of a city or town) and the power (establish a housing commission), with no stated conditions or criteria.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify which municipal body may establish a housing commission under section 110 of the Municipalities Act.

evidenceText: The council of a city or town may establish a housing commission.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 110 grants a single permissive power—the council of a city or town may establish a housing commission—with no conditions, criteria, or further mechanics. It is an operative permission and warrants a minimal standalone unit, though its simplicity makes P4 the appropriate priority.

rows.heading: Joint project housing
rows.groupTitle: Joint project housing: municipal agreement powers and Lieutenant-Governor in Council authorization
rows.groupReason: The agreement powers in (1) and (2) and the enabling authorization in (3) form one interdependent mechanism; recalling them separately would fragment the dependency between the agreements and the authorization that enables them.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two types of joint housing agreements a municipality may enter (with the Province and with Canada under the National Housing Act) and the three enabling measures the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may authorize (borrowing, capital funds under the Municipal Capital Borrowing Act, and municipal services).
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 111 is a short, tightly interdependent mechanism: municipal agreement powers (Province and Canada) plus the Lieutenant-Governor in Council's enabling authorization, all operating as one joint project housing scheme.

rows.heading: Generation of electricity
rows.groupTitle: Municipal generation facility: permission, distribution prohibition, and municipal distribution utility exception
rows.groupReason: The permission to generate and sell electricity, the prohibition on distributing to residents, and the municipal distribution utility exception form one interdependent rule/exception structure.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what a municipality may and may not do with electricity from a generation facility and identify the municipal distribution utility exception under section 88 of the Electricity Act.

evidenceText: A municipality may construct, own and operate a generation facility and may use the electricity for its own purposes or sell it to a distribution electric utility or another person, but shall not distribute it or provide it as a service to its residents.

Subsection (1) does not apply to a municipal distribution utility with respect to the distribution or provision of electricity as a service to its residents within the territorial limits provided for in section 88 of the Electricity Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 111.2 contains a core permission/prohibition rule with its exception (subs 1–2) and a distinct set of ancillary enabling powers (sub 3); these answer different recall questions for a learner.

rows.heading: Generation of electricity
rows.groupTitle: Enabling powers for municipal generation facilities: land and agreements
rows.groupReason: Subsection (3) lists three distinct enabling powers (adjacent land acquisition, cost-sharing agreements, joint-operation agreements) that are separately recallable from the core distribution rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the three enabling powers a municipality has under subsection (3) to acquire adjacent land and enter into cost-sharing or joint-operation agreements for a generation facility.

evidenceText: acquire land or an interest in land that is adjacent to the municipality and use the land for the purposes stated

enter into an agreement with one or more municipalities or rural communities or with any person, including the Crown, where the costs of construction and operation of a generation facility may be shared

enter into an agreement with one or more municipalities or rural communities or with any person, including the Crown, to provide for the joint acquisition, ownership, development, extension, management or operation of a generation facility.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 111.2 contains a core permission/prohibition rule with its exception (subs 1–2) and a distinct set of ancillary enabling powers (sub 3); these answer different recall questions for a learner.

rows.heading: Generation facility fund
rows.groupTitle: Duty to establish a generation facility fund
rows.groupReason: Creates a clear 'shall' obligation triggered by constructing, owning, or operating a generation facility; independently recallable duty distinct from the construction/ownership powers in 111.2 and the budget rules in 111.4.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the obligation imposed on a municipality that constructs, owns, or operates a generation facility under section 111.3.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 111.3 is a single-sentence mandatory duty: a municipality that constructs, owns, or operates a generation facility shall establish a generation facility fund. One trigger, one obligation, one recall task.

rows.heading: Budget for generation facility
rows.groupTitle: Budget requirements and year-end adjustments for a generation facility
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(3) set the budget submission and balancing duty with a fallback; (4)–(6) set year-end deficit, surplus, and transfer rules. Together they form one interdependent budgeting framework for the generation facility fund.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the budget submission deadline, the annually or quadrennially balanced requirement, the fallback charge against other operating funds, and the required treatment of deficits and surpluses (debit/credit to the second next ensuing year or spread over four years) and the council's authority to transfer an audited surplus.

evidenceText: A municipality that operates a generation facility shall annually, on or before the date fixed pursuant to subsection 87(2), submit to the Minister the budget with respect to its operation of the facility for that year.
When operating a generation facility, a municipality shall produce, with respect to such operation, (a) an annually balanced budget, or (b) a quadrennially balanced budget.

A municipality may transfer some or all of any audited surplus of the generation facility fund to other operating funds of the municipality at the discretion of the council, commencing with the second next ensuing year.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 111.4 is a short, coherent set of budgeting rules for municipal generation facilities (submission duty, balancing requirement, fallback charge, deficit/surplus handling, and surplus transfer). The subsections are interdependent stages of one budgeting framework and form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Reserve funds
rows.groupTitle: Municipal reserve funds for generation facilities
rows.groupReason: One permissive power with two parallel fund types (operating and capital) that a learner recalls as a single concept tied to generation-facility operations and the regulations.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two types of reserve funds a municipality may establish, manage, and contribute to in respect of its ownership or operation of a generation facility, and the requirement that this be done in accordance with the regulations.

evidenceText: A municipality may, in accordance with the regulations, with respect to its ownership or operation of a generation facility

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 111.5 is a single permissive power: a municipality may establish, manage, and contribute to operating and capital reserve funds for a generation facility, subject to regulations. The two parallel fund types form one coherent recall task and the provision is self-contained.

rows.heading: Borrowing
rows.groupTitle: Borrowing for generation facilities: temporary operating loan cap and section 89 exclusion
rows.groupReason: Both subsections are short, address borrowing for generation facilities, and together define the complete borrowing picture a learner must recall.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the cap on temporary borrowing for generation-facility operations and identify why construction/renovation borrowing for a generation facility is excluded from section 89 counting.

evidenceText: A municipality may borrow temporarily in each year for current expenditures in respect of the operation of a generation facility a sum or sums of money not exceeding 50% of the budgeted revenue for that year.
any money borrowed by a municipality for the construction or renovation of a generation facility is not considered as money borrowed.

rows.sourceMapReason: Two short subsections form one coherent generation-facility borrowing rule: a capped temporary borrowing permission and a section 89 counting exclusion.

rows.heading: Application to rural communities
rows.groupTitle: Extension of generation-facility rules to rural communities
rows.groupReason: Learner must recall that the generation-facility and borrowing provisions (111.1–111.6) apply to rural communities, not only municipalities.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that sections 111.1 to 111.6 apply with necessary modifications to a rural community.

evidenceText: Sections 111.1 to 111.6 apply with the necessary modifications to a rural community.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 111.7 extends the generation-facility and borrowing rules in sections 111.1–111.6 to rural communities with necessary modifications. It is a single application-scope sentence with no independent rule, so it carries only low independent recall value as a standalone unit.

rows.heading: Licences
rows.groupTitle: Municipal licensing by-law powers (s. 112)
rows.groupReason: All seven paragraphs are permissions granted to the municipality under the same trigger; recalling them as a complete set of licensing by-law powers is the natural recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the seven powers a municipality may exercise in a licensing by-law, including the fee cap in paragraph (b) and the delegation and information-gathering powers in paragraphs (f) and (g).

evidenceText: prohibit the doing without a licence of anything for which a licence is required
prescribe licence fees not exceeding the maximum fee established in this Act or prescribed by regulation for the licence

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 112 is a single enumerated list of seven municipal licensing by-law powers sharing one trigger, one actor, and one modality; the full list answers the recall task 'what may a municipality do in a licensing by-law?'

rows.heading: Licences
rows.groupTitle: Territorial Scope of Municipal Licensing By-laws
rows.groupReason: Single rule: licensing by-law applies regardless of partial out-of-municipality operation or absence of a local place of business.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that a municipal licensing by-law applies to a person even where the business operates partly outside the municipality and even where the person does not occupy or use a place of business in the municipality.

evidenceText: A by-law for the licensing of persons carrying on or engaged in a business applies to a person whether or not
he carries on or engages in such business partly within and partly outside the municipality

rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained rule on the territorial reach of municipal licensing by-laws; one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Licences
rows.groupTitle: Licence without examination for certificate holders
rows.groupReason: Single entitlement rule with two alternative certificate triggers (NB apprenticeship certificate or out-of-province certificate with Interprovincial Standards Seal) and one fee condition forming one recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two certificate types that entitle a person to a municipal trade licence without examination and the condition that must also be met.

evidenceText: is entitled, upon payment of the prescribed fee, to be issued a licence without examination.

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent entitlement rule: two alternative certificate conditions and a fee condition all serve the same recall task—identifying who gets a licence without examination.

rows.heading: Licences
rows.groupTitle: Offences by by-law licence holders (s. 115)
rows.groupReason: Both sub-paragraphs are alternative grounds for the same offence carrying the same penalty, forming one recallable unit on licence-holder offences.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two acts by which a by-law licence holder commits a category B offence under Part II of the Provincial Offences Procedure Act and the actors who may require production of the licence.

evidenceText: fails without reasonable excuse to produce his licence when required to do so by a peace officer or a judge of the Provincial Court
breaks any condition of his licence by an act which is not itself punishable
commits an offence punishable under Part II of the Provincial Offences Procedure Act as a category B offence

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 115 is a short, self-contained offence provision creating two alternative grounds for a single category B offence by a by-law licence holder, with one shared penalty.

rows.heading: Licences
rows.groupTitle: Municipal licence precondition: production and recording of provincial licence
rows.groupReason: The prohibition, invalidity consequence, and recording requirement are one tightly interdependent licensing rule; recalling them separately would fragment a single concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the precondition that a provincial licence must be produced before a municipal licence is issued, the invalidity of a municipal licence issued without it, and the obligation to record the production on the municipal licence.

evidenceText: No municipality or officer of a municipality shall issue a licence to a person who is required by law to obtain a provincial licence for the same purpose until the applicant has first produced the proper provincial licence and no municipal licence issued without such production is valid.
A municipal licence issued in such case shall state the fact that the licensee has produced his provincial licence.

rows.sourceMapReason: Both subsections form one interdependent licensing rule: the prohibition and invalidity consequence in 116(1) and the recording duty in 116(2) are needed together to recall the complete municipal licensing precondition when a provincial licence applies.

rows.heading: Power of municipality respecting local improvements
rows.groupTitle: Services a municipality may undertake as a local improvement
rows.groupReason: The four enumerated services, the authorization condition, and the resulting local-improvement power form one tightly interdependent rule answering a single recall question.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the four services (sewerage, sidewalks, roads and streets, water) a municipality may undertake as a local improvement under this part, and the condition that the municipality must be authorized to provide the service.

evidenceText: Where a municipality is authorized to provide any of the following services: (a) sewerage; (b) sidewalks; (c) roads and streets; or (d) water; it may undertake the provision of such service as a local improvement under this part.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single short provision stating the four services a municipality may undertake as a local improvement, conditional on the municipality being authorized to provide the service. One coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Part definitions – local improvements vocabulary
rows.groupReason: All active part-scoped definitions are interdependent (e.g. 'frontage' references 'work'; cost portions reference 'abutting parcel') and answer one recall task: the vocabulary that governs the local-improvements scheme.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Define the key terms governing local improvements under the Municipalities Act, including the scope of 'work' and 'street,' the cost-allocation portions, and the 'owner' and 'value' definitions.

evidenceText: “work” means a work that may be undertaken as a local improvement.
“municipality’s portion of the cost” means that part or proportion of the cost of a work which is not to be specially assessed
“owners’ portion of the cost” means that part or proportion of the cost of a work that is to be specially assessed upon abutting parcels

rows.sourceMapReason: Single part-scoped definitions section establishing the coherent vocabulary for the local-improvements scheme; all active terms interlock and form one study set.

rows.heading: Power of council to authorize work
rows.groupTitle: Classes of work a council may authorize as a local improvement
rows.groupReason: Subsection (1) enumerates the four classes and subsection (2) sets the combining rule; together they define the full scope of the council's local-improvement authorization power as one recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the four classes of work a council may authorize as a local improvement under s. 119(1) and the rule in s. 119(2) that two or more classes may be undertaken as one work.

evidenceText: The council may, subject to this part, authorize any work of the following classes to be undertaken as a local improvement
Work of two or more of the classes mentioned in subsection (1) may be undertaken as one work.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 119 grants the council a specific authorization power over four enumerated classes of local improvement work and adds a combining rule; both subsections form one coherent scope-and-combination concept.

rows.heading: Local improvements before paving of street
rows.groupTitle: Cost certification, conclusive evidence, owner liability, lien, and cost calculation basis
rows.groupReason: Subsections (4)–(6) and (8) form one interdependent chain: the engineer certifies cost calculated per subsection (8), the certificate is conclusive evidence, and on filing the cost becomes a payable lien on the owner's parcel.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain who must certify the cost, what the certificate must show, the cost calculation basis (centre of street to street line), the conclusive-evidence effect, and the point at which the cost becomes a lien on the abutting parcel.

evidenceText: The municipal engineer or person designated by the council, upon the completion of the work, shall determine the cost of the drain connections made, water service pipes laid and stop-cocks installed under the preceding subsections, and shall file with the clerk a certificate
The certificate referred to in subsection (4) is conclusive evidence of such cost and of the amount payable by the owner.

The cost of such drain connections, water service pipes and stop-cocks, as certified under subsection (4) shall on the filing of such certificate become payable by the owner of the parcel for or to which it was made, laid or installed, and shall constitute a lien upon such parcel.

The cost as shown by the certificate under subsection (4) shall be the actual or estimated cost of making drain connections or laying water service pipes from the centre of the street to the street line whether or not the sewer or water main is laid in the centre of the street.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 120 contains three distinct recall tasks: the council's permissive power to direct utility connections in three infrastructure contexts, the cost-certification-and-liability mechanism (certification, conclusive evidence, owner payable obligation, lien, and cost calculation basis), and the municipality's separate recovery-by-suit power with a specific interest rate and trigger period.

rows.heading: Local improvements before paving of street
rows.groupTitle: Council's power to direct utility connections before paving or during sewer and water-main work
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(3) share one actor (council), one modality (may by resolution direct), and apply the same power to three infrastructure triggers (paving, domestic sewer construction, water-main construction).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the circumstances under which a council may by resolution direct drain connections, water service pipes, stop-cocks, and alterations, and the specific items directed in each of the three infrastructure contexts.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 120 contains three distinct recall tasks: the council's permissive power to direct utility connections in three infrastructure contexts, the cost-certification-and-liability mechanism (certification, conclusive evidence, owner payable obligation, lien, and cost calculation basis), and the municipality's separate recovery-by-suit power with a specific interest rate and trigger period.

rows.heading: Local improvements before paving of street
rows.groupTitle: Municipal recovery by suit with six per cent interest after ninety days
rows.groupReason: Subsection (7) creates a distinct enforcement right: a separate actor (municipality as plaintiff), a separate trigger (non-payment), a specific court action, and a defined interest rate and accrual period not stated elsewhere in the section.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the municipality's right to recover the certified cost by suit, the applicable interest rate, and the date from which interest begins to accrue.

evidenceText: Such cost may be recovered by the municipality by suit in any court of competent jurisdiction from the owner, together with interest at the rate of six per cent per annum from the expiration of ninety days after the completion of the work as evidenced by the certificate under subsection (4).

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 120 contains three distinct recall tasks: the council's permissive power to direct utility connections in three infrastructure contexts, the cost-certification-and-liability mechanism (certification, conclusive evidence, owner payable obligation, lien, and cost calculation basis), and the municipality's separate recovery-by-suit power with a specific interest rate and trigger period.

rows.heading: What cost deemed to include respecting work
rows.groupTitle: Cost of a work: deemed inclusions
rows.groupReason: All five enumerated items answer the single question of what the cost of a work is deemed to include.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the five categories of cost deemed to be included in the cost of a work under section 121 of the Municipalities Act.

evidenceText: The cost of a work is deemed to include:
the compensation for lands taken for the purpose of the work or injuriously affected by it and the expenses incurred by the municipality in connection with determining such compensation
the interest on all borrowings in connection with such work and any expenses incidental to the entering on, carrying out and completing the work and raising the money to pay the cost thereof

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 121 is a single definitional rule listing five categories that constitute the cost of a work; all items answer one recall question and form one coherent concept.

rows.heading: Special frontage assessment
rows.groupTitle: Petition-based special frontage assessment procedure
rows.groupReason: All four subsections describe one procedural sequence: petition sufficiency, council by-law vote and content, three-year window, and partial-work limitation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the petition thresholds (two-thirds in number and one-half in value of abutting parcels), the two-thirds whole-council vote, the by-law's dual functions of authorizing work and ordering cost by special frontage assessment, the three-year undertaking window, and the requirement that a petition be sufficient for any partial work undertaken.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 122 sets out the complete petition-based pathway for special frontage assessment: petition thresholds, council by-law requirements, time limit, and partial-work restriction all form one interdependent procedure.

rows.heading: Special frontage assessment
rows.groupTitle: Council-initiated special frontage assessment procedure
rows.groupReason: The notice publication requirements, owner petition threshold, council by-law voting and timing conditions, and the one-year re-notice bar after a sufficient petition form one interdependent procedural mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the publication requirements for the council's notice of intention, the threshold for a sufficient owner petition against the work, the by-law voting and timing conditions under which the council may authorize the work and order special frontage assessment, and the one-year bar on issuing a second notice after a sufficient petition is filed.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 123 describes the complete council-initiated special frontage assessment procedure—notice publication, owner petition threshold, council by-law voting and timing, and the one-year re-notice bar—as one interdependent procedural sequence.

rows.heading: Special frontage assessment
rows.groupTitle: Council override of petition by unanimous vote — special frontage assessment
rows.groupReason: The override trigger (sufficient petition), the elevated vote threshold (unanimous whole council), and the three operative by-law components form one integrated recall task distinct from the standard two-thirds process in s. 123.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a council may proceed with a special frontage assessment over a sufficient petition, including the unanimous vote requirement and the three components the by-law must contain.

evidenceText: Notwithstanding that a sufficient petition is presented against a proposed work
order that the cost thereof or such portion of the cost as may be fixed by a general by-law shall be raised by special frontage assessment

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 124 is a short, self-contained override rule: despite a sufficient petition, the council may proceed by unanimous vote, declaring necessity, authorizing the work, and ordering special frontage assessment. The three sub-parts are tightly interlocked components of one procedural mechanism and form a single recallable concept distinct from the standard process in section 123.

rows.heading: Order respecting water or sewerage work
rows.groupTitle: Council procedure for Minister of Health water or sewerage work orders
rows.groupReason: All three subsections apply to the single trigger of a Minister of Health order for water/sewerage work and form one recall task covering publication, notice content, and the council's override power.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the notice publication requirements (weekly for two consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation, form by by-law, statement of Health Act order) and the council's power to proceed by by-law notwithstanding a petition, including the majority-vote threshold and the three required by-law actions.

evidenceText: Where the Minister of Health under authority of the Health Act orders changes or additions to be made to an existing system of water works, sewers or sewage disposal by the municipality the council may on its own initiative cause a notice of its intention to undertake any work ordered by the Minister of Health and specified in paragraph 119(1)(d) to be published once a week for two consecutive weeks
the council may by by-law passed by the affirmative vote of a majority of the council present at any regular meeting or at any special meeting called for the purpose

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 125 addresses one coherent procedural scenario: the council's steps when the Minister of Health orders water or sewerage work. The three subsections form a single sequence (notice publication, notice content, and the council's by-law power notwithstanding a petition) tied to that one trigger.

rows.heading: Petition respecting support for or opposition to work
rows.groupTitle: Filing, sufficiency, and finality of petitions for or against municipal works
rows.groupReason: All four subsections form one sequential petition procedure (file with clerk, clerk determines sufficiency conclusively, joint-ownership concurrence requirement, no withdrawal after sufficiency) that operates as a single recallable unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the filing requirement, the clerk's conclusive sufficiency determination, the majority-in-interest concurrence rule for co-owners of an abutting parcel, and the prohibition on withdrawing a name after sufficiency is determined.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 126 is a short, self-contained procedural rule set governing the petition process for municipal works: filing, clerk's conclusive sufficiency determination, joint-ownership eligibility, and post-determination finality. All four subsections form one coherent petition sequence that a learner would recall as a single procedure.

rows.heading: Assessment of work
rows.groupTitle: Exemption from special frontage assessment for purpose-built sewer and water mains
rows.groupReason: Subsections (3) and (6) set out the conditions under which abutting parcels may be exempted from special frontage assessment when a sewer main or water main was constructed solely to serve other properties.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the conditions that must be met for the council to exempt abutting parcels from special frontage assessment where a sewer main or water main was constructed to afford an outlet or water supply to other lands.

evidenceText: a sewer main is constructed along a street or through land in which it would not in the opinion of the council have been constructed except as a means of affording an outlet
a water main is constructed along a street or through land in which it would not in the opinion of the council have been constructed except as a means of affording a water supply

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 127 contains three distinct recall tasks: the general metre-frontage assessment rule with the council's by-law power, exemption conditions for purpose-built sewer and water mains, and the late-connection assessment procedure with accounting treatment.

rows.heading: Assessment of work
rows.groupTitle: General special frontage assessment rule and owners' portion by-law
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(2) state the default rule that the entire cost of a local improvement work is assessed on abutting parcels by an equal special rate per metre frontage, and the council's power to prescribe the owners' portion by general by-law.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the default special frontage assessment rule for local improvement works and identify the council's by-law power to set the owners' portion of the cost.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 127 contains three distinct recall tasks: the general metre-frontage assessment rule with the council's by-law power, exemption conditions for purpose-built sewer and water mains, and the late-connection assessment procedure with accounting treatment.

rows.heading: Assessment of work
rows.groupTitle: Late-connection assessment and accounting for sewer and water mains
rows.groupReason: Subsections (4)–(5) and (7)–(8) provide the procedure for assessing a property connected to a sewer or water main after the initial assessment, the rate to be applied, the clerk's duty to update the roll, and the destination account for collections.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the late-connection assessment procedure for a sewer main or water main, including the council's resolution authority, the applicable rate per metre frontage, the clerk's roll-update duty, the s. 135 mutatis mutandis reference, and the accounting treatment of collections.

evidenceText: the council may by resolution order that such lot or parcel of land shall be assessed by a special frontage assessment at the same rate per metre frontage as was assessed against the lands actually abutting

the clerk shall add to the local improvement assessment roll for the work, the name of the owner of each parcel of land when connected with the sewer main and the provisions of section 135 apply mutatis mutandis

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 127 contains three distinct recall tasks: the general metre-frontage assessment rule with the council's by-law power, exemption conditions for purpose-built sewer and water mains, and the late-connection assessment procedure with accounting treatment.

rows.heading: Assessment respecting sidewalk or curbing
rows.groupTitle: Sidewalk and curbing assessment allocation
rows.groupReason: Default one-sided assessment rule and the petition-based both-sided exception operate as a single rule/exception pair for sidewalk or curbing works.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the default assessment side for sidewalk or curbing works and identify the petition conditions under which the council may spread the cost to owners on both sides of the street.

evidenceText: only the abutting parcels on that side of the street upon which the work is constructed shall be specially assessed

where a petition to the council praying that a sidewalk be constructed on one side of a street only, is made by the owners of abutting parcels on both sides of the street or the portion thereof on which the sidewalk is proposed to be constructed, the council may order that the cost of the work shall be borne by the owners of abutting parcels on both sides of the street

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 128 states one coherent assessment rule for sidewalks and curbing: default one-sided allocation with a petition-triggered exception permitting both-sided cost sharing. The rule and its exception form a single recallable unit.

rows.heading: Estimate respecting special frontage assessment
rows.groupTitle: Council estimation duty and default instalment payment for special frontage assessment
rows.groupReason: Both subsections state the council's cost-estimation and by-law fixation duty plus the resulting equal-annual-instalment default, forming one recallable estimation-and-payment rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the council's duty to estimate work cost and fix the number of annual instalments by by-law, and the default rule that the owners' portion is paid in equal annual instalments over the fixed term.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 129 imposes two council duties (estimate cost, fix instalments by by-law) and sets the default equal-annual-instalment payment rule; both subsections form one cohesive estimation-and-payment concept with independent study value.

rows.heading: Assessment of lots or parcels
rows.groupTitle: Special frontage assessment: general metre-frontage rule and reduction grounds
rows.groupReason: The general rule and the three distinct reduction grounds (corner/irregular lots, lots unfit for building, unneeded works) form one coherent recall task: identifying when a special frontage assessment is reduced.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the general metre-frontage assessment rule and identify the three specific grounds on which a reduction in special frontage assessment is required.

evidenceText: every abutting parcel shall be assessed according to its actual metre frontage

a reduction shall be made in the special frontage assessment that otherwise would be chargeable thereon sufficient, having regard to the situation, value and superficial area of such lots as compared with the other lots, to adjust the assessment on a fair and equitable basis
Where a lot is for any reason wholly or in part unfit for building purposes a reduction shall be made

Where a lot, other than a corner lot, has two limits that abut on works and the size or nature of the lot is such that any or all the works are not required, a reduction in respect of the works that are not required

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 130 pairs a general rule with three parallel reduction grounds (130(1)–(4)) and a separate implementation block covering calculation method, municipal financing of the reduction, and the clerk's role (130(5)–(7)). The two halves answer distinct recall questions: when a reduction applies versus how it is calculated, financed, and administered.

rows.heading: Assessment of lots or parcels
rows.groupTitle: Method, municipal financing, and administration of frontage assessment reductions
rows.groupReason: Subsections 130(5)–(7) address how a reduction is mechanically calculated, that the municipality bears the reduction cost and the roll-entry treatment, and that the clerk administers the reduction — distinct from the grounds themselves.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how a frontage assessment reduction is calculated by frontage deduction, that the municipality (not abutting lots) bears the reduction cost on the roll, and that the clerk makes the reduction.

evidenceText: The reduction shall be made by deducting from the total frontage of the lot liable to special frontage assessment so much thereof as is sufficient to make the proper reduction, but the whole of the lot shall be charged with the special frontage assessment as so reduced

The amount of any reduction made in the assessment of any lot under the provisions of this section shall not be chargeable upon the lots liable to special frontage assessment but shall be paid by the municipality and shall be entered on the local improvement assessment roll as if the municipality were the owner of the frontage so deducted
A reduction under the provisions of this section shall be made by the clerk

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 130 pairs a general rule with three parallel reduction grounds (130(1)–(4)) and a separate implementation block covering calculation method, municipal financing of the reduction, and the clerk's role (130(5)–(7)). The two halves answer distinct recall questions: when a reduction applies versus how it is calculated, financed, and administered.

rows.heading: Calculation of total metre frontage
rows.groupTitle: Calculation of total metre frontage for special frontage assessment
rows.groupReason: One formula with one recall task: how total metre frontage is assembled from reduced and actual frontage components.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the formula for total metre frontage: reduced metre frontage of parcels under s.130 plus actual metre frontage of all other abutting parcels.

evidenceText: The total metre frontage of the abutting parcels to be assessed shall be determined by adding the reduced metre frontage of abutting parcels as determined pursuant to section 130, to the actual metre frontage of every other abutting parcel.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 131 is a single, self-contained formula for calculating total metre frontage that directly feeds the s.132 rate calculation. It has independent recall value distinct from the s.130 reduction rules and the s.132 division rule.

rows.heading: Removal of obstructions
