rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when a Survey Plan must be prepared after boundary monumentation, the applicable Standards Manual section, and the two conditions under which the requirement is excused.

evidenceText: All surveys that result in monuments being placed shall have a Survey Plan prepared according to Section G - 4 of the Standards Manual.

The exception to this is when the placed monumentation is in compliance with existing coordinated plans that are: a) referenced to the ANBLS Plan Validation Database, or b) registered in the Registry Office or Land Titles Office for the Province of New Brunswick.

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent duty-with-exception rule: when a Survey Plan is required after monumentation, the governing standard (G-4), and the narrow exception for compliant coordinated plans.

rows.heading: Application
rows.groupTitle: Application: Preservation of Existing Mining Rights and Supersession of the Expropriation Act
rows.groupReason: Both subsections together state the limits of the Act's operation: 2(1) preserves pre-existing mining rights under two other statutes, and 2(2) establishes priority over the Expropriation Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify which existing mining rights are preserved from orders under the Ownership of Minerals Act and which prior statute the Act supersedes.

evidenceText: No order made under this Act shall be construed to affect any mining licence or lease made or issued under An Act Respecting the Encouragement of the Discovery and Development of Oil and Natural Gas
This Act supersedes the Expropriation Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 2 contains two short application provisions that together define the Act's boundary of operation: preservation of existing mining rights and statutory supersession of the Expropriation Act.

rows.heading: Power of Cabinet to make orders
rows.groupTitle: Compensation and claims powers for mineral orders
rows.groupReason: Sub-paragraphs (e) and (f) form the compensation framework: the power to determine that compensation will be paid and its amount, and the power to set procedural terms for making claims or receiving compensation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Lieutenant-Governor in Council's power to provide for compensation to persons suffering loss or damage from an order under the Act, to set the amount, and to prescribe the terms and conditions for making a claim or receiving compensation.

evidenceText: to provide for compensation to persons sustaining loss or damage by reason of any order made under this Act and the amount of compensation
to prescribe the terms and conditions under which any claim may be made, or compensation may be made, for loss or damage sustained by reason of any order made under this Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3 grants the Lieutenant-Governor in Council a broad delegated power with three independently recallable legal effects: the core mineral-ownership powers (severance, vesting, retrospectivity, grant deeming), a separate compensation-and-claims framework, and a specific exclusive prospecting right for fee-simple owners. These create distinct recall tasks and should be tested separately.

rows.heading: Power of Cabinet to make orders
rows.groupTitle: Crown mineral ownership powers and scope of orders
rows.groupReason: Sub-paragraphs (a) through (d) and 3(2) establish the Lieutenant-Governor in Council's power to sever minerals from soil, vest them in the Crown, fix retrospective effective dates, deem all prior Crown grants to have reserved minerals, and issue orders of particular or general application.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the specific powers the Lieutenant-Governor in Council holds to declare minerals separate from soil, vest them in the Crown, give orders retrospective effect, deem prior Crown grants to have reserved minerals, and make orders particular or general in application.

evidenceText: to declare all or any minerals, whether owned by the Crown or by any other person, existing in a natural state beneath the surface of the land anywhere in the Province, or in any designated area in the Province, to be property separate from the soil
to vest in the Crown in right of the Province all or any of the minerals referred to in paragraph (a) or any part of them
to fix the effective date of any order made under paragraph (a) or (b) and for that purpose to give the order retrospective effect
to declare that every grant of land from the Crown made at any time previously shall be construed and held to have excepted and reserved to the Crown all the minerals
The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make any order under this Act particular or general in its application.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3 grants the Lieutenant-Governor in Council a broad delegated power with three independently recallable legal effects: the core mineral-ownership powers (severance, vesting, retrospectivity, grant deeming), a separate compensation-and-claims framework, and a specific exclusive prospecting right for fee-simple owners. These create distinct recall tasks and should be tested separately.

rows.heading: Power of Cabinet to make orders
rows.groupTitle: Exclusive prospecting and staking right for fee-simple owners
rows.groupReason: Sub-paragraph (g) grants a distinct, time-limited exclusive right to a specific class (fee-simple owners) for a specific activity (prospecting and staking), independent of the compensation or vesting powers.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may give fee-simple owners an exclusive right, for a minimum of one year, to prospect and stake for minerals taken under the Act on the lands they own.

evidenceText: to give the exclusive right for a period not less than one year as he or she may determine for prospecting and staking for any minerals taken under this Act to the owners in fee simple of the lands under which the minerals lie

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3 grants the Lieutenant-Governor in Council a broad delegated power with three independently recallable legal effects: the core mineral-ownership powers (severance, vesting, retrospectivity, grant deeming), a separate compensation-and-claims framework, and a specific exclusive prospecting right for fee-simple owners. These create distinct recall tasks and should be tested separately.

rows.heading: Effect of orders
rows.groupTitle: Legal Effect of Orders Under the Ownership of Minerals Act
rows.groupReason: One short rule establishing that orders under the Act carry the same legal force as legislation, forming a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the legal effect of an order made under the Ownership of Minerals Act relative to an Act of the Legislature.

evidenceText: Every order made under this Act has the same effect as if embodied in an Act of the Legislature.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 4 states a single, self-contained rule: orders under the Act have the same effect as an Act of the Legislature. This is an independently recallable legal-effect provision distinct from the power-to-make-orders rule in section 3.

rows.heading: Power of Cabinet to grant licence contrary to orders
rows.groupTitle: Cabinet power to grant mining rights despite the Mining Act
rows.groupReason: One conditional power: affected mineral right plus substantial development or expenditure triggers a Cabinet discretion to grant mining rights on its own terms, notwithstanding the Mining Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions a person must show to the Lieutenant-Governor in Council (affected mineral right, development or expenditure, substantiality finding) and the resulting power to grant mining rights on Cabinet-determined terms despite the Mining Act.

evidenceText: If any person shows to the satisfaction of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council that any right that person would have had to any mineral but for an order made under this Act is affected by the order and that that person has developed any such mineral or expended money for or in connection with any such mineral, and the Lieutenant-Governor in Council considers that development or expenditure to be substantial, the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may grant to that person mining rights in respect of the mineral or any part of it, in the manner and on the terms and conditions the Lieutenant-Governor in Council sees fit, despite the Mining Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 5 is a single conditional power provision: three linked showing requirements lead to one Cabinet power to grant mining rights despite the Mining Act. The conditions and the power are tightly interdependent and form one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Power to enter into agreements respecting Crown Lands
rows.groupTitle: Crown mineral interest transfer agreements
rows.groupReason: Single permissive power with one trigger condition and two symmetric transfer directions forming one recall concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the condition under which the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may enter into a mineral interest transfer agreement and the two permitted directions of transfer.

evidenceText: the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may enter into an agreement with that person for the transfer of the Crown's interest to that person or for the transfer to the Crown of that person's interest.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short operative section granting the Lieutenant-Governor in Council a permissive power to negotiate mineral interest transfers when Crown and another person hold overlapping interests; one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Compensation
rows.groupTitle: Compensation paid from the Consolidated Fund
rows.groupReason: One payment rule: all Act-awarded compensation and agreement-based payments are funded from the Consolidated Fund.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that money compensation awarded under the Ownership of Minerals Act or money payable under an agreement made under the Act is paid out of the Consolidated Fund.

evidenceText: Any money compensation awarded under this Act or money payable under an agreement made under this Act shall be paid out of the Consolidated Fund.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 7 is a single payment rule specifying the Consolidated Fund as the source for all compensation and agreement-based payments under the Act. It constitutes one independently recallable funding obligation.

rows.heading: Immunity
rows.groupTitle: Crown immunity for orders under the Ownership of Minerals Act and its two exceptions
rows.groupReason: General immunity rule and its two dependent exceptions form one interdependent recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the general rule of Crown immunity for orders and actions under the Act and identify the two specific exceptions: compensation awarded under section 3(1) and breach of an agreement made under section 6.

evidenceText: No action lies against the Crown for any order made under this Act or anything done under any such order except for compensation awarded under section 3(1) or for breach of an agreement made under section 6.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single immunity rule with two tightly linked carve-outs; recalling the rule and its exceptions separately would fragment one coherent concept.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Official Languages Act – Defined Terms and Scope
rows.groupReason: The definitions collectively define who is bound by the Act and what key terms mean; they form one coherent scope-setting unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall which entities qualify as an "institution" under the Act and identify the key defined terms (court, Crown corporation, linguistic community, official languages, peace officer) that determine the Act's scope.

evidenceText: "institution" means an institution of the Legislative Assembly or the Government of New Brunswick, the courts, any board, commission or council, or other body or office, established to perform a governmental function

"linguistic community" means either of the English linguistic community or the French linguistic community of New Brunswick within the meaning of section 16.1 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
"court" means any court or administrative tribunal in the Province

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 1 is a self-contained definitions provision that establishes the scope and key terms of the Official Languages Act; it does not impose duties but defines the entities and concepts the Act's operative sections rely on.

rows.heading: Purpose
rows.groupTitle: Purpose of the Official Languages Act (s. 1.1)
rows.groupReason: The three purposes are interdependent parts of a single legislative-intent statement and form one coherent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the three stated purposes of the Official Languages Act regarding respect for both languages, equality of status in institutions, and the setting out of institutional powers and duties.

evidenceText: to ensure respect for English and French as the official languages of New Brunswick;
to ensure that English and French have equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all institutions of the Province;
to set out the powers and duties of the institutions of the Province with respect to the two official languages.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 1.1 is a short, self-contained purpose statement with three interdependent objectives that together answer one recall question about the Act's founding rationale. It provides interpretive context for the entire Official Languages Act but does not itself create an operative duty, procedure, or power.

rows.heading: Act prevails, exception
rows.groupTitle: Act prevails over conflicting legislation, with exception for linguistic-equality measures
rows.groupReason: The supremacy rule and its exception are one interdependent concept; a learner must recall both to know when the Act prevails and when a competing measure is carved out.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the Official Languages Act prevails over any conflicting act or regulation, and identify the exception for the Education Act and any other measure that promotes equality of the two linguistic communities or establishes distinct educational or cultural institutions.

evidenceText: No act, or regulation under it, other than this Act, shall be interpreted so as to repeal, limit or contravene a provision of this Act and, in case of conflict, this Act prevails.

Subsection (1) does not apply to the Education Act or any other act, legislative provision or measure which promotes the equality of the two linguistic communities or establishes distinct educational institutions or distinct cultural institutions.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3 states a short supremacy rule in (1) with a directly dependent exception in (2); the two subsections form one interdependent rule/exception pair best recalled together.

rows.heading: Distinct institutions
rows.groupTitle: Exclusion of distinct educational and cultural institutions from the 'institution' definition
rows.groupReason: One coherent scoping rule: an exclusion with an illustrative list, all serving the single concept of what falls outside the Act's 'institution' definition.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the categories of distinct educational and cultural institutions (including the illustrative school-system and university list) that section 4 excludes from the section 1 definition of 'institution' in the Official Languages Act.

evidenceText: Distinct educational institutions and distinct cultural institutions and, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the school system in New Brunswick including the English and French sections of the Department of Education and Early Childhood Development including schools and their committees, councils and boards, community centres and universities and, where applicable, community colleges are not included in the definition of “institution” in section 1.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 4 is a single definitional exclusion removing distinct educational and cultural institutions from the section 1 'institution' definition, creating a clear scoping rule with independent recall value.

rows.heading: Secretariat of Official Languages
rows.groupTitle: Secretariat of Official Languages: Establishment and Duties
rows.groupReason: The establishment clause and the seven enumerated duties (a)–(g) form one recallable unit: what the Secretariat is and what it shall do.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Secretariat of Official Languages, its placement within the Department of Intergovernmental Affairs, and recall its seven enumerated duties from implementation-plan support through Premier-assigned tasks.

evidenceText: There is established a secretariat within the Department of Intergovernmental Affairs called the Secretariat of Official Languages

rows.sourceMapReason: One institution with a single coherent list of seven duties; all answer the same recall question about the Secretariat's establishment and responsibilities.

rows.heading: Implementation plan
rows.groupTitle: Required contents of the Province's implementation plan
rows.groupReason: The seven enumerated elements (a)–(g) form a substantial, independently recallable list of mandatory plan contents distinct from the governance structure that follows.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the seven elements the Province's implementation plan must include under section 5.1(1).

evidenceText: The Province shall prepare a plan setting out how it will meet its obligations under this Act, and the plan shall include the following:
performance measures for evaluating the effectiveness of the measures implemented under the plan and time frames within which they must be implemented

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 5.1 contains two distinct recall tasks: the seven mandatory contents of the Province's plan and the multi-tier coordination and reporting chain assigning duties to the Premier and each portion of the public service.

rows.heading: Implementation plan
rows.groupTitle: Implementation coordination and annual reporting chain
rows.groupReason: Subsections (2)–(5) assign distinct duties to the Premier and each portion of the public service in a sequential coordination and annual reporting chain that is best recalled as one connected structure.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the Premier's coordination role, the departmental action-plan duty, and the annual reporting sequence from each portion of the public service through the Premier to the Legislative Assembly.

evidenceText: The Premier is responsible for ensuring central government coordination and oversight of the implementation of the plan
each portion of the public service shall submit a report to the Premier with respect to the activities under its action plan
the Premier shall submit a report to the Legislative Assembly with respect to the activities under the plan

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 5.1 contains two distinct recall tasks: the seven mandatory contents of the Province's plan and the multi-tier coordination and reporting chain assigning duties to the Premier and each portion of the public service.

rows.heading: Language of the Legislature
rows.groupTitle: Official Languages of the Legislature and Right to Use Either
rows.groupReason: One tightly coupled rule: the bilingual declaration grounds the individual right to use either language in Legislative Assembly and committee proceedings.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the official languages of the Legislature and the right of everyone to use either language in any debate or other proceeding of the Legislative Assembly or its committees.

evidenceText: English and French are the official languages of the Legislature and everyone has the right to use either language in any debate and other proceeding of the Legislative Assembly or its committees.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 is a short, self-contained provision declaring the official languages of the Legislature and granting the right to use either in Assembly and committee proceedings. The declaration and the right are tightly interdependent and form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Interpretation of proceedings of the Legislative Assembly
rows.groupTitle: Duty to provide simultaneous interpretation in the Legislative Assembly
rows.groupReason: One operative duty: the Legislature shall make simultaneous interpretation of debates and other proceedings available.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that section 7 requires the Legislature to make simultaneous interpretation of the debates and other proceedings of the Legislative Assembly available.

evidenceText: Simultaneous interpretation of the debates and other proceedings of the Legislative Assembly shall be made available by the Legislature.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single-sentence provision imposing one clear duty on the Legislature to provide simultaneous interpretation of Legislative Assembly proceedings; independently recallable as a standalone obligation.

rows.heading: Records and journals of the Legislative Assembly
rows.groupTitle: Bilingual Publication and Equal Authority of Legislative Assembly Records
rows.groupReason: The provision creates one coherent recall task: what must be printed in both languages and the equal-authority consequence.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the records, journals, and reports of the Legislative Assembly and its committees shall be printed and published in English and French, and that both language versions are equally authoritative.

evidenceText: The records, journals and reports of the Legislative Assembly and its committees shall be printed and published in English and French and both language versions are equally authoritative.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 8 is a single operative sentence imposing a bilingual-publication duty on Legislative Assembly records, journals, and reports and stating the equal-authority effect; it is self-contained and needs no combine or split.

rows.heading: Equal authority of both language versions
rows.groupTitle: Equal authority of English and French legislation versions
rows.groupReason: States the single operative rule that both language versions of legislation carry equal legal authority.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the English and French versions of legislation are equally authoritative under the Official Languages Act.
rows.sourceMapReason: Single-sentence provision stating the equal-authority principle for bilingual legislation; one independently recallable legal rule with no sub-parts to split.

rows.heading: Introduction of bills
rows.groupTitle: Simultaneous bilingual introduction, adoption, and assent of bills
rows.groupReason: All three legislative stages (introduction, adoption, assent) are governed by the same simultaneity requirement in both official languages and answer a single recall question.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the requirement that bills must be simultaneously introduced in both official languages before the Legislative Assembly and simultaneously adopted and assented to in both official languages.

evidenceText: Bills shall be simultaneously introduced in both official languages before the Legislative Assembly and shall be simultaneously adopted and assented to in both official languages.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 11 states one coherent procedural rule: bills must be simultaneously introduced, adopted, and assented to in both official languages. The three stages share a single subject, modifier, and legal modality, forming one recallable obligation.

rows.heading: Acts of the Legislature
rows.groupTitle: Co-drafting and publication of Acts in both official languages
rows.groupReason: One shall-duty governing the form and production of enacted legislation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the requirement that Acts of the Legislature be co-drafted, printed, and published in both official languages under section 12 of the Official Languages Act.
rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative obligation: Acts of the Legislature shall be co-drafted, printed, and published in both official languages. One actor, one duty, one recall task.

rows.heading: Required publication in The Royal Gazette
rows.groupTitle: Bilingual publication of rules, orders, Orders-in-Council, and proclamations in The Royal Gazette
rows.groupReason: One rule, one duty, one venue; no internal subdivisions warranting a split.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the documents that must be printed and published in both official languages when required to appear in The Royal Gazette.
rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative duty requiring bilingual publication of specific government instruments in The Royal Gazette; independently recallable and distinct from adjacent sections covering other document categories.

rows.heading: Official documents
rows.groupTitle: Bilingual publication duty for official notices and announcements
rows.groupReason: One operative rule covering three document categories with a single modality (mandatory bilingual publication), best recalled as one unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the categories of official documents (notices, advertisements, and other announcements of an official nature) that must be printed and published in both official languages, and state that this duty applies whether or not publication in The Royal Gazette is required.

evidenceText: Notices, advertisements and other announcements of an official nature, whether required to be published in The Royal Gazette or not, shall be printed and published in both official languages.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 14 is a single, self-contained duty: official-nature notices, advertisements, and other announcements must be printed and published in both official languages, whether or not required in The Royal Gazette. It creates one clear recall task and needs no other provision to be understood.

rows.heading: Documents published under an Act of the Province
rows.groupTitle: Bilingual publication of documents required under an Act
rows.groupReason: One operative duty with identifiable scope, legislative trigger, and obligated actors forming a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the bilingual-publication obligation in section 15, including the scope of documents covered, the legislative trigger, and the actors on whom the duty falls.

evidenceText: Notices, announcements and other documents required to be published under this Act or any other Act by the Province or its institutions shall be printed and published in both official languages.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 15 imposes a single, self-contained bilingual-publication duty on the Province and its institutions for documents required to be published under legislation. It is distinct from section 14's broader official-announcements duty and needs no split.

rows.heading: Language of the courts
rows.groupTitle: Official languages of the courts
rows.groupReason: A single-sentence declarative rule establishing the bilingual framework for all courts; independently recallable as a distinct legal statement.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that English and French are the official languages of the courts under the Official Languages Act.

evidenceText: English and French are the official languages of the courts.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 16 is a single declarative legal rule stating the official languages of the courts. It is independently recallable as a foundational framework statement for court language rights and has clear, unambiguous scope.

rows.heading: Right to use language of choice
rows.groupTitle: Right to use language of choice in court matters
rows.groupReason: Creates one affirmative right with a defined scope covering proceedings, pleadings, and process before courts and administrative tribunals.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the language right in section 17, the persons to whom it applies, and the scope of court matters it covers, including the meaning of 'court' under section 1.

evidenceText: Every person has the right to use the official language of his or her choice in any matter before the courts, including all proceedings, or in any pleading or process issuing from a court.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained affirmative right with a single scope; no internal sub-structure requiring a split.

rows.heading: Person not to be disadvantaged by choice
rows.groupTitle: Right to use chosen official language in court and protection against disadvantage
rows.groupReason: The right to use a chosen official language in court (s.17) and the prohibition on disadvantaging a person for exercising that choice (s.18) are tightly interdependent and answer one recall question about the language-of-choice right and its guarantee.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the right to use a chosen official language in any court matter (s.17) and the prohibition on placing a person at a disadvantage by reason of exercising that choice (s.18).

evidenceText: Every person has the right to use the official language of his or her choice in any matter before the courts, including all proceedings, or in any pleading or process issuing from a court.
No person shall be placed at a disadvantage by reason of the choice made under section 17.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 18 is a single-sentence prohibition whose sole operative reference is 'the choice made under section 17.' It is the non-disadvantage guarantee attached to the language-of-choice right, and the two sections together form one recallable concept: the right and its protective guarantee.

rows.heading: Obligation placed on the court to understand language chosen
rows.groupTitle: Court's obligation to understand the language chosen by the parties
rows.groupReason: Both subsections state the court's comprehension duty; 19(2) is the specific application of 19(1) when parties choose different languages, so they are recalled together as one obligation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the court's obligation under section 19 to understand, without an interpreter or translation process, the official language chosen by a party, and the extension of that obligation to both official languages when the parties choose different languages.

evidenceText: A court before which a matter is pending must understand, without the assistance of an interpreter or any process of simultaneous translation or consecutive interpretation, the official language chosen under section 17 by a party to the matter.

A court before which a matter is pending must understand both official languages, without the assistance of an interpreter or any process of simultaneous translation or consecutive interpretation, if both English and French are the languages chosen by the parties to the proceedings.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19 imposes a clear, operative duty on courts to understand the chosen language without an interpreter; subsections (1) and (2) form one interdependent rule (base obligation and its extension when both parties choose different languages) that a learner recalls as a single concept.

rows.heading: Accused’s right to be heard in the language of choice
rows.groupTitle: Accused's right to proceedings in chosen language and judge's duty to inform
rows.groupReason: Both subsections define the scope, content, and procedural trigger of the accused's language right as one coherent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the offences to which the accused's language right applies, the two components of that right (proceedings in the chosen language and the court's duty to understand without an interpreter), and the presiding judge's duty to inform the accused before entering a plea.

evidenceText: has the right to have the proceedings conducted in the language of his or her choice and shall be informed of that right by the presiding judge before entering a plea

has the right to be understood by the court, without the assistance of an interpreter or any process of simultaneous translation or consecutive interpretation, in the official language chosen by the person

rows.sourceMapReason: Both subsections address one tightly interdependent concept: the accused's right to use their chosen official language in provincial and municipal offence proceedings, including the judge's duty to inform before plea and the court's obligation to understand the accused without an interpreter.

rows.heading: Rights of the witness
rows.groupTitle: Court's duty to ensure witness is heard in chosen official language
rows.groupReason: The unconditional hearing duty and the request-triggered translation duty are tightly interdependent and form one recallable court obligation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the court's duty to ensure a witness is heard in the official language of the witness's choice and the conditions under which simultaneous translation or consecutive interpretation services must be made available.

evidenceText: Every court has the duty to ensure that any witness appearing before it can be heard in the official language of his or her choice and upon the request of one of the parties or the witness, the court has the duty to ensure that services of simultaneous translation or consecutive interpretation are available to the person who made the request.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single short provision establishing one coherent court duty on witness language rights, with a directly dependent translation mechanism that is meaningless apart from the base duty.

rows.heading: Obligation on the Crown to use language of the parties
rows.groupTitle: Crown's duty to use chosen official language in civil proceedings
rows.groupReason: One actor (Crown in right of the Province or an institution), one trigger (party to civil proceedings before a court), one mandatory duty (shall use the other party's chosen language in oral or written pleadings and court process).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the obligation on the Crown or an institution regarding the official language to be used in pleadings and court process when it is a party to civil proceedings before a court.

evidenceText: the Crown or the institution concerned shall use, in any oral or written pleadings or any process issuing from a court, the official language chosen by the other party

rows.sourceMapReason: Single clear duty on the Crown or an institution to use the other party's chosen official language in civil proceedings; one actor, one trigger, one obligation with no internal sub-parts to separate.

rows.heading: Disagreement between parties as to language of use
rows.groupTitle: Default language rule when private parties fail to agree
rows.groupReason: One trigger (parties other than the Crown or an institution do not choose or fail to agree) produces one duty (Crown/institution uses a reasonable language), forming a single recallable rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the condition under which the Crown or institution selects the language in civil proceedings and the standard it must apply (reasonable, having regard to the circumstances).

evidenceText: the Crown or the institution concerned shall use such official language as is reasonable, having regard to the circumstances

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 23 is a single, self-contained default rule: when private parties to civil proceedings cannot agree on the official language, the Crown or institution must use whatever language is reasonable given the circumstances. It creates one operative duty triggered by one condition and is independently recallable as a distinct scenario from the language-choice rule in section 22.

rows.heading: Publication of decisions
rows.groupTitle: Bilingual publication of court decisions and sequencing exception
rows.groupReason: The general bilingual-publication duty, its two enumerated triggering grounds, and the dependent one-language-first sequencing rule are tightly interdependent and answer one recall question.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two conditions under which a court decision must be published in both official languages and the sequencing rule that applies when simultaneous bilingual publication would cause delay, injustice, or hardship to a party.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 24 contains a single coherent rule: the two triggering conditions for mandatory bilingual publication of court decisions and a directly dependent sequencing exception, forming one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Publication of Court of Appeal decisions
rows.groupTitle: Bilingual publication of court and Court of Appeal decisions
rows.groupReason: Section 25 extends section 24's publication framework to all Court of Appeal decisions; the two sections state one complete bilingual-publication rule for courts.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the criteria under which a final court decision must be published in both official languages and confirm that all Court of Appeal decisions fall within that requirement.

evidenceText: Any final decision, order or judgment of any court, including any reasons given therefor and summaries, shall be published in both official languages where
it determines a question of law of interest or importance to the general public, or

Where a final decision, order or judgment is required to be published under subsection (1), but it is determined that to do so would result in a delay or injustice or hardship to a party to the proceedings
All decisions of the Court of Appeal are deemed to fall within the scope of section 24.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 25 is a single-sentence scope extension that is meaningful only in conjunction with section 24's publication criteria; together they form one recallable rule on bilingual publication of court decisions.

rows.heading: Rendering of a judgment
rows.groupTitle: Rendering of a judgment in either official language
rows.groupReason: The section establishes one rule with a directly dependent validity clarification; splitting would fragment a single concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that sections 24 and 25 do not prevent a judgment and its reasons from being pronounced in either official language, and that such a judgment is not invalid solely for being pronounced in one official language.

evidenceText: Sections 24 and 25 shall not be construed so as to prevent the pronouncement of a judgment, including the reasons in support of the judgment, in either official language
the judgment is not invalid by reason only that it was pronounced in one official language

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 26 is a short, self-contained rule: judgments may be pronounced in either official language and are not invalid for that reason. The construction rule and the non-invalidity clause are tightly interdependent and form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Communications with government and its institutions
rows.groupTitle: Right to communicate in chosen official language
rows.groupReason: Single right provision defining the public's language choice in all dealings with institutions.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the right Section 27 grants members of the public regarding the language in which they may communicate with and receive services from any institution.

evidenceText: Members of the public have the right to communicate with any institution and to receive its services in the official language of their choice.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 27 states a single, self-contained right for members of the public to communicate with and receive services from any institution in the official language of their choice.

rows.heading: Obligations of institutions
rows.groupTitle: Institutional duty to ensure language-of-choice communication and service
rows.groupReason: One actor (institution), one modality (shall ensure), one obligation (enable communication and service in the official language of choice); a single coherent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the duty imposed on an institution regarding the language in which members of the public may communicate with and receive its services.

evidenceText: An institution shall ensure that members of the public are able to communicate with and to receive its services in the official language of their choice.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 28 imposes a single, clear ongoing duty on institutions to ensure public access to communication and services in the official language of choice; it is independently recallable and substantively operative.

rows.groupTitle: Institution's duty to inform the public of language availability
rows.groupReason: One duty on one actor (institution) with one trigger (public-facing services) and one obligation (ensure the public is informed); no internal split is warranted.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the obligation imposed on institutions under section 28.1 regarding informing members of the public that their services are available in the official language of their choice.

evidenceText: An institution shall ensure that appropriate measures are taken to make it known to members of the public that its services are available in the official language of their choice.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 28.1 imposes a single, self-contained duty on institutions to inform the public that services are available in the official language of their choice. It is a distinct recallable obligation (public notification) separate from section 28's substantive availability requirement, and forms one coherent study unit on its own.

rows.heading: Posting of signs and publications intended for the public
rows.groupTitle: Institutional duty to publish in both official languages
rows.groupReason: The entire section is one operative duty with a single actor, trigger, and requirement, forming one recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the obligation imposed on institutions regarding postings, publications, and documents intended for the general public, and identify the required languages.

evidenceText: Institutions shall publish all postings, publications and documents intended for the general public in both official languages.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 29 imposes a single, self-contained duty on institutions to publish all public-facing postings, publications, and documents in both official languages. One actor, one obligation, one scope — no internal structure warrants splitting.

rows.heading: Services provided by third parties
rows.groupTitle: Responsibility for third-party service provider compliance
rows.groupReason: Defines the trigger (engaging a third party) and the duty (ensuring the third party meets sections 27 to 29 obligations), forming one recallable responsibility rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the circumstance that triggers the duty and identify which obligations the Province or institution must ensure a third-party service provider meets.

evidenceText: When the Province or an institution engages a third party to provide a service on its behalf, the Province or the institution, as the case may be, is responsible for ensuring that its obligations under sections 27 to 29 are met by the third party.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative rule: the Province or institution engaging a third party remains responsible for ensuring that party meets the language-service obligations in sections 27 to 29.

rows.heading: Services provided by a peace officer
rows.groupTitle: Language Service Rights and Obligations in Policing (s. 31)
rows.groupReason: One integrated mechanism: the public's right to choose a language, the peace officer's duty to take measures when unable to comply, the police force or agency's duty to ensure means, and the court's consideration of institutional efforts form a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the public's language-choice right when communicating with a peace officer, the peace officer's obligation to take necessary measures within a reasonable time, the police force or agency's duty to ensure means, and the factor a court must consider in assessing compliance.
rows.sourceMapReason: The four subsections form one tightly interdependent service-delivery chain: the public's language right, the peace officer's fallback duty, the institutional means obligation, and the judicial consideration factor all build sequentially on each other.

rows.heading: Application of section 31
rows.groupTitle: Peace officer language service obligations and scope
rows.groupReason: Sections 31 and 32 together define the complete peace officer language service regime: the individual right, the measures and support obligations, the judicial standard, and the non-exhaustive scope.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the public's right to receive language services from a peace officer, the resulting obligations on the officer and the police force or agency, the court's consideration of those efforts, and that section 31 does not limit obligations under other Acts or law.

evidenceText: Members of the public have the right, when communicating with a peace officer, to receive service in the official language of their choice and must be informed of that right.

A police force or agency, as the case may be, shall ensure the availability of the means necessary to respond to the choice made by a member of the public under subsection (1) and to support the obligation placed on a peace officer under subsection (2).
Section 31 does not limit the obligations placed on peace officers under any other Act or law to deliver services to the public in both official languages.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 32 is a one-sentence savings clause titled 'Application of section 31'; it has no standalone recall value apart from the peace officer regime it modifies, so it forms one learning unit with section 31.

rows.heading: Health services
rows.groupTitle: Health services: institutional scope and Minister of Health bilingual-planning duty
rows.groupReason: The scoping definition in 33(1) and the Minister's bilingual-planning obligations in 33(2) form one interdependent recall task on how the Act's institutional obligations apply to health services.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify what 'institution' means for health services under sections 27–28 and state the Minister of Health's two duties when establishing a provincial health plan.

evidenceText: an institution in sections 27 and 28 refers to the network of health establishments, facilities and programs under the jurisdiction of the Department of Health or the regional health authorities under the Regional Health Authorities Act

the Minister of Health shall (a) ensure that the principles upon which the provision of health services are to be based include the delivery of health services in both official languages in the Province, and (b) consider the language of daily operations under section 34

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 33 is a short, coherent provision pairing the health-services redefinition of 'institution' (33(1)) with the Minister of Health's bilingual-planning duty (33(2)); both pieces are needed together to understand the Act's health-services framework.

rows.heading: Effect of section 33
rows.groupTitle: Effect of section 33 on hospital and facility language of daily operations
rows.groupReason: Single rule with one non-limitation and one attached condition; recalling them separately would fragment one concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that section 33 does not limit the use of one official language in the daily operations of a hospital or other facility under the Regional Health Authorities Act, and identify the condition that the public must still be served in the official language of their choice.

evidenceText: section 33 does not limit the use of one official language in the daily operations of a hospital or other facility as defined in the Regional Health Authorities Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 34 states one self-contained rule: section 33 does not limit the use of one official language in daily hospital or facility operations, subject to the obligation to serve the public in the official language of their choice.

rows.heading: By-laws, minutes of council
rows.groupTitle: Municipal and city bilingual by-law and council minutes requirements
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) set the qualifying thresholds, (3) imposes the ongoing bilingual obligation for new or amended by-laws, (4) set the one-time compliance deadline, and (5) extends the rule to council minutes; together they form one recallable duty set.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the population threshold for municipalities, the unconditional city requirement, the ongoing bilingual obligation for new or amended by-laws after December 31, 2002, the one-time December 31, 2005 compliance deadline (excluding Moncton), and the extension of subsection (3) to minutes of council proceedings.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 35 is a short, tightly interdependent set of subsections that together define who must publish by-laws bilingually, the ongoing obligation for new or amended by-laws, the one-time compliance deadline, and the extension to council minutes. Splitting would fragment one coherent municipal bilingual-by-law rule.

rows.heading: Communications and services
rows.groupTitle: Municipal duty to offer services and communications in both official languages
rows.groupReason: One coherent obligation on in-scope municipalities and cities, with the operative content of 'services and communications' prescribed by regulation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify which municipalities and cities are bound by section 36, the duty to offer services and communications in both official languages, and that the specifics are prescribed by regulation.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 36 creates a single clear municipal duty to offer services and communications in both official languages, with scope defined by cross-reference to s.35(1), (2), and s.37, and specifics delegated to regulation.

rows.heading: Opting-in by municipalities
rows.groupTitle: Municipal opting-in by by-law and non-limitation of bilingualism authority
rows.groupReason: The permissive by-law mechanism and the non-limitation savings clause are tightly interdependent; recalling one without the other would fragment the single opting-in rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State how a municipality may declare itself bound by the Official Languages Act, the instrument required, and what the non-limitation clause preserves for municipalities.

evidenceText: A municipality may, by by-law of its municipal council, declare itself bound by the provisions of this Act
nothing in this Act shall be interpreted so as to limit the authority of municipalities to promote the equality of status and use of English and French

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 37 is a single, self-contained rule: a permissive mechanism for a municipality to declare itself bound by the Act by by-law, paired with a non-limitation savings clause preserving municipal authority to promote bilingualism. Both elements answer one recall question and form one coherent concept.

rows.heading: Regional Service Commissions
rows.groupTitle: Regional Service Commission Bilingual Service Threshold
rows.groupReason: Recall the 20% official language minority population threshold and the resulting obligation to provide bilingual services under section 41.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the 20% official language minority population threshold that triggers a regional service commission's obligation under section 41 to offer services and communications in both official languages.

evidenceText: a regional service commission covering a geographical area with an official language minority population of at least 20% of the total population is subject to the obligations imposed by section 41

rows.sourceMapReason: Single-sentence threshold rule: a regional service commission in an area with at least 20% official language minority population is subject to section 41 bilingual service obligations. One actor, one trigger, one consequence — one recall task.

rows.heading: Cities and Municipalities
rows.groupTitle: Regional service commission bilingual obligation via municipal or city composition
rows.groupReason: One rule: an RSC area containing a s.35(1) or (2) municipality or city triggers s.41 obligations regardless of the s.39 percentage threshold.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the condition under which a regional service commission is subject to section 41 obligations irrespective of the section 39 population percentage requirement.

evidenceText: the regional service commission is subject to the obligations imposed by section 41 irrespective of the percentage required under section 39

rows.sourceMapReason: Single-rule provision setting a distinct trigger for regional service commission bilingual obligations based on inclusion of a section 35(1) or (2) municipality or city, independent of the section 39 population threshold.

rows.heading: Communications and services
rows.groupTitle: Regional Service Commission Bilingual Service Obligation
rows.groupReason: Sections 39 and 40 supply the two triggers that section 41 cross-references; together they state who is covered and the bilingual service duty.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the two triggers for regional service commission coverage (20% official language minority threshold; inclusion of a municipality or city subject to s. 35(1) or (2)) and the resulting duty to offer services and communications prescribed by regulation in both official languages.

evidenceText: A regional service commission to which section 39 or 40 apply shall offer the services and communications prescribed by regulation in both official languages.
A regional service commission covering a geographical area with an official language minority population of at least 20% of the total population is subject to the obligations imposed by section 41.

Where the geographical area of a regional service commission includes a municipality or a city to which subsection 35(1) or (2) applies, the regional service commission is subject to the obligations imposed by section 41 irrespective of the percentage required under section 39.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 41 states the duty but defers its trigger entirely to sections 39 and 40; the three sections form one inseparable rule identifying who is covered and what they must do.

rows.heading: Professional associations
rows.groupTitle: Professional association language duties and no-disadvantage protection
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(4) define the actor and create a single interdependent set of bilingual duties and a prohibition against disadvantage.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify what constitutes a 'professional association' under s. 41.1 and state the obligations to provide bilingual services and communications, to permit fulfilment of requirements in the person's chosen official language, and the prohibition on placing a person at a disadvantage for exercising that language choice.
rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained section creating interdependent bilingual service, requirement-fulfilment, and no-disadvantage obligations for professional associations; all subsections form one coherent framework.

rows.heading: Review of Act
rows.groupTitle: Mandatory review of the Official Languages Act by 2031
rows.groupReason: One small duty (Premier initiates review) with a fixed deadline and a regulatory form-and-manner qualifier; both subsections answer the same recall question and should not be separated.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Premier's duty to initiate a review of the Official Languages Act, the December 31, 2031 completion deadline, and the requirement that the review follow the form and manner prescribed by regulation.

evidenceText: The Premier shall initiate a review of this Act, and the review shall be completed no later than December 31, 2031.
A review under subsection (1) shall be in the form and manner prescribed by regulation.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 42 creates a single, tightly coupled duty-and-procedure unit: the Premier's obligation to initiate and complete a review by a fixed date, with the review's form and manner set by regulation. The two subsections are interdependent and form one recall task.

rows.heading: Mandate and responsibilities of Commissioner
rows.groupTitle: Establishment and appointment of the Commissioner

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the appointment mechanism for the Commissioner, the selection committee's composition and function, and the Commissioner's rank and exclusivity requirement.

rows.groupReason: Provides the complainant's right to apply to The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick for a remedy, the judge's discretion in granting an appropriate and just remedy, and a savings clause preserving other rights of action.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the complainant's application right, the court involved, the judge's remedy standard, and the savings for other rights of action.

evidenceText: the complainant may apply to The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick for a remedy
The judge of a court referred to in subsection (18) may grant such remedy as he or she considers appropriate and just in the circumstances

rows.groupReason: Requires an annual report to the Legislative Assembly with four specified content items: nature of complaints, types, investigation trigger, and repeat-complaint counts.

evidenceText: the Commissioner shall submit to the Legislative Assembly a report, prepared by the Commissioner, with respect to the activities of the Office of the Commissioner in the preceding year

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Commissioner's staffing and contracting powers and the salary and pension framework applicable to the Office.

rows.heading: Mandate and responsibilities of Commissioner
rows.groupTitle: Mandate and investigation authority of the Commissioner

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Commissioner's role under the Act, the two triggers for an investigation, and the Commissioner's discretion to resolve a complaint without a full investigation.

the Commissioner shall conduct and carry out investigations either pursuant to any complaint made to the Commissioner or on his or her own initiative
the Commissioner may attempt to resolve a complaint without conducting an investigation

rows.heading: Delegation of authority
rows.groupTitle: Delegation of Commissioner's authority
rows.groupReason: Covers the full delegation regime: what the Commissioner may and may not delegate, the conflict-of-interest exception restoring the report power, and the delegatee's obligation to produce evidence of authority.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the powers the Commissioner may delegate in writing, the two general exclusions, the conflict-of-interest exception, and the delegatee's duty to produce evidence of authority when required.
rows.sourceMapReason: Three short subsections form one coherent delegation regime (general scope, conflict-of-interest carve-back, delegatee evidence duty) that a learner would recall as a single concept.

rows.heading: Protection from reprisal
rows.groupTitle: Protection from Reprisal (s. 43.1)
rows.groupReason: One prohibition covering both taking and directing reprisal, triggered by good-faith complaint or investigation cooperation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the prohibited conduct (taking or directing a reprisal), the protected conduct (good-faith complaint to the Commissioner or cooperating in an investigation), and the scope of persons covered.

evidenceText: No person shall take a reprisal against a person or direct that one be taken against a person because the person has made a complaint in good faith to the Commissioner or cooperated in an investigation under this Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single self-contained prohibition against reprisal for good-faith complaints or investigation cooperation; one coherent recall concept.

rows.heading: Immunity
rows.groupTitle: Commissioner and Office Immunity
rows.groupReason: Immunizes the Commissioner and Office personnel from proceedings for acts, reports, or statements made in the course of their functions, with a single bad-faith carve-out.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the persons protected, the conduct covered, the jurisdictional scope, and the bad-faith exception in the Commissioner's Office immunity provision.

evidenceText: No proceedings lie against the Commissioner or against a person holding an office or appointment in the Office of the Commissioner for anything he or she may do, report or say in the course of the exercise or intended exercise of his or her functions under this Act regardless of whether that function was within his or her jurisdiction, unless it is shown the person acted in bad faith.

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent immunity rule with a single tightly interdependent bad-faith exception; a learner recalls it as one concept.

rows.heading: Appointment of Official Translators
rows.groupTitle: Appointment Power for Official Translators (s. 44)
rows.groupReason: One discrete executive appointment power tied to a specific purpose (court duties under the Act); independently recallable as a single concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the appointing authority (Lieutenant-Governor in Council), the office created (Official Translators), and the stated purpose (enabling a court to discharge its duties under the Act).

evidenceText: The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may appoint such Official Translators as are necessary to enable a court to discharge the duties conferred on it by this Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single-sentence appointment power with one actor, object, and purpose; forms one discrete recall unit on who appoints Official Translators and why.

rows.heading: Regulation-making authority

rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the enumerated subject areas within which the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make regulations under section 45.

evidenceText: The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make regulations

prescribing circumstances not otherwise provided for under this Act in which institutions have the duty to ensure that any member of the public can communicate with and obtain available services from the institutions in either official language
establishing any other measure necessary for the better administration of this Act

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Parks Act Defined Terms
rows.groupReason: All defined terms form one vocabulary framework; the 'provincial park' definition sets the Act's territorial and institutional scope, and the Minister/Department definitions allocate jurisdiction by park type.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the key Parks Act defined terms, particularly the three-part 'provincial park' definition (established parks, agreement-administered land, continued parks, and designated recreational trails) and the Schedule A.1-based allocation of Minister and Department responsibilities.

evidenceText: "provincial park" means(parc provincial)

in relation to the provincial parks listed in Schedule A.1 of the General Regulation - Parks Act, the Minister of Tourism, Heritage and Culture, and includes any person designated by the Minister to act on the Minister's behalf, or
in relation to the provincial parks listed in Schedule A.1 of the General Regulation - Parks Act, the Department of Tourism, Heritage and Culture, or

rows.sourceMapReason: Definitions section establishing the Act's vocabulary, including the scope-defining 'provincial park' definition and the Schedule A.1-based allocation of Minister and Department; the terms form one coherent definitional framework.

rows.heading: Designation of recreational trail
rows.groupTitle: Ministerial designation of recreational trail as a provincial park
rows.groupReason: The three subsections collectively define the designation power, its legal form, and its evidentiary proof as one coherent mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Minister's power to designate a recreational trail (or portion) as a provincial park, confirm that the Regulations Act does not apply to the designation, and identify the evidentiary effect of a copy of the designation.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 2 is a short, tightly interdependent mechanism: the Minister's power to designate a recreational trail as a provincial park, the legal form of that designation (exclusion of the Regulations Act), and the evidentiary treatment of a copy of the designation. Together they define one designation mechanism.

rows.heading: Purpose of provincial parks
rows.groupTitle: Purpose and dedication of provincial parks
rows.groupReason: The dedication to residents, visitors, and future generations combined with the four enumerated purposes form one recallable concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the four statutory purposes to which all provincial parks are dedicated and identify the three beneficiary groups named in the dedication.

evidenceText: permanently protect ecosystems, biodiversity and the elements of natural and cultural heritage
provide opportunities for recreational and outdoor educational activities to promote a healthy lifestyle

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3 is a short, self-contained purpose and dedication statement that answers one recall question: to whom provincial parks are dedicated and for what purposes. The four purposes and the dedication clause are tightly interdependent and form a single coherent concept.

rows.heading: Powers of Minister in relation to provincial parks
rows.groupTitle: Lieutenant-Governor in Council powers over provincial parks and the Minister's threshold authority
rows.groupReason: The lettered powers in 5(1)(a)–(g) form one list answering the same recall question, and 5(2) is the dependent delegation threshold that modifies who exercises them.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the specific powers the Lieutenant-Governor in Council holds over provincial parks (acquire, administer by agreement, increase/decrease area, delimit, terminate, dispose, set aside as park reserve) and the $15,000 real-estate-value threshold at which the Minister may exercise those powers independently.

evidenceText: The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may

If, with respect to a provincial park, land to be set apart, purchased or acquired, added or withdrawn, delimited or disposed of has a real estate value of less than $15,000, the Minister may do those things that the Lieutenant-Governor in Council is authorized to do under subsection (1).

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 5 is a single powers enumeration: the L-G in C may authorize, delimit, terminate, dispose, or set aside park land (5(1)), and 5(2) sets the $15,000 threshold at which the Minister may act in place of the L-G in C. Together they answer one recall task about who holds and exercises provincial park establishment and modification powers.

rows.heading: Powers of Minister in relation to fees and rental
rows.groupTitle: Minister's fee and rental powers in provincial parks
rows.groupReason: All subsections address the setting, conditioning, waiver, refund, and regulatory status of provincial park fees as one operational framework.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Minister's fee-fixing power, the public-notice requirement, the prohibition on fees that may be prescribed under s. 23(2)(k), the three waiver grounds, the pro rata seasonal-fee refund rule, and the inapplicability of the Regulations Act to fee instruments.
rows.sourceMapReason: The seven subsections form one cohesive fee-and-rental mechanism: the power to fix fees, the notice precondition, the 23(2)(k) prohibition, waiver grounds, the pro rata refund rule, and the Regulations Act exclusion all operate on the same fee-setting framework.

rows.heading: Acceptance of property by Minister
rows.groupTitle: Minister's power to receive property for provincial parks
rows.groupReason: One permissive power with defined scope: who, from whom, by what transfer methods, over what property, for what purpose.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the scope of the Minister's power to receive property for a provincial park, including the permitted transfer methods (grant, gift, devise, bequest), the types of property and interests covered, and the required purpose.

evidenceText: The Minister may receive from any person by grant, gift, devise or bequest real or personal property, or an interest in real or personal property, for the purpose of a provincial park.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 is a single, self-contained permissive power defining the Minister's authority to receive property for a provincial park; its scope (methods, property types, purpose) forms one coherent recall unit with no natural combine partner in adjacent sections.

rows.heading: Provincial park deemed separate entity
rows.groupTitle: Provincial park land separated from local government
rows.groupReason: Single deeming rule establishing that park land is separated from its prior local government for local government purposes while it remains park land.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the local government legal status of land once it is set apart as or added to a provincial park, including the temporal condition on that status.

evidenceText: For local government purposes, land set apart as a provincial park or added to a provincial park, so long as it remains part of the provincial park, shall be deemed to be separated from the local government of which it formed a part immediately before it became a provincial park or part of a provincial park.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short deeming rule with one clear legal effect; forms a single self-contained recall unit on local government status of park land.

rows.heading: Provincial park deemed part of county where located
rows.groupTitle: Provincial park land remains in its county for judicial purposes
rows.groupReason: One declarative rule fixing the county jurisdictional status of park land for judicial purposes.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State which county a provincial park's land remains part of for judicial purposes and when that county affiliation is determined.

evidenceText: For judicial purposes, land set apart as a provincial park or added to a provincial park shall continue to form part of the county of which it formed a part immediately before it became a provincial park or a part of a provincial park.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 9 states a single, self-contained jurisdictional rule: park land continues in its county for judicial purposes. It is independently recallable and complements but does not require Section 8.

rows.heading: Administration
rows.groupTitle: Minister's administration and provincial park powers
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) together establish the Minister's administrative role and the full scope of permissive powers over provincial parks as one governance concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Minister's administration responsibility under the Parks Act and enumerate the specific permissive powers the Minister holds in respect of a provincial park, including facility construction, historical preservation, agreements, advisory committee creation, and notice-based opening/closing times.

evidenceText: The Minister is responsible for the administration of this Act and the regulations.
Without limiting the generality of subsection (1), in respect of a provincial park, the Minister may
create an advisory committee including members of First Nations

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 10 assigns the Minister general administration responsibility and enumerates specific permissive powers over provincial park facilities, agreements, advisory committees, and opening/closing notices; together they form one coherent governance concept.

rows.heading: Resource management plans
rows.groupTitle: Resource management plan duty and cultural heritage park exclusion

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Minister's duty to ensure the Department prepares a resource management plan at least every ten years for each provincial park, list the required plan contents, and identify the exclusion for cultural heritage parks classified under the General Regulation - Parks Act.

evidenceText: The Minister shall ensure that the Department prepares a resource management plan at least every ten years for each provincial park that includes the different zones, resource protection measures, the use and development of resources and any other information the Minister considers appropriate.
Subsection (1) does not apply to a provincial park that is classified as a cultural heritage park under the General Regulation - Parks Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 10.1 states a single duty (Minister to ensure ten-yearly resource management plans) with one directly dependent exception (cultural heritage parks), forming one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Review of Act

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Minister's obligation to initiate and complete a review of the Parks Act, the initial completion deadline of December 31, 2024, and the ten-year recurrence thereafter.

evidenceText: The Minister shall initiate a review of this Act, and the review shall be completed no later than December 31, 2024 and every ten years after that.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short standalone duty requiring the Minister to initiate and complete a periodic review of the Act with a fixed initial deadline and ten-year recurrence.

rows.heading: Granting of lease, licence, privilege or concession

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 11 contains the core granting framework (leases and licences/privileges/concessions with their approval and duration rules) plus a distinct easement-in-perpetuity exception for recreational trails that operates 'despite subsection (2)' with its own purpose and location conditions.

rows.heading: Granting of lease, licence, privilege or concession

evidenceText: The Minister, with the approval of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, may grant a lease with respect to a provincial park

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 11 contains the core granting framework (leases and licences/privileges/concessions with their approval and duration rules) plus a distinct easement-in-perpetuity exception for recreational trails that operates 'despite subsection (2)' with its own purpose and location conditions.

rows.heading: Authorization to fix, impose, collect and retain fees or rental

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 12 is one coherent mechanism: the concession-holder's fee-setting and revenue-retention authority, the corollary restrictions on the Lieutenant-Governor in Council and Minister, and the Regulations Act exemption are tightly interdependent and form a single recall task.

rows.heading: Park wardens

rows.heading: Park wardens

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 14 contains two independently recallable concepts: who qualifies as a park warden (appointment pathway plus four office-based categories) and the substantive powers and charge of the office (peace officer powers under the Criminal Code). rows.sourceMapReason: One short operative provision establishing a single appointment power and the resulting duty of a security guard; no further split or combination warranted.

rows.heading: Items seized
rows.groupTitle: Detention period and release of seized items
rows.groupReason: The detention limit, owner's release-on-application triggers, Minister's return order, and automatic forfeiture after six months form one interdependent recall task about what happens to seized items over time.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the six-month detention period for items seized by a park warden and the specific conditions under which seized items are released, returned to the owner, or deemed forfeited to the Crown.

evidenceText: may be detained for a period of six months following the time of seizure or, if proceedings are instituted within the two months following seizure, until the proceedings are concluded
on application, shall be released to its owner
shall be returned to the owner on the Minister ordering its return, if it is not required for evidence in a court of law
shall be deemed to be forfeited to the Crown if, after a period of six months from the date of seizure, no application has been made and no proceedings have been instituted

rows.heading: Items seized

rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the two mandatory disposition options a judge must order for seized items when convicting a person of a Parks Act offence: return to the owner as soon as practicable or forfeiture to the Crown.

evidenceText: When a judge convicts a person of an offence against this Act, the judge shall order anything seized under the Provincial Offences Procedure Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 15 contains two distinct procedural stages: the detention/release/forfeiture framework operating on application or by lapse (15(1)–(2)), and the separate judicial disposition order a judge must make upon conviction (15(3)).

rows.sourceMapReason: All three subsections answer one recall question — which offence category applies to which type of Parks Act violation — and the default/exception pair in (1)-(2) is inseparable from the higher-tier rule in (3).

rows.heading: Orders prohibiting entry to provincial park

rows.sourceMapReason: The two subsections form one coherent exclusion-order mechanism: the issuing authority, grounds, and order requirements in 17(1), and the subject person's compliance duty in 17(2).

rows.heading: Evidentiary matters
rows.groupTitle: Certified copies: preparation and court admissibility

evidenceText: a document purporting to be signed by the Minister or the Minister's designate shall be received as evidence of the contents of the document in any court in the Province without proof of the appointment, authority or signature of the Minister or the Minister's designate.

rows.heading: Evidentiary matters
rows.groupTitle: Sign presumptions in prosecution
rows.groupReason: Creates two interdependent rebuttable presumptions regarding proper placement, maintenance, and temporal existence of a sign in a prosecution under the Act or regulations.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two rebuttable presumptions that apply to a sign in a prosecution under the Act or regulations under s.18(2)(a) and (b).

evidenceText: the existence of a sign is proof, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, that the sign was properly placed and maintained by the proper authorities
evidence that the sign was in existence both before and after the conduct in question is proof, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, that the sign was in existence at all material times.

rows.sourceMapReason: Three distinct evidentiary rules differ in actor, trigger, and legal effect: Minister's certification power (18(1)), sign presumptions in prosecution (18(2)), and location presumption (18(3)).

rows.heading: Evidentiary matters
rows.groupTitle: Location presumption for provincial park
rows.groupReason: Establishes a rebuttable presumption that a proven act was committed within a provincial park when so alleged, in a prosecution under the Act or regulations.
