evidenceText: if an act that the accused is proven to have done is alleged to have been done in a provincial park, the accused shall be deemed to have done the act in the provincial park in the absence of evidence to the contrary.

rows.sourceMapReason: Three distinct evidentiary rules differ in actor, trigger, and legal effect: Minister's certification power (18(1)), sign presumptions in prosecution (18(2)), and location presumption (18(3)).

evidenceText: the contravention may be restrained by action at the instance of the Minister

rows.heading: Opening or closing of roads by Minister

rows.heading: Protection of flora

"personal representative" includes, where the context permits, an executor, an administrator, a trustee under a will, the Public Trustee, and a guardian as may be appointed pursuant to law, or some or all of them
"persons beneficially interested" includes the Public Trustee, a representative appointed under the Supported Decision-Making and Representation Act, and a guardian of a minor

rows.sourceMapReason: The section defines the operative vocabulary of the Act, with several terms (common form business, personal representative, persons beneficially interested, probate, administration, will) carrying substantive scope and standing significance that a learner must recall independently of the provisions that use them.

rows.heading: The Probate Court of New Brunswick
rows.groupTitle: Establishment, Core Powers, and Cross-Reference Rule for The Probate Court of New Brunswick
rows.groupReason: Both subsections form one recall unit: what the court is, what powers it holds, how existing courts are absorbed, and how other Acts' references to 'a probate court' are deemed.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that The Probate Court of New Brunswick is a court of record with power to take probate of wills, grant or recall/revoke administration, and supervise estates; that existing probate courts are amalgamated into it; and that references to 'a probate court' in any other Act are deemed to reference it.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 2 is a short, self-contained establishment provision: it creates the court, enumerates its core powers, provides for amalgamation of existing courts, and supplies a cross-reference deeming rule. Both subsections answer one coherent recall task about the court's identity and mandate.

rows.heading: Powers vested in Court
rows.groupTitle: Probate Court Jurisdiction and Exclusive Powers
rows.groupReason: Learner must recall what jurisdiction is vested, its qualifications (not derogating from K'B, subject to Judicature Act, manner hitherto in use), and the three exclusive-jurisdiction items including the concurrent-jurisdiction qualifier in (c).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the scope of jurisdiction vested in the Probate Court under s.3(1), its qualifying conditions, and the three areas of exclusive jurisdiction under s.3(2)(a)–(c) including the concurrent-jurisdiction limitation in (c).

evidenceText: all jurisdiction and authority in relation to matters and causes testamentary and all matters arising out of or connected with the grant, recall or revocation of grant of probate or administration are vested in the Court
the Court has exclusive jurisdiction and authority in the following items

subject to the concurrent jurisdiction of the Court of King's Bench, in the issuance of any orders or directions in connection with the administration, passing of accounts and winding up of the estate

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3 is a single coherent jurisdictional framework: s.3(1) vests general testamentary and probate jurisdiction with qualifications, and s.3(2) specifies the exclusive-jurisdiction subset, explicitly subordinate to the general grant. The rule/condition structure is tightly interdependent and best recalled as one unit.

rows.heading: Seal of the Court
rows.groupTitle: Seal of the Court and Facsimile Seals
rows.groupReason: Both subsections together define the custody chain for the Court's seal and its facsimiles, forming one coherent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who has custody of the Seal of the Court, who approves the seal, and who receives and holds facsimile seals at each probate office.
rows.sourceMapReason: One short provision whose two interdependent subsections define the Court's seal custody hierarchy and approval authority as a single recall task.

rows.heading: Establishment of probate offices
rows.groupTitle: Establishment of Probate Offices and Court Sittings
rows.groupReason: 5(1) grants the Lieutenant-Governor in Council power to establish probate offices in judicial districts for common form business and other estate proceedings; 5(2) requires sittings to be held in those premises (or other judge-directed premises) under a judge's presiding.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the authority that may establish probate offices, the purpose those offices serve, where Court sittings must be held, and who presides over them.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 5 establishes the institutional framework for probate offices and Court sittings as one coherent unit; 5(2) directly depends on the offices created under 5(1).

rows.heading: Power to enforce judgments and orders
rows.groupTitle: Probate Court enforcement powers mirroring Court of King's Bench
rows.groupReason: One coherent rule: the Court's enforcement powers, writs, and process have the same scope and force as the Court of King's Bench province-wide.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that the Probate Court possesses the same enforcement powers as the Court of King's Bench, may issue the same writs and process, and those writs have the same force and effect as Court of King's Bench writs throughout the Province.

evidenceText: The Court has the same powers as are possessed by the Court of King's Bench of enforcing its judgments and orders in any part of the Province, and may issue the same writs and process as are issued out of the Court of King's Bench, and they have the same force and effect as writs and process issued out of the Court of King's Bench.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single short provision establishing the Probate Court's enforcement powers, writ-issuing authority, and process force and effect by reference to the Court of King's Bench province-wide.

rows.heading: Power to punish by fine or imprisonment
rows.groupTitle: Probate Court contempt power and statutory maximums
rows.groupReason: The power, its wilful-contempt trigger, and the $1,000 / six-month caps are one interdependent rule a learner recalls as a unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Court's contempt punishment power, its trigger (wilful contempt or resistance to process, rules, or orders), the available forms of punishment, and the statutory maximums of $1,000 fine and six months' imprisonment.

evidenceText: The Court may punish by fine or imprisonment, or by both, for every wilful contempt of or resistance to its process, rules or orders but the fine shall not in any case exceed one thousand dollars, nor shall the imprisonment exceed six months.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 7 is a short, self-contained operative provision establishing the Court's contempt power, its trigger (wilful contempt or resistance), and statutory maximums. All elements form one recallable rule and warrant a single StudyUnit.

rows.heading: Applicable rules of evidence
rows.groupTitle: Rules of evidence, practice, procedure, and powers applying to the Probate Court
rows.groupReason: Single borrowing-and-powers provision; the two exceptions qualify the borrowed rules and the powers grant operates over all matters within the Court's jurisdiction.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State which rules of evidence, practice, and procedure apply to the Probate Court, the two exceptions to that application, and the scope of powers the Court, judges, and officers may exercise.

evidenceText: The rules of evidence observed in and, except as herein otherwise provided and subject to the rules in contentious matters, the practice and procedure of the Court of King's Bench apply to the Court
the Court and the judges and officers thereof respectively have and may exercise all the powers of the Court of King's Bench and of the judges and officers thereof

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 8 is a short, single-sentence provision establishing that Court of King's Bench evidence rules, practice, procedure, and powers apply to the Probate Court, subject to two stated exceptions. One coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Court of King’s Bench judge ex officio judge
rows.groupTitle: Ex officio composition of the Probate Court
rows.groupReason: One recallable structural fact: the Probate Court's judgeship is held ex officio by every Court of King's Bench judge.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who holds the office of judge of the Probate Court and by what mechanism under section 9(1).
rows.sourceMapReason: Single-sentence structural rule stating that every Court of King's Bench judge is ex officio a judge of the Probate Court; minimal but operative institutional content.

rows.heading: Conclusion of business on retirement
rows.groupTitle: Conclusion of pending business on a judge's retirement
rows.groupReason: One coherent rule: the six-month conclusion period and its deeming consequence form a single recall task about what happens to pending cases on a judge's retirement.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the six-month period a retired judge has to conclude pending Court business and the legal effect that such business is deemed dealt with during the judge's tenure.

evidenceText: a judge shall have the period of six months from the date of commencement of the retirement to conclude such business of the Court as may at that date be pending before him
shall be considered to have been dealt with by him during his tenure as a judge of the Court

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 10 is a short, self-contained rule: a retiring judge gets six months to conclude pending business, and cases handled in that period are deemed dealt with during tenure. The timeframe and the deeming consequence are tightly interdependent parts of one recallable rule.

rows.heading: Appointment of Registrar and deputy registrars
rows.groupTitle: Registrar appointment and oath of office
rows.groupReason: One office-identity rule plus the directly attached oath/affirmation prerequisite constitute a single recallable appointment concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify that the Probate Court Registrar is the Court of King's Bench Registrar and state the oath or affirmation the Registrar must take or make before entering office, including the duty to protect wills and testamentary papers.

evidenceText: The Registrar and deputy registrars of the Court of King's Bench appointed under the Judicature Act shall be the Registrar and deputy registrars of the Court
I will not knowingly permit or suffer any alteration, obliteration or destruction to be made or done, of any will or testamentary paper, or other document or paper committed to my charge

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 11 establishes the Registrar's office identity (same as Court of King's Bench) and the mandatory oath or affirmation prerequisite before entering office, forming one tightly interdependent appointment unit.

rows.heading: Appointment of clerks and deputy clerks
rows.groupTitle: Appointment and role of clerks and deputy clerks
rows.groupReason: Identifies who appoints each office (Lieutenant-Governor in Council for clerks; Minister of Justice for deputy clerks), the scope of delegated powers, the official title, and the fee and remuneration rules.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the appointing authority for clerks and deputy clerks, the official title format, and the fee-receiving and remuneration provisions under subsections 12(1)–(4).
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 12 contains two distinct recall tasks: the appointment authorities, official title, and fee/remuneration structure for clerks and deputy clerks (12(1)–(4)), and the separately operative oath/affirmation prerequisite that gates when a clerk is deemed appointed (12(5)).

rows.heading: Appointment of clerks and deputy clerks
rows.groupTitle: Oath or affirmation requirement for clerks and deputy clerks
rows.groupReason: Section 12(5) imposes a distinct procedural prerequisite: a specific oath or affirmation before a judge, a certificate endorsed on the commission, and the operative consequence that the clerk is not deemed appointed until both are completed.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the content of the oath or affirmation, the administering officer, the certificate endorsement requirement, and the effect that the clerk is not deemed appointed until these steps are completed.

evidenceText: the clerk shall not be deemed to be appointed until the oath or affirmation is administered and the certificate thereof endorsed as aforesaid

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 12 contains two distinct recall tasks: the appointment authorities, official title, and fee/remuneration structure for clerks and deputy clerks (12(1)–(4)), and the separately operative oath/affirmation prerequisite that gates when a clerk is deemed appointed (12(5)).

rows.heading: Registrar and deputy registrar ex officio clerks
rows.groupTitle: Registrar and deputy registrars as ex officio clerks
rows.groupReason: Single designation of who holds the clerk role and the judicial-district scope; one recall question.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Registrar and deputy registrars as ex officio clerks and state their territorial scope as each judicial district.

evidenceText: The Registrar and deputy registrars of the Court are ex officio clerks for each judicial district.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 is a single-sentence provision designating the Registrar and deputy registrars as ex officio clerks for each judicial district, establishing their official role and territorial scope within the Probate Court. It is one recallable fact with minimal but independent study value.

rows.heading: Office hours of probate offices
rows.groupTitle: Probate office operating hours and holiday closure
rows.groupReason: The section-specific holiday definition and the mandatory opening-hours duty are interdependent and answer one recall question: when must probate offices be open and on which days are they closed?
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that every probate office shall be kept open from 9:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m. on all days except holidays, and identify the three categories of days defined as holidays for closure purposes (Interpretation Act holidays, Saturday, and other public-service holidays).

evidenceText: every probate office shall be kept open from 9:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m. each day
In this section “holiday” means (a) a holiday as defined in the Interpretation Act; (b) Saturday; and (c) any other day observed as a holiday within the public service of the Province

rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained provision setting a mandatory probate-office opening duty and a section-specific holiday definition; the two subsections are tightly interdependent and form one recallable operational rule.

rows.heading: Filing and preservation of documents
rows.groupTitle: Clerk's duty to file and preserve original wills and Court papers
rows.groupReason: Covers the full scope of the clerk's filing and preservation duty: original wills tied to granted probate/administration and all other papers used in Court matters, subject to the rules.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what a clerk must file and preserve (original wills where letters probate or letters of administration with the will annexed are granted, and all other papers used in Court matters) and the applicable limitation (subject to the rules).

evidenceText: A clerk shall file and preserve all original wills of which letters probate or letters of administration with the will annexed are granted, and all other papers used in any matter in the Court, subject to the rules.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single, clear duty on the clerk to file and preserve original wills (where probate or administration with will is granted) and all other Court papers, subject to the rules. One actor, one modality, one trigger — one recall task.

rows.heading: Forwarding of information to Registrar
rows.groupTitle: Clerk duty to forward grant information to the Registrar
rows.groupReason: Single operative rule: clerk forwarding duty tied to Registrar direction and request.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what each clerk must forward to the Registrar, at what intervals, in what manner, and whose direction governs the forwarding.

evidenceText: Each clerk shall forward to the Registrar at such intervals and in such manner as the Registrar may from time to time direct, such information in respect of grants of probate and administration made by the Court as the Registrar may request.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 17 imposes a single duty on clerks to forward probate and administration grant information to the Registrar at intervals and in a manner the Registrar directs. One simple recall task; no split needed.

rows.heading: Probate value of estate not exceeding $25,000
rows.groupTitle: Public Trustee administration of estates not exceeding $25,000
rows.groupReason: The threshold, the affidavit requirement to the Registrar, the resulting equal authority, and the mandatory issuance of letters of administration are one recallable procedural rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the probate-value threshold, the affidavit requirements to the Registrar, and the effect on the Public Trustee's authority and letters of administration under s. 20(2)–(3).

evidenceText: if the probate value of the estate does not exceed $25,000 it is not necessary for the Public Trustee to be appointed by order of the Court as administrator of the estate
letters of administration shall be issued to him

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 20(2) and 20(3) form one tightly coupled procedural mechanism: a probate-value threshold exempting the Public Trustee from court appointment, the affidavit requirement, and the resulting letters of administration. Recalling them separately would fragment a single concept.

rows.heading: Fees and reimbursement for expenses of administration
rows.groupTitle: Public Trustee fees and expense reimbursement in estate administration
rows.groupReason: Single short provision establishing the Public Trustee's fee-charging and reimbursement rights in probate contexts, governed by the Public Trustee Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the Public Trustee may charge fees and is entitled to expense reimbursement in estate administration, with both governed by the Public Trustee Act and its regulations.

evidenceText: the Public Trustee may charge such fees as are provided for in the Public Trustee Act and the regulations under that Act and is entitled to be reimbursed for expenses in accordance with that Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 23 is a short cross-reference confirming the Public Trustee's fee-charging permission and expense reimbursement entitlement in probate estate administration, with operative details governed by the Public Trustee Act. It creates a substantive right in this context and warrants a brief standalone unit.

rows.heading: Administration of pension estate
rows.groupTitle: Distribution, costs, and temporal applicability of pension estate administration
rows.groupReason: Distribution recipients, the costs prohibition, and the section's temporal scope are distinct recall tasks from the entry mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the categories of persons to whom the Public Trustee may distribute a pension estate, state the rule that administration costs are not a charge on the estate, and note the section's application to deaths occurring before the Act came into force.

evidenceText: The Public Trustee may pay the pension estate to any relative by blood or connection by marriage of a deceased pensioner or any other person appearing to him or her to be equitably entitled
The costs of administration of a pension estate shall not be a charge upon the estate
This section applies to the pension estates of deceased pensioners who died before the coming into force of this Act as well as those who die thereafter

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 25 is a self-contained procedure for Public Trustee administration of small pension estates. The entry conditions and evidentiary rules (subsections 1–4) form a distinct recall task from the distribution recipients, costs prohibition, and temporal scope (subsections 5–7), warranting two StudyUnits.

rows.heading: Administration of pension estate
rows.groupTitle: Pension estate definitions and Public Trustee entry conditions
rows.groupReason: Definitions, entry conditions, ipso facto effect, and evidentiary rule form one coherent 'entering administration' concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what constitutes a pension estate and a pensioner, the conditions under which the Public Trustee may enter upon administration without court order, the ipso facto legal effect, and the evidentiary role of cheque endorsement.

evidenceText: the Public Trustee may, without letters of administration or order from the Court, enter upon administration of the pension estate
he is, ipso facto, administrator of the pension estate
is sufficient evidence that he is administrator of the pension estate

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 25 is a self-contained procedure for Public Trustee administration of small pension estates. The entry conditions and evidentiary rules (subsections 1–4) form a distinct recall task from the distribution recipients, costs prohibition, and temporal scope (subsections 5–7), warranting two StudyUnits.

rows.heading: Administration of estates of deceased persons
rows.groupTitle: Public Trustee appointment to administer estates
rows.groupReason: One short power provision: the Public Trustee may be appointed to administer estates of deceased persons dying before or after the date of appointment.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Public Trustee's appointment power to administer estates of deceased persons and identify that it covers deaths occurring both before and after the date of appointment.
rows.sourceMapReason: Single-sentence provision stating the Public Trustee's permissive appointment power to administer estates, with a temporal scope covering deaths before and after the appointment date. One recall task.

rows.heading: Prohibition respecting legacy action
rows.groupTitle: Prohibition on legacy and residue distribution actions
rows.groupReason: One jurisdictional prohibition covering two closely related action types recalled as a single rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that the Probate Court shall not entertain an action for a legacy or for the distribution of a residue.

evidenceText: An action for a legacy or for the distribution of a residue shall not be entertained by the Court.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single, clear prohibition limiting the Probate Court's jurisdiction over legacy and residue distribution actions.

rows.heading: Where application presented
rows.groupTitle: Venue for probate and administration applications
rows.groupReason: One recall task: the two alternative grounds (deceased's residence at death or property location) that fix the judicial district for presenting the application.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two jurisdictional grounds that determine in which judicial district's probate office an applicant may present an application for letters probate or letters of administration.
rows.sourceMapReason: A single short venue rule stating the two alternative judicial districts where a probate or administration application may be presented; one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Letters in force until revoked
rows.groupTitle: Continuing force of letters probate and letters of administration
rows.groupReason: One short rule establishing that granted letters persist by default and are terminated only by revocation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the default continuing legal status of letters probate and letters of administration after grant and identify the sole condition stated in s. 30 that terminates that status.

evidenceText: Letters probate of a will and letters of administration granted by the Court shall remain in force until revoked.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 states a single, self-contained default rule: letters probate and letters of administration continue in force until revoked. This is a substantive, independently recallable legal status rule with no internal complexity requiring a split.

rows.heading: Effect of letters
rows.groupTitle: Province-wide effect of letters probate and letters of administration
rows.groupReason: One operative sentence establishing the geographic scope of probate and administration letters.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the geographic scope of effect for letters probate of a will and letters of administration granted by the Court.

evidenceText: Letters probate of a will and letters of administration have effect in all parts of the Province.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 31 states a single operative rule: letters probate of a will and letters of administration have effect in all parts of the Province. This is a substantive territorial-scope rule with independent recall value.

rows.heading: Order to produce documents, order to attend for examination
rows.groupTitle: Court power to order production of documents or examination in probate
rows.groupReason: Both subsections form one two-path document-compelment procedure: direct production where possession is shown, and examination/attendance where only knowledge is suspected, including default consequences and costs discretion.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the two triggers (possession shown vs. reasonable grounds of knowledge), the categories of documents covered, the three examination venues, and the default consequences under section 32 of the Probate Court Act.

evidenceText: the Court may, on motion or other proceeding in a summary manner, order any person to produce and bring before the clerk, or otherwise as the Court directs, any paper or writing being or purporting to be testamentary

If it is not shown that the paper or writing is in the possession or under the control of that person, but it appears that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the person has knowledge of the paper or writing, the Court may direct that person to attend for the purpose of being examined

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 32 provides one coherent procedural mechanism — the Court's power to compel document production or examination in probate matters — with two complementary paths (possession shown vs. knowledge suspected) that are best recalled together.

rows.heading: Removal of contentious proceedings to Court of King’s Bench
rows.groupTitle: Removal of contentious probate proceedings to the Court of King's Bench
rows.groupReason: Establishes the removal power, the judicial standard (necessary or desirable), and the statutory purpose as one coherent triggering rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a judge may order a contentious probate cause or proceeding removed to the Court of King's Bench, including the required judicial standard and the purposes of complete determination and avoiding multiplicity of proceedings.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 33 contains a distinct removal power with its own standard and purpose (33(1)) separate from the post-removal procedural mechanics (33(2)–(3)); each poses a different recall task for the learner.

rows.heading: Removal of contentious proceedings to Court of King’s Bench
rows.groupTitle: Post-removal cost terms and certification of judgment
rows.groupReason: These two short subsections impose the KB judge's power to set cost or security terms and the clerk's duty to certify the judgment back to the originating probate office, forming the post-removal procedural mechanics.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Court of King's Bench judge's power to impose terms as to payment of or security for costs, and the clerk of the probate office's duty to certify the resulting judgment back to the office from which the matter was removed.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 33 contains a distinct removal power with its own standard and purpose (33(1)) separate from the post-removal procedural mechanics (33(2)–(3)); each poses a different recall task for the learner.

rows.heading: Right of a party or person taking part in proceeding to appeal
rows.groupTitle: Probate Court appeal: property-value threshold and leave requirement
rows.groupReason: The $1,000 threshold and the leave requirement are interdependent halves of one appeal-eligibility rule; recalling one without the other would be incomplete.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who may appeal from a Probate Court order or judgment, the property-value threshold that triggers a direct right of appeal to the Court of Appeal, and the leave requirement when the threshold is not met.

evidenceText: Any party or person taking part in an action or other proceeding may appeal to the Court of Appeal from any order, determination or judgment of the Court or a judge thereof in any matter or cause if the value of the property affected by such order, determination or judgment exceeds one thousand dollars; in any other case appeal shall be by leave of the Court of Appeal only.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained appeal rule: one monetary threshold ($1,000) divides a direct right of appeal from a leave-based appeal, forming a single recall task.

rows.heading: Right of person beneficially interested to appeal
rows.groupTitle: Supplementary appeal by person beneficially interested
rows.groupReason: Creates a leave-based appeal right for persons beneficially interested in the estate, triggered by the inaction of the claimant or personal representative under section 34.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the actor (person beneficially interested in the estate), the triggering condition (claimant or personal representative does not appeal under section 34), and the leave requirement (leave of a judge of the Court of Appeal) for this supplementary appeal right.

evidenceText: Where the claimant or personal representative having a right of appeal pursuant to section 34 does not appeal from the order, determination or judgment, any person beneficially interested in the estate may, by leave of a judge of the Court of Appeal, appeal therefrom.

rows.sourceMapReason: One-sentence provision creating a conditional supplementary appeal right for persons beneficially interested in the estate; forms a single coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Application where deceased resident in Province, application where deceased member of forces, mariner or seaman
rows.groupTitle: Application requirements for resident deceased
rows.groupReason: Subsection (1) states the mandatory affidavit and proof requirements for the common-form grant where the deceased was a Province resident.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the affidavit and proof requirements that must be satisfied before letters probate or letters of administration may be granted where the deceased was resident in the Province at death.

evidenceText: his place of abode at the time of his death shall be made to appear by affidavit of the person or one of the persons making the application

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsection (1) sets the standard affidavit-and-proof requirement for resident deceased, while subsections (2)–(3) create a distinct evidentiary dispensation for military and maritime testators with unavailable witnesses, including a tightly bound definition.

rows.heading: Application where deceased resident in Province, application where deceased member of forces, mariner or seaman
rows.groupTitle: Alternative evidence for wills of military and maritime testators
rows.groupReason: Subsections (2) and (3) together create a self-contained evidentiary rule for military and maritime testators whose witnesses are unavailable, including the defining scope of 'member of the forces.'
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the circumstances under which the Court may accept alternative evidence of a will's validity and proper execution for a military or maritime testator, and state who qualifies as a 'member of the forces' for that purpose.

evidenceText: the Court may accept such evidence as it considers satisfactory as to the validity and proper execution of such will, notwithstanding anything in this Act, the rules or regulations
In subsection (2), "member of the forces" means a member of a component of the Canadian forces

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsection (1) sets the standard affidavit-and-proof requirement for resident deceased, while subsections (2)–(3) create a distinct evidentiary dispensation for military and maritime testators with unavailable witnesses, including a tightly bound definition.

rows.heading: Application where deceased had no fixed place of abode or was a non-resident
rows.groupTitle: Application requirements for non-resident or no-fixed-abode estates
rows.groupReason: The section states one procedural sequence: identifying the triggering factual scenario, the mandatory affidavit, and the grant condition upon proof of the will or intestacy.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the affidavit and proof requirements for an application for letters probate or administration where the deceased was a non-resident or had no fixed place of abode in the Province but left property in the Province.

evidenceText: where the deceased had no fixed place of abode in the Province or the deceased was a non-resident of the Province at the time of his death, and the deceased died leaving property in the Province, it shall be made to so appear by affidavit of the person or one of the persons making the application

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 37 is a single, tightly interdependent procedural rule governing applications where the deceased was a non-resident or had no fixed abode; the trigger, affidavit requirement, and grant condition form one recallable unit.

rows.heading: Court governed by principles of common law
rows.groupTitle: Common law as governing principle for probate and administration
rows.groupReason: One recall task: identify the governing legal principle (common law) and the three sources that can displace it (this Act, the rules, or another Act of the Legislature).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the default body of law governing the Court in granting probate or administration and the three sources of law that can displace it.

evidenceText: Except as otherwise provided in this Act or the rules, or in any other Act of the Legislature, the Court, in granting probate or administration, shall be governed by the principles of the common law.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 38 is a single, self-contained rule: the Court governs probate and administration by common law principles unless displaced by this Act, the rules, or another statute. The rule and its carve-out form one inseparable recall unit.

rows.heading: Application by person not next-of-kin
rows.groupTitle: Show-cause order for non-next-of-kin applicant for letters of administration
rows.groupReason: Trigger, mandatory show-cause order, and fallback service/publication form one interdependent procedural rule with no independent recall task separable from the rest.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when the Court must issue a show-cause order to in-Province interested parties for a non-next-of-kin applicant, and identify the required service or publication method when no such person resides in the Province.

evidenceText: an order shall be made requiring the next of kin, or others having or claiming to have an interest in the property of the deceased, resident in the Province, to show cause why the administration should not be granted to the person applying therefor
if neither the next of kin nor any person of the kindred of the deceased resides in the Province a copy of the order shall be served or published in the manner prescribed by the rules

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent procedural mechanism: a mandatory show-cause order to in-Province interested parties when a non-next-of-kin person applies for letters of administration, with a fallback service or publication step when no such person resides in the Province.

rows.heading: Grant of temporary administration
rows.groupTitle: Grant of temporary administration and administrator conditions
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) together state the absence trigger, the Court's grant power and temporal limits, and the administrator's security duty and Court-control status as one operative mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when the Court may grant a temporary administration, the temporal limits on the grant, and the security, powers, and Court-control conditions binding the temporary administrator.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 40 establishes one coherent temporary-administration mechanism: the Court's power to grant, the absence trigger, temporal limits, and the appointed administrator's security duty and status.

rows.heading: Notarial will made in Quebec
rows.groupTitle: Admission to probate of a notarial will made in Quebec
rows.groupReason: One recallable rule: a Quebec notarial will may be probated on a notarial copy plus other proper proofs, without the original.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when a notarial will made in the Province of Quebec may be admitted to probate without the original will and what must be filed to obtain a grant.

evidenceText: A notarial will made in the Province of Quebec may be admitted to probate without the production of the original will upon filing a notarial copy thereof together with the other proper proofs leading to a grant.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 41 states a single, self-contained procedural rule for admitting a notarial will made in Quebec to probate without the original, conditioned on filing a notarial copy and other proper proofs.

rows.heading: Stay of proceedings where two applications made
rows.groupTitle: Stay of proceedings for duplicate probate applications
rows.groupReason: Defines the trigger, mandatory stay, and direction to one judge when applications reach two or more probate offices.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the trigger (Registrar's certificate showing two or more applications), the judges' duty to stay proceedings, and the required direction to the parties.

evidenceText: Where it appears by the certificate of the Registrar that application for the grant of letters probate of a will or letters of administration has been made to two or more probate offices, the judges sitting in the judicial districts for those probate offices in which such applications have been made shall stay proceedings therein and shall direct the parties to apply to one of them for such direction in the matter as that judge considers necessary.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single procedural rule addressing duplicate probate filings; the stay duty and direction to one judge form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Determination of appropriate probate office
rows.groupTitle: Costs order in a probate-office determination
rows.groupReason: The costs-ordering power and its distinct Court of King's Bench enforcement are independently recallable from the underlying determination rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the judge's power to order costs in a s. 43 determination and the court responsible for enforcing the costs order.

evidenceText: The judge may order costs to be paid by any of the applicants, and the order shall be enforced by the Court of King's Bench.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 43 contains a core determination rule with a stated criterion and finality effect, plus a distinct collateral costs-ordering power with a separate enforcement body; these create independent recall tasks.

rows.heading: Determination of appropriate probate office
rows.groupTitle: Judge's determination of appropriate probate office
rows.groupReason: Covers the judge's summary inquiry, the balance-of-convenience criterion, and the finality and Registrar transmission duties as one interdependent procedural rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the judge's duty and criterion in determining the appropriate probate office under s. 43(1) and the legal effect of that determination under s. 43(3).

evidenceText: the judge shall inquire into the matter in a summary manner and may determine as to which probate office the application shall be made
the judge shall take into account the balance of convenience to those who have an apparent interest in the estate

The determination of the judge made pursuant to subsection (1) is final and conclusive, and the Registrar shall without delay transmit a certified copy of the judge's order to the clerks of the probate offices

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 43 contains a core determination rule with a stated criterion and finality effect, plus a distinct collateral costs-ordering power with a separate enforcement body; these create independent recall tasks.

rows.heading: Lodging of caveat
rows.groupTitle: Where a caveat may be lodged
rows.groupReason: Specifies the two permitted recipients for lodging a caveat against a probate or administration grant.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two officials with whom a caveat against a grant of letters probate of a will or letters of administration may be lodged.

evidenceText: A caveat against a grant of letters probate of a will or letters of administration may be lodged with the Registrar or with the clerk of a probate office.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 44 states a single procedural rule on where a caveat may be lodged; it is one self-contained recall task.

rows.heading: Summons to attend and parties to proceedings
rows.groupTitle: Summons of interested persons in contested will proceedings
rows.groupReason: The triggers (solemn-form proof, revocation for invalidity, other contested validity), the class of summonable persons (interested or claiming interest), and the limiting conditions (Act, rules, Court discretion) are interdependent parts of one procedural right.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the circumstances in which persons having or claiming an interest in will-affected property may be summoned to attend and permitted to become parties, and the conditions limiting that power.

evidenceText: Where proceedings are taken for proving a will in solemn form or for revoking the grant of letters probate of a will on the ground of the invalidity thereof, or where in any other contentious cause or matter the validity of a will is disputed, all persons having or claiming to have an interest in the property affected by the will may, subject to this Act and the rules, be summoned to attend the proceedings and may be permitted to become parties, subject to the rules and to the discretion of the Court.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 45 is a single, self-contained procedural rule setting out when interested persons may be summoned to attend and become parties in contested will proceedings, with one trigger set, one class of persons, and one set of limiting conditions that form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Summons to executor
rows.groupTitle: Court's power to summon a named executor
rows.groupReason: Single summons power with enumerated and catch-all objects forming one recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the matters to which the Court may summon a person named as executor under section 46.

evidenceText: The Court may summon any person who has been named as an executor of any will to prove or to refuse to prove such will, and to bring in inventories and to do every other thing necessary or expedient concerning the will.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 46 is a single, self-contained power granting the Court authority to summon a named executor; one actor, one power, one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Cessation of executorship
rows.groupTitle: Cessation of executorship and devolution of administration
rows.groupReason: Both triggering events (death before probate; failure to appear after summons) lead to the same operative consequence and are recalled as one rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two circumstances in which an executor's right wholly ceases under s. 47 and state the devolution rule that applies without further renunciation.

evidenceText: When an executor survives a testator, but dies without having taken probate, or when an executor is summoned to take probate and does not appear, his right in respect of the executorship wholly ceases, and the representation on behalf of the testator and the administration of his property without any further renunciation go, devolve, and are committed in the same manner as if that person had not been named executor.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short self-contained provision stating two triggering events and one devolution consequence; the triggers and effect form a single coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Renunciation by executor
rows.groupTitle: Effect of executor's renunciation of probate
rows.groupReason: Covers the trigger (renunciation of probate), the cessation of executorship rights, and the automatic devolution of administration as if the person had never been named.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the legal effect on executorship rights and the devolution of administration when a named executor renounces probate of a will.
rows.sourceMapReason: One short provision stating the single legal effect of an executor's renunciation; the trigger and the resulting devolution are interdependent and form one recall task.

rows.heading: Infant as sole executor
rows.groupTitle: Administration and probate where a minor is sole executor
rows.groupReason: Interim administration with the will annexed and the mandatory-at-majority letters probate are tightly linked parts of one continuous rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the type of grant made to the guardian or Court-appointed person during a minor's minority and the point at which letters probate of the will may be granted to the minor.
rows.sourceMapReason: Short self-contained rule covering the interim grant during minority and the transition to letters probate at majority; one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Power of guardian or other person
rows.groupTitle: Scope of powers of interim administrator appointed under s. 49
rows.groupReason: The provision defines one substantive rule: the interim administrator holds the same powers as a standard administrator during minority of the next-of-kin.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the scope of powers held by the guardian or person appointed under section 49 during the minority of the next-of-kin.

evidenceText: has the same powers as an administrator has by virtue of an administration granted to him during the minority of the next-of-kin

rows.sourceMapReason: Single-sentence provision establishing the scope of powers of the interim administrator appointed under section 49 during minority; one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Obtainment of official copies
rows.groupTitle: Obtaining official copies of wills and probate or administration grants
rows.groupReason: One short permission with a fee condition; all elements form a single recallable procedural rule about which documents are available as official copies and from whom.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the categories of official documents obtainable from the clerk under section 51 and the fee condition attached to obtaining them.

evidenceText: An official copy of the whole or any part of a will, or an official certificate of the grant of any letters probate of a will or of letters of administration may be obtained from the clerk on payment of the fee as prescribed by the rules.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 51 is a single-sentence procedural permission: it states what official copies may be obtained (whole or part of a will, or certificate of letters probate/administration), from whom (the clerk), and on what condition (fee as prescribed by the rules). It is short but creates a permission and a fee rule, giving it modest independent study value for Probate Court practice.

rows.heading: Appointment of administrator pending validity of will
rows.groupTitle: Appointment of Administrator Pending Validity of Will
rows.groupReason: The trigger, appointment power, residue-distribution limitation, Court control, and remuneration form one tightly interdependent interim-administrator concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Court may appoint an administrator pending will-validity proceedings, the appointed administrator's powers and the residue-distribution exclusion, the Court's continuing control, and the remuneration mechanism.

evidenceText: Pending an action or other proceeding concerning the validity of the will of a deceased person or for obtaining, recalling or revoking any grant of letters probate of a will or letters of administration, the Court may appoint an administrator of the property of the deceased person

the administrator so appointed has all the rights and powers of an administrator, other than the right of distributing the residue of the property, and every such administrator is subject to the immediate control and direction of the Court, and the Court may direct that such administrator receive out of the property of the deceased such reasonable remuneration as the Court considers proper

rows.sourceMapReason: Single coherent provision defining the Court's power to appoint an interim administrator during will-validity proceedings, that administrator's limited powers, Court control, and remuneration.

rows.heading: Appointment of administrator
rows.groupTitle: Default appointment of administrator and next-of-kin priority
rows.groupReason: Covers the primary triggers (dies wholly intestate; executor refuses upon citation), the eligible persons (spouse, next-of-kin, spouse of next-of-kin), and the Court's discretion among competing next-of-kin of equal degree.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the triggers for administration, the classes of persons the Court may appoint, and how competing claims among next-of-kin of equal degree are resolved under s. 53(1).
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 53 contains three distinct appointment mechanisms with different triggers, decision-makers, and legal effects, each independently recallable as a separate study concept.

rows.heading: Appointment of administrator
rows.groupTitle: Court appointment in special circumstances: insolvency and limitation
rows.groupReason: Covers the special-circumstances override (insolvency, other special circumstances), the Court's discretion to deviate from the normal entitlement, the security requirement, and the power to limit the administration.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which the Court may appoint a person other than the normally entitled one under s. 53(3), and identify the security and limitation powers available to the Court.

evidenceText: it appears to the Court to be necessary or convenient by reason of insolvency of the estate of the deceased, or other special circumstances

it is not obligatory upon the Court to grant administration to the person who if this subsection had not been enacted would have been entitled to a grant thereof, but the Court may appoint such person as it considers proper upon his giving such security as it directs, and every such administration may be limited as the Court considers best

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 53 contains three distinct appointment mechanisms with different triggers, decision-makers, and legal effects, each independently recallable as a separate study concept.

rows.heading: Appointment of administrator
rows.groupTitle: Transfer of administration right upon request and trust company eligibility
rows.groupReason: Covers the mechanism by which entitled persons (or a majority resident in the Province) transfer their administration right to a requested person, and the trust company eligibility under s. 53(4).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how the right to administration transfers to a requested person under s. 53(2) and identify the trust company eligibility rule in s. 53(4).

evidenceText: the right that such persons possessed to have administration granted to them in respect of it belongs to that person
A trust company authorized to do business in the Province may be appointed as administrator under subsection (2) or (3), either alone or jointly with another person.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 53 contains three distinct appointment mechanisms with different triggers, decision-makers, and legal effects, each independently recallable as a separate study concept.

rows.heading: Power of administrator to sue or prosecute or to act as personal representative of deceased
rows.groupTitle: Exclusive power of administrator to sue or act as personal representative
rows.groupReason: One rule: only the administrator may act as personal representative, and that exclusivity ends on recall or revocation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the exclusive holder of the power to sue, prosecute, or act as personal representative after a grant of letters of administration, and the event that ends that exclusivity.

evidenceText: no person, other than the administrator, has power to sue or prosecute any action or otherwise act as personal representative of the deceased as to the property comprised in or affected by such grant of administration until such administration has been recalled or revoked

rows.sourceMapReason: Short single-rule provision establishing the administrator's exclusive power to sue or act as personal representative and the temporal limit until recall or revocation; one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Limited letters
rows.groupTitle: Limited letters of administration
rows.groupReason: The entire section is one recallable concept: the eligibility, permissive nature, and Court-discretion condition for limited letters.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the eligibility requirement, permissive nature, and Court-discretion condition for taking out limited letters of administration.

evidenceText: A person entitled to a grant of letters of administration to the property of a deceased person may, at the discretion of the Court, take out limited letters.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single permissive rule stating who may take limited letters of administration and that the grant is at the Court's discretion.

rows.heading: Necessity to deliver statement of total value of property
rows.groupTitle: Statement of total value of estate property
rows.groupReason: Subsections 56(1)–(3) together set the pre-grant duty, the post-grant supplemental duty for newly discovered property, and the scope rule for partial applications.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when the statement of total value must be delivered, by whom, the two-month deadline for newly discovered property, and the scope limitation for partial applications or grants.
rows.sourceMapReason: All three subsections establish and modify a single procedural duty (delivering a verified statement of total value to the clerk) and form one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Bonds
rows.groupTitle: Enforcement of a broken bond
rows.groupReason: Subsection (4) establishes a distinct enforcement procedure with its own trigger (broken condition), actors (Court, clerk, assignee), and remedy (suit in own name, recovery as trustee).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the summary-application procedure for enforcing a broken bond, including the Court's order to assign the bond to a named person and the assignee's right to sue and recover as trustee for all persons interested.

evidenceText: on an application made in a summary manner and on being satisfied that the condition of a bond has been broken, may order the clerk to assign the bond to some person to be named in the order
he shall recover thereon, as trustee for all persons interested, the full amount recoverable in respect of any breach of the condition of the bond

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 57 contains three distinct recall tasks: who must or may be required to give a bond, the bond's amount and the Court's modification powers, and the enforcement procedure on breach. Each addresses different actors, triggers, and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Bonds
rows.groupTitle: Mandatory and discretionary bond requirements
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (1.1) together define the full scope of who must or may be required to give a bond and the bond's purpose and surety conditions.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify when a bond is mandatory (creditor of the deceased, non-resident of the Province) versus when the Court may discretionarily require one, and state the bond's purpose, surety requirement, and form.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 57 contains three distinct recall tasks: who must or may be required to give a bond, the bond's amount and the Court's modification powers, and the enforcement procedure on breach. Each addresses different actors, triggers, and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Bonds
rows.groupTitle: Bond amount, form, and Court modification powers
rows.groupReason: Subsections (2) and (3) govern the practical terms of the bond (amount, multiple bonds to limit surety liability) and the Court's power to modify or dispense with the bond under special circumstances.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the required bond amount, the Court's power to direct multiple bonds to limit surety liability, and the Court's power to reduce, revise conditions of, or dispense with a bond under special circumstances.

evidenceText: in an amount equal to the amount under which the property of the deceased has been sworn
the Court may at any time under special circumstances reduce the amount of, revise the conditions of, or dispense with, a bond

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 57 contains three distinct recall tasks: who must or may be required to give a bond, the bond's amount and the Court's modification powers, and the enforcement procedure on breach. Each addresses different actors, triggers, and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Exemptions from bond requirement
rows.groupTitle: Exemptions from bond requirement
rows.groupReason: One operative subsection creates a single negative-obligation rule for enumerated public and financial entities.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the entities exempt from giving security under section 58(1) and the fiduciary offices to which the exemption extends.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 58(1) is a single, self-contained exemption rule specifying which public and financial entities are relieved of the bond requirement in fiduciary offices.

rows.heading: Just and full account when lawfully required
rows.groupTitle: Limitation on requiring a just and full account from a personal representative
rows.groupReason: One rule: the account-rendering obligation in oaths, bonds, letters probate, and letters of administration applies only when lawfully required, not unconditionally in every instrument.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the condition under which oaths, bonds, letters probate, or letters of administration may require a personal representative to render a just and full account of executorship or administration.

evidenceText: shall require the personal representative to render a just and full account of his executorship or administration only when lawfully required

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 59 states a single, self-contained limitation: instruments given to personal representatives may require a just and full account only when lawfully required. This is one recallable rule with no internal split points.

rows.heading: Additional security
rows.groupTitle: Court power to require additional security and revoke letters of administration
rows.groupReason: Triggers, Court's power, revocation consequence, and initiation mechanism form one coherent recall task on when and how the Court enforces adequate security from a personal representative.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the conditions under which the Court may require other or additional security (surety death, insolvency, or other inadequacy), the consequence of non-compliance (revocation of the grant of letters of administration), and that the order may issue on the Court's own initiative or on the application of any person interested.
rows.sourceMapReason: A short, self-contained provision stating the triggers, the Court's power to require additional security, the revocation consequence, and the procedural trigger for the order, all tightly interdependent as one rule.

rows.heading: Substitution of surety
rows.groupTitle: Substitution of surety for a personal representative
rows.groupReason: Triggers (surety discharge or PR substitution), Court's discretionary power and terms, discharge conditions (substituted security and optionally passed accounts), and the ex parte or on-notice application procedure form one mechanism a learner recalls as a unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two triggering scenarios, the Court's power and discretion over terms, the conditions for discharging the surety, and how an application under section 61(1) may be made.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 61 states one coherent Court power (allowing substitution of security for a personal representative) with its triggers, discharge conditions, and a short application-procedure rule; all pieces are tightly interdependent and form a single recall task.

rows.heading: Cancellation of bond or security
rows.groupTitle: Prerequisites for Court Direction Cancelling an Administrator's Bond
rows.groupReason: One recall task: the two conditions (final accounts passed; property paid into Court or distributed) that trigger the Court's permissive power to direct cancellation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two prerequisites an administrator must satisfy before the Court may direct that the administrator's bond or other security be delivered up to be cancelled.

evidenceText: Where an administrator has passed his or her final accounts and has paid into Court or distributed the whole of the property of the deceased that has come to his or her hands, the Court may direct any bond or other security furnished by the administrator to be delivered up to be cancelled.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 62 states a single, self-contained rule: the two prerequisites under which the Court may direct an administrator's bond or security to be cancelled. No split or combine is warranted.

rows.heading: Notice to guardian, representative and others before bond or security cancelled
rows.groupTitle: Conditions for cancelling an administrator's bond and mandatory notice for vulnerable beneficiaries
rows.groupReason: The general cancellation condition and the mandatory notice safeguard for minors and SDMA-represented persons are one interdependent rule; recalling them separately would fragment the single procedural concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the evidence the administrator must produce for the Court to cancel a bond or security and identify to whom notice must be given when a minor or a person with a representative under the Supported Decision-Making and Representation Act was or is entitled to part of the estate.

evidenceText: If an administrator has produced evidence to the satisfaction of the Court that the debts of the deceased have been paid and the residue of the estate has been duly distributed, the Court may make an order directing any bond or other security furnished by the administrator to be delivered up to be cancelled

if a minor or a person for whom a representative has been appointed under the Supported Decision-Making and Representation Act was or is entitled to a part of the estate under the distribution, the order shall not be made until after such notice as the Court directs has been given to the guardian or the representative, as the case may be, and to any person beneficially interested in the estate

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 63 is a short, self-contained procedural rule: the condition for the Court to cancel an administrator's bond (debts paid, residue distributed, evidence to the Court's satisfaction) plus a tightly linked mandatory notice safeguard for minors and Supported Decision-Making and Representation Act–represented persons. The rule and its condition form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Priority of payment of debts
rows.groupTitle: Deficiency of assets: pari passu rule, security preservation, and affidavit proof
rows.groupReason: Subsection (2) combines the pari passu treatment in a deficiency, the Crown and existing-security savings, and the affidavit precondition into one interdependent deficiency framework.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the pari passu rule for estate debts when assets are deficient, the preserved rights of the Crown and existing liens, mortgages, or other security, and the affidavit proof requirement before a debt may be paid or an action brought.

evidenceText: all debts due shall be paid pari passu and without any reference to priority of debts of one rank or nature over those of another
nothing herein prejudices any rights of the Crown or any lien, mortgage or other security existing during the lifetime of the deceased
no debt due by the deceased shall be paid by the personal representative, or action brought therefor, until the debt is proven by affidavit

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 64 contains two distinct recall tasks: the fixed priority waterfall in subsection (1) and the deficiency-of-assets framework in subsection (2), each independently testable.

rows.heading: Priority of payment of debts
rows.groupTitle: Priority order for applying estate assets
rows.groupReason: Subsection (1) sets a fixed six-step waterfall for applying estate assets, forming one ordered recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the six priority categories for applying estate assets in the order set out in section 64(1)(a)–(f).
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 64 contains two distinct recall tasks: the fixed priority waterfall in subsection (1) and the deficiency-of-assets framework in subsection (2), each independently testable.

rows.heading: Contestation of claim
rows.groupTitle: Notice of contestation and claimant's response deadline
rows.groupReason: The notice trigger, the claimant's response obligation with filing requirements, and the forever-barred consequence form one interdependent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the personal representative's written notice requirements, the claimant's 30-day (or 3-month) application deadline and verified-statement filing, the Court's hearing role, and the consequence of deemed abandonment and permanent bar.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 65 contains a multi-stage estate-claim contestation procedure with distinct recall tasks for notice and response, procedural routing, evidentiary powers, fees, and enforcement.

rows.heading: Contestation of claim
rows.groupTitle: Procedural routing, participation, and scope
rows.groupReason: Subsections (3)–(6) and (8) together determine the applicable procedure (Small Claims or King's Bench), required notice, standing of interested persons, and the section's application to claims not presently payable.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how Small Claims–eligible and non-Small Claims claims are routed, the notice and standing rules for each track, the consent exception in subsection (6), and that the section applies even where the claim is not presently payable.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 65 contains a multi-stage estate-claim contestation procedure with distinct recall tasks for notice and response, procedural routing, evidentiary powers, fees, and enforcement.

rows.heading: Contestation of claim
rows.groupTitle: Evidentiary powers for contested claim proceedings
rows.groupReason: Subsections (9)–(12) collectively define the Court's evidentiary powers—commissions, evidence de bene esse, witness summonses—and the applicable Rules of Court and cost tariff.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Court's powers to issue commissions for out-of-Province witnesses, take evidence de bene esse for sick, aged, infirm, or departing witnesses, issue witness summonses, and apply the Judicature Act Rules of Court with King's Bench cost tariffs.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 65 contains a multi-stage estate-claim contestation procedure with distinct recall tasks for notice and response, procedural routing, evidentiary powers, fees, and enforcement.

rows.heading: Contestation of claim
rows.groupTitle: Fees and costs in contested claim proceedings
rows.groupReason: Subsection (7) sets a multi-branch fee structure keyed to whether the Small Claims procedure or another procedure applies.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that Small Claims–procedure claims pay the SCA tariff, other claims pay fees equivalent to an estate audit of the same value, and the Court fixes counsel or solicitor fees based on the amount involved and the importance of the contest.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 65 contains a multi-stage estate-claim contestation procedure with distinct recall tasks for notice and response, procedural routing, evidentiary powers, fees, and enforcement.

rows.heading: Contestation of claim
rows.groupTitle: Enforcement of established claims
rows.groupReason: Subsections (13) and (14) form a two-step enforcement mechanism: Court permission is required, then the order is filed in the Court of King's Bench for execution as a judgment.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that no enforcement proceeding may be taken without Court permission, and that once permission is given the order is filed in the Court of King's Bench with execution issuing as upon a judgment of that Court, including costs.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 65 contains a multi-stage estate-claim contestation procedure with distinct recall tasks for notice and response, procedural routing, evidentiary powers, fees, and enforcement.

rows.heading: Idem
rows.groupTitle: Claimant application and bar consequence for non-s.65(1) claims
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(3) form one procedural obligation: scope trigger, the claimant's filing requirements and time limits, the seven-day notice to the PR and others, and the bar consequence of inaction.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the scope of claims covered by s. 66, the claimant's filing requirements (affidavit-verified statement and copy of notice of contestation), the time limits, the notice requirement to the personal representative and others, and the consequence of failing to apply (deemed abandoned and forever barred).

evidenceText: if the claimant does not make the application he shall be deemed to have abandoned his claim or demand and it is forever barred

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 66 extends the contestation procedure to claims outside s. 65(1) and contains two distinct recall tasks: the claimant's filing obligation with a bar consequence, and the Court's directional powers plus appeal rights of beneficially interested persons.

rows.heading: Idem
rows.groupTitle: Court's directional powers and appeal rights under s. 66
rows.groupReason: Subsections (4)–(8) cover the Court's discretionary directions (order to bring an action, prescribe timing), the consent-trial option, the cross-reference to s. 65(9)–(12), and the two distinct paths by which a person beneficially interested may appeal or appear.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the Court's powers to direct the claimant to bring an action or prescribe a timing, the consent-trial option, and the two separate paths by which a person beneficially interested in the estate may obtain leave to appeal or appear.

evidenceText: direct the claimant to bring an action for recovery or establishment of his claim or demand on such terms and conditions as it considers just

If the personal representative does not appeal from an order made under subsection (2) or (4), any person beneficially interested in the estate may by leave of a judge of the Court of King's Bench appeal therefrom

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 66 extends the contestation procedure to claims outside s. 65(1) and contains two distinct recall tasks: the claimant's filing obligation with a bar consequence, and the Court's directional powers plus appeal rights of beneficially interested persons.

rows.heading: Resolution of dispute in summary manner
rows.groupTitle: Summary Resolution of Disputed Ownership of Estate Personal Property
rows.groupReason: States the triggering conditions (personal representative, personal property, Small Claims threshold, disputed claim) and the applicable procedure (summary manner, section 65 with modifications) as one interdependent rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the conditions under which a personal representative's ownership claim for personal property may be determined in a summary manner and confirm that section 65 applies with necessary modifications.

evidenceText: Where the personal representative of a deceased person claims the ownership of any personal property not exceeding in value the amount prescribed under the Small Claims Act, and his claim is disputed by any other person, the dispute may be determined in a summary manner and section 65 shall apply with the necessary modifications.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 67 is a single, self-contained provision establishing a summary-dispute mechanism for personal representative ownership claims within the Small Claims threshold, incorporating section 65 with modifications.

rows.heading: Application of Limitation of Actions Act
rows.groupTitle: Notice to Preserve a Claim Against an Estate Under the Limitation of Actions Act
rows.groupReason: Subsection 1 sets out the content, verification, timing, and filing-destination requirements for a notice that preserves a claim against a deceased person's estate.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the requirements for filing a notice to preserve a claim against an estate: full particulars, affidavit or affirmation verification, filing before the limitation deadline, and the filing hierarchy (executor/administrator, then probate office, then Registrar).
rows.sourceMapReason: Subsection 1 states one coherent procedural mechanism for preserving estate claims against limitation; subsection 2 is repealed and carries no operative content.

rows.heading: Accounting of executor as trustee
rows.groupTitle: Accounting by executor who is also trustee
rows.groupReason: One rule: when a person holds both executor and trustee roles under a will, trusteeship accounts may be required in the same manner as executorship accounts.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the accounting requirement and the applicable manner when an executor under a will also serves as trustee.

evidenceText: An executor who is also a trustee under a will may be required to account for his trusteeship in the same manner as he may be required to account in respect of his executorship.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single short provision stating an independently operative accounting rule for a dual fiduciary role (executor-trustee); one coherent recall task with no structural ambiguity.

rows.heading: Binding effect of approval by Court
rows.groupTitle: Binding Effect of Court Approval of Accounts
rows.groupReason: The trigger (filing, Court approval, subsequent passing in the Court of King's Bench), the binding effect, the mistake-or-fraud exception, and the scope of persons bound form one coherent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a Probate Court's approval of a personal representative's account is binding, identify the mistake-or-fraud exception, and name the persons and claimants against whom the approval operates.

evidenceText: such approval, except so far as mistake or fraud is shown, is binding upon any person who was notified of the proceedings taken before the Court or who was present or represented thereat, and upon everyone claiming under any such person

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 70 states a single interdependent rule: the binding effect of a Probate Court's approval of a personal representative's account, including trigger conditions, the mistake-or-fraud exception, and the class of persons bound. All elements are needed together to recall the rule correctly.

rows.heading: Power of the Court to make inquiry
rows.groupTitle: Court's inquiry jurisdiction over a personal representative's accounts
rows.groupReason: The core jurisdictional grant: scope, evidentiary power, dispute resolution, and appealability form one recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the scope of the Court's inquiry power over a personal representative's accounts, including its power to take evidence, decide disputed matters, and the appealability of its decisions.

evidenceText: has jurisdiction to enter into and make a full inquiry and accounting of and concerning the whole property of which the deceased died possessed or entitled, and the administration and disbursement thereof in as full and ample a manner as the Court considers necessary, and for such purpose may take evidence and decide disputed matters arising in such accounting, subject to appeal

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 71 contains five distinct recall tasks: the Court's core inquiry jurisdiction, the misconduct/damages remedy and its trial mechanism, notice rules for interested persons (including protective notices), Public Trustee notice triggers, and the power to appoint an expert. These involve different actors, triggers, and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Power of the Court to make inquiry
rows.groupTitle: Inquiry into personal representative misconduct and trial of issues
rows.groupReason: The substantive misconduct/damages remedy (71(2)) and its dedicated trial mechanism (71(3)) are tightly coupled: one states the claim and remedy, the other provides the procedural vehicle for contested issues.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the Court's power to inquire into a personal representative's misconduct, neglect, or default causing financial loss, the remedy it may order, and the trial-of-issue procedure available for contested claims.

evidenceText: power to inquire into any complaint or claim, by any person interested in such accounts, of misconduct, neglect or default on the part of the personal representative occasioning financial loss to the estate or trust fund, and the Court, on proof of such claim, may order the personal representative to pay such sum by way of damages or otherwise as it considers proper and just to the estate or trust fund

may order the trial of an issue of any complaint or claim under subsection (2), and in such case it shall make all necessary directions as to pleadings, production of documents and otherwise in connection with the issue

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 71 contains five distinct recall tasks: the Court's core inquiry jurisdiction, the misconduct/damages remedy and its trial mechanism, notice rules for interested persons (including protective notices), Public Trustee notice triggers, and the power to appoint an expert. These involve different actors, triggers, and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Power of the Court to make inquiry
rows.groupTitle: Notice requirements for interested persons (general and protective notices)
