rows.groupReason: The general seven-day notice rule (71(4)) and the protective twenty-one-day notice rules for minors, persons of unsound mind, and psychiatric facility patients (71(5)-(6)) with the 'not bound' consequence form one coherent notice-to-interested-persons unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the general and protective notice requirements before accounts are passed, including the different notice periods, the persons to be served for vulnerable parties, and the consequence of non-service.

evidenceText: if resident in the Province, entitled to not fewer than seven days' notice thereof, and if resident out of the Province are entitled to such notice as the Court may direct

his notice shall be served upon his guardian not fewer than twenty-one days before the day appointed for the passing of the accounts, and unless such notice is so given such person is not bound by the passing of the accounts

his notice shall be served upon one of his next-of-kin not fewer than twenty-one days before the day appointed for the passing of the accounts, and unless such notice is so given such person is not bound by the passing of the accounts

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 71 contains five distinct recall tasks: the Court's core inquiry jurisdiction, the misconduct/damages remedy and its trial mechanism, notice rules for interested persons (including protective notices), Public Trustee notice triggers, and the power to appoint an expert. These involve different actors, triggers, and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Power of the Court to make inquiry
rows.groupTitle: When the Public Trustee must be served with notice of an application to pass accounts
rows.groupReason: Both subsections impose the same obligation (serve notice on the Public Trustee) under two distinct triggering circumstances: charitable/religious trust property under a will or instrument (71(7)) and intestate death with doubtful next-of-kin (71(8)).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two circumstances requiring service of notice on the Public Trustee before an application to pass accounts: charitable/religious trust property and intestate death with doubtful surviving next-of-kin.

evidenceText: notice of an application for the passing of accounts shall be served upon the Public Trustee, unless the Public Trustee is himself or herself the executor, administrator or trustee

Where a person has died intestate in the Province and administration has been granted to some person who is neither the Public Trustee nor one of the next-of-kin, and it appears to be doubtful whether the intestate left any next-of-kin surviving him or her or that there are no known next-of-kin resident in the Province, notice of an application for the passing of accounts shall be served upon the Public Trustee

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 71 contains five distinct recall tasks: the Court's core inquiry jurisdiction, the misconduct/damages remedy and its trial mechanism, notice rules for interested persons (including protective notices), Public Trustee notice triggers, and the power to appoint an expert. These involve different actors, triggers, and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Power of the Court to make inquiry
rows.groupTitle: Court's power to appoint an expert for complex accounts
rows.groupReason: A discrete, conditional procedural power triggered by account complexity, distinct from the Court's own inquiry jurisdiction.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which the Court may appoint an accountant or other skilled person to assist in auditing accounts.

evidenceText: Where accounts submitted to the Court are of an intricate or complicated character and in the opinion of the Court require expert investigation, it may appoint an accountant or other skilled person to investigate and to assist it in auditing the accounts

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 71 contains five distinct recall tasks: the Court's core inquiry jurisdiction, the misconduct/damages remedy and its trial mechanism, notice rules for interested persons (including protective notices), Public Trustee notice triggers, and the power to appoint an expert. These involve different actors, triggers, and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Rendering of account by inventory
rows.groupTitle: Compelling an executor or administrator to account: inventory as the exclusive form
rows.groupReason: 72(1) states the general rule (inventory-only) and its exception (interested person or creditor), and 72(2) protects the rule from prior bond terms; together they answer one recall question about when and how an executor or administrator may be compelled to account.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that an executor or administrator cannot be compelled to render an account other than by inventory unless a person interested in the property or a creditor of the deceased requests otherwise, and that this rule applies notwithstanding any contrary provision in a prior bond or security.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 72 is a short, self-contained rule: inventory is the exclusive compellable form of account, the exception is an interested person or creditor requesting otherwise, and 72(2) ensures the rule overrides prior bonds. All parts are interdependent and form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Sealing of letters or other legal documents grant by a Court of another jurisdiction
rows.groupTitle: Resealing procedure, jurisdictional scope, and legal effect
rows.groupReason: Conditions, jurisdictional scope, the Quebec deemed provision, and the like-force-and-effect rule form one coherent resealing mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the conditions for resealing out-of-jurisdiction probate documents and state the legal effect of sealing in the Province.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 73 contains a general resealing procedure with its legal effect, plus a distinct security prerequisite that applies only to letters of administration and involves a different actor and requirement.

rows.heading: Sealing of letters or other legal documents grant by a Court of another jurisdiction
rows.groupTitle: Security prerequisite for resealing letters of administration
rows.groupReason: A distinct condition applying only to letters of administration, involving the issuing court's clerk or registrar and a security bond as a bar to resealing.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the security and certification requirements that must be satisfied before letters of administration may be resealed by the Court.

evidenceText: The letters of administration or other legal document purporting to be of the same nature shall not be sealed with the Seal of the Court until a certificate has been filed with the Court, signed by the clerk or the registrar of the court that issued the letters or document, certifying that security has been given in the court in a sufficient amount to cover the assets outside the jurisdiction of the Court as well as the assets within the Province or, in the absence of such certificate, until like security is given to the Court covering the assets within the Province as in the case of granting original letters of administration.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 73 contains a general resealing procedure with its legal effect, plus a distinct security prerequisite that applies only to letters of administration and involves a different actor and requirement.

rows.heading: Rehearing before another judge
rows.groupTitle: Rehearing trigger, application, and Chief Justice's order
rows.groupReason: Covers the trigger conditions, the party's right to apply, the Chief Justice's order requirements, and the interim procedural freeze as one initiation sequence.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the circumstances under which a rehearing may be sought before another judge, the application procedure to the Chief Justice of the Court of King's Bench, and the requirements of the resulting order including the interim freeze on proceedings.

evidenceText: Where the judge before whom any action, cause, matter or other proceeding under this Act is tried dies or retires, or for any other reason ceases to hold office, before disposing of it, or having heard it has not disposed of it within six months thereafter, any party may, upon notice to all of the parties, apply to the Chief Justice of the Court of King's Bench for an order
An order made under subsection (1) shall name the place where the action, cause, matter or other proceeding is to be reheard or otherwise disposed of
No proceedings in the action, cause, matter or other proceeding shall thereafter be taken without the order of the Chief Justice after such notice as he may provide

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 74 is a complete rehearing procedure with distinct procedural stages and different actors; the initiation/order stage (74(1)–(3)) and the conduct/costs/appeal stage (74(4)–(6)) are independently recallable.

rows.heading: Rehearing before another judge
rows.groupTitle: Rehearing procedure, costs, and appeal rights
rows.groupReason: The rehearing conduct, cost allocation, and appeal rights form a distinct post-order procedural stage with separate recall tasks.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe how a rehearing is conducted (evidence read, argument, treated as original trial), who fixes costs and directs payment, and the manner of appeal from the rehearing judgment.

evidenceText: the evidence, exhibits and papers used at the trial shall be read and, after argument by counsel, the presiding judge shall deal with the action as on an original trial
The costs of the rehearing or other disposition shall be fixed by the judge presiding at the rehearing, who shall also direct by whom they are to be paid
An appeal lies from such judgment or finding in the same manner and on the same terms as if the judgment had been pronounced at the trial

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 74 is a complete rehearing procedure with distinct procedural stages and different actors; the initiation/order stage (74(1)–(3)) and the conduct/costs/appeal stage (74(4)–(6)) are independently recallable.

rows.heading: Calculation of fees payable
rows.groupTitle: Fee calculation on estate value
rows.groupReason: Both subsections together define the single calculation rule: the whole estate (real and personal) is the fee base, and the actual value of encumbrances is deducted from real property.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the estate value base on which fees are calculated and the encumbrance deduction applied to real property.
rows.sourceMapReason: Two short subsections form one coherent fee-calculation rule: fees are assessed on the whole estate value, with encumbrances deducted from real property.

rows.heading: Tax payable
rows.groupTitle: Probate tax: triggers, payer, and calculation basis
rows.groupReason: Subsection (1) sets the two trigger events and the duty to pay; subsections (2) and (3) supply the interdependent valuation rule (whole estate, deduct encumbrances) that completes the same tax calculation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two events that trigger probate tax under s.75.1(1), state who pays and to whom, and explain that the tax is calculated on the whole estate (real and personal) with the actual value of any encumbrance deducted from real property.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 75.1 establishes one coherent tax obligation: the triggering events, the payer (the estate), the recipient (Crown in right of the Province), and the valuation rules, all forming a single recallable probate-tax concept.

rows.heading: Functions of Rules Committee
rows.groupTitle: Functions of the Rules Committee
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) are interdependent: the recommendation power in (2)(b) is explicitly tied to the inquiry in (1), forming one coherent set of committee functions.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the three matters the Rules Committee may examine and the two categories of recommendations it may make to the Lieutenant-Governor in Council.

evidenceText: The Rules Committee may inquire into and examine
The Rules Committee may make recommendations to the Lieutenant-Governor in Council

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 76 is a short, self-contained provision defining the Rules Committee's inquiry and recommendation powers; the two subsections are tightly interdependent and form one recallable institutional function.

rows.heading: Regulations
rows.groupTitle: Regulation-making power and authorized areas (s. 77)
rows.groupReason: The enumerated regulatory areas and the delegation power form one recall task: what may the Lieutenant-Governor in Council regulate, and what may those regulations do.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify each area in which the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make regulations for the Court under s. 77(1)(a)–(e) and the delegation or discretion power in s. 77(2).

evidenceText: The Lieutenant-Governor in Council may make regulations
Regulations made under paragraph (1)(a) may delegate a matter to or confer discretion on the Court.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 77 is a single coherent regulation-making power: it identifies the maker (Lieutenant-Governor in Council), enumerates the regulatory areas in (1)(a)–(e), and adds one delegation qualification in (2). All elements answer the same recall question and are tightly interdependent.

rows.groupTitle: Estate tax schedule under s. 75.1(1)(a)
rows.groupReason: Three-tier estate tax formula with distinct thresholds and per-$1,000 rates; independently recallable as a single calculation rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three estate-value thresholds ($20,000; $100,000) and the applicable base-plus-incremental rates for each tier of the s. 75.1(1)(a) tax.

evidenceText: if the value of the estate or the part of the estate being administered does not exceed $20,000, $200
if the value of the estate or the part of the estate being administered exceeds $20,000 but not $100,000, $200 plus $5 per $1,000 or part of $1,000 by which the value of the estate exceeds $20,000
if the value of the estate or the part of the estate being administered exceeds $100,000, $600 plus $15 per $1,000 or part of $1,000 by which the value of the estate exceeds $100,000

rows.sourceMapReason: Schedule A contains two independently recallable tax schedules tied to different subsections of s. 75.1(1), with different triggers, tier structures, and rates; a learner would be tested on each calculation separately.

rows.groupTitle: Passing-of-accounts tax under s. 75.1(1)(b)
rows.groupReason: Separate two-tier tax on passing of accounts with its own trigger and rates, distinct from the main estate tax formula.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the two-tier passing-of-accounts tax: flat $40.00 at or below $20,000 and $2.00 per $1,000 or part thereof above $20,000.

evidenceText: on every passing of accounts, including all services in connection with the passing of accounts, where the amount of capital and income
exceeds $20,000, the sum of $2.00 per $1000 or part thereof of the value of the capital and income

rows.sourceMapReason: Schedule A contains two independently recallable tax schedules tied to different subsections of s. 75.1(1), with different triggers, tier structures, and rates; a learner would be tested on each calculation separately.

rows.heading: Employee benefit plans
rows.groupTitle: Exemption of Employee Benefit Plan Trusts from Perpetuity Rules
rows.groupReason: One rule with a defined scope of covered plans, trusts, funds, and beneficiaries.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the rules of law and statutory enactments relating to perpetuities do not apply, and are deemed never to have applied, to trusts of a plan, trust, or fund established to provide pensions, retirement allowances, annuities, or sickness, death, or other benefits to employees or their widows, widowers, dependants, or other beneficiaries.
rows.sourceMapReason: A single, self-contained rule exempting employee benefit plan trusts from perpetuity rules; one recallable concept with no internal split needed.

rows.heading: Apportionment of rent, annuity, dividend or periodic payment
rows.groupTitle: Daily accrual and apportionability of periodic payments
rows.groupReason: One rule covering the scope of covered payments (rents, annuities, dividends, other periodical income) and the daily-accrual/apportionability principle.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the categories of periodic payments covered by section 4 and the rule that they accrue from day to day and are apportionable in respect of time.

evidenceText: All rents, annuities, dividends and other periodical payments in the nature of income, whether reserved or made payable under an instrument in writing or otherwise, shall be considered as accruing from day to day, and shall be apportionable in respect of time accordingly.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 4 states one self-contained rule: listed periodic income payments accrue daily and are apportionable by time. No internal split is needed.

rows.heading: Recovery of apportionment
rows.groupTitle: Timing of recovery for apportioned parts (s. 5)
rows.groupReason: Both sub-paragraphs define the single rule for when an apportioned part becomes payable, covering the continuing-payment and determined-payment scenarios as two faces of the same timing concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two timing rules in s. 5 for when an apportioned part of a rent, annuity, dividend, or other payment becomes payable or recoverable: (a) for a continuing payment, when the entire portion becomes due; and (b) for a payment determined by re-entry, death, or otherwise, when the next entire portion would have been payable had the payment not so determined.

evidenceText: shall be payable or recoverable at the following times and not before
in the case of a continuing rent, annuity or other such payment when the entire portion, of which such apportioned part forms part, becomes due and payable
in the case of a rent, annuity or other such payment determined by re-entry, death or otherwise, when the next entire portion of the same would have been payable if the same had not so determined

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 5 states one coherent timing rule — when an apportioned part becomes payable or recoverable — with two scenarios (continuing vs. determined payment) that together answer a single recall question. It is independently operative and distinct from s. 4 (the apportionment principle) and s. 6 (remedies and recovering parties).

rows.heading: Idem
rows.groupTitle: Remedies for recovering apportioned parts of rents and other payments
rows.groupReason: General remedy parity with proportionate allowances, plus the specific recovery mechanism for rents reserved or charged on lands, including the requirement to sue in a court of competent jurisdiction.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the general remedy parity available to holders of apportioned parts (including proportionate allowances) and explain how recovery differs for rents reserved or charged on lands, including the court-action requirement to recover the apportioned part from the person entitled to the entire rent.

evidenceText: shall have such or the same remedies for recovering the apportioned parts as aforesaid when payable, allowing the proportionate parts of all just allowances, as they respectively would have had for recovering such entire portions as aforesaid if entitled thereto respectively

persons liable to pay rents reserved out of, or charged on lands or other hereditaments, and the same lands or other hereditaments shall not be resorted to for any such apportioned part forming part of an entire or continuing rent
such apportioned part shall be recoverable from the executor or other person by other parties entitled under this Act to the same, by action in any court of competent jurisdiction

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 states the general remedy parity for apportioned parts and a directly dependent exception for rents charged on lands; together they form one coherent recall unit on recovering apportioned shares.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Defined terms for apportionment: annuities, dividends, rents
rows.groupReason: All three defined terms establish the scope of periodic payments subject to apportionment under sections 4–6.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the scope of the defined terms 'annuities,' 'dividends,' and 'rents' for apportionment, including the daily-increment accrual rule and the capital-return exclusion for dividends.
rows.sourceMapReason: Three interrelated definitions scoping the apportionment provisions in sections 4–6 form one coherent vocabulary unit of limited length.

rows.heading: No apportionment
rows.groupTitle: Exclusions from Apportionment
rows.groupReason: The two subsections together define the boundaries of the apportionment regime by excluding insurance-policy annual sums and cases with an express no-apportionment stipulation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two categories in which the apportionment provisions of sections 4–7 do not apply.
rows.sourceMapReason: Both subsections state exclusions from the apportionment regime in sections 4–7 and together answer the same recall question: when do those rules not apply?

rows.heading: Contingent remainder
rows.groupTitle: Contingent remainder survives determination of preceding estate
rows.groupReason: One operative rule on when a contingent remainder takes effect and the three modes of preceding-estate determination that do not defeat it.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the three modes of determination (forfeiture, surrender, merger) that do not defeat a contingent remainder and the rule that the remainder takes effect as if the determination had not happened.

evidenceText: capable of taking effect, notwithstanding the determination by forfeiture, surrender or merger of any preceding estate of freehold, in the same manner in all respects as if such determination had not happened

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 9 states one self-contained rule: a contingent remainder takes effect notwithstanding determination of a preceding freehold estate by forfeiture, surrender, or merger, with a standard savings for pre-commencement creations.

rows.heading: Power of aliens, conveyance by grant or livery
rows.groupTitle: Property rights of aliens
rows.groupReason: Substantive rule placing alien acquisition, holding, and title derivation of property on equal footing with Canadian citizens.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that an alien may take, acquire, hold, and dispose of real and personal property in the same manner as a Canadian citizen, and that title may be derived through, from, or in succession to an alien in the same manner as through a Canadian citizen.
rows.sourceMapReason: The two subsections address independently recallable concepts: alien property rights and the grant/livery conveyance rule, with different subjects and legal effects.

rows.heading: Power of aliens, conveyance by grant or livery
rows.groupTitle: Freehold conveyance by grant or livery
rows.groupReason: Rules that corporeal tenements and hereditaments lie in grant as well as in livery for the conveyance of the immediate freehold.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that all corporeal tenements and hereditaments are deemed to lie in grant as well as in livery as regards the conveyance of the immediate freehold.
rows.sourceMapReason: The two subsections address independently recallable concepts: alien property rights and the grant/livery conveyance rule, with different subjects and legal effects.

rows.heading: Necessity of deed, tortious operation of feoffment
rows.groupTitle: Deed requirement for land transactions and abolition of feoffment (s. 11)
rows.groupReason: Both subsections state the operative post-1904 rule: enumerated transactions are void without a deed, and feoffments carry no tortious operation; recalling them together answers the single question of what form and effect the law gives to these conveyances.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify each type of land transaction that is void at law unless made by deed under s. 11 and state the effect on feoffments made after July 1, 1904.

evidenceText: A feoffment made after July 1, 1904, is void at law unless evidenced by deed
A feoffment made after July 1, 1904, shall not have any tortious operation.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short section establishing the deed-form requirement for enumerated land transactions and abolishing tortious operation of feoffments; both subsections form one coherent conveyancing-form concept.

rows.heading: Voiding of exchange or partition, interpretation
rows.groupTitle: Interpretation rules for deed language under s. 12
rows.groupReason: All three subsections state concise interpretive rules about what deed words do and do not imply, answerable as a single recall task on statutory deed interpretation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what implied conditions or covenments are excluded in exchanges, partitions, and deeds using 'give' or 'grant' after July 1, 1904, and identify the sufficient words to limit a fee simple estate without using 'heirs'.
rows.sourceMapReason: Three short interpretive rules for deed language (no implied condition in exchanges/partitions, no implied covenant from 'give'/'grant', 'heirs' not required for fee simple) form one coherent recall unit on deed interpretation.

rows.heading: Words “grant, bargain and sell”
rows.groupTitle: Effect of 'grant, bargain and sell' in fee simple conveyances
rows.groupReason: Single interpretive rule with its directly dependent exception; recalling them separately would fragment one concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what the words 'grant, bargain and sell' amount to in a fee simple conveyance limited to grantee and heirs, and identify the limitation on that interpretation.

evidenceText: the words "grant", bargain and sell," therein only amount to a covenant by the grantor or bargainor that he has done no act to encumber the land
nothing in this section shall be held or construed to prevent those words from amounting to a conveyance, or to prevent the same from being sufficient to convey and transfer all the right and title

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 states one tightly interdependent interpretive rule: the default legal effect of 'grant, bargain and sell' in a fee simple conveyance (covenant of non-encumbrance) plus its directly dependent savings clause. Both parts are needed to recall the rule correctly.

rows.heading: Interest of person not named in indenture, deed purporting to be indenture
rows.groupTitle: Unnamed taker of estate or interest under an indenture
rows.groupReason: Standalone permission rule: a taker need not be a named party to take an immediate estate, interest, or covenant benefit under an indenture executed after July 1, 1904.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the condition under which a person not named a party to an indenture may still take an immediate estate, interest, or the benefit of a condition or covenant, and identify the temporal boundary (indentures executed after July 1, 1904).

evidenceText: an immediate estate or interest in any land, and the benefit of a condition or covenant respecting any land, may be taken although the taker thereof is not named a party to the indenture

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsection 14(1) is a permission rule about who may take under an indenture; 14(2) is a separate declarative-effect rule about document form. They answer different recall questions and involve different legal modalities, making them independently studyable despite their brevity.

rows.heading: Interest of person not named in indenture, deed purporting to be indenture
rows.groupTitle: Effect of deed purporting to be an indenture
rows.groupReason: Separate declarative rule: a deed that purports to be an indenture carries indenture effect regardless of whether it is physically indented.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the legal effect of a deed that purports to be an indenture when the document is not actually indented.

evidenceText: A deed purporting to be an indenture shall have the effect of an indenture, although not actually indented.

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsection 14(1) is a permission rule about who may take under an indenture; 14(2) is a separate declarative-effect rule about document form. They answer different recall questions and involve different legal modalities, making them independently studyable despite their brevity.

rows.heading: Interest disposed of by deed
rows.groupTitle: Disposal by deed of contingent, executory, future interests and rights of entry
rows.groupReason: All enumerated interests and rights of entry share one operative rule — disposition by deed — forming a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the categories of land interests (contingent, executory, future; possibility coupled with an interest; right of entry) that section 15 permits to be disposed of by deed, including the stated qualifiers (ascertained or unascertained object; immediate or future; vested or contingent).

evidenceText: A contingent, an executory, or a future interest, or a possibility coupled with an interest, in any land, whether the object of the gift or limitation of such interest or possibility is or is not ascertained, or a right of entry, whether immediate or future and whether vested or contingent, into or upon any land may be disposed of by deed.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single permission (disposition by deed) applied to enumerated interest types with shared qualifiers; no separate actors, modalities, or procedural stages warrant splitting.

rows.heading: Release of rent charge
rows.groupTitle: Effect of partial release from a rentcharge
rows.groupReason: One recall task: what a partial rentcharge release does and does not do, including the protection of non-consenting interest holders in remaining lands.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the legal effect of a partial release from a rentcharge on the charge as a whole, on rent recovery from released lands, and on the rights of persons in remaining unreleased lands who do not concur in the release.

evidenceText: A release from a rentcharge of part of the lands charged therewith does not extinguish the whole rentcharge but operates only to bar the right to recover any part of the rent charged out of the lands released, without prejudice nevertheless to the rights of any person interested in the lands remaining unreleased and not concurring in or confirming the release.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single coherent rule on the effect of a partial rentcharge release, with tightly interdependent limitation and third-party protection clauses that form one recall task.

rows.heading: Release of land from judgment
rows.groupTitle: Effect of Partial Release on Judgment Charge
rows.groupReason: Single operative rule preserving judgment validity on unreleased land while protecting rights of non-concurring interested persons; the two elements are interdependent and should be recalled together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the effect on a judgment of releasing only part of the charged lands and identify the rights preserved for interested persons in the remaining unreleased lands who do not concur in or confirm the release.

evidenceText: A release from a judgment of part of any lands charged therewith does not affect the validity of the judgment as to the lands remaining unreleased, without prejudice nevertheless to the rights of any person interested in the lands remaining unreleased, and not concurring in or confirming the release.

rows.sourceMapReason: One-sentence rule with a tightly coupled savings clause forming a single recallable concept about partial release from a judgment charge.

rows.heading: Use
rows.groupTitle: Operation of uses and non-necessity of continued seisin
rows.groupReason: One rule with one operative effect: uses take effect by relation to the original vesting and no continued seisin or scintilla juris is required or deemed to subsist.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State how uses under an instrument take effect under s. 18 and explain why continued seisin to uses or scintilla juris is not necessary for future, contingent, or executory uses.

evidenceText: all uses thereunder, whether expressed or implied by law and whether immediate or future or contingent or executory or to be declared under any power therein contained, shall take effect when and as they arise by force of and by relation to the estate and seisin originally vested in the person seised to the uses
the continued existence in him or elsewhere of any seisin to uses or scintilla juris, shall not be deemed necessary for the support of or to give effect to future or contingent or executory uses

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 18 is a single coherent rule on how uses take effect and why continued seisin or scintilla juris is not required; it forms one independently recallable property-law concept.

rows.heading: Abolition of estate tail
rows.groupTitle: Abolition and conversion of estates tail
rows.groupReason: One coherent legal reform: abolition of the estate tail, conversion to fee simple or fee simple absolute, and the attendant conveyance, devising, and descent rules form a single recallable classification rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the effect of s. 19 on estates tail, the resulting estate classification (fee simple vs. fee simple absolute), and the tenant in tail's power to convey, devise, or see descent.

evidenceText: Estates tail are abolished, and every estate that would hitherto have been adjudged a fee tail shall be adjudged a fee simple

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19 is a single, self-contained conversion rule: it abolishes estates tail, reclassifies them as fee simple (or fee simple absolute absent a valid remainder), and states the resulting conveyance, devising, and descent powers. All elements interlock as one recall task.

rows.heading: Joint interest
rows.groupTitle: Default co-ownership form and fiduciary co-tenancy
rows.groupReason: General default (tenancy in common), its express-declaration exception, and the separate trustee/executor rule form one tightly interdependent recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the default form of co-ownership for an estate created to two or more persons in their own right, the effect of an express joint-tenancy declaration, and the holding form required for estates vested in trustees or executors as such.

evidenceText: shall be a tenancy in common, unless expressly declared to be a joint tenancy
every estate vested in trustees or executors as such shall be held by them in joint tenancy

rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained provision establishing the default co-ownership form for co-vested estates, the express-declaration exception, and the contrasting holding rule for trustees and executors; one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Change of joint trustees
rows.groupTitle: Continuity of Joint Tenancy on Trustee Change
rows.groupReason: One rule with two interdependent clauses (no severance; tenancy continues with full force); splitting would fragment a single concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the effect on title and the joint tenancy when trustees in a joint estate are changed pursuant to the powers of the original trust.

evidenceText: A change of the trustees in a joint estate, pursuant to the powers of the original trust, does not sever the title, but after the change, the joint tenancy exists in the whole body of the trustees, with all the force and effect of the original trust.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative rule stating that a trustee change in a joint estate does not sever title and the joint tenancy continues; self-contained and independently recallable.

rows.heading: Effect of conveyance
rows.groupTitle: Effect of conveyance: what transfers with the land
rows.groupReason: The inclusion lists (savings clauses) and their limiting conditions form one recall task: the scope and limits of what a land conveyance operates to transfer.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the categories of property, rights, and appurtenances a conveyance of land is deemed to include, the additional estate transferred when the beneficial owner conveys to the grantee and his heirs, and the conditions that limit that inclusion (no contrary intention expressed, no better title than the grantor's, and the 1904 temporal scope).

evidenceText: A conveyance of land shall be deemed to include, and shall by virtue of this Act operate to convey with the land all buildings, erections, fixtures, commons, trees, woods, underwoods, hedges, ditches, fences, ways, waters, watercourses, liberties, privileges, easements, rights, hereditaments, appurtenances and advantages whatsoever
This section applies only if, and as far as a contrary intention is not expressed in the conveyance, and has effect subject to the terms of the conveyance and to the provisions therein contained.

This section shall not be construed as giving to any person a better title to any property, right or thing mentioned in this section than the title which the conveyance gives to him to the land expressed to be conveyed

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 22 states a single coherent rule on what a conveyance of land operates to include, with subsections (3)–(5) providing tightly interdependent conditions and limits on the inclusion lists in (1) and (2).

rows.heading: Conveyance of land
rows.groupTitle: Permitted self-conveyance and spousal conveyance of freehold land (s. 23)
rows.groupReason: One compact rule-set: a person may convey freehold land to himself jointly with another, a spouse may convey to his or her spouse (alone or with another), and a person may convey or vest land in himself.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three categories of land conveyance expressly permitted under s. 23 involving self-conveyance or spousal conveyance, including the section-local definition of 'spouse' as a married person.
rows.sourceMapReason: All three operative subsections state short, interdependent permissions for self-referential or spousal land conveyances and collectively answer one recall question: what conveyances are expressly permitted where grantor and grantee overlap.

rows.heading: Assignment of personalty to self and another
rows.groupTitle: Assignment of personal property to self and another
rows.groupReason: One permission, one scope (assignable personal property including chattels real), one mechanism (same means as assignment to another); no basis to split.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the scope of personal property a person may assign jointly to himself and another under s. 24 and the means by which that assignment operates.

evidenceText: A person may assign personal property now by law assignable, including chattels real, jointly to himself and another person or other persons by the like means as he may assign the same to another.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single-sentence permission to assign personal property jointly to self and another; one coherent recall task with no independent sub-concepts.

rows.heading: Grant of easement, right, liberty or privilege
rows.groupTitle: Vesting of easement or similar interest through conveyance of freehold land
rows.groupReason: One recall task: the conveyance-to-the-use mechanism that creates and vests an easement or similar interest, its duration cap, and its passage to title-deriving successors.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the mechanism by which a conveyance of freehold land vests an easement, right, liberty, or privilege in a person, the duration limitation on that interest, and who may exercise it after the original grantee.

evidenceText: operates to vest in possession in that person that easement, right, liberty or privilege for the estate or interest expressed to be limited to him
for an estate or interest not exceeding in duration the estate conveyed in the land
he, and the persons deriving title under him shall have, use and enjoy the same accordingly

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 25 states one coherent rule: a conveyance of freehold land to the use of an easement, right, liberty, or privilege vests that interest in possession, limited by the duration of the estate conveyed and running to persons deriving title. All elements are interdependent parts of a single vesting mechanism.

rows.heading: Idem
rows.groupTitle: Non-appurtenant infrastructure easements
rows.groupReason: The permission to hold listed infrastructure easements in non-appurtenant form by the enumerated classes of holders, together with the rule's retrospective and prospective temporal scope, forms one coherent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the classes of infrastructure easements (drains, pipes, transmission lines, wires for water, electric power, telecommunication, forest products, oil, gas, sewage, or like purposes) that may be held in non-appurtenant form, the permitted holders, and the section's application to easements granted before and after enactment.

evidenceText: may be granted, created or acquired, transferred or assigned in favour of the Crown, a Crown corporation, a telephone or telegraph company, a local government or rural district, a railway, a public utility company or commission, a pulp or timber company or a company authorized to transport oil or gas, or both oil and gas, in the same manner and with the same effect as any other interest in land, notwithstanding that the benefit of the right of way or easement is not appurtenant or annexed to any land
This section applies to all rights of way or easements granted, created or acquired, transferred or assigned before and after its enactment.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 26 contains a core non-appurtenant infrastructure easement rule (ss.26(1)–(2)) and a separate Easements Act s.9 exclusion (s.26(3)) with different legal modalities and independently recallable content.

rows.heading: Idem
rows.groupTitle: Easements Act s.9 exclusion for power and telecommunication wires
rows.groupReason: Operates as a separate exclusion of a specific provision of another statute for a narrower easement subset, creating a distinct recall task from the general non-appurtenant holding rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that, under Property Act s.26(3), section 9 of the Easements Act does not apply to prevent the acquisition of an easement for electric power or telecommunication wires or cables.

evidenceText: Section 9 of the Easements Act does not apply to prevent the acquisition of an easement for electric power or telecommunication wires or cables.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 26 contains a core non-appurtenant infrastructure easement rule (ss.26(1)–(2)) and a separate Easements Act s.9 exclusion (s.26(3)) with different legal modalities and independently recallable content.

rows.heading: Reservation of legal estate
rows.groupTitle: Operation and deeming rule for reservations of legal estates
rows.groupReason: Both subsections define the reservation mechanism: 27(1) sets the operative effect (no execution/regrant; creates and vests estate) and 27(2) extends it by deeming subject-to conveyances as reservations absent contrary intention.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State how a reservation of a legal estate operates without grantee execution or regrant, and identify when a conveyance subject to another not-yet-existing estate operates as a reservation under s. 27.

evidenceText: A reservation of a legal estate operates without any execution of the conveyance by the grantee of the legal estate out of which the reservation is made, or any regrant by him, so as to create the legal estate reserved and so as to vest the same in possession in the person, whether the grantor or not, for whose benefit the reservation is made.

A conveyance of a legal estate expressed to be made subject to another legal estate not in existence immediately before the date of the conveyance shall operate as a reservation, unless a contrary intention appears.

rows.sourceMapReason: Two short, interdependent subsections: 27(1) states how a reservation operates (no grantee execution or regrant needed; creates estate and vests possession), and 27(2) deems a conveyance subject to a not-yet-existing estate to operate as a reservation unless contrary intention. Together they form one coherent reservation mechanism.

rows.heading: Injury done by accidental fire
rows.groupTitle: Accidental fire immunity and its limits
rows.groupReason: The immunity in 28(1) is incomplete without the Forest Fires Act carve-out (28(2)) and the landlord-tenant contract preservation (28(3)); together they answer one recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions for immunity from legal action where a fire accidentally begins on a person's property, and identify the two express limits: the Forest Fires Act is unaffected and landlord-tenant agreements are not defeated.
rows.sourceMapReason: One immunity rule (28(1)) with two directly dependent carve-outs (28(2), 28(3)) forming a single rule/exception structure that a learner must recall together.

rows.heading: Relief against forfeiture
rows.groupTitle: Court power to relieve against forfeiture of fire-insurance covenant
rows.groupReason: One judicial power with three conditions defining when it may be exercised; recalling them separately would fragment a single rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick's power to relieve against forfeiture of a fire-insurance covenant and the three conditions that must be met (no fire loss occurred, no fraud or gross negligence, conforming insurance on foot at time of application).

evidenceText: The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick has power, upon such terms as it sees fit, to relieve against a forfeiture for breach of a covenant or condition to insure against loss or damage by fire

where no loss or damage by fire has happened and the breach has, in the opinion of the Court, been committed through accident or mistake or otherwise without fraud or gross negligence, and there is an insurance on foot, at the time of the application to the Court, in conformity with the covenant to insure

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 29 is a single self-contained rule: the Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick's discretionary power to relieve against forfeiture of a fire-insurance covenant, with three tightly interdependent conditions. The power and its conditions form one recallable legal rule.

rows.heading: Record of relief against forfeiture
rows.groupTitle: Recording requirement for relief against forfeiture
rows.groupReason: One recallable rule: the form and trigger for documenting court-granted relief against forfeiture on the lease.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the recording direction the Court must give when it grants relief against forfeiture and the prescribed form of that record.

evidenceText: The Court, when relief is granted, shall direct a record of such relief having been granted to be made by endorsement on the lease, or otherwise.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 states a single, self-contained procedural duty: upon granting relief against forfeiture, the Court shall direct a record to be made by endorsement on the lease or otherwise. It is a distinct recall task separate from the relief power (s.29) and the limitations (s.31).

rows.heading: Limitation on court
rows.groupTitle: Limitations on the Court's Power to Grant Relief Against Forfeiture
rows.groupReason: Both prohibitions—no double relief for the same covenant and no relief after an out-of-court waiver of the forfeiture—define the outer boundary of the Court's relief jurisdiction and are best recalled together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the two circumstances in which the Court is prohibited from granting relief under the Property Act: when the same person has already been relieved in respect of the same covenant or condition, and when the forfeiture has already been waived out of Court in favour of the person seeking relief.

evidenceText: The Court shall not, under this Act, relieve the same person more than once in respect of the same covenant or condition, nor grant any relief under this Act where a forfeiture under the covenant in respect of which relief is sought has been already waived out of Court in favour of the person seeking the relief.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 31 is a short, self-contained provision imposing two interrelated prohibitions on the Court's relief power. Both limitations answer the same recall question (what are the limits on the Court granting relief under this Act) and form one coherent rule under the heading 'Limitation on court.'

rows.heading: Breach of covenant by lessee or mortgagor
rows.groupTitle: Benefit-holder's advantage from non-conforming fire insurance
rows.groupReason: One operative rule: on fire loss, the covenant benefit-holder recovers under any subsisting insurance even if not effected in conformity with the covenant.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the rule that a person entitled to the benefit of a lessee's or mortgagor's fire-insurance covenant has the same advantage from any then subsisting insurance, even if not effected in conformity with the covenant, as from conforming insurance.

evidenceText: have the same advantage from any then subsisting insurance relating to the building covenanted to be insured, effected by the lessee or mortgagor in respect of his interest under the lease or in the property, or by any person claiming under him, but not effected in conformity with the covenant, as he would have from an insurance effected in conformity with the covenant

rows.sourceMapReason: Single self-contained rule granting a fire-insurance covenant benefit-holder the same advantage from non-conforming subsisting insurance as from conforming insurance; one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Protection of B.F.P.’s
rows.groupTitle: Protection of bona fide purchasers against pre-purchase insurance covenant breaches
rows.groupReason: Conditions (rent receipt, subsisting insurance), scope of the no-liability protection, and the preservation of the lessor's remedy against the lessee operate as one integrated rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two conditions that must be met for a bona fide purchaser of a leasehold interest to be shielded from liability for pre-purchase breaches of an insurance covenant, and identify the remedy that the provision does not take away.

evidenceText: the purchaser is furnished with the written receipt of the person entitled to receive the rent, or his agent, for the last payment of rent accrued due before the completion of the purchase, and there is subsisting at the time of the completion of the purchase an insurance in conformity with the covenant

shall not be subject to any liability by way of forfeiture or damages or otherwise, in respect of any breach of the covenant, committed at any time before the completion of the purchase, of which the purchaser had not notice before the completion of the purchase
this provision does not take away any remedy that the lessor or his legal representatives may have against the lessee or his legal representatives for breach of covenant

rows.sourceMapReason: One integrated rule protecting bona fide purchasers from pre-purchase insurance-covenant breaches; conditions, effect, and saving clause form a single recallable concept.

rows.heading: Covenants to insure
rows.groupTitle: Lease types covered by covenant-to-insure provisions (s. 34)
rows.groupReason: Single recall task: identify the lease types to which the covenant-to-insure provisions (ss. 29–33) extend.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the categories of leases to which the covenant-to-insure provisions (ss. 29–33) apply under s. 34.

evidenceText: Sections 29, 30, 31, 32 and 33 are applicable to leases for a term of years absolute, or determinable on a life or lives, or otherwise, and also to a lease for the life of the lessee or the life or lives of any other persons.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short scope provision extending the covenant-to-insure rules (ss. 29–33) to life leases and leases determinable on lives; independently recallable as the boundary of applicability for those sections.

rows.heading: Necessity of attornment
rows.groupTitle: Effect of conveyances without attornment
rows.groupReason: The dispensation from attornment and the tenant notice protection are two sides of one rule; recalling either without the other would be incomplete.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State which conveyances (rents, reversions, remainders) are effective without attornment and the condition under which a tenant is protected from prejudice before receiving notice from the grantee.

evidenceText: Grants or conveyances of any rents, or of the reversion or remainder of lands, shall be good and effectual to all intents and purposes, without any attornment
no tenant shall be prejudiced or damaged by payment of rent to the grantor, or by breach of any condition or non-payment of rent, before notice shall be given to him of such grant by the grantee

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent rule: conveyances of rents, reversions, and remainders are effective without attornment, with a directly coupled tenant-protection condition tied to notice from the grantee.

rows.heading: Attornment to stranger
rows.groupTitle: Voidness of attornment to a stranger and its exceptions
rows.groupReason: General rule and its four carve-outs are inseparable for correct application; splitting them would fragment one recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when attornment of a tenant to a stranger claiming the landlord's title is void and identify the four categories of attornment the voidness rule does not affect.

evidenceText: Every attornment of a tenant of any lands to a stranger claiming title to the estate of the landlord is void, and the possession of the landlord shall not be deemed or construed to be affected in any way by the attornment

nothing herein contained extends to vacate or affect an attornment made pursuant to, or in consequence of a judgment or an order of The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick, or made with the privity and consent of the landlord, or to any mortgagee after the mortgage is become forfeited, or under the Landlord and Tenant Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single voidness rule for attornment to a stranger with four directly dependent exceptions in one 'nothing herein contained extends to' clause; the rule and exceptions form one interdependent recall unit.

rows.heading: Death of mortgagor
rows.groupTitle: Death of mortgagor: primary liability of charged land, contrary-intention construction, and chargee's preserved rights
rows.groupReason: 37(1)–(3) form one interdependent rule: primary proportional liability of charged land, the will-construction limits on contrary intention, and the chargee's preserved right to full payment.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State how an equitable charge follows charged land at a mortgagor's death (primary proportional liability), what does and does not constitute a contrary intention in a will, and that the chargee's right to full payment from the personal estate is preserved.

evidenceText: the land so charged is, as between the different persons claiming through or under the deceased person, primarily liable for the payment of all sums of money with which it is charged, every part thereof according to its value bearing a proportionate part of the sums charged on the whole thereof
a general direction that all the debts of the testator shall be paid out of his personal estate shall not be deemed to be a declaration of such contrary or other intention

Nothing herein affects or diminishes any right of the person entitled to such sum of money so charged on such lands to obtain full payment or satisfaction of such sum either out of the personal estate of the person so dying or otherwise

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent rule on how equitable charges follow charged land at a mortgagor's death, with the will-construction rule and chargee savings clause as interdependent parts of the same mechanism.

rows.heading: Assignment of mortgage
rows.groupTitle: Assignment of mortgage on redemption
rows.groupReason: Rule, possession exception, and application clause are tightly interdependent and answer one recall task: the terms of a mortgagor's assignment right on redemption.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the conditions, possession exception, and overriding effect of a mortgagor's right to require a mortgagee to assign the mortgage debt and convey the mortgaged property to a third person on redemption.

evidenceText: he may require the mortgagee, instead of reconveying, and on the terms on which he would be bound to reconvey, to assign the mortgage debt and convey the mortgaged property to any third person as the mortgagor directs, and the mortgagee shall be bound to assign and convey accordingly
This section does not apply in the case of a mortgagee being or having been in possession
This section applies to all mortgages whenever made, and shall have effect notwithstanding any stipulation to the contrary

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 38 states one coherent rule: the mortgagor's right to require assignment of the mortgage to a third person on redemption, its possession exception, and its override of contrary stipulations.

rows.heading: Redemption of mortgage in exceptional circumstances
rows.groupTitle: Grounds for court-ordered mortgage discharge
rows.groupReason: Subsection 38.1(1) and 38.1(5) set out the distinct triggering circumstances (mortgagee missing, dead without probate, money already paid, undue delay or expense) that justify court-ordered discharge, forming one coherent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the circumstances under which the court may order payment into court and discharge a mortgage where the mortgagee cannot be found, has died without probate, or a discharge cannot be obtained without undue delay and expense.

evidenceText: the court on application may permit payment into court of the amount due upon the mortgage and may make an order discharging the mortgage

The court on application may make an order discharging a mortgage (a) where a mortgagee has died and all money due upon the mortgage was paid to him in his lifetime or has been paid to a person entitled to receive the money after his death, or (b) where in any other case it appears that all money due upon the mortgage has been paid, and for any reason a discharge or reconveyance cannot be obtained without undue delay and expense.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 38.1 contains two independently recallable concepts: the substantive grounds on which the court may order a mortgage discharged, and the payment conditions, notice requirements, registration, legal effect, and appeal path for that order.

rows.heading: Redemption of mortgage in exceptional circumstances
rows.groupTitle: Conditions, notice, registration, and effect of mortgage discharge order
rows.groupReason: Subsections 38.1(2)–(10) govern the payment mechanics (including excess sums for disputed amounts and costs), notice requirements, registration in the registry office, the cancelling and reconveying effect of registration, and the appeal path, forming the procedural and effectual framework distinct from the substantive grounds.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions the court may impose on payment into court, the notice requirements for application and order, the legal effect of registering the discharge order in the registry office, and the available appeal.

evidenceText: The money paid into court, with any accrued interest, shall be paid out of court to the mortgagee or as the court by order may direct.

The registration in the appropriate registry office of an order made under this section discharging a mortgage shall have the effect of cancelling the mortgage and of reconveying to the mortgagor any estate conveyed by the mortgage.
An appeal lies to the Court of Appeal from any order made under this section, or from the refusal to make an order.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 38.1 contains two independently recallable concepts: the substantive grounds on which the court may order a mortgage discharged, and the payment conditions, notice requirements, registration, legal effect, and appeal path for that order.

rows.heading: Redemption of mortgage
rows.groupTitle: Independent redemption of a mortgage (s. 39)
rows.groupReason: Section 39(1) grants the mortgagor the right to redeem one mortgage without paying money due under other mortgages on other property; 39(2) limits the section where the mortgage deeds express a contrary intention.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the mortgagor's right to redeem a mortgage without discharging other mortgages on different property, and identify the condition under which the section does not apply.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 39 states a single coherent rule: a mortgagor may redeem one mortgage without discharging other mortgages on other property, subject to the deeds not expressing a contrary intention. Both subsections form one interdependent rule.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Definitions for mortgage redemption sections
rows.groupReason: The three expanded definitions operate together to scope the mortgagee-mortgagor relationship and the instruments covered by sections 38, 38.1, and 39.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall how 'mortgage,' 'mortgagor,' and 'mortgagee' are defined for sections 38, 38.1, and 39, including the extension of 'mortgage' to any charge on property for securing money or money's worth and the inclusion of successors and persons entitled to redeem.
rows.sourceMapReason: Three interrelated definitions (mortgage, mortgagor, mortgagee) extend term meanings for sections 38–39 and form one coherent definitional unit; splitting would fragment a single recall task.

rows.heading: Action by mortgagor
rows.groupTitle: Mortgage as a Defence in a Mortgagor's Action
rows.groupReason: One integrated rule: the general prohibition on defendants setting up the mortgage, the mortgagee/successor exception, and the two barred effects (bar recovery, defeat title) form a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify which defendants may and may not set up a mortgage to bar the right of recovery or defeat title in an action brought by a mortgagor or the mortgagor's heirs, executors, or assigns.

evidenceText: no defendant except the mortgagee, his devisee, executor or assigns, shall set up the mortgage to bar the right of recovery, or defeat the title of the mortgagor, his heirs, executor or assigns

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 41 states a single, self-contained rule restricting which defendants may set up a mortgage to bar recovery or defeat title in a mortgagor's action, with the mortgagee and successors as the exception; all elements are interdependent and recallable as one concept.

rows.heading: Abolition of doctrine of tacking
rows.groupTitle: Abolition of doctrine of tacking for registered encumbrances
rows.groupReason: Single operative rule on encumbrance priority; one independently recallable concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that under section 42 a mortgage, judgment, or other encumbrance on land cannot claim priority over another encumbrance solely because the same person also holds a prior registered encumbrance on that land.

evidenceText: No mortgage, judgment or other encumbrance on land shall have priority by reason of being held by or vested in a person who has a prior registered mortgage or encumbrance of the same land.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 42 states a single, self-contained rule abolishing the doctrine of tacking for registered encumbrances on land. One recall task, no subsections, no need to split or combine.

rows.heading: Repayment to joint mortgagee
rows.groupTitle: Joint Mortgagee Repayment and Discharge
rows.groupReason: The joint-account characterization, last-survivor discharge mechanism, and contrary-intention savings are tightly interdependent and form one recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which mortgage money owed to multiple persons is deemed a joint account, the effect of a last-survivor's written receipt as complete discharge, and the contrary-intention limitation in 43(2).

evidenceText: the receipt in writing of the survivors or last survivor of them, or of the personal representatives of the last survivor, shall be a complete discharge for all money or money's worth for the time being due, notwithstanding any notice to the payer of a severance of the joint account

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent rule: the joint-account deeming of mortgage money and the last-survivor receipt discharge, with a directly dependent contrary-intention limitation in 43(2).

rows.heading: Powers of mortgagee
rows.groupTitle: Mortgagee's Statutory Powers under Deed Mortgage (s.44)
rows.groupReason: Covers both the power of sale and power to insure, their conditions, ancillary rights, and the deed-variation and savings framework as a unified statutory package.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the mortgagee's statutory powers of sale and fire insurance, their triggering conditions, methods, ancillary rights, and how the mortgage deed may vary or extend those powers.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 44 establishes a coherent package of default mortgagee powers (sale and insurance) with shared deed-variation and savings provisions forming one recallable statutory framework.

rows.heading: When power of sale exercised
rows.groupTitle: Conditions for exercising the mortgagee's power of sale
rows.groupReason: The prohibition, the written-notice requirement, the newspaper-publication requirement, and the two supplementary sufficiency rules all answer one recall question about what must be done before the mortgagee may sell.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the notice, service, and publication conditions a mortgagee must satisfy before exercising the power of sale, and identify what constitutes sufficient publication and sufficient property description in the notice.

evidenceText: A mortgagee shall not exercise the power of sale conferred by section 44 unless
at least four weeks in advance of the sale, he has served upon the mortgagor or he has mailed by registered or certified mail
notice of the sale has been published weekly for two consecutive weeks in a daily or weekly newspaper having general circulation in the county

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 45 is a short, self-contained prohibition with specific notice and publication conditions that govern how a mortgagee may exercise the section 44 power of sale; all three subsections address one recall task and form a single coherent study unit.

rows.heading: Conflict of laws
rows.groupTitle: Conflict-of-laws presumption for mortgage-secured obligations (s. 46)
rows.groupReason: One coherent rule: the conclusive presumption of New Brunswick governing law for obligations secured by a mortgage or charge on in-province real estate, displaceable only by express agreement, applying to all undischarged obligations.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conflict-of-laws presumption in s. 46: the governing law, the trigger (mortgage or charge on real estate in the Province), the express-agreement exception, and the application to all obligations not fully and completely discharged whether due, accruing, or past due.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 46 states one conflict-of-laws rule (conclusive presumption that New Brunswick law governs mortgage-secured obligations) and its application clause (all undischarged obligations, due, accruing, or past due). The two subsections are tightly interdependent and form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Effect of power of sale
rows.groupTitle: Nature of conveyance under power of sale
rows.groupReason: Subsection 47(1) defines the estate conveyed and the priority rules governing what passes to the purchaser, a core concept of the sale itself.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the estate the mortgagee may convey under the power of sale and how prior and subordinate interests affect the property sold.

evidenceText: A mortgagee exercising the power of sale conferred by section 44 may convey the property sold, for such estate and interest therein as is the subject of the mortgage, freed from all estate, interests and rights to which the mortgage has priority, but subject to all estates, interests and rights that have priority to the mortgage.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 47 contains five distinct legal concepts across its seven subsections: the nature of the conveyance, purchaser protection and damages remedy, application of proceeds, incidents of the power (who exercises, foreclosure preserved, liability limit), and recovery of documents. Each poses a separate recall task for a learner.

rows.heading: Effect of power of sale
rows.groupTitle: Purchaser protection and remedy for improper exercise
rows.groupReason: Subsection 47(2) pairs the purchaser's title protection from specified challenges with the damages remedy available to a damnified person, forming one rule-and-limitation concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the grounds on which a purchaser's title under a professed exercise of the power of sale cannot be impeached and state the remedy available to a person damnified by an unauthorized or improper exercise.

evidenceText: the title of the purchaser is not impeachable on the ground that no case had arisen to authorize the sale, or that due notice was not given, or that the power was otherwise improperly or irregularly exercised; but any person damnified by an unauthorized or improper or irregular exercise of the power shall have his remedy in damages against the person exercising the power.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 47 contains five distinct legal concepts across its seven subsections: the nature of the conveyance, purchaser protection and damages remedy, application of proceeds, incidents of the power (who exercises, foreclosure preserved, liability limit), and recovery of documents. Each poses a separate recall task for a learner.

rows.heading: Effect of power of sale
rows.groupTitle: Application of sale proceeds
rows.groupReason: Subsection 47(3) establishes the trust-based order of application of sale proceeds in a specific sequence, a highly testable financial rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the order in which a mortgagee must apply money received from a sale under the power of sale and identify who receives the residue.

evidenceText: in the first place in payment of all costs, charges and expenses, properly incurred by the mortgagee as incident to the sale or any attempted sale of the mortgaged premises;
in the second place in discharge of all unpaid money and interest secured by the mortgage;
the residue of the money so received shall be paid to the person entitled to the mortgaged property
