rows.groupReason: The enumerated permitted activities and their express override of s.11/12 prohibitions form the core substantive recall task of the permit power.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the four categories of activities a s.15 permit may authorize and recognize that the permit may cover activities otherwise prohibited under section 11 or 12.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 15 contains a distinct substantive scope (four categories of permitted activities that override s.11/12 prohibitions) and a separate administrative framework (application, conditions, cancellation, renewal, compliance) serving different recall tasks.

rows.heading: Permits to carry on certain activities
rows.groupTitle: Permit application, conditions, and administration
rows.groupReason: These subsections form the administrative lifecycle of a s.15 permit: form-and-fee application, Ministerial conditions and amendment, cancellation or suspension, reinstatement or renewal, and the holder's compliance duty.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the application requirements, the Minister's powers to impose and amend conditions and to cancel or suspend a permit, the reinstatement and renewal procedure, and the permit holder's duty to comply with permit terms.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 15 contains a distinct substantive scope (four categories of permitted activities that override s.11/12 prohibitions) and a separate administrative framework (application, conditions, cancellation, renewal, compliance) serving different recall tasks.

rows.heading: Requirement to produce permit upon request
rows.groupTitle: Permit holder's duty to produce permit on request
rows.groupReason: Single operative duty with one actor (permit holder), one trigger (entering or carrying on an activity in a protected natural area under the permit), and one requesting authority (conservation officer under s. 5.1(1) Crown Lands and Forests Act).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when a permit holder must produce the permit (entering or carrying on an activity in a protected natural area under the permit) and to which officer the permit must be produced upon request.

evidenceText: the holder of the permit shall produce the permit when requested by a conservation officer appointed under subsection 5.1(1) of the Crown Lands and Forests Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 16 imposes a single, self-contained duty on permit holders to produce their permit when requested by a specifically identified conservation officer. One actor, one trigger, one obligation, one requesting authority — a clean standalone recall unit.

rows.heading: Recreational and access roads
rows.groupTitle: Recreational and access roads: Ministerial powers and designation by regulation
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(3) form one interdependent mechanism: the road power references subsection (2), and the content requirement in (3) applies directly to regulations under (2), making them a single coherent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the scope of the Minister's road development and management powers in protected natural areas, the regulatory designation process requiring Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval, and the mandatory description or plan content of designation regulations.

evidenceText: The Minister may develop, construct, maintain and manage roads within any protected natural area on Crown Lands for the purposes of access or within a Class II Protected Natural Area on Crown Lands for the purposes of recreation
The Minister may, with the approval of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, make regulations
A regulation made under paragraph (2)(a) or (b) shall contain a description or plan of the road or portion of road designated as an access road or recreational road.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 17 is a compact, internally cross-referenced mechanism: the Minister's road power (1), the regulatory designation process with Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval (2), and the mandatory content of designation regulations (3) are directly linked and best recalled as one unit.

rows.heading: Closure of protected natural areas, recreational roads or access roads
rows.groupTitle: Closure of protected natural areas, recreational roads, and access roads
rows.groupReason: The closure power, the entry prohibition it triggers, and the enumerated exceptions form one interdependent mechanism that a learner must recall as a unit to understand when and by whom a closed PNA may be entered.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Minister's authority and method for closing a protected natural area, recreational road, or access road, the resulting prohibition on entry, and the three categories of persons excepted from that prohibition.

evidenceText: the Minister may by a notice in writing, posted or placed in accordance with the regulations, close temporarily or for a specified period of time to public use any protected natural area, recreational road or access road

no person other than the Minister shall enter a protected natural area or portion of a protected natural area or enter upon a recreational road or access road or portion of a recreational road or access road during the time that it is closed to public use under subsection (1) without the authorization of the Minister

Subsection (2) does not apply to (a) an emergency service provider in carrying out and exercising activities or services for (i) the public safety, (ii) the protection of public health, (iii) the protection of private lands or other private property, or (iv) the protection of the environment

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 18 is one coherent closure mechanism: the Minister's power to close (18(1)), the resulting entry prohibition (18(2)), and the enumerated exceptions (18(3)) are structurally interdependent and answer a single recall task about how PNA closure operates.

rows.heading: No disposing or encumbering of Crown Lands within a protected natural area
rows.groupTitle: Prohibition on disposing of or encumbering Crown Lands in a protected natural area
rows.groupReason: All three sub-paragraphs are parallel prohibitions on the same actor for the same lands, forming one coherent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three categories of Crown Lands dealings (disposal, right-of-way/easement, lease/licence of occupation/encumbrance) the Minister is prohibited from undertaking within a protected natural area, and the notwithstanding clause that overrides any other Act.

evidenceText: Notwithstanding any other Act, the Minister shall not
lease, issue a licence of occupation under the Crown Lands and Forests Act or otherwise encumber Crown Lands within a protected natural area

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19 is a single, self-contained prohibition on the Minister dealing with Crown Lands within a protected natural area, with one actor and one legal modality across three parallel sub-paragraphs.

rows.heading: Exceptions
rows.groupTitle: Exceptions for private land access and public utility easements
rows.groupReason: These two exceptions address providing access to private lands and public utility easements, distinct from the infrastructure-management and recreational-trail categories.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the conditions under which the Minister may grant a right-of-way or easement to a private land owner or a public utility despite the Section 19 prohibition, including the surrounding/adjacency requirement and the public-interest condition for utility easements.

evidenceText: a right-of-way or easement granted by the Minister under the Crown Lands and Forests Act to the owner of private lands for the purpose of providing access to the private lands where the private lands are otherwise inaccessible

an easement to a public utility granted by the Minister under the Crown Lands and Forests Act where the easement is adjacent to an easement that was in existence immediately before the commencement of this section, the additional easement is for the same purposes as the existing easement, and the Minister is of the opinion that the granting of the additional easement is in the public interest

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 20 lists three materially distinct categories of exception to the Section 19 prohibition, each with different purposes, instruments, and (for Class II) area classification, creating three independent recall tasks.

rows.heading: Exceptions
rows.groupTitle: Class II Protected Natural Area recreational trail exceptions
rows.groupReason: These two exceptions are limited to Class II Protected Natural Areas and to outdoor recreational trails, a distinct purpose and area classification not available under the general infrastructure exceptions.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the lease and licence of occupation instruments the Minister may use for outdoor recreational trails specifically within Class II Protected Natural Areas, distinguishing these from the general infrastructure exceptions.

evidenceText: a lease of Crown Lands within a Class II Protected Natural Area issued by the Minister under the Crown Lands and Forests Act where the approved use of the lands, as specified in the lease, is a trail for the carrying on of an outdoor recreational activity

a licence of occupation authorizing the occupancy and use of Crown Lands within a Class II Protected Natural Area issued by the Minister under the Crown Lands and Forests Act where the approved use of the lands, as specified in the licence of occupation, is a trail for the carrying on of an outdoor recreational activity

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 20 lists three materially distinct categories of exception to the Section 19 prohibition, each with different purposes, instruments, and (for Class II) area classification, creating three independent recall tasks.

rows.heading: Exceptions
rows.groupTitle: Exceptions for infrastructure maintenance and management in protected natural areas
rows.groupReason: These three exceptions cover the instruments available for managing existing infrastructure within any protected natural area, sharing the same purpose but using distinct legal vehicles.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three instruments (right-of-way or easement, lease, and licence of occupation) by which the Minister may access and manage infrastructure located within a protected natural area, and the required approved use for each.

evidenceText: a right-of-way or easement granted by the Minister under the Crown Lands and Forests Act for the purpose of providing access to Crown Lands for the maintenance, management, repair, rehabilitation or operation of infrastructure located within the boundaries of a protected natural area

a lease issued by the Minister under the Crown Lands and Forests Act where the approved use of the Crown Lands, as specified in the lease, is the maintenance, management, repair, rehabilitation or operation of infrastructure located within the boundaries of a protected natural area

a licence of occupation granted by the Minister under the Crown Lands and Forests Act where the approved use of the lands, as specified in the licence of occupation, is the maintenance, management, repair, rehabilitation or operation of infrastructure located within the boundaries of a protected natural area

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 20 lists three materially distinct categories of exception to the Section 19 prohibition, each with different purposes, instruments, and (for Class II) area classification, creating three independent recall tasks.

rows.heading: Infrastructure within a protected natural area
rows.groupTitle: Minister's Infrastructure Powers in Protected Natural Areas
rows.groupReason: Covers both the Minister's direct infrastructure powers and the agreement-based delegation mechanism as one interdependent grant of authority.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the five infrastructure activities the Minister may undertake within a protected natural area and the power to enter into an agreement delegating those activities to one or more persons.

evidenceText: maintain, manage, repair, rehabilitate and operate infrastructure that is located within the boundaries of a protected natural area
enter into an agreement with one or more persons for the maintenance, management, repair, rehabilitation or operation of infrastructure referred to in paragraph (a)

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 21 grants the Minister a unified set of infrastructure powers and a delegation mechanism within protected natural areas, forming one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Existing and future interests and agreements
rows.groupTitle: Preservation of Pre-Existing Interests in Protected Natural Areas
rows.groupReason: The savings rule, the permission to carry on otherwise-prohibited activities under sections 11 and 12, and the enumerated list of protected interests and agreements (a)–(j) are structurally interdependent and answer one coherent recall question.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify which pre-existing interests and agreements in relation to lands within a protected natural area are preserved from the operation of the Act and regulations, and state the permission granted to persons acting pursuant to those interests regarding activities otherwise prohibited under sections 11 or 12.

evidenceText: Nothing in this Act or the regulations affects the rights, duties, obligations or responsibilities of any person in respect of any of the following interests and agreements in relation to lands within a protected natural area, and any person acting pursuant to such an interest or agreement may carry on an activity that is otherwise prohibited under section 11 or 12
a licence to search or a lease granted under the Oil and Natural Gas Act and in effect immediately before the establishment of the protected natural area

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 22 is a single coherent savings provision: one operative rule preserving pre-existing interests, one permission for otherwise-prohibited activities, and an enumerated list defining scope. These elements are interdependent and form one recall task.

rows.heading: Erection of notices and other markers
rows.groupTitle: Minister's power to post and remove notices and markers
rows.groupReason: Covers the posting power with its four enumerated purposes and the companion removal power as a single recallable mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the four purposes for which the Minister may post or place notices, plaques, markers, or signs in a protected natural area, and the Minister's power to remove them.
rows.sourceMapReason: Short Ministerial power to post and remove notices or markers in protected natural areas, with four enumerated purposes; both subsections form one coherent administrative concept.

rows.heading: Prohibitions respecting notices and other markers
rows.groupTitle: Prohibition on unauthorized notices and markers in protected natural areas
rows.groupReason: The prohibition in 24(1) and the evidentiary presumptions in 24(2) are tightly interdependent; the presumptions exist solely to support enforcement of the 24(1) prohibition.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two acts prohibited without lawful authority in a protected natural area under 24(1) and the two evidentiary presumptions that apply in a prosecution under the Act or the regulations under 24(2).

evidenceText: No person shall without lawful authority (a) post or place any notice, plaque, marker, sign or other device in a protected natural area, or (b) damage, deface or remove any notice, plaque, marker, sign or other device posted or placed in a protected natural area under subsection 18(1) or 23(1).

the posting or placing of a notice, plaque, marker, sign or other device under subsection 18(1) or 23(1) that shows the Province of New Brunswick galley logo and bears the inscription "Department of Natural Resources" or "Natural Resources" is, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, proof that the notice, plaque, marker, sign or other device was posted under the authority of that subsection

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 24 contains a single prohibition on posting/placing or damaging markers in protected natural areas (24(1)) with tightly coupled evidentiary presumptions for prosecution (24(2)); both form one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Definition of “conservation officer”
rows.groupTitle: Part IV definition of 'conservation officer'
rows.groupReason: Single part-level definition cross-referencing the Crown Lands and Forests Act appointment provision.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Part IV definition of 'conservation officer' and the Crown Lands and Forests Act subsection under which the appointment is made.

evidenceText: In this Part, “conservation officer” means a conservation officer appointed under subsection 5.1(1) of the Crown Lands and Forests Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Part-level definition that narrows 'conservation officer' for Part IV to those appointed under subsection 5.1(1) of the Crown Lands and Forests Act, distinct from the broader section 1 'enforcement officer' definition; minimal but real recall value for understanding who exercises Part IV powers.

rows.heading: Powers of conservation officers and forest service officers
rows.groupTitle: Conservation officer peace officer status under the Act
rows.groupReason: 25(1) designates the conservation officer's legal status as a Criminal Code peace officer, a distinct recall task from the specific search and entry powers in 25(2) and 25(3).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the peace officer status conferred on a conservation officer carrying out duties under the Protected Natural Areas Act and the scope of powers and immunities that follows.

evidenceText: is a person employed for the preservation and maintenance of the public peace and has and may exercise all the powers, authorities and immunities of a peace officer as defined in the Criminal Code (Canada)

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 25 contains three independently recallable officer powers: peace officer status, a specific warrantless search power, and a trespass-immunity entry power involving different actors and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Powers of conservation officers and forest service officers
rows.groupTitle: Conservation officer warrantless search power in protected natural areas
rows.groupReason: 25(2) creates a specific warrantless search power with defined conditions (location, grounds, evidentiary purpose) that is a separate recall task from general peace officer status or entry rights.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the conditions under which a conservation officer may search without warrant lands within a protected natural area and distinguish this power from those under the Provincial Offences Procedure Act.

evidenceText: the power to search without warrant any lands within a protected natural area in or on which he or she has reasonable and probable grounds to believe there is anything that may provide evidence of the commission of an offence under this Act or the regulations

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 25 contains three independently recallable officer powers: peace officer status, a specific warrantless search power, and a trespass-immunity entry power involving different actors and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Powers of conservation officers and forest service officers
rows.groupTitle: Entry on private lands without trespass liability
rows.groupReason: 25(3) extends to forest service officers and accompanied persons and grants a trespass immunity on private lands, a distinct actor set, legal effect, and scope from the other two subsections.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who may enter private lands without trespass liability under this Act, the conditions attached to that entry, and who else is covered by the immunity.

evidenceText: A conservation officer or a forest service officer, in carrying out his or her duties under this Act or the regulations, and any person accompanied by him or her, may enter upon and pass through private lands without being liable for trespass

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 25 contains three independently recallable officer powers: peace officer status, a specific warrantless search power, and a trespass-immunity entry power involving different actors and legal modalities.

rows.heading: Duty to report violation
rows.groupTitle: Duty to report violation – application to officers
rows.groupReason: Establishes that the reporting duty in s.13 FWA binds conservation officers and forest service officers under this Act and its regulations.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify that conservation officers and forest service officers owe a duty to report violations under s.13 of the Fish and Wildlife Act as applied by s.25.1 of the Protected Natural Areas Act.

evidenceText: Section 13 of the Fish and Wildlife Act applies to a conservation officer and a forest service officer for the purposes of this Act and the regulations.

rows.sourceMapReason: One-sentence cross-reference that operatively applies s.13 of the Fish and Wildlife Act to conservation officers and forest service officers under this Act; thin but independently operative duty provision.

rows.heading: Prohibitions respecting statements to or obstruction of conservation officer or forest service officer
rows.groupTitle: Prohibited statements to and obstruction of conservation or forest service officers
rows.groupReason: Two short prohibitions (false/misleading statements and obstruction/incitement to obstruct) directed at the same officers in the same duties context form one recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two categories of knowingly prohibited conduct toward a conservation officer or forest service officer carrying out duties under the Act or regulations, including the extension of the obstruction prohibition to persons assisting the officer.

evidenceText: knowingly make a false or misleading statement to a conservation officer or a forest service officer engaged in carrying out his or her duties under this Act or the regulations

knowingly obstruct, cause to be obstructed or incite others to obstruct a conservation officer or a forest service officer engaged in carrying out his or her duties under this Act or the regulations, or any person assisting the conservation officer or the forest service officer

rows.sourceMapReason: Short dual-prohibition section protecting conservation and forest service officers; both paragraphs share the same actors, 'knowingly' mental standard, and enforcement context, forming one coherent recallable concept.

rows.heading: Search, seizure and return or forfeiture of property seized
rows.groupTitle: Forfeiture of property upon conviction
rows.groupReason: Subsections 2(11) and 2(12) govern automatic forfeiture of Crown property and judicial forfeiture orders for non-Crown property on conviction, plus the Minister's 30-day restriction on using or disposing of forfeited property.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain what happens to Crown and non-Crown seized property upon a conviction and the 30-day restriction on the Minister's use or disposal of forfeited property.

evidenceText: any property belonging to the Crown seized under this Act or the Provincial Offences Procedure Act is, upon the conviction, in addition to any penalty imposed, forfeited to the Minister

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 27 contains five distinct recall concepts: seizure powers, post-seizure duties, the return procedure, forfeiture on conviction, and mandatory return without forfeiture. Each block answers a separate legal question and involves different actors or triggers.

rows.heading: Search, seizure and return or forfeiture of property seized
rows.groupTitle: Mandatory return of property without forfeiture
rows.groupReason: Subsections 2(13) and 2(14) impose two automatic return obligations: the 6-month no-prosecution rule and the 30-day post-charge-disposition rule where no forfeiture order was made.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two time-limited conditions under which a conservation officer must return seized non-Crown property without a forfeiture order.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 27 contains five distinct recall concepts: seizure powers, post-seizure duties, the return procedure, forfeiture on conviction, and mandatory return without forfeiture. Each block answers a separate legal question and involves different actors or triggers.

rows.heading: Search, seizure and return or forfeiture of property seized
rows.groupTitle: Post-seizure reporting and notice duties
rows.groupReason: Subsection 2(4) imposes two immediate duties on a conservation officer who seizes evidentiary property: report to the Minister and give written notice to the person in possession.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the two mandatory steps a conservation officer must take after seizing property that may afford evidence of an offence.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 27 contains five distinct recall concepts: seizure powers, post-seizure duties, the return procedure, forfeiture on conviction, and mandatory return without forfeiture. Each block answers a separate legal question and involves different actors or triggers.

rows.heading: Search, seizure and return or forfeiture of property seized
rows.groupTitle: Return of seized non-Crown property
rows.groupReason: Subsections 2(5)–2(10), with the section's definitions in 2(1), set out both the Minister's administrative return authorization and the full judicial application, notice, hearing, and execution procedure for returning seized non-Crown property.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe the two pathways for returning seized non-Crown property (Minister's authorization and judicial application), the 14-day notice requirement and its contents, and the judge's power to order return with security.

evidenceText: a person with an interest in the property seized may apply to a judge for the return of the property after giving to the prosecutor and any other person known by the person making the application to have or to claim an interest in the property 14 days' notice in writing

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 27 contains five distinct recall concepts: seizure powers, post-seizure duties, the return procedure, forfeiture on conviction, and mandatory return without forfeiture. Each block answers a separate legal question and involves different actors or triggers.

rows.heading: Search, seizure and return or forfeiture of property seized
rows.groupTitle: Conservation officer seizure powers
rows.groupReason: Subsections 2(2) and 2(3) together define when and what a conservation officer may seize: vehicles on two grounds and plain-view items, all requiring reasonable and probable grounds.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the specific grounds on which a conservation officer may seize a vehicle and the plain-view seizure power over fauna, flora, or other things.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 27 contains five distinct recall concepts: seizure powers, post-seizure duties, the return procedure, forfeiture on conviction, and mandatory return without forfeiture. Each block answers a separate legal question and involves different actors or triggers.

rows.heading: Disposal where owner unknown or not found
rows.groupTitle: Minister's disposal power for seized property with unknown or unfound owner
rows.groupReason: One rule: property seized under this Act or the Provincial Offences Procedure Act, owner unknown or not found within 3 months, triggers the Minister's power to direct disposal in any manner the Minister considers appropriate.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions (seizure under this Act or the Provincial Offences Procedure Act, owner unknown or not found for 3 months) that allow the Minister to direct disposal of seized property and the scope of the Minister's discretion in choosing the manner of disposal.

evidenceText: the owner is unknown or cannot be found within 3 months after the seizure, the Minister may direct that it be disposed of in any manner the Minister considers appropriate

rows.sourceMapReason: Single provision creating one Minister's disposal power triggered by a specific 3-month owner-not-found condition; forms one independent recall task.

rows.heading: Designation and certificate of qualified technician
rows.groupTitle: Designation and Certificate of Qualified Technician
rows.groupReason: All four subsections operate as one procedural rule governing how a qualified technician's certificate enters evidence in a prosecution under the Act.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Minister's power to designate qualified technicians, the admissibility and prima facie proof effect of the certificate in a prosecution, the party's right to require cross-examination with court leave, and the reasonable-notice precondition before the certificate may be received.
rows.sourceMapReason: Four short subsections form one coherent evidentiary mechanism: the Minister's designation power, the certificate's admissibility and proof effect, the cross-examination right, and the notice precondition are tightly interdependent and recallable as a single unit.

rows.heading: Offences and penalties
rows.groupTitle: Continuing offence fine multiplication
rows.groupReason: A cross-cutting penalty-mechanism rule (multiplying min and max fines by days of continuation) that applies across all other subsections and is independently recallable.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain that when an offence continues for more than one day, both the minimum and maximum fine set by subsection (1), (2), (3), (4), or (5) are multiplied by the number of days the offence continues.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 sets distinct penalty rules keyed to different actors (individual, corporation, person), different underlying provisions (serious s.11/12/15(6) vs. lesser s.16/18(2)/24(1)/26 vs. regulations), and a separate continuing-offence multiplier, each independently recallable.

rows.heading: Offences and penalties
rows.groupTitle: Corporate serious offences
rows.groupReason: Different actor (corporation) with a distinct penalty range and no imprisonment option makes this a separate recall task from the individual penalties in 30(1)/(2).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a corporation violating s.11(a)/(b), s.12(a)/(b), or s.15(6) commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine of not less than $5,000 and not more than $1,000,000.

evidenceText: A corporation that violates or fails to comply with paragraph 11(a) or (b), subparagraph 12(a)(i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), (vii), (viii), (ix), (x), (xi) or (xii), clause 12(a)(xiii)(A), (B), (C) or (D), paragraph 12(b) or subsection 15(6) commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine of not less than $5,000 and not more than $1,000,000.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 sets distinct penalty rules keyed to different actors (individual, corporation, person), different underlying provisions (serious s.11/12/15(6) vs. lesser s.16/18(2)/24(1)/26 vs. regulations), and a separate continuing-offence multiplier, each independently recallable.

rows.heading: Offences and penalties
rows.groupTitle: Individual serious offences and financial-motive enhanced penalty
rows.groupReason: 30(1) sets the base individual penalty and 30(2) is its directly dependent enhancement for financial-motive offences; together they form one rule/condition pair covering the core serious prohibitions.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the offences under s.11(a)/(b), s.12(a)/(b), and s.15(6) for which an individual is liable, the base penalty ($500–$100,000 fine or up to 6 months imprisonment, or both), and the enhanced minimum of $5,000 where a judge finds the offence was committed for financial advantage or to avoid the financial burden of compliance.

evidenceText: an individual who violates or fails to comply with paragraph 11(a) or (b), subparagraph 12(a)(i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), (vii), (viii), (ix), (x), (xi) or (xii), clause 12(a)(xiii)(A), (B), (C) or (D), paragraph 12(b) or subsection 15(6) commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine of not less than $500 and not more than $100,000 or a term of imprisonment of not more than 6 months, or both.

Where, in the opinion of a judge, an individual has committed an offence referred to in subsection (1) for financial advantage or to avoid the financial burden of compliance with the law, the judge may impose a fine of not less than $5,000 and not more than $100,000 or a term of imprisonment of not more than 6 months, or both.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 sets distinct penalty rules keyed to different actors (individual, corporation, person), different underlying provisions (serious s.11/12/15(6) vs. lesser s.16/18(2)/24(1)/26 vs. regulations), and a separate continuing-offence multiplier, each independently recallable.

rows.heading: Offences and penalties
rows.groupTitle: Person offences for lesser Act violations
rows.groupReason: A distinct set of lower-severity offences tied to specific provisions (s.16, s.18(2), s.24(1), s.26(a), s.26(b)), each with its own fine range, forming one recall exercise on lesser person offences.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Match each listed provision (s.16, s.18(2), s.24(1)(a)/(b), s.26(a), s.26(b)) to its applicable fine range for a person who violates or fails to comply with that provision.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 sets distinct penalty rules keyed to different actors (individual, corporation, person), different underlying provisions (serious s.11/12/15(6) vs. lesser s.16/18(2)/24(1)/26 vs. regulations), and a separate continuing-offence multiplier, each independently recallable.

rows.heading: Offences and penalties
rows.groupTitle: Offences under the regulations
rows.groupReason: Distinct trigger (regulations rather than a named Act section) with its own penalty range and the 'unless otherwise provided' qualifier, making it a separate recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a person who violates a regulation (unless the Act provides otherwise) commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine of $100 to $500.

evidenceText: Unless otherwise provided in this Act, a person who violates or fails to comply with a provision of the regulations commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine of not less than $100 and not more than $500.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 sets distinct penalty rules keyed to different actors (individual, corporation, person), different underlying provisions (serious s.11/12/15(6) vs. lesser s.16/18(2)/24(1)/26 vs. regulations), and a separate continuing-offence multiplier, each independently recallable.

rows.heading: Additional penalties
rows.groupTitle: Additional penalty orders a judge may impose on conviction
rows.groupReason: All four subsections form one sentencing toolkit: the enumerated remedial/restraining directions (a)(i)–(vi), the exclusion order (b), and the procedural constraints (effective date, five-year cap, trust-fund deposit) that attach to the (a) orders.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Describe each remedial direction, the exclusion order, and the procedural requirements (effective date, five-year maximum, trust-fund deposit) that apply to a judge's additional penalty orders under s. 31.

evidenceText: a judge may, (a) after considering the nature of the offence and the circumstances surrounding its commission, in addition to any other penalty that may be imposed, make an order directing the person to do one or more of the following
make an order prohibiting the person from entering or being in a protected natural area or any portion of a protected natural area for such period of time as the judge considers appropriate
The judge shall specify in an order made under paragraph (1)(a) the period of time during which it is in effect, which period shall not exceed five years.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 31 is a coherent sentencing-power provision whose subsections form one interdependent rule set: enumerated remedial directions, an exclusion order, and the procedural constraints (effective date, five-year maximum, trust-fund deposit) binding on those orders.

rows.heading: Administration of Act
rows.groupTitle: Minister's administrative responsibility and delegation power
rows.groupReason: Single provision combining the Minister's administrative duty and the authority to delegate; both elements form one recallable concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who is responsible for administering the Act and the Minister's power to designate persons to act on the Minister's behalf.

evidenceText: The Minister is responsible for the administration of this Act and may designate persons to act on the Minister's behalf.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short administrative provision establishing the Minister's responsibility for the Act and the delegation power to designate persons; one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Agreements for the protection, conservation and management of protected natural areas
rows.groupTitle: Minister's Power to Enter Protection Agreements for Protected Natural Areas
rows.groupReason: One permissive power with a single actor, trigger, and purpose; no internal subdivision needed.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who may enter a protection agreement, the permitted counterparties, and the stated purposes (protection, conservation, and management of a protected natural area or portion thereof) under section 33.

evidenceText: The Minister may enter into an agreement with one or more persons for the protection, conservation and management of a protected natural area or any portion of a protected natural area.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 33 is a single, self-contained permissive power granting the Minister authority to enter into protection, conservation, and management agreements for protected natural areas. It has clear independent study value as a core management mechanism of the Act.

rows.heading: Service of notice or other document
rows.groupTitle: Service of notices and documents under the Protected Natural Areas Act
rows.groupReason: One recall task: identify the permitted service methods and the seven-day deemed-receipt rule for registered mail, subject to subsection 27(7).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the three permitted methods of service for a notice under the Act and the day on which registered-mail service is deemed received.

evidenceText: may be served personally on the person or on an adult residing at the last known residence of the person, or sent by registered mail to such residence, and when sent by registered mail shall be deemed to have been received by the person not later than the seventh day after the day of mailing

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 34 is a single, tightly interdependent procedural rule: permitted service methods (personal, adult at residence, registered mail) plus the seven-day deemed-receipt rule for registered mail, all answering one recall question. The subsection 27(7) cross-reference and the methods are inseparable from the deemed-receipt consequence.

rows.heading: Regulations
rows.groupTitle: Scope of Regulatory Power – Protected Natural Areas Act s.35
rows.groupReason: All fifteen paragraphs state one permissive power of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council and enumerate the subjects of that power; recalling them as a set answers the single question of what the Act authorises the executive to regulate.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the regulatory authority (Lieutenant-Governor in Council on the Minister's recommendation) and enumerate the principal subject matters the Lieutenant-Governor in Council may address by regulation under section 35 of the Protected Natural Areas Act.

evidenceText: establishing a protected natural area on Crown Lands or on private lands
respecting any other matter or thing the Lieutenant-Governor in Council considers necessary or advisable to carry out effectively the purposes of this Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 35 is a single enabling provision granting the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, on the Minister's recommendation, the power to make regulations across fifteen enumerated subjects. All paragraphs share the same actor, same legal modality (permissive regulatory power), and one recall task: the scope of regulatory authority under the Act.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Disease surveillance and health monitoring definitions
rows.groupReason: These terms define the disease-reporting and public health monitoring framework and form one coherent recall set.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the enumerated Group I notifiable diseases, how a notifiable disease is established by regulation or order, the infectious-state requirement for 'contact', the components of 'examination', and the four categories of 'health hazard'.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 1 contains 27 active defined terms that cluster into three thematically distinct recall tasks: disease surveillance terminology, food/water/premises regulatory definitions, and inspector/institutional actor definitions.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Food, water, premises, and sewage system definitions
rows.groupReason: These terms define the physical and environmental regulatory scope of the Act and form a distinct recall set from disease-monitoring and actor terms.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the activities and inclusions/exclusions defining 'food premises', the three 'occupier' categories, the five 'on-site sewage disposal system' types, and the distinctions among 'water supply system', 'public water supply system', and 'water circulation system'.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 1 contains 27 active defined terms that cluster into three thematically distinct recall tasks: disease surveillance terminology, food/water/premises regulatory definitions, and inspector/institutional actor definitions.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Inspector framework and institutional definitions
rows.groupReason: These terms define the administrative actors and institutional framework and are independently recallable from the subject-matter definitions.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three inspector classes and the umbrella 'inspector' definition, the scope of 'medical officer of health' (including chief and deputy chief), the 'Minister' definition, and the 'institution' categories.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 1 contains 27 active defined terms that cluster into three thematically distinct recall tasks: disease surveillance terminology, food/water/premises regulatory definitions, and inspector/institutional actor definitions.

rows.heading: Act binds the Crown
rows.groupTitle: Act Binds the Crown
rows.groupReason: One recallable rule: the Act applies to and binds the Crown, removing Crown immunity from its provisions.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the Public Health Act binds the Crown, meaning the Crown is not immune from the Act's provisions.

evidenceText: This Act binds the Crown.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 2 is a single operative rule stating the Act binds the Crown; it removes Crown immunity and has independent legal effect, but is too short to split.

rows.heading: Inconsistency
rows.groupTitle: Prevailing effect on inconsistency
rows.groupReason: One short rule: where this Act or its regulations conflict with another act or regulation, the Public Health Act side prevails to the extent of the inconsistency.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the prevailing rule that applies when the Public Health Act or a regulation made under it is inconsistent with another act of the Legislature or a regulation made under that act.

evidenceText: the provision of this Act or the regulation prevails to the extent of the inconsistency

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 3 is a single, self-contained rule of legal precedence: the Act or its regulations prevail over other legislation to the extent of any inconsistency. One clear recall task.

rows.heading: Reporting of health hazard
rows.groupTitle: Duty to report a health hazard and food premises notification offence
rows.groupReason: The general duty in 4(1) and the specific offence in 4(2) are tightly interdependent and form one recallable reporting obligation with its enforcement consequence.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the duty of any person with reasonable grounds to notify a medical officer of health or public health inspector of a health hazard without delay, and identify the offence committed by a food premises licence holder or manager who fails to do so.
rows.sourceMapReason: Subsection 4(1) states a general notification duty and 4(2) specifies the offence for food premises operators who fail to comply; together they form one tightly interdependent rule-and-consequence concept.

rows.heading: Investigation of health hazard
rows.groupTitle: Duty to investigate a suspected health hazard
rows.groupReason: One actor, one trigger, one mandatory action — the investigation duty forms a single recallable procedural rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the trigger (reasonable grounds to believe a health hazard may exist) and the mandatory duty of a medical officer of health or public health inspector to investigate or cause an investigation to be carried out under section 5.
rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative duty on a named officer with a clear trigger and purpose; independently recallable as one procedural step in the health hazard response chain.

rows.heading: Order respecting health hazard
rows.groupTitle: Compliance duty, communication requirement, and Part III non-prevention
rows.groupReason: Subsections (11)–(13) impose the duty on the directed person to comply and to communicate the order's contents as required, and clarify that Part III does not prevent orders regarding non-human premises or substances infected or contaminated with a notifiable disease.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a person directed by an order shall comply, that the officer or inspector may require that person to communicate the order's contents to others, and that Part III does not prevent a section 6 order in relation to non-human premises or substances infected or contaminated with a notifiable disease agent.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 contains at least four independently recallable legal concepts: the authority and grounds for issuing orders, the permissible content and addressees, effectiveness and oral-order form rules, and downstream compliance and communication duties. Splitting yields the smallest useful set of recall units.

rows.heading: Order respecting health hazard
rows.groupTitle: Permissible content and addressees of health hazard orders
rows.groupReason: Subsections (3)–(6) define what an order may specify (time, the ten non-exhaustive requirement types, the specific legal effect of a closing order) and the three categories of persons to whom it may be directed; they answer 'what can the order require and who does it apply to?'
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the non-exhaustive list of requirements a health hazard order may include (vacating, closing, placarding, doing work, removal, isolation, cleaning, destruction, food regulation, use regulation), the specific legal effect of a closing order, and the three categories of persons to whom an order may be directed.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 contains at least four independently recallable legal concepts: the authority and grounds for issuing orders, the permissible content and addressees, effectiveness and oral-order form rules, and downstream compliance and communication duties. Splitting yields the smallest useful set of recall units.

rows.heading: Order respecting health hazard
rows.groupTitle: Effectiveness, oral order procedure, and form sufficiency
rows.groupReason: Subsections (7)–(10) set out when an order is effective (reasons must be stated), the oral-order exception where delay would increase the hazard, the 72-hour written-confirmation requirement, and the rule that a description of persons is sufficient even if not all are named.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that an order is not effective unless reasons are set out, that an oral order is permitted where writing would substantially increase the hazard (dispensing with the reasons requirement), that the oral order must be reduced to writing and served within seventy-two hours without invalidity upon failure, and that describing rather than naming persons is sufficient.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 contains at least four independently recallable legal concepts: the authority and grounds for issuing orders, the permissible content and addressees, effectiveness and oral-order form rules, and downstream compliance and communication duties. Splitting yields the smallest useful set of recall units.

rows.heading: Order respecting health hazard
rows.groupTitle: Authority and grounds for health hazard orders
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) together state who may issue the order, the required written form, and the two-part reasonable-ground belief that must precede it; they are a single recallable authority-and-conditions unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a medical officer of health or public health inspector may by written order require a person to act or refrain from acting, and that the officer or inspector must believe on reasonable grounds both that a health hazard exists and that the specified requirements are necessary to prevent, decrease, or eliminate it.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 6 contains at least four independently recallable legal concepts: the authority and grounds for issuing orders, the permissible content and addressees, effectiveness and oral-order form rules, and downstream compliance and communication duties. Splitting yields the smallest useful set of recall units.

rows.heading: Seizure and destruction
rows.groupTitle: Minister's cost recovery for destroyed or disposed items
rows.groupReason: A separate Ministerial power to recover destruction or disposal costs from the owner, with sections 10 and 11 applying with modifications.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Minister's authority to recover the cost of destruction, disposal, or other action taken to eliminate a confirmed health hazard from the owner or person from whom the item was seized, and note that sections 10 and 11 apply with the necessary modifications. (7(6))
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 7 contains a coherent seizure-and-outcome procedure (ss. 1–5), a separate Ministerial cost-recovery power (s. 6), and a food-specific exception (s. 7) that are independently recallable.

rows.heading: Seizure and destruction
rows.groupTitle: Food-specific seizure exception
rows.groupReason: Subsection (7) exempts food from the examination and reclaim steps in (2)–(4), permitting immediate destruction or disposal.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain how seizure of food differs from other items: subsections (2) to (4) do not apply, and the officer may destroy or dispose of the food without further examination or inspection when the condition is a health hazard. (7(7))
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 7 contains a coherent seizure-and-outcome procedure (ss. 1–5), a separate Ministerial cost-recovery power (s. 6), and a food-specific exception (s. 7) that are independently recallable.

rows.heading: Seizure and destruction
rows.groupTitle: Seizure power and post-seizure procedure
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(5) form one procedural sequence from authorization through detention, examination, and the two outcome paths (release or destruction).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the authorized officers, the reasonable-grounds standard, the scope of seizable items, the detention duty, and both outcome paths: release with a three-working-day reclaim period when no hazard is found, and destruction or other action when a hazard is confirmed. (7(1)–(5))
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 7 contains a coherent seizure-and-outcome procedure (ss. 1–5), a separate Ministerial cost-recovery power (s. 6), and a food-specific exception (s. 7) that are independently recallable.

rows.heading: Action by Minister in respect of health hazard
rows.groupTitle: Minister's direct intervention for a health hazard
rows.groupReason: Triggers, entry conditions, and permissible actions form one operational power the learner recalls as a unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the four circumstances that authorize the Minister's direct entry and action, the scope of force, persons, and equipment permitted on entry, and the non-exhaustive list of actions the Minister may take.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 8 is one coherent mechanism: the Minister's direct intervention power, with trigger conditions, entry authority, and illustrative actions forming a single recall unit.

rows.heading: Effect of order or action
rows.groupTitle: Legal non-effects of health hazard orders and Ministerial actions
rows.groupReason: Both (a) and (b) are parallel 'shall not' limitations on the same triggering event, together defining the full scope of what a section 6 order or section 8 action does not do.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two legal non-effects of a section 6 order or section 8 Ministerial action: no effect on the validity or force of other orders under the Act, and no inference or deeming that the health hazard was caused by the person to whom the order is directed.

evidenceText: affect the validity or force of any other order that is made under this Act, whether before, during or after the making of that order or taking of that action

rows.sourceMapReason: The two sub-parts jointly state the complete legal non-effect of section 6 orders and section 8 Ministerial actions, forming one coherent recall unit on what those acts do not do.

rows.heading: Recovery of expenses of Minister
rows.groupTitle: Recovery of Minister's health-hazard expenses as a Crown debt
rows.groupReason: One recallable rule: who may be charged, the legal characterization of the expense as a Crown debt, and the required court-action route.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the mechanism by which the Minister recovers health-hazard expenses, including the debtor, the 'with costs' element, the court-action route, and the characterization as a debt owed to the Crown in right of the Province.

evidenceText: The expenses incurred by the Minister in respect of a health hazard may be recovered with costs from any person to whom an order is or would be directed under subsection 6(6) in respect of a health hazard by action in a court of competent jurisdiction as a debt owed to the Crown in right of the Province.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 10 is a single coherent payment/cost rule stating that the Minister may recover health-hazard expenses with costs by court action as a Crown debt; all elements form one recall task and the provision has clear independent study value.

rows.heading: Certificate of Minister for expenses
rows.groupTitle: Minister's certificate of unrecovered expenses: creation and evidentiary effect
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) are interdependent: (2) gives evidentiary force to the specific certificate signed under (1), so they recall together as one procedural mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which the Minister may sign a certificate of unrecovered expenses and identify the two matters the certificate proves in the absence of contrary evidence in an action under section 10.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 11 is a coherent evidentiary mechanism: the Minister's power to sign a certificate of unrecovered expenses (11(1)) and its admissibility and proof effect in a section 10 action (11(2)) form one tightly coupled procedural rule.

rows.heading: Food premises
rows.groupTitle: Food premises licensing requirement and application
rows.groupReason: The licensing prerequisite and its application procedure are tightly interdependent and recallable as one rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that a food premises may not be operated without a licence and identify the application requirements: application to the Minister on the prescribed form with the prescribed fee paid.

evidenceText: No person shall operate a food premises unless the person is the holder of a licence issued in accordance with this Act and the regulations.
shall apply to the Minister on a form provided by the Minister for a licence to operate the food premises and shall pay the prescribed application fee at the time the application is made.

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsection 12(1) states the licensing prerequisite and 12(2) provides its directly dependent application procedure; together they form one coherent food premises licensing concept too small to split meaningfully.

rows.heading: Duties of a person who holds a licence to operate a food premises
rows.groupTitle: Core maintenance duty and licence conditions
rows.groupReason: The duty to maintain premises per prescribed standards and the dual source of licence terms (regulatory and Minister-specified) form one interdependent compliance framework.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the standard a food premises licensee must meet and the two sources of terms and conditions to which the licence is subject.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 contains two distinct recall tasks: (1) the baseline compliance standard and dual source of licence conditions, and (2) the operational information, record-keeping, and reporting duties. These are independently testable concepts for a food premises licensee.

rows.heading: Duties of a person who holds a licence to operate a food premises
rows.groupTitle: Information, record-keeping, and reporting duties
rows.groupReason: These subsections collectively define the licensee's operational duties: furnishing information to named officers on request, keeping prescribed records, and making prescribed reports and returns.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall to whom a licensee must furnish information upon request, what records must be kept and how, and the obligation to make prescribed reports and returns.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 contains two distinct recall tasks: (1) the baseline compliance standard and dual source of licence conditions, and (2) the operational information, record-keeping, and reporting duties. These are independently testable concepts for a food premises licensee.

rows.heading: Duty to operate under sanitary conditions
rows.groupTitle: Duty to ensure sanitary conditions for food on licensed premises
rows.groupReason: One actor, one duty, one standard (sanitary conditions) covering six enumerated food-handling activities; a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the specific duty a food premises licence holder owes to ensure that food manufactured, processed, prepared, stored, handled, or displayed on or in the premises is handled under sanitary conditions.

evidenceText: A person who holds a licence to operate a food premises shall ensure that food that is manufactured, processed, prepared, stored, handled or displayed on or in the premises is manufactured, processed, prepared, stored, handled or displayed under sanitary conditions.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 14 is a single, self-contained duty imposing a specific sanitary-conditions obligation on food premises licence holders; it is independently recallable and distinct from the general maintenance duty in section 13.

rows.heading: Duty of a person who is employed on or in a food premises
rows.groupTitle: Employee compliance duty in food premises
rows.groupReason: A single compliance duty owed by food premises employees to meet prescribed regulatory standards.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the compliance duty imposed by section 15 on a person employed on or in a food premises regarding standards and requirements prescribed by the regulations.
rows.sourceMapReason: One actor, one duty, one modality — a single regulatory compliance obligation with no internal subdivisions warranting a split.

rows.heading: Food unfit for human consumption
rows.groupTitle: Prohibition on selling food unfit for human consumption
rows.groupReason: One operative prohibition with an enumerated set of unfitness reasons; all elements are needed to recall the rule completely.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the prohibition in s. 16: no person shall sell or offer for sale food unfit for human consumption by reason of disease, adulteration, impurity, or other cause.

evidenceText: No person shall sell or offer for sale any food that is unfit for human consumption by reason of disease, adulteration, impurity or other cause.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single, self-contained prohibition: no person shall sell or offer for sale food unfit for human consumption by reason of disease, adulteration, impurity, or other cause. One actor, one modality, one recall task.

rows.heading: Milk and milk products
rows.groupTitle: Milk and milk product pasteurization and sterilization requirements
rows.groupReason: The prohibition, its exception, and the defined term form one interdependent rule set a learner recalls as a single dairy-safety requirement.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the pasteurization or sterilization requirement for selling, offering for sale, delivering, or distributing milk, cream, and milk products, the licensed-plant condition for in-province and out-of-province plants, the exception in 17(3) for delivery to a Minister-licensed plant, and the definition of "milk product" in 17(4).

evidenceText: No person shall sell, offer for sale, deliver or distribute milk or cream that has not been pasteurized or sterilized in a dairy plant licensed by the Minister
Subsection (1) does not apply in respect of milk or cream that is sold, offered for sale, delivered or distributed to a plant licensed by the Minister
In subsection (2), "milk product" means a product processed or derived in whole or mainly from milk and intended for human consumption

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent dairy-safety prohibition scheme: the same pasteurization/sterilization rule applied to raw milk/cream and to processed milk products, with a tightly bound exception and an in-section definition.

rows.heading: Meat and meat products
rows.groupTitle: Sale requirements for meat and meat products
rows.groupReason: The two alternative compliance paths, the derivative meat-product rule, and the in-subsection definition are one interdependent prohibition a learner must recall together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the two alternative compliance paths for selling meat (CFIA inspection legend or Minister-licensed abattoir) and how that requirement extends to meat products.

evidenceText: No person shall sell or offer for sale any meat unless it (a) bears the inspection legend of the Canadian Food Inspection Agency or such other jurisdiction as may be prescribed by regulation, or (b) is from an animal slaughtered in an abattoir licensed by the Minister.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 18 states one prohibition (selling meat or meat products) with two alternative compliance paths and a short definitional gloss; all subsections form a single recall task on lawful sale requirements.

rows.heading: Poultry meat and poultry products
rows.groupTitle: Prohibition on selling poultry meat and poultry products without inspection or licensed abattoir
rows.groupReason: All three subsections form one interdependent prohibition: the base rule, its extension to derived products, and the term that scopes the extension.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two alternative requirements (CFIA inspection legend or Minister-licensed abattoir) that poultry meat must meet before sale, confirm that the prohibition extends to poultry products derived from such meat, and recall the statutory definition of 'poultry product' in subsection (3).

evidenceText: No person shall sell or offer for sale any poultry meat unless it
is from poultry slaughtered in an abattoir licensed by the Minister
a product processed or derived in whole or mainly from poultry meat and intended for human consumption

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 19 is a self-contained prohibition scheme for poultry meat and poultry products: a primary sale prohibition (19(1)), its extension to derived products (19(2)), and the scoping definition (19(3)) form one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Seizure and destruction of food in unlicensed food premises
rows.groupTitle: Seizure and destruction of non-compliant food
rows.groupReason: One seizure-to-disposal sequence: parallel grounds for four food categories followed by the destruction/disposal power.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the officers with seizure power, the four food categories and their linked sections (12, 17, 18, 19), the reasonable-grounds standard, and the destruction or disposal options for seized items.
rows.sourceMapReason: A single enforcement mechanism with one actor set, parallel seizure grounds across four food categories, and a dependent destruction power; recalls as one unit.

rows.heading: Public water supply system
rows.groupTitle: Duties of a public water supply system owner or operator
rows.groupReason: All three duties (consumer information, monitoring/reporting, and MOH notification) operate on the same actor within one short section and form a single coherent recall set of operator obligations.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the three duties imposed on the owner or operator of a public water supply system: providing consumer information when the Minister requires it, monitoring and reporting on water quality, and promptly notifying a medical officer of health of malfunctions that may affect potability.

evidenceText: An owner or operator of a public water supply system shall, when required by the Minister, ensure that persons who consume water from the system are provided forthwith with such information in relation to the water from the system
monitor the water supply for such substances and at such frequencies as may be necessary or as required by the Minister, and report the results of the monitoring as required by the Minister
promptly notify a medical officer of health of any malfunctions or occurrences in the public water supply system that may affect the potability of the water

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 21 imposes three short, parallel duties on the same actor (owner/operator of a public water supply system): consumer information provision, ongoing monitoring and reporting, and prompt MOH notification of potability-affecting malfunctions. All three are concise, share the same actor and operational context, and answer one coherent recall task, so one StudyUnit suffices.

rows.heading: On-site sewage disposal systems
rows.groupTitle: Ongoing information, record-keeping, and reporting duties of licence holders
rows.groupReason: Subsections (3), (4), and (5) impose three distinct ongoing duties on the licence holder—responding to inspector requests, maintaining records, and making reports—each deferred to regulation for specifics.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the three ongoing duties of an on-site sewage disposal licence holder: furnishing information to inspectors, keeping prescribed records, and making prescribed reports and returns.

evidenceText: A person who holds a licence referred to in subsection (1) shall furnish a public health inspector or public safety inspector with any information that he or she requests in respect of the installation, construction, repair or replacement of an on-site sewage disposal system.

A person who holds a licence referred to in subsection (1) shall keep such records in respect of the installation, construction, repair or replacement of an on-site sewage disposal system as are prescribed by regulation and shall keep such records in such form, with such detail and for such length of time as are prescribed by regulation.
A person who holds a licence referred to in subsection (1) shall make such reports and returns as are prescribed by regulation.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 23 contains a clear licensing requirement with its licence terms (23(1)-(2)) and three distinct ongoing duties of the licence holder (23(3)-(5)), forming two independently recallable study concepts.

rows.heading: On-site sewage disposal systems
rows.groupTitle: Licensing requirement and licence terms for on-site sewage disposal systems
rows.groupReason: The licensing prohibition in 23(1) and the licence terms in 23(2) are tightly interdependent: the terms describe the content of the licence the prohibition requires.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who must be licensed by the Minister to install, construct, repair, or replace an on-site sewage disposal system and state the two categories of terms to which the licence is subject.

evidenceText: No person shall install, construct, repair or replace an on-site sewage disposal system or carry out the business of installing, constructing, repairing or replacing on-site sewage disposal systems unless the person is licensed by the Minister in accordance with the regulations.

A licence referred to in subsection (1) is subject to (a) the terms and conditions prescribed by regulation, and (b) such additional terms and conditions the Minister considers appropriate and specifies in the licence.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 23 contains a clear licensing requirement with its licence terms (23(1)-(2)) and three distinct ongoing duties of the licence holder (23(3)-(5)), forming two independently recallable study concepts.

rows.heading: Approval by the Minister
rows.groupTitle: Legal limits of Minister's approval: no warranty and no injurious affection or compensation
rows.groupReason: Subsections (5)–(6) define what the Minister's approval does not do: it is not a warranty and does not by itself create injurious affection or a compensation right.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two legal limits of the Minister's approval: it does not constitute a warranty and it does not by itself render land injuriously affected or give rise to a compensation claim.

evidenceText: An approval given under this section does not constitute a warranty.

Land shall not be deemed or found to be injuriously affected by reason only of an approval given under this section and no compensation shall be payable by reason only of an approval given under this section.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 24 contains the operational approval mechanism (triggers, required approvals, compliance duty) and a separate set of legal limits on the approval's effect (no warranty, no injurious affection or compensation). These form two distinct recall tasks.

rows.heading: Approval by the Minister
rows.groupTitle: Minister's approval requirements and compliance for on-site sewage disposal systems
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1)–(4) establish the approval triggers by activity type, what must be approved in each case, and the post-approval duty to work in accordance with the approval.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify which activities (install, construct, repair, replace, bring into use) require Minister's approval, what design/location/plan elements must be approved for each, and the obligation to carry out work in accordance with the approval.

evidenceText: A person shall not install or construct an on-site sewage disposal system unless the design and location of the on-site sewage disposal system is approved by the Minister.

A person shall not repair or replace an on-site sewage disposal system unless the design, location and plan for repair or replacement of the on-site sewage disposal system is approved by the Minister.

Where an approval is given under this section, no person shall install, construct, repair or replace, or bring into use or operation an on-site sewage disposal system other than in accordance with the approval.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 24 contains the operational approval mechanism (triggers, required approvals, compliance duty) and a separate set of legal limits on the approval's effect (no warranty, no injurious affection or compensation). These form two distinct recall tasks.

rows.heading: Requirement to provide notice before covering a system
rows.groupTitle: Notice to the Minister before covering an on-site sewage disposal system
rows.groupReason: One actor, one written-notice duty, one trigger (covering the system), and one minimum advance period form a single recallable obligation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify who must give written notice to the Minister before covering an on-site sewage disposal system, what the notice must state, and the minimum advance period required.

evidenceText: A person who holds a licence under subsection 23(1) shall give the Minister written notice that an on-site sewage disposal system is ready for inspection at least three working days before covering the system.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative duty with one actor, one trigger, and one timing requirement; independently recallable as a pre-covering notice obligation.

rows.heading: Orders respecting on-site sewage disposal systems
rows.groupTitle: Powers to issue orders for on-site sewage disposal systems
rows.groupReason: Covers the two distinct order powers (inspection and remedial), the duty to comply, and the restriction barring a public safety inspector from issuing a remedial order for a health hazard.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the types of written orders a medical officer of health, public health inspector, or public safety inspector may issue, the parties to whom they are directed, the duty to comply, and the prohibition on a public safety inspector issuing a remedial order in respect of a health hazard.
rows.sourceMapReason: The section divides into the power to issue inspection and remedial orders (with the duty to comply and the public safety inspector restriction) and the separate post-order obligations on covering and inspection fees.

rows.heading: Orders respecting on-site sewage disposal systems
rows.groupTitle: Obligations after a remedial order: covering and inspection fees
rows.groupReason: Covers the prohibition on covering a system subject to a remedial order until inspected and the licensee's obligation to pay prescribed fees for each compliance inspection.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that a person must not cover an on-site sewage disposal system that is the subject of a remedial order until it is inspected for compliance, and that the licensee under subsection 23(1) must pay the prescribed fee for each such inspection.
rows.sourceMapReason: The section divides into the power to issue inspection and remedial orders (with the duty to comply and the public safety inspector restriction) and the separate post-order obligations on covering and inspection fees.

rows.heading: Certificate of compliance
rows.groupTitle: Certificate of compliance for on-site sewage disposal systems
rows.groupReason: One actor must both furnish a content-specific certificate to the owner and mail a copy to the Minister within a fixed deadline after the system is covered.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State who must issue the certificate of compliance for an on-site sewage disposal system, what the certificate must state, and the deadline and recipient for mailing a copy to the Minister.

evidenceText: A person who installs, constructs, repairs or replaces an on-site sewage disposal system shall provide to the owner of the system a certificate signed and dated by the person stating that the system has been installed, constructed, repaired or replaced in accordance with the approval given by the Minister under section 24 and that this Act and all applicable regulations have been complied with
shall mail a copy of the completed certificate to the Minister within ten days after the on-site sewage disposal system is covered

rows.sourceMapReason: Both subsections impose sequential duties on the same actor (the installer/repairer) and together form one small certificate-of-compliance procedure; splitting would fragment a tightly interdependent two-step obligation.

rows.heading: Water circulation systems
rows.groupTitle: Water circulation system licensing requirement and application
rows.groupReason: The prohibition on unlicensed operation and the application procedure to the Minister are mutually dependent parts of one licensing regime.
