rows.groupTitle: Minister's power to take possession of land, waters, or watercourse
rows.groupReason: The sole power to take possession of land, waters, or watercourse, which is qualitatively distinct from the temporary entry and modification powers in the other subsections.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the scope of the Minister's power to take possession of land, waters, or watercourse under subsection (b), including the standard (Minister's opinion) and the two stated purposes (carrying out work or obtaining access).

evidenceText: take possession of any land, waters or watercourse that in the Minister's opinion is necessary to carry out work on a public work, or for obtaining access to that public work

rows.sourceMapReason: The possession power in (b) is qualitatively distinct from the entry-and-modification powers in (a), (c), (d), and (e), creating two independent recall tasks for the learner.

rows.heading: Power of Minister to enter buildings and on lands designated as public works
rows.groupTitle: Minister's entry power for project-designated public works
rows.groupReason: One power with one trigger (Ministerial designation for a project) and one purpose (carry out work); no internal split needed.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which the Minister and delegated persons may enter a building, structure, or land designated as a public work for a project to carry out work on that public work.

evidenceText: The Minister may enter, by himself or herself or by his or her architects, engineers, agents and workers, a building or other structure or enter on any land that is, for the purposes of a project, designated as a public work by the Minister in order to carry out work on that public work.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 10 is a single, self-contained entry power triggered by Ministerial designation of land or structures as public works for a project, distinct from the broader general land powers in section 9.

rows.heading: Power of Minister to make contract
rows.groupTitle: Minister's power to contract for property
rows.groupReason: One permissive power with defined method (purchase or lease), defined property scope, and dual purposes (public work or government use) forming a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Minister's power to contract for the purchase or lease of land, buildings, and other structures and identify the two purposes that justify such a contract.

evidenceText: The Minister may contract for the purchase or lease of land, buildings and other structures required for a public work or for the use and purposes of government.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single permissive power granting the Minister authority to contract for property acquisition; one coherent recall unit with no internal division warranting a split.

rows.heading: Notice of intention to designate
rows.groupTitle: Minister's duty to serve written notice before designating a public work for a project
rows.groupReason: One procedural duty with tightly interdependent elements (timing, form, recipient, content) forming a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what the Minister must do, in what form, to whom, and before what action, when designating land, a building, or other structure as a public work for a project.

evidenceText: Before the Minister designates any land, building or other structure as a public work for the purposes of a project, the Minister shall serve notice in writing of the intention to designate on the owner of the land, building or other structure.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 12 states a single, self-contained pre-designation duty: the Minister shall serve written notice of intention to designate on the owner before designating land, building or structure as a public work for a project. All elements (actor, trigger, form, recipient, content) form one recallable procedural rule.

rows.heading: Service of notice
rows.groupTitle: Service of section 12 notice by registered mail
rows.groupReason: Both subsections together define the single operative rule for how section 12 notice is served and when it is deemed effective; recalling them separately would fragment one procedural concept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the method that constitutes sufficient service of a section 12 notice (registered mail to the owner's latest known address) and the date on which such service is deemed effected.

evidenceText: A notice under section 12 shall be sufficiently served if it is mailed by registered mail to the latest known address of the owner.
Service by registered mail shall be deemed to be effected 30 days after the date of mailing.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 13 is a short, self-contained procedural rule: it specifies the method of serving the section 12 notice (registered mail to the owner's latest known address) and the deemed service date (30 days after mailing). The two subsections form one coherent service-of-notice concept and constitute a single recall task.

rows.heading: Exemption from the Community Planning Act
rows.groupTitle: Minister's Exemption from the Community Planning Act
rows.groupReason: One exemption rule: the Minister is exempt from CPAA compliance (by-law, regulation, order, demand, term, condition, and Assessment and Planning Appeal Board decision) for lands, buildings, and structures designated as public works for a project.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the condition that triggers the Minister's exemption and identify the specific forms of Community Planning Act compliance from which the Minister is exempt for designated public works.

evidenceText: the Minister is exempt from compliance with
designated as public works by the Minister

rows.sourceMapReason: A single exemption rule with one triggering condition (designation as public works for a project) and one enumeration of Community Planning Act instruments from which the Minister is exempt; all pieces form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Permits, licences and approvals
rows.groupTitle: Minister's permit and licence dispensation for public works (s. 15)
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) together state one mechanism: the Minister's power to apply despite other Acts and the issuing ministers' authority to grant even absent normal compliance.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Minister's power to apply for permits, licences, or approvals for work on designated public works despite any other Act, and the authority of issuing ministers to grant them even if the Minister does not meet normal issuance requirements.

evidenceText: Despite any other Act, the Minister may apply for a permit, licence or approval that he or she considers necessary to carry out work on the lands, buildings and other structures that are, for the purposes of a project, designated as public works by the Minister.

the ministers of the Crown responsible for the issuance of the permits, licences and approvals referred to in subsection (1) may issue those permits, licences and approvals to the Minister, even if the Minister is unable to meet the requirements or comply with the terms and conditions for their issuance.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 15 is a short, self-contained operative provision granting the Minister a special permit pathway for public works and allowing issuing ministers to grant those permits even absent normal compliance. The two subsections are tightly interdependent and form one coherent dispensation mechanism.

rows.heading: Compensation for damages
rows.groupTitle: Minister's compensation duty and claim procedure under the Public Works Act
rows.groupReason: The Minister's mandatory duty to compensate and the claimant's written-claim requirement are two halves of one compensation mechanism and are best recalled together.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Minister's obligation to compensate for damages done under the Act and the contents required in a person's written claim for compensation.

evidenceText: The Minister shall compensate a person for damages suffered by virtue of anything done under this Act.
A person claiming to be entitled to compensation shall deliver to the Minister a written claim setting forth full particulars of the claim and of his or her right and title to the compensation.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 16 creates a mandatory compensation duty on the Minister and a written-claim procedure for the claimant; both subsections form one tightly interdependent recall unit on how compensation under the Act is triggered and claimed.

rows.heading: Arbitration
rows.groupTitle: Arbitration procedure for compensation disputes
rows.groupReason: Subsections 17(1) and 17(2) are interdependent stages of one procedure, from the Minister's offer duty through the deemed arbitration agreement.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Minister's 120-day offer-and-notice duty, the claimant's 120-day acceptance period, and the automatic submission to arbitration with the deemed written arbitration agreement.
rows.sourceMapReason: The two subsections form one sequential arbitration procedure (Minister's offer duty, two 120-day windows, automatic submission, deemed arbitration agreement) that a learner would recall as a single procedural concept.

rows.heading: The Court of King’s Bench may extend time limit
rows.groupTitle: Court power to extend section 17 time limits
rows.groupReason: One procedural power with a single recall task: who may apply, which court, which time limits are extendable, and the before-or-after flexibility.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the court, the applicants, the specific section 17 time limits subject to extension, and the timing rule (before or after expiration).

evidenceText: The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick may extend a time limit under subsection 17(1) or (2), either before or after the expiration of the time limit.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 18 is a short, self-contained provision granting the Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick a single procedural power: extending section 17 time limits on application. It forms one coherent recall task without needing to combine or split.

rows.heading: Application of Arbitration Act
rows.groupTitle: Arbitration Act application and conflict priority
rows.groupReason: Both clauses (incorporation and conflict priority) are needed together to answer 'which law governs an arbitration under this Act?'
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that the Arbitration Act applies to arbitrations under the Public Works Act and that a provision of this Act prevails over a conflicting provision of the Arbitration Act.

evidenceText: The Arbitration Act applies to an arbitration under this Act but, if there is a conflict between a provision of this Act and a provision of the Arbitration Act, the provision of this Act prevails.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single undivided section stating two interdependent rules — incorporation of the Arbitration Act and the conflict priority in favour of this Act — that form one coherent recall task on the applicable-law framework for arbitrations under the Act.

rows.heading: Exclusive jurisdiction of arbitral tribunal
rows.groupTitle: Exclusive arbitral jurisdiction and court intervention exceptions
rows.groupReason: 20(1) is a self-contained jurisdictional rule: the tribunal exclusively hears compensation matters, and a court may intervene only for three listed purposes.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the arbitral tribunal's exclusive jurisdiction over compensation matters under the Public Works Act and the three specific purposes for which a court may intervene in the arbitration.

evidenceText: An arbitral tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine all matters of compensation under this Act and no court shall intervene in the matter of compensation, except for the following purposes:
to prevent unfair or unequal treatment of a party to an arbitration agreement

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 20 contains two independently recallable rules with different modalities: 20(1) allocates exclusive compensation jurisdiction to the arbitral tribunal with three court-intervention exceptions, while 20(2) prohibits seeking compensation under the Expropriation Act or any other Act for damages from this Act.

rows.heading: Exclusive jurisdiction of arbitral tribunal
rows.groupTitle: Prohibition on compensation claims under the Expropriation Act or other Acts
rows.groupReason: 20(2) imposes a separate prohibition on seeking compensation through alternative statutory schemes for damages arising from this Act, distinct from the jurisdictional allocation in 20(1).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the prohibition in section 20(2) preventing any person from applying for compensation under Part 2 of the Expropriation Act or any other Act for damages suffered by virtue of anything done under the Public Works Act.

evidenceText: No person shall apply for compensation under Part 2 of the Expropriation Act or any other Act for damages suffered by virtue of anything done under this Act.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 20 contains two independently recallable rules with different modalities: 20(1) allocates exclusive compensation jurisdiction to the arbitral tribunal with three court-intervention exceptions, while 20(2) prohibits seeking compensation under the Expropriation Act or any other Act for damages from this Act.

rows.heading: Appointment of arbitral tribunal
rows.groupTitle: Appointment of the arbitral tribunal
rows.groupReason: One constitution procedure with sequential fallbacks from sole arbitrator to three-arbitrator panel to court-appointed backstop; recalling the stages separately would fragment the process.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the sequential steps and deadlines for constituting the arbitral tribunal, including the three-arbitrator composition, the 10-day and 20-day appointment windows, and when The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick steps in to appoint.

evidenceText: Within ten days after the date on which the Minister submits a matter to arbitration, the Minister and the person claiming compensation shall appoint a sole arbitrator.

If the Minister or the person claiming compensation fails to appoint an arbitrator within ten days after the expiration of the time period referred to in subsection (2), The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick shall appoint an arbitrator on behalf of the Minister or the person, as the case may be.

If the arbitrators appointed under paragraphs (2)(a) and (b) are unable to agree on the appointment of the chair within 20 days after the appointment of the second arbitrator, The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick shall appoint the chair on their behalf.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 21 is a single sequential appointment procedure: sole-arbitrator first, then three-arbitrator fallback with deadlines and court backstop. The subsections are interdependent stages of one constitution process.

rows.heading: Fees and expenses of arbitral tribunal
rows.groupTitle: Arbitral tribunal fee and expense allocation
rows.groupReason: Two tribunal-size scenarios of one cost-allocation rule form a single recall task on who bears arbitration expenses.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State which party is responsible for the fees and expenses of each arbitrator and other arbitration costs under both the sole-arbitrator and three-arbitrator tribunal configurations.

evidenceText: the Minister is responsible for the fees and expenses of the arbitral tribunal and any other expenses related to the arbitration
the person claiming compensation is responsible for the fees and expenses of the arbitrator appointed by that person

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent cost-allocation rule with two tribunal-size scenarios; a single recall task on who bears arbitration fees and expenses.

rows.heading: Decision of arbitral tribunal
rows.groupTitle: One-year deadline for arbitral tribunal compensation decision
rows.groupReason: A single mandatory time limit on the arbitral tribunal, triggered by the Minister's submission to arbitration.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the deadline the arbitral tribunal must meet to decide a compensation matter and the event that starts the one-year period.

evidenceText: Within one year after the date on which the Minister submits a matter of compensation to arbitration, the arbitral tribunal shall make a decision on the matter of compensation.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 23 states a single mandatory deadline: the arbitral tribunal shall decide a compensation matter within one year of the Minister's submission. It is one clear procedural obligation, independently recallable, and does not require splitting or combining.

rows.heading: Arbitral tribunal may extend the time for making a decision
rows.groupTitle: Arbitral tribunal's power to extend the decision deadline
rows.groupReason: The provision sets out one procedural rule: who may extend, when, and the required form of notice with reasons to two named parties.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which the arbitral tribunal may extend the one-year decision deadline in section 23, including the timing limit and the notice-with-reasons requirement to the Minister and the person claiming compensation.

evidenceText: an arbitral tribunal may extend the time for making a decision by giving notice of the extension with reasons to the Minister and to the person claiming compensation

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 24 is a single, coherent procedural rule: the arbitral tribunal's power to extend the one-year decision deadline, its timing limit, and the notice-with-reasons requirement to both the Minister and the claimant. One actor, one modality, one procedure — one recallable unit.

rows.heading: Vesting of property; sale or lease of public work
rows.groupTitle: Vesting, sale or lease, and proceeds of public works
rows.groupReason: The vesting rule, the conditional disposal power with Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval, the Great Seal conveyance mechanism, and the proceeds treatment form one tightly interdependent recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall where public works are vested, the conditions and conveyance procedure for their sale or lease, and how the proceeds must be accounted for or deposited.

evidenceText: All public works shall be vested in the Crown in right of the Province
when a public work is not required, the Minister, with the approval of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, may enter into an agreement for the sale or lease of the public work
the proceeds of the sale or leasing shall be accounted for as public money or on the direction of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, deposited to the credit of the Land Management Fund

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 25 is a short, self-contained provision establishing the vesting of public works, the conditional sale or lease power, the conveyance mechanism, and proceeds treatment as one interdependent rule set.

rows.heading: Sale or disposal of public works without Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval
rows.groupTitle: Minister's power to dispose of a public work without LGiC approval and appraisal requirement
rows.groupReason: The disposal power, its conditions (no longer required, ≤ $150,000 appraised value, override of s.25 and s.55), and the qualifying appraiser designation form one interdependent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which the Minister may sell or dispose of a public work without Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval and identify the professional designation required to determine the appraised value.

evidenceText: the Minister, without the approval of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, may sell or otherwise dispose of a public work that is no longer required by the Minister if the public work has an appraised value not exceeding $150,000

The appraised value of a public work shall be determined by a member of the New Brunswick Association of Real Estate Appraisers/Association des évaluateurs immobiliers du Nouveau-Brunswick holding the designation of Canadian Residential Appraiser (CRA) or Accredited Appraiser Canadian Institute (AACI), as applicable

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 26 contains the Minister's conditional power to dispose of a public work without LGiC approval plus an appraisal-qualification requirement (26(1)-(2)), and a separate mandatory proceeds-accounting rule (26(3)) involving a different legal operation and trigger stage.

rows.heading: Sale or disposal of public works without Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval
rows.groupTitle: Disposition of proceeds from a sale under section 26
rows.groupReason: The mandatory accounting or deposit rule for sale proceeds is a distinct legal obligation triggered after the sale and involves a different operative requirement from the disposal power itself.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State how the proceeds of a public work sale made under section 26 must be accounted for and to which fund they may be deposited.

evidenceText: the proceeds of the sale shall be accounted for as public money or, on the direction of the Minister, be deposited to the credit of the Land Management Fund

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 26 contains the Minister's conditional power to dispose of a public work without LGiC approval plus an appraisal-qualification requirement (26(1)-(2)), and a separate mandatory proceeds-accounting rule (26(3)) involving a different legal operation and trigger stage.

rows.heading: Transfer of land, buildings and other structures from other ministers
rows.groupTitle: Transfer of unneeded Crown property to the Minister
rows.groupReason: The transfer duty and the public work consequence are one recallable concept; splitting them would fragment the mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the trigger, the other minister's transfer duty, and the resulting public work status when unneeded Crown property passes to the Minister under section 27.
rows.sourceMapReason: Two short, tightly linked subsections form one transfer mechanism: the other minister's duty to transfer unneeded Crown property and the resulting public work status upon transfer.

rows.heading: Transfer of public works to other ministers or the New Brunswick Housing Corporation
rows.groupTitle: Minister's duty to distribute lists and power to transfer surplus public works
rows.groupReason: Covers both the mandatory distribution of surplus lists and the permissive transfer at book value plus costs to other ministers or the New Brunswick Housing Corporation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Minister's mandatory duty to distribute surplus public works lists and the permissive transfer power priced at book value plus transportation and incidental costs.

evidenceText: the Minister shall distribute lists of public works that are no longer required to other ministers of the Crown and to the New Brunswick Housing Corporation and may transfer a public work to another minister of the Crown or to the New Brunswick Housing Corporation by transfer at book value plus the cost of transportation and any other costs incidental to the transfer

rows.sourceMapReason: Single provision pairing the Minister's duty to distribute surplus lists with the permissive transfer power at book value; same actor, recipients, and trigger form one coherent unit.

rows.heading: Sale of public works to non-profit organizations or other governments
rows.groupTitle: Sale of public works to non-profit organizations or other governments (s.29)
rows.groupReason: Single permissive power whose price cap, eligible buyer list, and s.28 scope limitation are tightly interdependent conditions of one rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Minister's s.29 sale power, including the eligible buyer categories, the price cap (cost, appraised or book value), and the requirement that the public work was not transferred under section 28.

evidenceText: the Minister may sell a public work that is not transferred under section 28 for any amount up to the cost, appraised or book value of the public work to a charitable, religious or non-profit organization, a local government, a government of another province or territory, the Government of Canada or a corporation or agency in which the Province has a majority interest

rows.sourceMapReason: One coherent permissive sale power with interdependent conditions (eligible buyer categories, price cap, scope limitation) that function as a single recall task.

rows.heading: Sale of public works other than under sections 28 and 29
rows.groupTitle: Default sale methods for public works and Treasury Board override
rows.groupReason: Subsections (1) and (2) form a rule/exception pair defining the four default sale channels and the Treasury Board override; they are needed together to recall when each channel applies.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the four prescribed sale methods under subsection (1) and the two Treasury Board grounds for applying a different method under subsection (2).

evidenceText: the Minister shall sell a public work that is not transferred under section 28 or sold under section 29

Subsection (1) does not apply to the sale of a public work under that subsection if the Treasury Board determines that a sale is impractical or that a public benefit is likely to result from the sale of the public work by another method.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 contains three independently recallable rule sets: the default sale methods with Treasury Board override, the salvage/no-value disposal rules, and the records duty. Each answers a distinct recall question.

rows.heading: Sale of public works other than under sections 28 and 29
rows.groupTitle: Record-keeping for sale and disposal of public works
rows.groupReason: Subsection (5) imposes a freestanding records duty with three specific data items; it is independently recallable as an audit/compliance obligation distinct from the sale or disposal methods.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three categories of information the Minister must record for each sale or disposal transaction: buyer name, description and serial number, and location and date.

evidenceText: The Minister shall maintain adequate records of each transaction relating to the sale or disposal of a public work under this Act

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 contains three independently recallable rule sets: the default sale methods with Treasury Board override, the salvage/no-value disposal rules, and the records duty. Each answers a distinct recall question.

rows.heading: Sale of public works other than under sections 28 and 29
rows.groupTitle: Sale and disposal of salvage-value and valueless public works
rows.groupReason: Subsections (3) and (4) cover the low-value spectrum with distinct triggers, methods, and a hazardous-waste exception involving a different minister; together they answer how the Minister handles items with no meaningful market value.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the required sealed-offer method for salvage-value items, the landfill disposal option for valueless items, and the hazardous-disposal requirement under the Minister of Environment and Climate Change.

evidenceText: If the Minister determines that the only value in a public work is salvage value, the Minister shall sell the public work by sealed offer solicited from more than one source.

If the Minister determines that a public work has no value, the Minister may dispose of it at the local sanitary landfill site, but if the public work may be hazardous to the health of the public, disposal shall be made in the manner required by the Minister of Environment and Climate Change.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30 contains three independently recallable rule sets: the default sale methods with Treasury Board override, the salvage/no-value disposal rules, and the records duty. Each answers a distinct recall question.

rows.heading: Vacant land
rows.groupTitle: Minister's disposal of vacant land from failed Real Property Tax Act sales
rows.groupReason: The whole section states one coherent disposal mechanism: the two conjunctive conditions, the website sale channel, the exclusion of sections 28/29/30(1), the optional appraisal, and the Land Management Fund proceeds rule all serve the same recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the conditions under which the Minister may dispose of vacant land transferred under section 27 without Lieutenant-Governor in Council approval, and state the applicable sale channel, excluded sections, appraisal option, and proceeds destination.

evidenceText: the Minister, without the approval of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, may sell or otherwise dispose of any vacant land that is transferred or has been transferred, whether before, on or after the commencement of this section, to the Minister under section 27 if

the amount of the taxes and penalties on the land that were due and unpaid under the Real Property Tax Act on the date that the proceedings to sell the land were held under that Act does not exceed $10,000
The proceeds of the sale of vacant land under this section shall be deposited to the credit of the Land Management Fund

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 30.1 is a compact, self-contained mechanism giving the Minister a specific disposal power for vacant land from failed Real Property Tax Act sales, with its own conditions, sale channel, exclusion from normal procedures, appraisal option, and proceeds rule. All parts are tightly interdependent and form one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Report of sale of a public work under section 26 or 30.1
rows.groupTitle: Minister's annual sale report and Royal Gazette publication
rows.groupReason: Both subsections form one short reporting-and-publication cycle; recalling them separately would fragment a single two-step accountability procedure.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the Minister's duty to report fiscal-year sales under sections 26 or 30.1 to Executive Council within six months of fiscal year-end and the requirement to publish the accepted report in the Royal Gazette within one month of Executive Council acceptance.

evidenceText: the Minister shall provide to Executive Council a report on all such sales occurring in the fiscal year in the form approved by Executive Council within six months after the end of each fiscal year
A report under subsection (1) shall be published in the Royal Gazette within one month after the report is accepted by Executive Council

rows.sourceMapReason: Creates two linked operative duties—Minister's annual report to Executive Council and Royal Gazette publication—forming one small accountability mechanism for public-work sales under sections 26 and 30.1.

rows.heading: Land Management Fund
rows.groupTitle: Land Management Fund Establishment and Custodianship
rows.groupReason: Establishment, custodianship, and account location form one coherent recall unit on who holds the fund and where it is kept.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Minister's custodianship role over the Land Management Fund and confirm that the fund is held in a separate account in the Consolidated Fund.

evidenceText: There is established a fund to be known as the Land Management Fund.
The Minister shall be the custodian of the Land Management Fund and the Land Management Fund shall be held in trust by the Minister.
The Land Management Fund shall be held for the purposes of this section in a separate account in the Consolidated Fund.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 32 establishes the Land Management Fund, defines its purposes and charges, grants a purchase power, and vests acquired land. These create distinct recall tasks: fund administration, statutory purposes and payable charges, and the acquisition mechanism with its vesting consequence.

rows.heading: Land Management Fund
rows.groupTitle: Minister's Purchase Power and Crown Vesting
rows.groupReason: The Minister's purchase power and the automatic vesting of acquired lands in the Crown form a cause-and-effect pair distinct from the fund's general purposes.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Explain the conditions under which the Minister may contract for a land purchase using Fund money and state that acquired lands vest in the Crown in right of the Province as public works under the Minister's control.

evidenceText: The Minister may, with money from the Fund and with the approval of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, contract for the purchase of land and lands and buildings and other structures.

Land and lands and buildings and other structures acquired under this section are public works that shall be vested in the Crown in right of the Province under the general administration, management, direction and control of the Minister.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 32 establishes the Land Management Fund, defines its purposes and charges, grants a purchase power, and vests acquired land. These create distinct recall tasks: fund administration, statutory purposes and payable charges, and the acquisition mechanism with its vesting consequence.

rows.heading: Land Management Fund
rows.groupTitle: Fund Purposes and Payable Charges
rows.groupReason: The three statutory purposes and the corresponding charge rules in subsections 5 and 6 are tightly interdependent and answer one recall question about what the fund may be used for.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the three statutory purposes of the Land Management Fund and identify which costs and expenses are payable out of it.

evidenceText: The purposes for the Land Management Fund are (a) with the approval of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, to acquire land and lands and buildings and other structures, (b) to maintain properties that have been designated by the Minister for management under the Fund, and (c) to develop and maintain a land inventory system.

The following are payable out of the Land Management Fund: (a) costs associated with acquiring and selling land and lands and buildings and other structures; and (b) expenses prescribed by regulation relating to the administration of the Land Management Fund.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 32 establishes the Land Management Fund, defines its purposes and charges, grants a purchase power, and vests acquired land. These create distinct recall tasks: fund administration, statutory purposes and payable charges, and the acquisition mechanism with its vesting consequence.

rows.heading: Public works development area
rows.groupTitle: Consent requirement for construction and renovation in a public works development area
rows.groupReason: Subsections (10)–(12) form a tightly linked prohibition/exception/consequence structure: the $5,000 annual cost threshold, the Minister's written consent requirement, the ordinary-repairs carve-out, and the no-allowance consequence for contravention.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the $5,000-per-year cost threshold triggering the Minister's written consent requirement for construction, additions, alterations, or renovations in a public works development area, the ordinary-repairs exception, and the rule that no increase in value from a contravention is allowed to the owner.

evidenceText: Unless the Minister gives his or her written consent to the owner of land in a public works development area, if there is involved a cost in excess of $5,000 in any year to the land, the owner shall not (a) construct any building or improvement on the land, (b) make any addition or alteration to a building on the land, or (c) renovate any building or improvement on the land.
Nothing in subsection (10) prohibits an owner from making ordinary repairs to his or her buildings.
If an owner contravenes subsection (10), nothing shall be allowed to the owner for any increase in value resulting from the contravention.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 33 contains at least four materially distinct legal concepts with different actors, triggers, and modalities: the sale restriction and right-of-first-refusal procedure, expropriation interaction rules, the construction/renovation consent regime, and the Minister's registration notice duties.

rows.heading: Public works development area
rows.groupTitle: Interaction of public works development area rules with expropriation
rows.groupReason: Subsections (8) and (9) address how the development area scheme interacts with the Expropriation Act and section 25: preserving government powers and setting a compensation standard that disregards the area designation.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that the public works development area does not diminish the Minister's expropriation or section 25 disposal powers, and that expropriation compensation is calculated as though the land were outside the development area.

evidenceText: Nothing in this section shall diminish or detract from the right of the Minister to expropriate land at any time according to the Expropriation Act or to dispose of land according to section 25 of this Act.
if land within a public works development area is expropriated, the owner shall be compensated for that land as though the land were not in a public works development area.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 33 contains at least four materially distinct legal concepts with different actors, triggers, and modalities: the sale restriction and right-of-first-refusal procedure, expropriation interaction rules, the construction/renovation consent regime, and the Minister's registration notice duties.

rows.heading: Public works development area
rows.groupTitle: Minister's duty to register notices of inclusion and exclusion from the development area
rows.groupReason: Subsections (13) and (14) impose paired registration duties on the Minister to notify owners at the registry office when lands enter or leave the public works development area.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall that the Minister must register a notice at the proper registry office advising owners when lands become subject to the public works development area provisions and again when the lands are no longer within the area.

evidenceText: The Minister shall cause to be registered in the proper registry office a notice to the persons who appear from the records of that registry office to be the owners of the lands in a public works development area at the time the lands became affected by this section, that the lands are so affected.

the Minister shall cause to be registered in the proper registry office a notice to all persons appearing on the records of that registry office to be the owners of those lands that those lands are no longer within the public works development area.

rows.heading: Public works development area

rows.sourceMapReason: Single operative rule stating the Board's factual findings are binding and conclusive; distinct recall task from the jurisdiction and evidence rules in section 36.

rows.heading: Procedure
rows.groupTitle: Board procedural powers and fairness duty
rows.groupReason: One procedural framework unit: the Board's procedural autonomy, its evidence and study powers, and its mandatory duty of procedural fairness operate as a single set of rules governing how the Board inquires into matters.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Board's procedural autonomy, its power to request or require evidence and studies, and its mandatory duty to ensure procedural fairness to all affected persons when inquiring into, hearing, or determining matters.

evidenceText: is the master of its own procedure and may give directions about process and procedure that it considers appropriate in the circumstances
may request from anyone, and require anyone to gather, evidence or require anyone to prepare studies relevant and incidental to the matter over which it is exercising its jurisdiction
shall ensure procedural fairness to all affected persons

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 38 sets out the Board's procedural framework in three tightly interdependent sub-parts (procedural autonomy, evidence-gathering power, and the mandatory fairness duty) that together answer one recall question about the Board's procedure. The section is short and cohesive; splitting would fragment a single procedural concept.

rows.heading: Orders respecting application
rows.groupTitle: Board's Ordering Power on Applications
rows.groupReason: All elements—partial/whole grant, conditional orders, and further or other relief—answer one recall question about the scope of the Board's order-making power on applications.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the forms of order the Board may make on an application: granting whole or part only, making a conditional order, or granting further or other relief as if originally sought.

evidenceText: the Board may make an order granting the whole or part only of the application, make a conditional order or grant further or other relief besides or instead of that applied for, as fully and in all respects as if the application had been for such partial, further or other relief.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 39 states one coherent Board power—the scope of relief available on an application—with no internal subdivisions or distinct recall tasks warranting a split.

rows.heading: Interim orders
rows.groupTitle: Board power to make interim orders and directions on final outcome
rows.groupReason: Both subsections form one recall task: the trigger, scope, and conditions of the Board's interim order power, including how it handles divergence from the final order.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall when the Board may make an interim order, what terms it may impose, and its power to issue directions if the interim order differs from the final order.

evidenceText: The Board may, with respect to any matter before it or on application, make an interim order where it considers it advisable to do so, and may impose such terms and conditions as it considers appropriate.
The Board may provide directions in the event that the interim order is different from the final order.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 40 grants the Board a coherent interim-order-making power with a closely tied transition mechanism (directions when interim differs from final); 40(3) is repealed and carries no study value.

rows.heading: Ex parte orders
rows.groupTitle: Board's ex parte order power and duration limit
rows.groupReason: The ex parte order power and its built-in temporal limitation are tightly interdependent and answer a single recall question.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Board's authority to make an interim ex parte order and the requirement that the order not extend beyond the time necessary for determination through normal procedures.

evidenceText: The Board may make an interim ex parte order, but it shall make no ex parte order for any longer time than it considers necessary to enable the matter to be determined by means of its normal procedures.

rows.sourceMapReason: Short self-contained provision granting the Board power to make interim ex parte orders with an integral duration limit; the power and its constraint form one recall task.

rows.heading: Substantial compliance
rows.groupTitle: Substantial compliance standard for Board actions
rows.groupReason: The provision states one rule (substantial compliance suffices) and its direct protective consequence (no voidness for technical omissions or non-material defects); both are needed to recall the complete standard.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the standard of compliance required for Board rules, decisions, orders, regulations, and acts to have effect, and identify the category of omissions or defects that cannot render them inoperative, illegal, or void.

evidenceText: A substantial compliance with the requirements of this Act or any other Act conferring jurisdiction, power or authority on the Board is sufficient to give effect to all the rules, decisions, orders, regulations and acts of the Board

no rules, decisions, orders, regulations or acts of the Board shall be declared inoperative, illegal or void for any omission of a technical nature in respect of such matter or for any non-material defect

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 42 is a short, self-contained operative rule establishing the substantial-compliance standard for Board actions and shielding them from being declared inoperative, illegal, or void for technical or non-material defects. It forms one coherent recallable concept.

rows.heading: Board may review, rescind or vary order
rows.groupTitle: Board power to reconsider, rescind or vary its own order
rows.groupReason: One actor (the Board), one trigger (its own advisability standard), and a defined set of actions (reconsider, review, rescind, vary) over its own orders; no internal split is warranted.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the actions the Board may take over its own orders (reconsider, review, rescind, vary) and the standard it applies (considers it advisable to do so).

evidenceText: The Board may reconsider any order made by it and review, rescind or vary the order if it considers it advisable to do so.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 43 is a single, self-contained power granting the Board discretion to reconsider, review, rescind, or vary its own orders; it forms one recallable concept.

rows.heading: Rehearing
rows.groupTitle: Board's power to require a rehearing
rows.groupReason: Single discretionary power of the Board to order a rehearing before deciding an application.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Board's power under section 44 regarding a rehearing of an application before a decision is made.

evidenceText: The Board may require a rehearing of an application before making a decision on it.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 44 grants the Board a single, discrete procedural power to require a rehearing before deciding an application; it is one recall task and has no sub-parts to split.

rows.heading: Effective date of order or decision
rows.groupTitle: Effective Date of Board Orders and Decisions
rows.groupReason: One default rule plus its modification exception form a single recall unit.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the default effective date for a Board order or decision and the condition under which it may be set otherwise.
rows.sourceMapReason: A single default rule with its directly dependent modification exception forms one coherent recall task on when Board orders take effect.

rows.heading: Final decision
rows.groupTitle: Contents and publication of a Board final decision
rows.groupReason: Subsections 46(1) and 46(2) together define what a final decision must contain and when it must be published, forming one coherent recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the three mandatory elements a Board final decision must include and the 60-day publication requirement.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 46 sets the mandatory contents of a Board final decision and its publication deadline; together they form one compact, recallable procedural rule about the final decision.

rows.heading: Security for costs
rows.groupTitle: Board power to require security for costs
rows.groupReason: One operative power with a single reasonableness standard; independently recallable as a Board procedural tool.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the scope of the Board's power to require security for costs, including who may be required to provide it and the reasonableness standard applied.

evidenceText: The Board may require from any person such security for the costs incurred or to be incurred by the Board in respect of any matter as it considers reasonable.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single short provision granting the Board one discretionary power to require security for costs from any person; no internal split is warranted.

rows.heading: Costs
rows.groupTitle: Board costs in proceedings (s. 47.1)
rows.groupReason: Definition, general power, two exceptions, and procedural duty are tightly interdependent and recallable as one costs mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the definition of "intervener" under s. 47.1, identify the Board's general costs-ordering power, name the two situations where a costs order is prohibited, and note the Board's duty to adopt intervener costs procedures.

evidenceText: The Board may, in any proceeding before it, order, subject to subsection (3), the costs of and incidental to any proceeding be paid in the amounts or proportions by or to a party to the proceeding.

The Board shall not make an order under subsection (2) (a) when the proceeding results from financial and consumer services legislation, and (b) with respect to the Public Intervener referred to in section 49.
The Board shall adopt procedures with respect to costs to be paid to an intervener under subsection (2).

rows.sourceMapReason: Short, self-contained costs provision: a local definition, a general costs power, two directly dependent exceptions, and a linked procedural duty all form one coherent Board costs mechanism.

rows.heading: Notification to Public Intervener
rows.groupTitle: Public Intervener's procedural position in Board proceedings
rows.groupReason: The three subsections collectively state the Board's notification duty, its duty to forward materials, and the Public Intervener's automatic party status, which together answer how the Public Intervener participates in Board proceedings.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State when the Board must notify the Public Intervener, what materials the Board must forward on request, and the Public Intervener's automatic party status in Board proceedings.

evidenceText: when a proceeding is initiated before the Board, the Board shall notify the Public Intervener
the Public Intervener shall be deemed to be a party to all proceedings before the Board, regardless of whether the Public Intervener has notified the Board of his or her intention to intervene

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 49 is a short, self-contained procedural provision: three subsections together define the Public Intervener's procedural position in Board proceedings (notification, materials on request, deemed party status). They form one coherent recall package.

rows.heading: Assisting the Board
rows.groupTitle: Regulator assistance to the Board in financial and consumer services proceedings
rows.groupReason: One procedural mechanism: the Board's application trigger, the regulator's permission to assist without joining as a party, and the Board's power to accept information regardless of court admissibility.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which a regulator may render assistance to the Board in financial and consumer services proceedings and the Board's power to receive and accept information whether or not it would be admissible in a court of law.
rows.sourceMapReason: Short self-contained procedural mechanism for regulator assistance to the Board in financial and consumer services proceedings, including the Board's power to accept information regardless of court admissibility.

rows.heading: Assessment of expenses
rows.groupTitle: Expense assessment: payors, definitions, and determination
rows.groupReason: Definitions, the enumerated list of persons bearing expenses by Act, and the Board's determination, categorization, timing, and allocation duties form one coherent assessment-framework recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the persons who bear the Board's annual expenses under each Act, define direct and common expenses, and state the Board's assessment timing (December 1 and April 1) and allocation method.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 50 contains two distinct recall tasks: the assessment determination and allocation framework (who pays, how much, when) and a separate notice-payment-enforcement procedure with a court-filing consequence.

rows.heading: Assessment of expenses
rows.groupTitle: Notice, payment deadline, and enforcement of assessments
rows.groupReason: The notice-by-registered-mail requirement, the 30-day payment deadline, and the Board's power to file an enforcement order with The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick form a separate procedural stage with distinct actors and a court-filing consequence.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the registered-mail notice requirement, the 30-day payment deadline after posting, and the Board's power to make and file an enforcement order with The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick on non-payment.

evidenceText: The Board shall notify each person by registered mail of the amount so assessed upon it.
A person shall, on receipt of a notice under subsection (6), pay the assessed amount to the Board within 30 days after the posting of the notice.

the Board may make an order requiring the payment and file the order with The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick, and the order, on filing, shall have the same force and effect as an order of the Court.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 50 contains two distinct recall tasks: the assessment determination and allocation framework (who pays, how much, when) and a separate notice-payment-enforcement procedure with a court-filing consequence.

rows.heading: Judicial review
rows.groupTitle: Judicial review of Board decisions
rows.groupReason: Covers who may seek judicial review, the applicable court, the 30-day time limit, the financial and consumer services legislation exclusion, and the effect of filing on the operation of the Board's order.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the conditions for applying for judicial review of a Board decision (aggrieved person, The Court of Appeal of New Brunswick, 30-day limit, financial and consumer services legislation exclusion) and whether filing stays the order (no automatic stay; judge may order stay; Board may suspend).

evidenceText: a person aggrieved by an order or decision of the Board in a matter may make an application for judicial review of the order or decision to The Court of Appeal of New Brunswick within 30 days after the later of the making of the order or decision

An application for judicial review does not stay the operation of the order or decision of the Board, unless a judge of The Court of Appeal of New Brunswick orders otherwise, but the Board itself may suspend the operation of the order or decision until the Court has rendered its decision

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 52 is a short, self-contained judicial review provision stating the right to apply and its operative effect on the Board's order; the two subsections form one coherent recall unit.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Definition of 'public utility' (six categories)
rows.groupReason: The six sub-parts distinguish persons, local governments (when specified by regulation), and municipal distribution utilities across water, gas, and electricity services; a learner must recall which actors and conditions create a public utility.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the six categories of 'public utility' under s. 53, including the regulation-triggered local government and municipal distribution utility provisions and the controlling-interest condition in (f).

evidenceText: a person who owns, operates, manages or controls any plant or equipment for the transmission, distribution, delivery or furnishing of water, or that provides such other service as may be prescribed by regulation, either directly or indirectly, to or for the public,

a municipal distribution utility as defined in the Electricity Act that generates or distributes electricity if the utility's controlling interest is held by a person other than the municipality that is served by the utility.

rows.sourceMapReason: The 'public utility' definition (a)–(f) is a multi-part substantive scope definition independently recallable from the simpler cross-reference and vocabulary terms that surround it.

rows.heading: Definitions
rows.groupTitle: Part 3 supporting definitions: tariff, toll, railway terms, and cross-references
rows.groupReason: These seven shorter definitions establish the Part's supporting vocabulary, including cross-references to other Acts and the tariff/toll pricing pair, and form one recall unit of regulatory terminology.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Recall the definitions of tariff, toll, interconnect, interswitch, running rights, and the cross-referenced terms gas distribution system and local government as used in this Part.
rows.sourceMapReason: The 'public utility' definition (a)–(f) is a multi-part substantive scope definition independently recallable from the simpler cross-reference and vocabulary terms that surround it.

rows.heading: Supervision of public utilities and others
rows.groupTitle: Board supervision and enforcement powers over public utilities (s. 54)
rows.groupReason: All three subsections define one coherent supervisory power: the jurisdictional scope, the enforcement orders (compel and forbid), and the own-motion trigger are interdependent and answer a single recall task on the Board's enforcement role.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the scope of the Board's supervisory jurisdiction, the two categories of matters it may inquire into, the specific enforcement orders it may make (order to act, forbid contrary action), and the own-motion inquiry trigger.

evidenceText: The Board has supervision of the activities of public utilities and other persons subject to this Part and has full jurisdiction to inquire into, hear and determine any matter
order and require any person to do, forthwith, or within or at any specified time and in any manner it may determine, any act, matter or thing

The Board may of its own motion inquire into, hear and determine any matter that under this Part it may inquire into, hear and determine that does not expressly require an application before the Board.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 54 establishes the Board's unified supervisory and enforcement power over public utilities: jurisdiction to inquire (s. 54(1)), specific orders to compel or forbid (s. 54(2)), and own-motion trigger (s. 54(3)). These three subsections are tightly interdependent facets of one supervisory mechanism.

rows.heading: Review by Board
rows.groupTitle: Board Power to Review Public Utility Affairs, Earnings, and Accounts
rows.groupReason: One short permissive power grant covering three review objects (affairs, earnings, accounts) directed at any public utility; a single recall task.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the scope of the Board's review power under section 55, including the three categories reviewed and the class of entities to which it applies.

evidenceText: The Board may review the affairs, earnings and accounts of any public utility.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 55 grants the Board a single, self-contained permissive power to review the affairs, earnings, and accounts of any public utility, forming one discrete recall task.

rows.heading: Books and records of public utility
rows.groupTitle: Books and records duty and restriction on changing accounting practices
rows.groupReason: The duty to keep records and maintain GAAP-based accounts (s. 56(1)) and the prohibition on substantially changing those practices without prior Board approval (s. 56(2)) are inseparable recall tasks.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the books-and-records obligations of a public utility under s. 56(1) and the Board-approval requirement that applies before substantially changing accounting practices under s. 56(2).
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 56 imposes one coherent books-and-records duty on public utilities, with the subsection (2) prohibition tightly bound to the subsection (1) practices it restricts, forming a single interdependent recall unit.

rows.heading: Reports to the Board
rows.groupTitle: Public utility reporting duties under s. 57
rows.groupReason: Covers the annual return deadline, its three required content items, and the separate 10-day officer-change notification as one reporting regime.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the deadline, required contents, and Board discretion for the annual return, and the 10-day notification duty on officer or director changes.

evidenceText: within 3 months after the end of its financial year, or within such further period of time as the Board may allow, file with the Board a return
notify the Board within 10 days after every change in its officers or directors

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 57 imposes two short, related reporting duties on public utilities (annual return and officer-change notification) that together form one coherent 'Reports to the Board' regime suitable for a single StudyUnit.

rows.heading: Filing of schedules
rows.groupTitle: Public utility tariff schedule filing duty
rows.groupReason: One filing duty with two attached requirements (public inspection; tariff content) that together answer a single recall question.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State what a public utility must file with the Board, the requirement that schedules be open to public inspection, and the tariff content they must show.

evidenceText: A public utility shall file with the Board schedules, which shall be open to public inspection, showing the tariffs that it has established for any services provided by it.

rows.sourceMapReason: A single short duty: a public utility must file tariff schedules with the Board, open to public inspection. One recallable obligation with no internal split.

rows.heading: Charges to be in accordance with filed schedule
rows.groupTitle: Prohibition on charges outside filed schedules
rows.groupReason: One prohibition covering both compensation limits and unauthorized tolls relative to the filed schedules.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two charging prohibitions imposed on a public utility under section 59 regarding compensation and tolls relative to the filed schedules.

evidenceText: A public utility shall not charge, demand or collect or receive a greater or lesser compensation for any service that is prescribed in the schedules than are at the time established, or demand, collect or receive any tolls not specified in such schedules.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 59 imposes a single prohibition with two closely linked limbs on public utility charging, forming one recallable rule tied to the filed schedules under s.58.

rows.heading: Change in tariff
rows.groupTitle: Duty to apply to the Board before tariff change or new service
rows.groupReason: Establishes the mandatory application requirement for tariff changes and new services.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the obligation of a public utility to apply to the Board for approval before changing a tariff or providing a service for which no current tariff exists.

evidenceText: If a public utility wishes to change any tariff, or provide for another service to the public for which there is no current tariff, it shall apply to the Board to approve the change or the provision of the service.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 60 imposes a single clear duty: a public utility must apply to the Board for approval before changing a tariff or providing a service with no current tariff. One actor, one trigger, one obligation — a self-contained procedural rule.

rows.heading: Hearing to change tariff
rows.groupTitle: Board's mandatory hearing duty on tariff-change application
rows.groupReason: The provision states one operative rule: the Board is obligated to hold a hearing when it receives a tariff-change application, then proceed under section 62.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the Board's mandatory obligation upon receiving a public utility's application to change tariffs and the provision that governs the hearing procedure.

evidenceText: it shall hold a hearing and proceed under section 62

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 61 imposes a single, clear mandatory duty on the Board to hold a hearing upon receiving a tariff-change application, with a procedural cross-reference to section 62. The operative content is one recallable obligation.

rows.heading: Notice of hearing
rows.groupTitle: Notice requirement for tariff-change hearing
rows.groupReason: Single procedural duty with one trigger, one default method, one Board discretion, and one exception, all answering the same recall question.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the default notice period, method, and the Board's discretion over means for a tariff-change hearing under section 62.

evidenceText: be given by advertisement for a period of not less than 20 days, in one or more newspapers as directed by the Board or by any other means as the Board may direct

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 62 is a short, self-contained procedural rule setting the notice requirement for tariff-change hearings; all elements form one coherent recall task.

rows.heading: Burden of proof
rows.groupTitle: Burden of proof in tariff applications
rows.groupReason: Assigns the burden of proof to the applicant specifically in tariff applications before the Board.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the party who bears the burden of proof in an application regarding tariffs under the Act.

evidenceText: the burden of proof is on the applicant

rows.sourceMapReason: Single procedural rule assigning the burden of proof to the applicant in tariff applications; independently operative and recallable.

rows.heading: Approval of Board required
rows.groupTitle: Board approval and tariff compliance for public utilities
rows.groupReason: One recall task: the approval prerequisite and the prohibition on deviating from the Board-approved tariff are two facets of the same Board-control rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Board-approval prerequisite for charging or changing a toll or tariff and the prohibition on charging compensation greater or lesser than the Board-approved tariff.
rows.sourceMapReason: Both subsections state a single coherent rule: a public utility must obtain Board approval before charging or changing a toll or tariff, and must not charge compensation different from the Board-approved tariff. They are tightly interdependent and form one recall task.

rows.heading: Decision of Board
rows.groupTitle: Board's Tariff Decision Duties at Conclusion of Hearing
rows.groupReason: Both sub-obligations share the same actor, trigger, and modality and are interdependent; a learner recalls them as one decision rule.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the two mandatory actions the Board must take at the conclusion of a tariff hearing, including the just-and-reasonable criterion and the effective-date requirement.

evidenceText: approve the tariff, if it is satisfied that the tariff applied for is just and reasonable or, if not so satisfied, fix such other tariff as it finds to be just and reasonable
set the time at which any change in the tariff is to take effect

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 65 imposes two tightly linked duties on the Board at the conclusion of a tariff hearing — the substantive tariff decision and the effective-date determination — forming one recallable decision-making rule.

rows.heading: Order in the public interest
rows.groupTitle: Public-interest terms and conditions on Board orders (s.66)
rows.groupReason: One recall task: identify the condition that attaches to every Board order under this Part and the standard the Board applies in imposing it.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that any Board order under this Part is subject to terms and conditions the Board considers necessary in the public interest.

evidenceText: Any order of the Board made under this Part is subject to such terms and conditions as the Board considers necessary in the public interest.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 66 states a single, self-contained rule: every Board order under this Part carries public-interest terms and conditions the Board considers necessary. It creates an independent recall task distinct from the tariff-decision rule in s.65 or the alternative-regulation power in s.67.

rows.heading: Alternative form of regulation
rows.groupTitle: Alternative form of regulation and Board's methodological freedom
rows.groupReason: Definition and power are inseparable: the power references the defined term, and the definition gives it operative content.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the definition of 'alternative form of regulation' and identify that the Board may adopt any method or technique it considers appropriate for tolls and tariffs of water, electricity, and natural gas.
rows.sourceMapReason: The section defines 'alternative form of regulation' and grants the Board methodological freedom in tariff-setting; the definition and power form one tightly interdependent concept.

rows.heading: Forbearance from regulation
rows.groupTitle: General discretionary forbearance and resumption of regulation
rows.groupReason: The discretionary forbearance power and the resumption power form one paired concept: the Board's broad may-forbear authority and its power to resume when warranted.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the conditions under which the Board may exercise its discretionary forbearance power and the condition under which it may resume a greater degree of regulation.

evidenceText: The Board may forbear, in whole or in part and conditionally or unconditionally, from the exercise of any power or the performance of any duty of its own making where the Board finds as a question of fact that forbearance would be consistent with the purpose of this Part.
If the Board does forbear from regulation, it may later resume a greater degree of regulation if it considers that its level of forbearance is no longer warranted.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 68 contains a discretionary forbearance power (68(1)) paired with a resumption power (68(3)), and a distinct mandatory competition-based forbearance obligation (68(2)) with a different trigger and modality. The may/shall shift and separate factual triggers support two recall tasks.

rows.heading: Forbearance from regulation
rows.groupTitle: Mandatory forbearance on effective competition finding
rows.groupReason: This subsection imposes a mandatory (shall) obligation triggered by a specific factual finding of effective competition, distinct in modality and trigger from the general discretionary power in 68(1).
rows.approximateLearningGoal: Identify the factual finding that compels the Board to forbear from regulating tolls, tariffs, or contractual provisions and the scope of that mandatory forbearance.

evidenceText: Where the Board finds as a question of fact that a service offered by a public utility is or will be subject to effective competition sufficient to protect customer's interests, it shall make a determination to forbear, to the extent that it considers appropriate, conditionally or unconditionally, from regulating the tolls or tariffs or other contractual provisions of that service or class of service

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 68 contains a discretionary forbearance power (68(1)) paired with a resumption power (68(3)), and a distinct mandatory competition-based forbearance obligation (68(2)) with a different trigger and modality. The may/shall shift and separate factual triggers support two recall tasks.

rows.heading: Extension of service by public utility
rows.groupTitle: Board power to order extension of public utility service
rows.groupReason: The power, the mandatory rate-of-return consideration, and the hearing requirement are tightly interdependent facets of one regulatory mechanism.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the Board's power to order a public utility to extend service to an unserved area, the rate-of-return factor the Board must consider, and the hearing prerequisite before any such order may be made.
rows.sourceMapReason: Section 69 is a short, self-contained provision stating the Board's power to order a public utility to extend services, the mandatory rate-of-return consideration, and the hearing prerequisite. All three subsections form one interdependent recall task and should be studied together.

rows.heading: Duty of public utility to provide adequate service
rows.groupTitle: Duty to furnish reasonably adequate and safe services
rows.groupReason: Core service standard imposed on every public utility under section 70.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the service standard that section 70 requires every public utility to meet.

evidenceText: Every public utility shall furnish reasonably adequate and safe services and facilities.

rows.sourceMapReason: Single-sentence duty imposing a 'reasonably adequate and safe' service standard on every public utility; one actor, one obligation, one recall task.

rows.heading: Discontinuance of service by public utility
rows.groupTitle: Right and procedure for discontinuing public utility service for non-payment
rows.groupReason: One coherent recall task: the non-payment trigger, the permission to discontinue, and the entry/disconnection procedure (notice, time window, scope of property taken or disconnected).

evidenceText: Where any person supplied with a service provided by a public utility neglects or refuses to pay the amount due for the same, or for the rent of the meter or other articles, the public utility may discontinue service and stop the supply.
after 24 hours' notice, enter the premises of such person between the hours of nine o'clock in the forenoon and four o'clock in the afternoon

rows.sourceMapReason: Subsections 71(1) and 71(2) form one tightly interdependent concept: the trigger for and procedure of discontinuing public utility service for non-payment, with 71(2) explicitly operating 'in such cases' as 71(1) describes.

rows.heading: Existing contracts and jurisdiction of Board
rows.groupTitle: Board jurisdiction not limited by existing contracts or legislation

rows.approximateLearningGoal: State that the Board's jurisdiction under this Part may be exercised notwithstanding any existing contract, agreement, or Act of the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick.

evidenceText: The jurisdiction of the Board under this Part may be exercised by it notwithstanding any existing contract or agreement or Act of the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 72 is a single operative jurisdictional rule stating that the Board's jurisdiction under this Part is not limited by existing contracts, agreements, or Acts of the Legislative Assembly. It forms one coherent recall task with no internal split points.

rows.heading: Provincial railways
rows.groupTitle: Board power to order interconnection of two provincial railways
rows.groupReason: The three subsections form one recall task: the scope, the Board's discretionary interconnection order, and the enforcement path via The Court of King's Bench.
rows.approximateLearningGoal: State the applicability conditions, the Board's power to order track interconnection and interswitching between two provincial railways, and the mechanism for enforcing such an order as an order of The Court of King's Bench of New Brunswick.

evidenceText: This section applies to railways whose construction or operation is authorized by an Act of the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick and whose tracks intersect or run into the same local government.

rows.sourceMapReason: Section 73 is a short, self-contained provision granting the Board a single interconnection power over two provincial railways, with scope, the discretionary order, and court enforcement forming one tightly interdependent mechanism.

rows.heading: Provincial and federal railways
